sections.content_zh:
四、石桥村的家族性集体住宅

（一）家族性集体住宅的产生

闽南的方形、圆形家族性集体住宅早已闻名世界，南靖县的家族性集体住宅主要集中在书垟、梅林两乡。书垟乡有方形的二百四十座，圆形的一百零四座。梅林乡有方形的九十七座，圆形的五十三座。石桥村就在书垟乡。

石桥村主要由十来座独立的家族性集体住宅组成，有长方形的、方形的和圆形的几种。在一个小盆地内，有几种形式的楼交错地建在一起，不但村落景观十分丰富，而且楼形变化发展脉络清晰。

闽南人和客家人，经过长途的迁徙，历经艰难，最后在闽南一带安居下来，靠的是家族的集体力量。他们要在新的居住地发展仍然要靠家族的内聚力，于是就采用了内向的集体住宅。但各户的经济是独立的。为了准备家族的发展，楼房大都建得规模较大，留有余地。例如石桥村方形的永安楼，清初兴建时虽然张氏家族只有不足十口人，但有上下四层，六十四间房。

这些楼都有坚固的防御性，有如堡垒。闽南一带山高林密，为防盗匪、猛兽，也因为民系之间和村落之间频繁发生争斗，凡聚族性的方楼和圆楼大都是外围厚夯土高墙，向外很少开窗，只有一个大门出入。大型楼房居住的人很多，便开两个或三个大门。门上大多有严密的防御措施，如射击孔和泼热水驱敌的缝隙。有一些集体住宅，顶层设环廊，便于守卫者调动位置，打击来犯的敌人。楼内院中有粮仓和水井，可以长期坚守待援。

围墙之内的居住部分则全用木材建造。

家族性集体住宅，方的或圆的，环绕着内院形成一圈。一般为四层，都按梁架划分标准房间，上下垂直的四间为一户。底层做厨房、餐厅，二层做谷仓，三层住人，四层为杂物贮存间，也可住人。有些大宅，每户都有水井，有些则只在大院里有公用水井。住户的单元又可分为两大类，一类是通廊式，即每一层沿内院设一圈公共走廊。全大宅只有三四个公共楼梯，各户人家，从自家厨房上楼到自家卧室，也要从公共楼梯和走廊过去。另一类是单元式，即上下四间为一个独立的单元，每个单元有左右隔墙，有自己内部的小楼梯，厨房前还有一个天井。大宅中央仍有公共大院落。通廊式的集体住宅在永定县及南靖县书垟乡一带十分普遍。少数圆楼还做成两环、三环，内外环或同高，或外环高内环低。

大院中央还建一座祖堂，大的为小三合院式，小的只有一间，有院墙。

这种家族性集体住宅型制的起源可能和唐代陈元光把所辖大军五十八姓全部在漳州地区解甲为民有关系。陈元光军队落籍的地区，正是后来家族性集体住宅流行的地区。大军落籍，第一是带来了军营式的建筑观念，对外防御，内部一律标准化、统一化；第二是带来了一些中原地区的建筑影响，如家庙的型制，因为部队是从中原来的。

石桥村的集体住宅在张氏二十几代的建设过程中，规模从小到大，型制从封闭的方形到半开敞的长方形，又到圆形。每个发展阶段都深深地烙上了那个时期的社会、经济、文化、人口等多方面的印记。

（二）方形家族性集体住宅

石桥村张氏开基祖张念三郎，15世纪中叶在东山脚下建立了最早的家族性集体住宅昌楼。由于当时人口少，经济弱，昌楼建得很小，仅有十米左右见方。

四世祖宗华公时，家族人口增多，经济好于第一代，在溪背垟建起大型集体住宅永安楼，方形，外墙全部夯土，内部建筑为木结构。这种型制十分符合当时客家人要求聚族而居、共同对外防御的需要。

通常方形集体住宅的每个居住单元仍区分正房、厢房和倒座房。倒座房的当心间为户门门厅，两侧是厢房。它们的规模无一定之规，据当时的经济和人口而定。如规模最大的长篮楼，四层，正房及倒座均为九间，左右厢房各五间。永安楼及昭德楼，正房及倒座均为五开间，四个角落上是黑房间，正房当心间稍宽，为祖堂，供奉本楼开基祖的牌位。在石桥村附近，河坑村的绳庆楼等，为方形集体住宅，院落中间建一座小四合院，做专门的祖堂。到民国以后，石桥村的集体住宅已打破了小房派界限，插花居住。不能在祖堂祭本房派先祖，便改为供奉观音和土地菩萨。小房派子孙每年便到东山祠祭奠祖先。

方形的楼一般为四层，也有三层的和一半四层一半三层的。通常有四座楼梯位于楼的转角处。楼梯宽达一点五米左右，为的是担粮上楼进仓便利。从第二层起走廊均外挑，形成院内环廊。

张氏十三代以前所建的方形住宅，住的都是同一小房派的族人。尽管房间的优劣没有大的区别，但遵从家族制度，仍要按照辈分的高低来分配，有高辈分老人的家庭，一般住在正房上下各四间里，无高辈分老人的家庭，住在两厢上下四间里。待儿子成婚，女儿出嫁，人口有了变化之后，再重新调整住房。有经济实力的会另建新房搬出去，而经济实力不强的，或人丁不旺的人家，仍然住在拥挤的老楼里。年深日久，最初的分配方式被打乱，插花居住，共享厨房，以致杂物间也住人。这种杂乱的称为"梅花间"。

外墙以内的建筑都是木结构，厨房内又常常堆满柴禾，集体住宅极易发生火灾。永安楼失过火，幸被扑灭；德源楼烧成了一堆废墟。因火灾焚毁的楼还有顺源楼及一座现在已不知其名的楼。

外墙墙体都很厚，一方面因为都是夯土承重墙，另一方面为防御兵匪祸乱。而且外墙在一、二层不开窗。大门门扇十分厚重，约有十至二十厘米厚，外面包铁皮，内侧设重闩门和门杠。楼的二层正房与角房的上方都有瞭望孔和射击孔。晚期的住宅，为了美观，大门框以外四周夯土墙面还做泥塑彩绘。

大门门厅往来人多，是楼内人们交流信息、休闲和重要的生活场所。货郎担下乡，也都歇在这门厅里。通常门厅的左侧放一块石条或木凳，供人们乘凉、休息、谈天甚至开家族会。另一侧放一架脚踏的石臼，这是家族共有的财产，每家都用它舂米、捣年糕。

小农经济，家家需要一些辅助房间，集体住宅内不能满足，便在楼外建造一座三合式前院，正对大门。前院占地面积与住宅楼所占相差不多。如为两层，下层大多敞开不分隔，供楼内住户公用，多养牛、家禽及作茅厕。上层有的不分间。有分间的，一户一间或两三户合用一间，存放农具和柴草等。

除永安楼建在河滩上，其他的楼为避水患，又要不占用垟田，便建在山坡上，因此，昭德楼、长篮楼等，都是楼的位置高于前院。

（三）外向的长方形家族性集体住宅

在建造封闭的、防御性的方形集体住宅的同时，在长篮村沿河的陡坎间由石桥的张氏十三代子谦公几兄弟建起了新的家族性集体住宅，即长源楼、逢源楼、振德楼和一幢被称为"十间房"的楼。这批住宅沿河建造，长方形、外向的。子伦则在洪坑坝上建了形状不规则的向月楼和向日楼。

建筑型制出现这样的突变，大致有以下两个原因：其一，风水因素。石桥人很重视风水，房子在建造之前，都要请地理师看地形，选择一个能使子孙发达的地方，而地理师选定的是一条狭窄的地段。其二，由于长篮下地形狭窄，不可能再像以前那样建造大型方形住宅，只能因地制宜，建造适应狭小地段的住宅。同时，坎陡坡高处，敌人来犯不易，可以降低住宅的防御性。

长方形的家族集体住宅的平面型制比较自由，如长源楼。这是一座长方形建筑。楼坐西朝东，面河而建，长三十六米，宽十二米，正房与倒座均为十一间。正房为三层楼，厢房为两层。倒座房临溪，因为在人工填起的地基上，只造单层。正房的当心间是祖堂，全部敞开，向前凸出，进深大于左右次间。

长源楼视野开阔，比起方形的建筑来大大改善了房间的采光、通风，居住更加舒适。

（四）圆形集体住宅

清末太平天国农民战争爆发，农民军在南靖活动十分频繁，石桥村遭到严重破坏，战乱过后，经济很难恢复，直到1927年，村中的居住状况实在不能持续而不得不建新屋时，就回复到封闭的、防御性很强的、可容纳众多人口的圆形家族性集体住宅。

1927年，大型的圆楼顺裕楼开工了，于1949年前大体建成。圆形集体住宅比方形的更有优越性，例如房间的面积和质量更均等，分配容易。圆形的抗震性能更好，等等。

顺裕楼是南靖县境内最大的一座圆形集体住宅，它有内外两圈，外环外径达七十四米。上下四层，每层七十二个开间，共两百八十八间。二层全部为各户的粮仓，有特殊处理。四个楼梯，均匀分布。内环与外环相距四米，两层，可惜只建成四分之一连楼梯间都没有造便停工了。外环底层外墙用大块蛮石砌一米多高的墙裙，上面用夯土筑墙，厚一点六米。内环之内为圆形院落，有一口井和一间独立的庙堂。

顺裕楼也采用通廊式做法，一个开间，从底层到四层上下为一组，供一户使用。底层为厨房、餐厅兼客厅，二层是粮仓，三层四层做卧室。

它在建筑上有些新特点，首先是因为它在建造时集资不限房派，所以楼中不建祖堂而建庙堂，不祭开基祖而供奉观音和土地。

其次是出入口加强了防御能力。顺裕楼在门厅上层安装竹管穿过楼板通到大门扇外侧的上方，平时将竹管封闭，一旦攻楼的敌人放火烧门时，守御的人可由竹管向下灌水灭火。

再次，圆楼各间不像早期的方楼有正位偏位之分，它各间平等而无差别，便于用抽签的方式来分配。

最后，四层楼上的卧室为木板隔断，木板房门，木棂格窗。夯土的外墙上也有比较大一点的窗，比起早期的方形家族性集体住宅更讲究居住的舒适。
sections.content_en:
4. Clan Collective Residences of Shiqiao Village

(1) Origins of Clan Collective Residences

The square and round clan collective residences of southern Fujian are world-famous. In Nanjing County, they are concentrated mainly in Shuyang and Meilin townships. Shuyang has 240 square and 104 round buildings; Meilin has 97 square and 53 round. Shiqiao Village is in Shuyang.

Shiqiao consists mainly of about ten independent clan collective residences—rectangular, square, and round. In a small basin, several building forms are interspersed, creating rich village landscape and a clear evolutionary trajectory of building types.

Minnan and Hakka people, after long migrations and hardships, settled in southern Fujian through clan collective strength. To develop in their new homes, they relied on clan cohesion and adopted inward-looking collective residences. But each household's economy was independent. To prepare for clan growth, buildings were usually large with spare capacity. For example, Yong'an Tower (永安楼), a square building in Shiqiao, was built in the early Qing dynasty when the Zhang clan had fewer than ten people—yet it had four floors and 64 rooms.

These buildings are strongly defensive, like fortresses. Southern Fujian has high mountains and dense forests; to guard against bandits, wild beasts, and frequent conflicts between ethnic groups and villages, clan square and round buildings generally have thick rammed-earth outer walls, few outward-facing windows, and only one main gate. Large buildings housing many people have two or three gates. Gates usually have elaborate defensive measures—firing slits and gaps for pouring boiling water. Some collective residences have a top-floor ring corridor for defenders to move and attack enemies. The inner courtyard has granaries and wells, allowing long-term defense.

The residential parts inside the walls are entirely timber-built.

Clan collective residences, square or round, form a ring around an inner courtyard. Usually four stories, with standard rooms divided by beam frames; four vertically aligned rooms form one household. Ground floor: kitchen and dining; second floor: granary; third floor: dwelling; fourth floor: storage (can also house people). Some large buildings have a well per household; others have only shared wells in the main courtyard. Household units fall into two types: (1) corridor type—each floor has a ring of public corridors along the inner courtyard; the whole building has only 3–4 public staircases, and each household goes from its kitchen up to its bedroom via public stairs and corridors. (2) unit type—four vertical rooms form an independent unit with left/right partition walls, its own internal small staircase, and a skylight before the kitchen. The building center still has a public courtyard. Corridor-type collective residences are common in Yongding and Shuyang, Nanjing. A few round buildings have two or three rings—same height, or outer ring higher than inner.

In the courtyard center stands an ancestral hall—large ones are small three-sided courtyard style, small ones just one room with walls.

The origin of this building type may relate to Tang dynasty Chen Yuanguang, who demobilized his army of 58 surnames in Zhangzhou. The area where Chen's army settled is exactly where clan collective residences later flourished. Military settlement brought: (1) military-camp architectural concepts—outward defense, internal standardization and uniformity; (2) Central Plains architectural influences, such as ancestral hall form, since the troops came from the Central Plains.

Over 20+ generations of Zhang clan construction, Shiqiao's collective residences grew from small to large, from enclosed square to semi-open rectangular, then to round. Each stage bears deep imprints of that period's society, economy, culture, and population.

(2) Square Clan Collective Residences

Zhang clan founder Zhang Niansanlang built the earliest clan collective residence, Chang Tower (昌楼), at the foot of East Mountain in the mid-15th century. With small population and weak economy, Chang Tower was small—only about 10 m square.

By the 4th generation, Zonghua Gong, with more people and better economy, built the large collective residence Yong'an Tower at Xibeiyang—square, fully rammed-earth exterior, timber interior. This type perfectly suited Hakka needs for clan cohabitation and joint external defense.

Each residential unit in a square collective residence still distinguishes main rooms (正房), wing rooms (厢房), and reverse-set rooms (倒座房). The reverse-set room's central bay is the entry hall, with wings on both sides. Sizes vary by economy and population. The largest, Changlan Tower (长篮楼), four stories, main and reverse rooms each 9 bays, wings 5 bays each. Yong'an and Zhaode Towers: main and reverse rooms each 5 bays, four corners are dark rooms, main room's central bay slightly wider as ancestral hall enshrining the building founder's tablet. Near Shiqiao, Hejing Village's Shengqing Tower etc. are square collective residences with a small four-sided courtyard in the center as a dedicated ancestral hall. After the Republic era, Shiqiao's collective residences broke sub-lineage boundaries, with interspersed living. Unable to worship sub-lineage ancestors in the hall, they switched to enshrining Guanyin and Earth God; sub-lineage descendants worship annually at East Mountain Shrine.

Square buildings are usually four stories, some three, some half-four-half-three. Typically four staircases at the corners. Stairs ~1.5 m wide for easy grain-carrying upstairs. From the second floor, corridors cantilever outward, forming inner-courtyard ring corridors.

Square residences built before the 13th Zhang generation housed only the same sub-lineage. Though room quality differed little, clan rules required allocation by seniority: families with senior elders lived in the main rooms' four vertical bays; families without senior elders lived in the wings' four vertical bays. After sons married, daughters married out, populations changed, housing was reallocated. Those with means built new homes and moved out; those without means or with small families stayed in crowded old buildings. Over time, the original allocation broke down—interspersed living, shared kitchens, even storage rooms occupied. This disorder is called "梅花间" (plum-blossom rooms).

Timber interiors plus firewood-stacked kitchens make collective residences highly fire-prone. Yong'an Tower had a fire, luckily extinguished; Deyuan Tower burned to ruins. Shunyuan Tower and one now-unnamed building also burned.

Outer walls are very thick—both as rammed-earth load-bearing walls and for defense against soldiers and bandits. First and second floors have no outward windows. Main gates are very heavy, 10–20 cm thick, iron-sheathed outside, with heavy inner bolts and bars. Second-floor main and corner rooms have lookout and firing holes above. Late-period buildings, for aesthetics, have clay sculpture and painting on rammed-earth walls around the gate frame.

The gate hall sees much traffic—it is the building's information exchange, leisure, and important living space. Peddlers rest there. Usually the hall's left side has a stone slab or wooden bench for cooling off, resting, chatting, even clan meetings. The other side has a foot-operated stone mortar—clan communal property, used by every household for pounding rice and rice cakes.

Small-scale peasant economy needed auxiliary rooms unavailable inside collective residences, so a three-sided front courtyard was built outside, facing the gate. Its area roughly equals the residence building. If two stories: lower floor mostly open, shared by all residents—for cattle, poultry, latrines. Upper floor sometimes undivided; when divided, one room per household or shared by 2–3 households for tools and firewood.

Except Yong'an Tower built on a riverbank, other buildings, to avoid floods and not占用 farmland, were built on hillsides—so Zhaode, Changlan, etc. have the building higher than the front courtyard.

(3) Outward-Looking Rectangular Clan Collective Residences

While enclosed defensive square buildings were being built, the 13th-generation Zhang brothers (Ziqian Gong et al.) built new clan collective residences on the steep riverbank terraces of Changlan Village—Changyuan Tower, Fengyuan Tower, Zhende Tower, and one called "Ten-Room Building." These are rectangular, outward-looking, built along the river. Zilun built irregularly shaped Xiangyue and Xiangri Towers on Hongkeng Dam.

This sudden type change had two main causes: (1) Feng shui. Shiqiao people value feng shui highly; before building, a geomancer examines terrain to choose a site for descendants' prosperity—and the geomancer chose a narrow strip. (2) Changlan's narrow terrain made large square buildings impossible; they had to adapt to the narrow site. Also, steep high banks are hard for enemies to attack, reducing defensive needs.

Rectangular clan collective residences have freer plans, e.g., Changyuan Tower. A rectangular building, facing west with back to east, built facing the river—36 m long, 12 m wide, main and reverse rooms each 11 bays. Main rooms three stories, wings two stories. Reverse rooms face the stream; built on人工 fill, only single story. Main room's central bay is the ancestral hall—fully open, projecting forward, deeper than adjacent bays.

Changyuan Tower has open views, greatly improving lighting and ventilation compared to square buildings—more comfortable living.

(4) Round Collective Residences

The late-Qing Taiping Rebellion saw frequent peasant-army activity in Nanjing; Shiqiao was severely damaged. Post-war economy was slow to recover. By 1927, living conditions were unsustainable and new housing was needed—so they returned to enclosed, strongly defensive, high-capacity round clan collective residences.

In 1927, the large round building Shunyu Tower (顺裕楼) began construction, largely completed before 1949. Round collective residences have advantages over square ones: room area and quality are more equal, easier to allocate. Round buildings have better earthquake resistance, etc.

Shunyu Tower is the largest round collective residence in Nanjing County—two concentric rings, outer ring diameter 74 m. Four stories, 72 bays per floor, 288 rooms total. Second floor entirely granaries for each household, with special treatment. Four staircases evenly distributed. Inner ring 4 m from outer ring, two stories—unfortunately only one-quarter built, not even staircase rooms completed before work stopped. Outer ring ground-floor wall has 1+ m high rubble stone plinth, above which rammed-earth wall 1.6 m thick. Inside the inner ring is a round courtyard with a well and an independent shrine hall.

Shunyu Tower also uses corridor-type construction: one bay, from ground to fourth floor vertically as one unit for one household. Ground floor: kitchen, dining/living room; second: granary; third and fourth: bedrooms.

It has several new architectural features. First, because construction funding was not limited to sub-lineages, the building has no ancestral hall but a shrine hall—worshipping Guanyin and Earth God, not the founder.

Second, enhanced entrance defense. Shunyu Tower has bamboo pipes installed in the gate hall's upper floor, passing through the ceiling to above the outer side of the main gate. Normally sealed; if enemies set fire to the gate, defenders pour water down through the pipes to extinguish it.

Third, unlike early square buildings with primary/secondary bay distinctions, round building bays are all equal—facilitating allocation by drawing lots.

Finally, fourth-floor bedrooms have wood-board partitions, wood doors, wood lattice windows. The rammed-earth outer wall also has somewhat larger windows—more comfort-oriented than early square clan collective residences.

sections.name: 关麓村住宅的别厅
sections.content_zh:
五、关麓村住宅的别厅

（一）别厅中的生活

关麓村在安徽省黟县。老村在太平天国战争时几乎全部焚毁，现在的房子多是战后重建的。一共三十七幢住宅，倒有十四幢上规模成独立院落的别厅，建筑质量很高，一般都建造在住宅的一旁。它们兼有书房和小客厅的功能，主人读书、写文、作画、吟诗、会友，都在别厅里，是徽商退休养老最好的场合。

别厅的用途，除起居和读书外，重要的是接待宾客。一般外客不进正房厅堂，厅堂太肃穆，不自在，而且有客来时妇女要避开，很不方便。

徽商多从十二三岁离家学做生意，在外奔波几十年，到五十来岁还乡，家务琐事，不堪烦扰，要有个颐养天年的安乐之所，于是便另建小院作安身之处，这便是别厅。别厅也是那些在家闲居靠收店息过日子的人的安乐窝。这些人吃喝有佣人照料，闲时读书绘画。因为别厅小而紧凑，容易保暖，一到冬季，更喜欢在别厅过日子。清初许友著《贫贱快活》中有一则："春新秋残，村屋山斋，丝雨骤至，幽寒上人手，老妻涤洁衫袜送至，夜来加授一层，读书无穷安稳。"它所描绘的便是类似的生活情趣。

平时别厅小院无人惊扰，一片宁静。回归乡里的退隐商人，有文化有见识，有钱有闲，别厅中的生活方式便颇有品位。如"三家"的汪丕洽外出经商，年老回家，与在村中做私塾老师的"八家"汪觉民友善，两人都喜欢古文学，常在一起谈论切磋。一年冬天，汪觉民不慎在烤火时将汪丕洽送他的一幅字画烧残，丕洽知道后心疼而懊恼，便连夜秉烛写了一首诗批评。第二天送到汪觉民手中，汪觉民见诗，心中深感委屈，又不好找丕洽辩解，便也赋诗一首。两人你一首我一首地写诗笺来往直到芥蒂冰释，重叙旧好。

有一位安庆隆兴福商号名旭的，给丕洽来信，在生动地叙述了所见的天灾人祸之后，说："老弟到家，例应从俗拜年一番，想必日在竹阁兄处靠榻清谈。老弟聪明过人，聆竹阁兄之言论，必更有进益。"

"靠榻清谈"和"秉烛写诗"，都是别厅里的情趣。因此，别厅往往有个雅致的、书卷气很浓的名称，如原令铎的别厅称"淡月山房"，原令锺的别厅则称"临溪书房"。

（二）别厅的型制

别厅虽独立，但多靠近住宅的正房而建，规格比住宅要小。它大致有三种型制。一种只有一开间，贴建在住宅正房的山墙面，上下两层。前后墙与正房的平齐。由于进深大，在中央横置一个楼梯间，把它分为前后间。从正房通过敞厢进入别厅，别厅没有自己的对外门户。第二种是一幢缩小的三间房，面向正房侧墙，有一个窄缝一样的吸壁天井。也是两层的。进深相当于正房的一个开间的面阔，面阔相当于正房的进深。由于所有尺寸都很小，所以光线较弱。它有自己独立的大门，甚至可能有青砖门楼。从正房也有小门进入别厅。第三种别厅比较大，是一幢独立的三间楼屋，从前廊一端有门通正房的敞厢。别厅庭院两侧各做一间小敞厢。一侧敞厢的前檐柱间做半高的花栏杆，另一侧在前檐柱间做平板坐凳。庭院中间种南天竺、石榴、金桂等有姿有色有香而格调清雅的花木。地面用碎石块铺垫，清静整齐。

又如"八家"长房令銮所建的前后进式住宅，贴住宅右侧墙建起别厅。别厅分前后两间，隔着一个小院子。前后间由三间廊子相连，廊子开间每间不足两米。当中一间留做通道，另两间则在檐柱间做美人靠栏杆。每间的枋子下还有菱花挂落。前后两间别厅的上下层均朝小庭院做菱花格扇窗。小院有门开向住宅与学堂屋"吾爱吾庐"之间的窄巷，院门不大却十分讲究，采用内外双面雕砖门楼，与小巧的别厅游廊相配格外漂亮。

三房令锨的住宅建在令銮的宅后，东端有别厅。住宅和别厅都有前院，院之间有隔墙，墙上有空花窗，并有小门相通。门上镶水磨青砖的小匾，一侧书"瑞霭晴岚"，一侧书"延禧"。篆体，石绿色。

（三）别厅的风格

在家族住宅团组中，型制变化最多的就是别厅，它没有一定的格式，不受一般规矩的束缚。别厅的建筑比起住宅正房和学堂厅就显得小巧、活泼、轻快、舒朗，工艺很精。它们的风格力求亲切雅致，但作为商人的生活环境，仍不免华丽，所以别厅又称"花厅"。天花板上满绘彩画，不过色调比较淡雅，以墨菊为多，略施黄色，添一点渊明情趣。不论为官为商，赋老恬退之后，真真假假都是要标榜这一份悠然姿态的。樘板有的漆朱红，如双桂书屋别厅；有的漆象牙白，如原令镓家别厅；有的作壁画，如原令铎宅别厅。也有的用素木，润泽温暖，天然亲切。别厅楼上前檐做通间的槅扇窗。原令铎家的小别厅，楼上明间廊前是美人靠栏杆，次间为空花栏杆。别厅与正房不同，楼上侧墙上常开宽大的窗子，眺望山水秀色，使自然与住房渗透交融。这些窗子或有砖花格，或有砖披檐，装饰性很强，是村落街景景观中的点缀。因为别厅楼上并不封闭内向，也不用高墙围合，所以楼上的槅扇、栏杆等在户外可以见到，给村落增添了美和生气。
sections.content_en:
5. Bieting (Ancillary Halls) of Guanlu Village Residences

(1) Life in the Bieting

Guanlu Village is in Yixian County, Anhui. The old village was almost entirely destroyed during the Taiping Rebellion; most current houses were rebuilt afterward. Of 37 residences, 14 have sizable, independent-courtyard bieting (别厅, ancillary halls) of high construction quality, usually built beside the residence. They combine study and small reception room functions—the master reads, writes, paints, composes poetry, and receives friends in the bieting—the ideal place for Huizhou merchants' retirement.

Besides daily living and reading, the bieting's important use is receiving guests. Ordinary outsiders do not enter the main residence hall—it is too solemn and uncomfortable, and women must withdraw when guests arrive, very inconvenient.

Huizhou merchants often left home at age 12–13 to learn business, traveling for decades, returning around age 50. Household琐事 became unbearable; they needed a peaceful place for their later years, so they built small courtyards as personal retreats—the bieting. Bieting are also havens for those living idly at home on shop interest. These people have servants for meals, and spend leisure reading and painting. Because bieting are small and compact, easy to heat, they are especially favored in winter. Early Qing writer Xu You wrote in 《贫贱快活》 (Happiness in Humble Circumstances): "New spring, late autumn, village house mountain study, sudden fine rain, chill creeping to the hands, old wife brings clean clothes and socks, at night adds another layer—reading in endless peace." This describes a similar lifestyle.

Normally the bieting courtyard is undisturbed, serene. Retired merchants returning home—cultured, knowledgeable, wealthy, with leisure—developed refined lifestyles in the bieting. For example, Wang Piqia of the "Three Families" (三家), after years of business, returned old and befriended Wang Juemin of the "Eight Families" (八家), a village private-school teacher. Both loved ancient literature and often discussed it together. One winter, Wang Juemin accidentally burned a calligraphy painting Wang Piqia had given him while warming himself by the fire. Piqia, heartbroken and annoyed, wrote a critical poem by candlelight that night. Next day he sent it to Juemin, who felt wronged but could not argue—so he wrote a poem in reply. They exchanged poem after poem until the grievance melted and their friendship was restored.

A merchant named Xu from Anqing's Longxingfu shop wrote to Piqia, vividly describing natural disasters and human misfortunes he had seen, then said: "Younger brother, upon arriving home, you must make the customary New Year visits; I imagine you spend days reclining and chatting at Brother Zhuge's place. You are intelligent beyond others; listening to Brother Zhuge's discourse will surely bring further progress."

"Reclining and chatting" (靠榻清谈) and "writing poetry by candlelight" (秉烛写诗) are bieting pleasures. Hence bieting often have elegant, scholarly names—e.g., Yuan Lingduo's bieting called "淡月山房" (Pale Moon Mountain Studio), Yuan Lingzhong's called "临溪书房" (Streamside Study).

(2) Bieting Typology

Though independent, bieting are usually built close to the residence's main rooms, smaller in scale. There are roughly three types:

Type 1: single bay, attached to the main residence's gable wall, two stories. Front and rear walls align with the main residence. Due to deep plan, a staircase room is placed transversely in the center, dividing into front and rear rooms. Accessed from the main residence through an open wing (敞厢); no independent exterior entrance.

Type 2: a scaled-down three-bay building, facing the main residence's side wall, with a narrow slit-like attached skylight (吸壁天井). Also two stories. Depth equals one bay width of the main residence; width equals the main residence's depth. All dimensions small, so lighting is weak. Has its own independent main gate, possibly with a blue-brick gatehouse. A small door also connects from the main residence.

Type 3: larger—an independent three-bay two-story building, with a door from one end of the front porch to the main residence's open wing. The bieting courtyard has a small open wing on each side. One side's front eave columns have half-height flower railings; the other has flat bench seats between eave columns. The courtyard center plants nandina, pomegranate, golden osmanthus—elegant plants with form, color, and fragrance. Ground paved with broken stone, clean and orderly.

Another example: the forward-and-rear style residence built by Lingluan, eldest son of the "Eight Families," has a bieting attached to the residence's right wall. The bieting has front and rear rooms separated by a small courtyard, connected by a three-bay corridor—each bay less than 2 m wide. The middle bay serves as passage; the other two have beauty-rest railings (美人靠) between eave columns. Each bay has ling-flower (菱花) hanging ornaments under the lintel. Both front and rear bieting rooms' upper and lower floors have ling-flower lattice windows facing the small courtyard. The small courtyard's gate opens into the narrow alley between the residence and the school house "吾爱吾庐" (I Love My Hut); the gate is small but elaborate—double-sided carved brick gatehouse inside and out, beautifully matching the compact bieting veranda.

Sanfang Lingxian's residence, built behind Lingluan's, has a bieting at its east end. Both residence and bieting have front courtyards, separated by a partition wall with open lattice windows and a small connecting door. The door has a small water-polished blue-brick plaque—one side reads "瑞霭晴岚" (Auspicious Mist, Clear Mountain Haze), the other "延禧" (Extended Blessing), in seal script, stone-green color.

(3) Bieting Style

Among clan residence complexes, the bieting has the most typological variation—no fixed format, unbound by conventional rules. Compared to the residence's main rooms and school hall, bieting appear small, lively, light, open, and exquisitely crafted. Their style strives for intimacy and elegance, but as merchants' living environment they are inevitably ornate—hence bieting are also called "花厅" (flower hall). Ceilings are fully painted, though tones are restrained—mostly ink chrysanthemums with touches of yellow, evoking Tao Yuanming's rustic charm. Whether official or merchant, after retirement, one genuinely or performatively advertises this leisurely posture. Door panels (樘板) are sometimes vermilion lacquered (e.g., Shuanggui Study bieting), sometimes ivory-white (e.g., Yuan Lingjia's bieting), sometimes mural-painted (e.g., Yuan Lingduo's bieting). Some use plain wood—moist, warm, naturally intimate. Bieting upper front eaves have full-width lattice windows. In Yuan Lingduo's small bieting, the upper central bay's porch has beauty-rest railings, side bays have open lattice railings. Unlike main rooms, bieting upper side walls often have wide windows overlooking landscape, blending nature with dwelling. These windows have brick lattice or brick eaves, highly decorative—accents in the village streetscape. Because bieting upper floors are not enclosed inward or walled off, their lattice windows and railings are visible from outside, adding beauty and vitality to the village.

sections.name: 宗祠的兴起
sections.content_zh:
一、宗祠的兴起

在中国国土的很大范围里，主要是东南各省区，宗祠是乡土社会里宗法制度下除了住宅之外最重要的建筑，也是血缘村落里最华丽、最高大的建筑。宗祠的基本功能是供奉宗族祖先的神位，定时祭祀。也就是说，它的基本功能是利用祖先崇拜，加强宗族的内聚力，而宗族是乡土社会主要的、基本的组织力量、管理力量和教化力量。所以，宗祠产生的主要前提是，在农耕时代，一处地方的一位"始迁祖"的直系后裔一代又一代地聚居在一起，形成宗族，同时形成血缘村落。正如清人赵吉士在《寄园寄所寄》卷十一《故老杂记》中描述的徽州的情况："新安各姓，聚族而居，绝无杂姓搀入者，其风最为近古，出入齿让。姓各有宗祠统之，岁时伏腊，一姓村中千丁皆集。"集就集在宗祠里。

在农耕时代，人们相对固定在一定范围的土地上从事生产，凡开沟洫、辟山林、整田亩、建道路，以及保卫自己的利益和安全不受侵犯，都不是个别家庭所能承担的，而需要人际的合作，并形成有内部结构的社会单元。这种社会单元，最自然的是建立在血脉亲情之上的宗族。因此，聚族而居，形成血缘村落，是农耕时代最普遍的现象。加强宗族的内聚力，也便是血缘认同，就是加强人际合作的社会单元的能量。宗族是人们生存并发展的最重要依靠，从而促成了祖先崇拜，以致《礼记·郊特牲》要特别强调一句："万物本乎天，人本乎祖"。宗祠主要是举行祖先崇拜仪式的场所，它的重要性由此决定。

中国的祖先崇拜由来已久，在商代，它超过了神鬼崇拜。不过，那时对祖先的崇拜还没有完全摆脱神鬼崇拜，敬畏有余而缺乏人情味。到了周代，人们认识到，为了使宗族稳定，便要利用宗族内部血缘关系的天然秩序，赋予这种天然秩序以浓郁的伦理意义，使它神圣化，于是提倡孝悌。《论语》里记录了孔子和他弟子论孝悌的一些话，有若说："君子务本，本立而道生，孝悌也者，其为仁之本与！"曾子说："慎终追远，民德归厚矣。"（均见《学而》篇）后来，《仪礼》和《礼记》里用了大量篇幅制定出亲族关系、祖先祭祀、婚丧礼仪等极其繁琐严格的规矩。这就把含情脉脉的伦理关系进一步制度化了。

因此，《礼记·祭法》里规定了王、诸侯、大夫、适士、官师等人建庙和祭祀规矩，但是，地位低的士和庶人"无庙，死曰鬼"。因为奉祀祖先有它天然的情感基础，又有它重要的社会意义，所以在百姓生活中盛行不衰。据东汉末年崔寔记的《四民月令》，可知到了汉代，平民祭祖已经成为普遍的礼俗。一年之内，六月、七月、八月、冬至、腊月都有祭祖的活动。不过，祭祖往往和社祭合一，或者到坟上去祭扫，坟地有小屋叫"祠"。当时百姓还没有祖庙，更没有如后来所称的宗祠。所祭的，也不是全宗族的共祖。

这种情况大致一直延续到宋代。宋代的理学家们认识到了宗族的社会意义，大力提倡"三纲五常"，说"生民之德莫大于孝"，并且致力于使敬老的礼俗更谨严，因而也更繁杂。最有代表性也最有权威性的是托名朱熹编定的《朱文公家礼》。《家礼》卷一《通礼·祠堂》里规定："君子将营宫室，先立祠堂于正寝之东，为四龛以奉先世神位。"后来以考证典章名物见长的乾隆进士阮葵生在《茶余客话·庙制》里解释：有一品至三品官职的，家庙五间；四品以下的，家庙三间；没有官职的士庶则"于寝之北为龛，奉高、曾、祖、祢"四代祖先，这就是《家礼》所说的"四龛"所奉的先祖，不过从正寝的东侧搬到了北侧。从这两则资料看，就礼俗上说，宋代的庙制还是等级森严的，士庶依旧不应有祖庙。不过，等级已经从周代的宗法分封制改为官阶品位制，这是隋唐以后科举制代替承袭制的成果。科举制度打开了士庶和品官之间的通道，既然品官可建祖庙，就为祖庙的建造向庶民开放创造了条件。有同样意义的是，士庶都有资格奉祀四代祖先，不再是先人死了便称"鬼"。但是按古礼，士庶祭祖先不能建庙，所以《家礼》把士庶祭祀祖先的建筑叫做"祠堂"，这是从坟地小屋取用过来的名称，和"鬼"还沾一点边。朱熹很重视祭祀，在给《论语·述而》写的注里，他说："慎终者，丧尽其礼；追远者，祭尽其诚。"《朱文公家礼》再三宣扬建祠堂的重大意义，说这个措施表达了子孙"报本反始之心，尊祖敬宗之意，实有家礼名分之守，所以开业传世之本"。这样就论证了建祠堂的普遍意义，为日后的民间祠堂大发展建立了理论基础。略早于朱熹的北宋程颐则主张除四代先祖外，还要祭血缘村落内一个宗族自始迁祖以下所有的先祖，后来的祠庙祭祀制度遵守了这个主张。

《家礼》认为，庶民祭祖限于四代，是因为五代以上的祖先不可能见到，祭五代以上便没有感情根据。所以亲情"五世而斩"，考诸古礼，多余的不必要的祭祀是要反对的。

或许，更重要的理由是统治者害怕百姓中产生大而有力的宗族。在农耕时代，最能威胁统治者地位的力量是宗族和"邪教"。强宗豪族是社会上的不稳定因素，统治者历来要设法加以抑制。隋唐废门阀世袭制之后，强宗豪族有所削弱，但历次农民"造反"，不论大小，宗族关系大都和"邪教"一同起了"啸聚"的作用。所以统治者还是不放松警惕，以致对庶民庙祭上溯的世代作了限制。

虽然《朱文公家礼》可能是一本伪托的书，但影响很大，后世官方和民间的宗族都长期以它为执礼的根据。不过《家礼》中所说的，有许多其实是已经存在的事实，北宋陆九渊、范仲淹等高位人物都早已为本族建立了家庙，而且径称为祠堂。其后宋、元两代各地士庶之家建祠堂的事已可见于记载。南宋淳佑十年（1250年）朱熠为浙江省平阳县顺溪村陈氏写的《宜都陈氏家乘·序》说："夫同宗之人，亲虽有戚疏，服虽有隆杀，而禴、祠、烝、尝必相会，冠婚丧祭必相赴，以至患难也、缓急也，则又未尝不相扶持，岂非由于谱谍之修而然哉！"序中说到禴、祠（祀）、烝、尝，就是夏、春、冬、秋四季的敬祖祭祀，既然届时"同宗之人"都要相会，则可证已有固定的奉祀的场所，这应该便是家庙，而且至迟建于南宋。

明初宋濂撰广东《惠州何氏先祠碑》，记何氏早在宋代已"率族人建祠置田以礼其众祖"。"礼其众祖"，则可能祠堂奉祀的已不止四代。据安徽《新安黄氏大宗谱·卷二》里《古林黄氏家祠碑记》，休宁县古林镇黄氏也已在宋代就建造了宗祠。宋濂写的《莆田林氏重建先祠记》记述元代林氏"汲汲于先祠之建"，"患祠之规制卑狭，不足以交神明，而即故宅之基建屋三楹间，蔽以外门"。（以上宋濂两则均见《宋学士文集》）这四例都说明，宋、元时有一些非高官显宦之家也已经建造了脱离住宅的独立的祠堂。浙江省建德市新叶村的叶氏总祠"西山祠堂"和外宅派总祠有序堂，也都是元代始建的。有了"总祠"，大约所祀的也已不止四代。到了明代，庶民建祠堂的就更多了，不过大概都属草创而且还有所顾忌，不敢造得多么堂皇。浙江省永嘉县渠口村《渠川叶氏宗谱·重修叶氏大宗祠碑记》说："明弘治甲子……肇建宗祠，敬宗为族……祠仅一重，草创而已。"这应该是事实，只是不知道当时的祭制如何，是只祭四代，还是向上直溯始迁祖。

不奉祀祖先，不能团结聚居在一个血缘村落里的全体族人，不免势单力薄。生产和生活的不可改变的要求便是形成并团结整个宗族。事实是，在庶民普遍建祠之前，不少宗族都已在祭祀共同祖先，除了一部分宗族可能已有祭祀"众祖"的"总祠"外，祭祖活动还在其他各种公共建筑中举行。这些公共建筑之一是社庙。社祭是中国人很原始的信仰活动，明代初年立法规定庶民可以祭祀五种对象，"里社"是其中之首（《明会典·祭祀通例》）。社神是地方的保护神，大概与大地崇拜有关，遍及中国城乡各地，并且社又成为地缘性的基层单位，《礼记·祭法》郑玄注："与民族居百家以上，则共立一社。"在农耕文明时代的血缘村落中，大多以族立社，族社合一，所以祭祖仪式可以在社庙中举行。二是显祖的庙。一个宗族如果在历史上出过功业赫奕的祖先，就可能奏请旌表，敕建庙宇。"古忠臣烈士有俊功大惠于世，有国者必崇祀之，著于令。"（《篁墩文集》卷十四，程敏政《休宁汉口世忠行祠记》）显祖的庙可以有"行祠"建在同族拆分出去的村落里，有的很远，甚至隔省，由各地族裔筹资建造。这种显祖庙和它的行祠往往是宗族祭共祖的场所，如皖南、赣北和浙西的越国公汪华的庙。三是寺院。农村中多数寺院也是大体由一个血缘村落建造并供养的。"施主"和"香客"多为族人，所以，也有极少数宗族暂时利用寺院祭祀祖先。四是祖屋，通常是一个血缘村落的始迁祖或者其他早期祖先住过的古老住宅，本身对宗族多少有些纪念意义。
sections.content_en:
1. The Rise of Ancestral Halls

Across much of China, especially the southeastern provinces, the ancestral hall (宗祠) is—after the residence—the most important building in the patriarchal clan system of rural society, and the most ornate and tallest building in a blood-kin village. Its basic function is to enshrine the spirit tablets of clan ancestors and hold scheduled sacrifices. That is, its basic function is to use ancestor worship to strengthen clan cohesion; the clan is the primary organizational, administrative, and educational force in rural society. Thus the main precondition for ancestral halls' emergence was that, in the agrarian era, the direct descendants of a "founding ancestor" (始迁祖) in one place lived together generation after generation, forming a clan and simultaneously a blood-kin village. As Qing scholar Zhao Jishi described Huizhou in 《寄园寄所寄》, vol. 11, 《故老杂记》: "The various surnames of Xin'an live in clans, with no alien surnames mixed in—a custom closest to antiquity, yielding precedence by age. Each surname has an ancestral hall to govern it; at seasonal festivals, all thousand males of a one-surname village gather." They gather in the ancestral hall.

In the agrarian era, people worked relatively fixed plots of land. Digging irrigation ditches, clearing forests, leveling fields, building roads, and defending interests and safety—none could be borne by individual households; they required cooperation and structured social units. The most natural such unit was the clan, built on blood kinship. Hence clan cohabitation and blood-kin villages were the most common agrarian-era phenomenon. Strengthening clan cohesion meant strengthening blood-kin identity and the energy of cooperative social units. The clan was people's most important reliance for survival and development, fostering ancestor worship—so much so that 《礼记·郊特牲》 (Book of Rites, Special Sacrifices) emphasizes: "All things originate from Heaven; humans originate from their ancestors." The ancestral hall is primarily the venue for ancestor-worship rituals; its importance follows from this.

Chinese ancestor worship is ancient—in the Shang dynasty it surpassed spirit-god worship. Yet early ancestor worship had not fully shed spirit-god worship: more awe than human warmth. By the Zhou dynasty, people recognized that to stabilize the clan, they must use the natural order of intra-clan blood relations, imbue it with rich ethical meaning, and sanctify it—hence promoting filial piety and brotherly respect (孝悌). 《论语》 records Confucius and disciples on filial piety: You Ruo said, "The gentleman devotes himself to the root; the root established, the Way grows. Filial piety and brotherly respect—are they not the root of benevolence!" Zengzi said, "Careful attention to funeral rites and sacrifices to distant ancestors brings the people's virtue to fullness." (Both in 《学而》) Later, 《仪礼》 and 《礼记》 devoted extensive space to elaborate rules for kinship, ancestor sacrifice, and wedding/funeral rituals—institutionalizing tender ethical relations.

Thus 《礼记·祭法》 (Book of Rites, Sacrifice Laws) stipulated temple-building and sacrifice rules for kings, dukes, grand masters, senior officers, and officials—but low-ranking shi and commoners had "no temple; at death they are called ghosts." Because ancestor worship had both natural emotional basis and important social meaning, it flourished among common people. According to Eastern Han Cui Shi's 《四民月令》 (Monthly Instructions for the Four Classes), by Han dynasty commoner ancestor sacrifice was widespread—June, July, August, winter solstice, and twelfth month all had activities. However, ancestor sacrifice was often combined with earth-god sacrifice (社祭), or performed at graves with small huts called "祠" (ci). Commoners then had no ancestral temples, let alone later-style ancestral halls. What they sacrificed was not the whole clan's common ancestor.

This situation lasted roughly until the Song dynasty. Song neo-Confucians recognized the clan's social significance, vigorously promoting "三纲五常" (Three Bonds and Five Constants), saying "no virtue among people exceeds filial piety," and working to make elder-respect rituals stricter and more elaborate. Most representative and authoritative was 《朱文公家礼》 (Master Zhu's Family Rituals), attributed to Zhu Xi. 《家礼》, vol. 1, 《通礼·祠堂》 stipulated: "When a gentleman builds a residence, he first establishes a ancestral hall east of the main bedroom, with four niches for ancestral spirit tablets." Later, Qianlong-era jinshi Ruan Kuisheng, known for textual scholarship, explained in 《茶余客话·庙制》: officials rank 1–3 had five-bay family temples; rank 4 and below, three bays; commoners without office "made a niche north of the bedroom, enshrining four generations—great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father." This is the "four niches" of 《家礼》, though moved from east to north of the bedroom. These sources show Song temple system was still rank-stratified; commoners still should not have ancestral temples. However, rank had shifted from Zhou's feudal-patriarchal system to official-rank system—a result of Sui-Tang's examination system replacing hereditary privilege. The examination system opened channels between commoners and officials; since officials could build temples, conditions were created for temple-building to extend to commoners. Equally significant: commoners could enshrine four generations, no longer called "ghosts" at death. But by ancient ritual, commoners could not build temples for ancestor sacrifice—so 《家礼》 called commoner ancestor-sacrifice buildings "祠堂" (ancestral hall), a name borrowed from grave huts, still faintly associated with "ghosts." Zhu Xi valued sacrifice highly; in his commentary on 《论语·述而》 he wrote: "Careful funeral means full ritual; distant sacrifice means full sincerity." 《朱文公家礼》 repeatedly emphasized the great significance of building ancestral halls, expressing descendants' "heart of returning to the root and origin, intention of honoring ancestors and respecting the clan, indeed upholding family ritual and status—thus the foundation for continuing the lineage." This argued for the universal significance of hall-building, laying theoretical groundwork for later folk temple expansion. Slightly before Zhu Xi, Northern Song's Cheng Yi advocated sacrificing, beyond four generations, all ancestors from the founding ancestor down within a blood-kin village clan—later temple-sacrifice systems followed this.

《家礼》 held commoner sacrifice limited to four generations because ancestors five generations back could not be known personally; sacrificing beyond lacked emotional basis. Thus kinship "cuts off at five generations" (五世而斩); per ancient ritual, unnecessary extra sacrifice was opposed.

Perhaps more importantly, rulers feared large, powerful clans among commoners. In the agrarian era, the forces most threatening to rulers were clans and "heterodox cults." Powerful clans were destabilizing; rulers always sought to suppress them. After Sui-Tang abolished hereditary aristocracy, powerful clans weakened, but every peasant rebellion—large or small—clan relations and "heterodox cults" together served to "gather crowds." So rulers remained vigilant, limiting how many generations commoners could sacrifice upward.

Though 《朱文公家礼》 may be a forged text, its influence was enormous; later official and folk clans long used it as ritual authority. Yet much of what 《家礼》 describes was already fact: Northern Song figures like Lu Jiuyuan and Fan Zhongyan had built family temples for their clans, directly calling them "ancestral halls." Thereafter Song-Yuan commoner families' hall-building is recorded. In Southern Song Chunyou 10 (1250), Zhu Yi wrote for Chen clan of Shunxi Village, Pingyang, Zhejiang, in 《宜都陈氏家乘·序》: "People of the same clan, though kinship varies close or distant, mourning grades vary high or low—yet at seasonal sacrifices (禴祠烝尝) they all gather; at weddings, funerals, and sacrifices they all attend; in hardship and emergency they support one another—is this not due to maintaining genealogy?" The four seasonal sacrifices mentioned mean summer, spring, winter, autumn ancestor worship; since "same-clan people" gather at these times, there must have been a fixed place of worship—a family temple, built no later than Southern Song.

Early Ming Song Lian wrote Guangdong's 《惠州何氏先祠碑》, recording He clan in Song dynasty already "led clansmen to build a hall and set aside fields to honor their many ancestors." "Honoring many ancestors" suggests the hall enshrined more than four generations. According to Anhui's 《新安黄氏大宗谱·卷二》, 《古林黄氏家祠碑记》, Huang clan of Gulin Town, Xiuning, also built an ancestral hall in Song. Song Lian's 《莆田林氏重建先祠记》 records Yuan dynasty Lin clan "eagerly building the ancestral hall," "finding the hall's规制 humble and narrow, insufficient to commune with spirits, so built a three-bay house on the old residence site, enclosed by an outer gate." (Both Song Lian pieces in 《宋学士文集》) These four cases show Song-Yuan non-official families already built independent halls separate from residences. Ye clan's main hall "西山祠堂" and outer-branch main hall "有序堂" in Xinye Village, Jiande, Zhejiang, were also founded in Yuan. With "main halls," what was sacrificed likely exceeded four generations. By Ming, commoner hall-building increased, though mostly rudimentary and cautious, not built grandly. Zhejiang Yongjia Qukou Village's 《渠川叶氏宗谱·重修叶氏大宗祠碑记》 says: "Ming Hongzhi Jiazi year... founded ancestral hall, honoring ancestors for the clan... hall only one layer, rudimentary." This is likely factual—though we don't know the sacrifice system: only four generations, or tracing up to the founding ancestor.

Without sacrificing common ancestors, a clan living together in a blood-kin village could not unite all clansmen, remaining weak. Production and life's immutable demand was to form and unite the whole clan. In fact, before commoners universally built halls, many clans already sacrificed common ancestors—besides some clans possibly having "main halls" for "many ancestors," sacrifice also occurred in other public buildings. One was the earth-god temple (社庙). Earth-god sacrifice is a very ancient Chinese belief; early Ming law allowed commoners to sacrifice five objects, with "village earth-god" (里社) first (《明会典·祭祀通例》). The earth god is a local protector, likely related to earth worship, found throughout China; "she" also became a territorial base unit. 《礼记·祭法》, Zheng Xuan's note: "Clans living together of 100+ households jointly establish one she." In agrarian blood-kin villages, most established she by clan—clan and she merged—so ancestor sacrifice could be held in earth-god temples. Second was the temple of an illustrious ancestor. If a clan had an ancestor of great merit, it might petition for imperial recognition and a state-built temple. "Ancient loyal ministers and martyrs with great merit and benefit to the world are necessarily worshipped by the state, recorded in law." (《篁墩文集》 vol. 14, Cheng Minzheng's 《休宁汉口世忠行祠记》) Illustrious-ancestor temples could have "branch temples" (行祠) in villages where the clan split off—some far away, even across provinces—built by local descendants. These temples and branch halls were often venues for clan common-ancestor sacrifice, e.g., the temple of Duke Wang Hua of Yue in southern Anhui, northern Jiangxi, and western Zhejiang. Third was Buddhist temples. Most rural temples were built and supported by a blood-kin village; "donors" and "worshippers" were mostly clansmen—so a few clans temporarily used temples for ancestor sacrifice. Fourth was the ancestral house (祖屋), usually the old residence where the founding ancestor or other early ancestors lived, itself having commemorative meaning for the clan.

sections.name: 宗祠与宗族
sections.content_zh:
二、宗祠与宗族

朝廷官方总是大大落后于民间，明代初年，不顾民间实在情况，仍然颁律法规定："庶民祭里社、乡厉及祖父母、父母，并得祀灶，余俱禁止。"这以后将近两百年，朝廷对祭祀祖先的礼制屡定屡改，反复多次而不能确立。不过，在民间，建祠庙以祭祖先的事还是不断地发生着，尤其在宋代，未成制度而已。浙江省永嘉县枫林镇的"徐氏大宗"就是初建于宋代。

这种情况到明代嘉靖年间（1522—1566）发生了大转折。这时期，朝政腐败，各地农民起义频繁，社会动荡，一些有识之士率先改变了对宗族的看法。他们看到，宗族既可能是反政府的力量，也可能改造成协助政府镇抚农民的力量。宗族既可能是"慎终报远"的纯伦理性组织，也可能改造成一个类政权性组织。政府的官僚机构不可能直接对广大的农村实行有效的统治，最好的办法是求助于宗族，利用宗族作为基层的类自治性政权机构，以稳定局面。嘉靖十五年（1536年），礼部尚书夏言（1482—1548）上《令臣民得祭始祖立家庙疏》，其中有"乞诏天下臣工建立家庙"：

伏惟皇上扩推因心之孝，诏令天下臣民，许如程子所言，冬至祭厥初生民之始祖，立春祭始祖以下高祖以上之先祖。皆设两位于其席，但不许立庙以逾分，……庶皇上广锡类之孝，臣下无禘袷之嫌，愚夫愚妇得以尽其报本追远之诚，溯源徂委，亦有以起其敦宗睦族之谊，其于化民成俗，未必无小补云。（《桂洲夏文愍公奏议》卷二十一）

奏疏提到了允许百姓"敦宗睦族"可以"化民成俗"，也就是教育百姓遵礼守法。这在当时是很迫切的事，也是只靠官僚机构做不到的事，所以世宗嘉靖皇帝准奏，下诏"许民间皆得联宗立庙"。"联宗立庙"，而不仅仅是家家在正寝之东建龛祭祀四代祖先，这正是平民百姓一直盼望着的，并在一定规模上已经实现了的。于是，一旦开禁，极短期内，便宗祠遍天下，如浙江省江山市清漾村毛氏大宗祠就是嘉靖二十年（1541年）建造的。

至于夏言建议中说宗祠只祭高祖以上的先祖，这是因为遵照古制，宜将高祖以下祭于宅内。经过世代更迭，后人再将已经升为高祖以上的先人送入宗祠，叫做"祧"。这也是《礼记》的古制，"远庙为祧，统祭远祖"。不过这个制度在不少地方早已被突破了。

统治者终于确认了扶植宗族对稳定社会的好处，其实，早在春秋时期一些读书人就已经再三强调指出过孝与忠的关系。《论语·学而》记孔子弟子有若的话："其为人也孝悌而好犯上者鲜矣。不好犯上而好作乱者未之有也。"《礼记·祭统》说："忠臣以事其君，孝子以事其亲，其本一也。"《孝经》里也说："以孝事君则忠"，以及"求忠臣于孝子之门"。事过将近两千年，统治者更加明白，为了要臣民忠于他，就得从提倡孝道下手。要提倡孝道，必须依靠宗族的力量，也就要推广宗祠的建设，以利于臣民的"慎终追远"。

于是，宗族的意义和作用扩大了。明太祖朱元璋曾颁过《圣谕六条》，说的是："孝顺父母，尊敬长上，和睦乡里，教训子弟，各安生理，毋作非为。"都是有关宗族内部凝聚的事。后世许多宗族的《族规》里都规定要在祠堂大祭的时候由宗长讲解这个《圣谕六条》。到了清初，皇家标榜以孝治国，把宗族的任务扩大到了外部的国家事务上去，把宗族真正当成了国家体制中的基础单位。康熙九年（1670年），颁布《上谕十六条》，确定了宗族的功能，内容是：

敦孝悌以重人伦，笃宗族以昭雍睦，和乡党以息争讼，重农桑以足衣食，尚节俭以惜财用，隆学校以端士习，黜异端以崇正学，讲法律以儆愚顽，明礼让以厚风俗，务本业以定民志，训子弟以禁非为，息诬告以全善良，诫匿逃以免株连，完钱粮以省催科。联保甲以弭盗贼，解仇忿以重身命。

比较明太祖朱元璋的《圣谕》和康熙的《上谕》，可以清晰地看到二者对宗族作用的看法有了很大的差别。康熙《上谕》实际上已经把宗族当成了国家的基层政府机构和司法机构，宗族的功能从此确定，宗族制度从此完备。后来雍正皇帝的《圣谕广训》："立家庙以荐丞尝，设家塾以保子弟，置族田以赡贫乏，修族谱以联疏远"，虽然把宗族作用的范围又缩小了很多，更突出了宗族的自身建设，不过，实际生活中一直起作用的仍然是康熙的《上谕》。

自从康熙朝赋予宗族类似地方自治政权的功能之后，各宗族的族谱中必有的《族规》也改变了内容，几乎把康熙《上谕》一条条都涵括进去了。有些族谱，径直就把《上谕》十六条作为族规。
sections.content_en:
2. Ancestral Halls and Clans

Official court policy always lagged far behind folk practice. Early Ming, ignoring actual folk conditions, law still stipulated: "Commoners may sacrifice village earth-gods, township ghosts, grandparents, and parents, and may worship the stove god; all else is forbidden." For nearly two centuries after, the court repeatedly set and revised ancestor-sacrifice ritual, never settling it. Yet among commoners, hall-building for ancestor sacrifice continued—especially in Song, though not yet institutionalized. The "Xu Clan Main Hall" in Fenglin Town, Yongjia, Zhejiang, was first built in Song.

A major turning point came in Ming Jiajing era (1522–1566). This period saw corrupt government, frequent peasant uprisings, social unrest. Some enlightened thinkers first changed their view of clans: they saw clans could be either anti-government forces or transformed into forces assisting government in pacifying peasants. Clans could be purely ethical organizations ("careful funeral, distant sacrifice") or transformed into quasi-governmental organizations. Government bureaucracy could not directly rule vast rural areas effectively; the best approach was to rely on clans as grassroots quasi-autonomous governing bodies to stabilize the situation. In Jiajing 15 (1536), Minister of Rites Xia Yan (1482–1548) submitted 《令臣民得祭始祖立家庙疏》 (Memorial on Allowing Subjects to Sacrifice Founding Ancestors and Establish Family Temples), including "begging the emperor to order all officials and people to establish family temples":

"May Your Majesty extend the filial piety of the heart, ordering all subjects to, as Master Cheng said, sacrifice the founding ancestor at winter solstice, and ancestors from founding ancestor down to great-great-grandfather at spring beginning. Set two spirit positions at their seats, but do not allow temple-building to exceed rank... May Your Majesty broadly bestow filial piety, subjects have no suspicion of imperial sacrifice, common men and women may fulfill their sincerity of returning to root and tracing the distant, tracing source to branch, thus arousing their affection for respecting clan and harmonizing kin—this may not be without small benefit to transforming the people and forming custom." (《桂洲夏文愍公奏议》 vol. 21)

The memorial noted that allowing commoners to "respect clan and harmonize kin" could "transform the people and form custom"—i.e., educate commoners to observe ritual and law. This was urgent then and impossible through bureaucracy alone, so Emperor Jiajing approved, issuing edict "allowing all commoners to unite clans and establish temples." "Uniting clans and establishing temples"—not merely each household building a niche east of the bedroom for four generations—was exactly what commoners had long desired and already achieved on some scale. Once permitted, in a very short time ancestral halls spread everywhere. For example, the Mao Clan Main Hall in Qingyang Village, Jiangshan, Zhejiang, was built in Jiajing 20 (1541).

As for Xia Yan's suggestion that ancestral halls sacrifice only ancestors above great-great-grandfather: this followed ancient ritual, where ancestors below great-great-grandfather should be sacrificed within the residence. Over generations, descendants later move those who have risen to above-great-great-grandfather status into the ancestral hall—called "祧" (tiao, distant-ancestor transfer). This is also 《礼记》 ancient system: "distant temple is tiao, collectively sacrificing distant ancestors." But this system was already broken in many places.

Rulers finally confirmed the benefit of supporting clans for social stability. In fact, as early as Spring-Autumn period, scholars repeatedly emphasized the relationship between filial piety and loyalty. 《论语·学而》 records Confucius's disciple You Ruo: "Few are those who are filial and brotherly yet like to offend superiors; none are those who do not offend superiors yet like rebellion." 《礼记·祭统》 says: "A loyal minister serves his lord; a filial son serves his parents—the root is one." 《孝经》 (Classic of Filial Piety) also says: "Serving the lord with filial piety yields loyalty," and "seek loyal ministers among the gates of filial sons." After nearly two thousand years, rulers understood more clearly: to make subjects loyal, start with promoting filial piety. To promote filial piety, rely on clan power—and promote ancestral hall construction to facilitate subjects' "careful funeral and distant sacrifice."

Thus the clan's significance and role expanded. Ming Taizu Zhu Yuanzhang issued 《圣谕六条》 (Six Sacred Edicts): "Be filial to parents, respect elders, harmonize with villagers, teach children, each pursue proper livelihood, do no wrong." All concerned intra-clan cohesion. Later many clans' 《族规》 (Clan Rules) stipulated that the clan head explain the Six Sacred Edicts during major hall sacrifices. By early Qing, the imperial house proclaimed ruling by filial piety, expanding clan tasks to external state affairs, truly treating clans as basic units of the state system. In Kangxi 9 (1670), 《上谕十六条》 (Sixteen Imperial Edicts) was issued, defining clan functions:

"Promote filial piety to value human relations; strengthen clans to manifest harmony; reconcile villagers to end lawsuits; value agriculture to ensure food and clothing; esteem frugality to conserve wealth; promote schools to rectify scholar conduct; reject heterodoxy to honor orthodox learning; explain law to warn the foolish; clarify courtesy to enrich customs; pursue proper occupation to settle people's will; train children to forbid wrongdoing; suppress false accusations to protect the good; warn against harboring fugitives to avoid collective punishment; pay taxes to reduce collection demands; organize mutual defense to eliminate bandits; resolve enmity to value life."

Comparing Zhu Yuanzhang's Sacred Edict and Kangxi's Imperial Edicts, one clearly sees a great difference in views of clan role. Kangxi's Edicts effectively treated clans as state grassroots government and judicial bodies—clan functions henceforth fixed, clan system henceforth complete. Later Yongzheng's 《圣谕广训》 (Expanded Sacred Edicts): "Establish family temples for seasonal sacrifice, set up family schools to protect children, set aside clan fields to support the poor, repair genealogy to connect distant kin"—though narrowing clan role's scope and emphasizing clan self-building, in actual life Kangxi's Edicts continued to operate.

After Kangxi赋予 clans quasi-local-autonomy government functions, the 《族规》 (Clan Rules) mandatory in every clan genealogy changed content, almost incorporating Kangxi's Edicts item by item. Some genealogies directly adopted the Sixteen Edicts as clan rules.

sections.name: 宗祠与礼法
sections.content_zh:
三、宗祠的分布

不过，宗祠之设，南方与北方大有不同，南方盛而丽，但北方则大多既少又简陋。这大约是因为一来北方历代多战乱，亲人离散或外迁，宗族组织不如南方普及、发达和健全，而且宗族性血缘村落很少，多的是杂姓共居的村落；二来北方农村大多远不如南方的富有，以致文化水平也落后；三来少数族又不断侵入，以致宗族观念更加淡化。清代初年大学者顾炎武曾描述山东情况："余来往山东省十余年，则见夫巨室之日以微而世族之日以败，货贿之日以乏，科名之日以衰，而人心之日以浇且伪；盗诬其主人而奴讦其长；日趋于祸败而莫知其所终。"（《皇朝经世文编》卷五十八，《莱州任氏族谱序》）乾隆《徐州府志·风俗》说：府境里"有庙者少，无庙者多"。过了一百年左右，光绪《太平县志·风俗》还说："祠堂之设唯缙绅家有之。"差不多同时，光绪《绛州志·风俗》说："祭祀营庙，唯缙绅家为然，然亦同堂异龛而已。"杂姓村落如山西省介休县张壁村，只有张姓、贾姓两大户晋商有宗祠，很狭小，型制完全与小型民居一般，无"拜殿"和"寝室"，单间而已，甚至无谱，只有一张世系图，画在白布上。贾氏宗祠是道光年间（1821—1850）造的，张氏的已不可考，当也是建于清中叶。河北省蔚县有二百多座村堡，在调查过的几十个中，只宋家庄有一座苏氏宗祠，仅仅一个开间，土墙，室内墙面画满了世系图。更多的是由某姓某长辈把一张布质世系图存在家里。更小的姓没有任何家族活动。

相反，南方宗祠很普遍。因为南方战乱少，长期稳定，因而多血缘村落，宗族势力大。清初康熙朝人赵吉士在《寄园寄所寄·泛叶寄》里写道："新安各姓，聚族而居，……千年之冢，不动一抔；千丁之族，未尝散处；千载之谱系，丝毫不紊……"

新安就是皖南徽州。池州地区各县，"每逾一岭，进一溪，其中烟火万家，鸡犬相闻者，皆巨族大家之所居也。一族所聚，动辄数里或十数里，即在城中，亦各占一区，无异姓杂处。以故千百年犹一日之亲，千百世犹一父之子。"（康熙《石埭桂氏宗谱·序》）江苏省苏州，"兄弟析烟亦不远徙，祖宗庐墓，永以为依。故一村之中，同姓者至数十家或数百家。"（《同治苏州府志》卷三）在这种宗族关系牢固的地方，宗祠自然就多了、大了而且壮观了。所以早在乾隆初年，江西巡抚陈宏谋在《寄杨朴园书》里说："直省惟闽中、江西、湖南皆聚族而居，族皆有祠，此古风也"。安徽黟县乾隆时知县孙维龙有《黟山杂诵》诗（见《黟续志》道光二十二年）：

祠堂高耸郁云烟，松柏苍苍不记年，
最爱土风犹近古，苏公族谱范公田。

从首句看，祠堂都已经很有规模了。原诗有注："邑中族姓俱有祠宇，以为岁时俎豆之地"，诗中末句所言"范公田"，指义田，以济贫族婚葬之用。

血缘村落里一姓可能有许多各级宗祠，是因为宗族内部天然地会分房分支。在南方许多村落里，宗族内一系人有了五代，就可以自立房派，当然，如人财两不旺，不立房派也可以。房派以下，三代可建支派。房派和支派都可以建造宗祠，在浙江省把它们叫做"厅"、"众厅"而不叫"祠堂"。房派以下的厅叫"私己厅"。不足三代的，不能建厅，只许在老祖屋里设龛祭祀，叫香火堂。众厅和私己厅也有很堂皇的，如浙江省建德市的新叶村，叶氏一个房派的崇仁堂，前后一共四进，规模竟和"外宅派"总祠有序堂相当且稍稍超出。总祠内存全族高祖以上的先祖的神主，"厅"内另有一套本房派的。

南方血缘村落内大小宗祠之多，还有别的原因。如江西省乐安县流坑村，一些人到了晚年，不愿身后子孙因分家而伤了老宅，便把自己的住房立为祠堂或把自己建造的书院立为祠堂，以致祠堂的数量大增，现存竟有八十三座之多，而大部分的型制和规模则仅仅同于一所普通小住宅而已。它们通常以原来的房主个人名号命名，如"卓然公祠"、"蕃昌公祠"等等。

也有一些村落，为有功于宗族的人立专祠，如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的金氏，有明代嘉靖年间（1522—1566）的桂林公兴建了全县最好的水利系统和街巷网，统建了一批大宅，筑坝蓄水建成楠溪江村落中最大的园林，也兴建了极为典雅的书院。他身后，子孙们便把书院改为桂林公祠。因为书院中央原有两方宽阔的水池，水池正中有凉亭翼然，所以又得名为"水亭祠"。桂林公生前兴水利，殁后与水长相厮守，亦可谓得其所哉了！

又如清代晚期光绪壬辰年（1892年）福建西部连城县培田村的吴拔祯考中了武进士，钦点蓝翎侍卫，御前听差。在农村里，这就是光宗耀祖的大事了，吴拔祯的家宅务本堂便挂上了"进士第"的匾额。吴拔祯告老还乡后，仍住在务本堂里，他去世后，后人举行升堂点主仪式，并把他的牌位供奉在上厅，将务本堂的香火堂辟为祭祀他的专祠。

清代乾隆二十九年（1764年）凌某在《江西视臬记事》里载，全省有宗祠九千多座。道光江西《宁都直隶州志》记载：州城内外"为祠宇者十之三四，为民居者十之六七"，祠宇竟占建筑总量的三分之一左右。浙江省富阳县龙门镇，有孙氏宗祠五十余座；同省兰溪市诸葛村，有诸葛氏宗祠四十六座。永嘉县枫林镇有三十六座叶氏宗祠，被日本侵略者烧毁了九座，包括建于宋代的叶氏大宗。这许多祠的来历大致和流坑村的相似了。

清代南方地区不但祠堂多，并且大而壮美。如广东顺德县，"俗以祠堂为重，大族祠至二三十区，其宏丽者所费数千金"。（《同治广州府志·卷一》引《顺德志》）"乡中建祠，一木一石，俱极选采，在始建者务求壮丽，以尽孝敬而肃观瞻。"（《佛山忠义乡志·乡俗》）这些祠堂，都已经是规模宏大，装饰华奢，左钟右鼓，戏台翼然，是村子里最重要的建筑了。永嘉县渠口村那座在明代"草创而已"的叶氏大宗祠，"康熙癸亥（1683年）……重建，拓地二十余弓，翼以两廊，奄有两重，规模略备。乾隆壬辰（1772年）……重建头门，前后历三重，宏敞高深，堂堂乎巨构矣！"（《渠川叶氏宗谱》）
sections.content_en:
3. Distribution of Ancestral Halls

However, ancestral halls differ greatly between north and south: prosperous and ornate in the south, but few and crude in the north. This is likely because: (1) the north saw frequent wars through dynasties, with kin scattered or migrated—clan organization less widespread, developed, and complete than the south; blood-kin villages are rare, mostly multi-surname villages; (2) northern rural areas were far less wealthy than the south, with lower cultural levels; (3) continuous ethnic-minority incursions further diluted clan consciousness. Early Qing scholar Gu Yanwu described Shandong: "I have traveled in Shandong for over ten years, seeing great families daily dwindle, hereditary clans daily decline, wealth daily scarce, academic degrees daily fade, while people's hearts daily become shallow and false; servants falsely accuse masters, slaves malign elders—daily heading toward disaster without knowing its end." (《皇朝经世文编》 vol. 58, 《莱州任氏族谱序》) Qianlong 《徐州府志·风俗》 says in the prefecture "few have temples, many do not." About a century later, Guangxu 《太平县志·风俗》 still says: "Ancestral halls exist only in gentry families." Around the same time, Guangxu 《绛州志·风俗》 says: "Sacrificial temple-building is done only by gentry, and even then only shared halls with separate niches." In multi-surname villages like Zhangbi Village, Jiexiu, Shanxi, only the two large Shanxi-merchant families Zhang and Jia have ancestral halls—very small, identical in type to small residences, no "worship hall" or "sleeping chamber," just single rooms, even without genealogy—only a lineage chart painted on white cloth. Jia's hall was built in Daoguang era (1821–1850); Zhang's is undatable, likely mid-Qing. Yu County, Hebei, has over 200 village forts; among dozens surveyed, only Songjiazhuang has a Su clan ancestral hall—just one bay, earthen walls, interior walls covered with lineage charts. More often, an elder of a surname keeps a cloth lineage chart at home. Smaller surnames have no clan activities at all.

In contrast, ancestral halls are common in the south. With fewer wars and long-term stability, the south has many blood-kin villages and strong clan power. Early Qing Kangxi-era Zhao Jishi wrote in 《寄园寄所寄·泛叶寄》: "The various surnames of Xin'an live in clans... thousand-year tombs, not a handful of earth moved; thousand-male clans, never scattered; thousand-year genealogies, not a thread disordered..."

Xin'an is Huizhou in southern Anhui. In Chizhou prefecture's counties: "Crossing every ridge, entering every stream, where ten thousand households live with cocks and dogs hearing each other—all are great clan families. One clan occupies several li or over ten li; even in towns, each occupies a district, no alien surnames mixed. Hence a thousand years still feel like one day's kinship, a hundred generations still like one father's children." (Kangxi 《石埭桂氏宗谱·序》) In Suzhou, Jiangsu: "Brothers dividing property do not move far; ancestral homes and graves remain forever relied upon. Hence in one village, the same surname numbers tens or hundreds of households." (《同治苏州府志》 vol. 3) Where clan bonds are strong, ancestral halls are naturally numerous, large, and imposing. So as early as early Qianlong, Jiangxi Governor Chen Hongmou wrote in 《寄杨朴园书》: "Among provinces, only Fujian, Jiangxi, and Hunan have clans living together, each with a hall—this is ancient custom." Sun Weilong, Qianlong-era magistrate of Yixian, Anhui, wrote a poem 《黟山杂诵》 (see 《黟续志》, Daoguang 22):

"Ancestral halls tower amid mist and clouds,
Pines and cypresses dark, years uncounted,
Most love the local custom still near antiquity,
Su's genealogy, Fan's charitable fields."

From the first line, halls were already substantial. The poem's note says: "All surnames in the county have halls as places for seasonal sacrifice"; the final line's "Fan's fields" refers to charitable fields (义田) to aid poor clansmen with weddings and funerals.

A blood-kin village may have many levels of ancestral halls because clans naturally branch into sub-lineages. In many southern villages, once a lineage within a clan reaches five generations, it may establish its own branch (房派)—though if population and wealth are weak, it may not. Below branches, three generations may establish sub-branches (支派). Both branches and sub-branches may build halls; in Zhejiang these are called "厅" (ting, hall) or "众厅" (public hall), not "祠堂" (ancestral hall). Halls below the branch level are called "私己厅" (private hall). Those under three generations cannot build halls; they may only set up niches in the old ancestral house, called "香火堂" (incense hall). Public and private halls can be quite grand—e.g., in Xinye Village, Jiande, Zhejiang, the Chongren Hall of one Ye branch has four courtyards front to back, its scale matching or slightly exceeding the "outer-residence branch" main hall Youxu Hall. The main hall stores spirit tablets of ancestors above great-great-grandfather for the whole clan; each "hall" has its own set for its branch.

There are other reasons for the abundance of halls in southern blood-kin villages. In Liukeng Village, Le'an, Jiangxi, some people in old age, not wanting descendants to damage the old house through division, designated their own residence or their built academy as an ancestral hall—greatly increasing hall count. Eighty-three survive today, most no larger or more elaborate than ordinary small residences. They are usually named after the original owner's personal style name, e.g., "卓然公祠" (Zhuoran Gong Hall), "蕃昌公祠" (Fanchang Gong Hall).

Some villages build dedicated halls for clansmen of merit. In Yantou Village, Yongjia, Zhejiang, the Jin clan's Guilin Gong (Ming Jiajing era, 1522–1566) built the county's best irrigation system and street network, constructed a batch of large residences, dammed water to create Nanxi River's largest garden, and built an elegant academy. After his death, descendants converted the academy into Guilin Gong Hall. Because the academy's center had two broad pools with a pavilion in the middle, it was also named "水亭祠" (Water Pavilion Hall). Guilin Gong built waterworks in life; in death he abides with water—fitting indeed!

Another example: in late Qing Guangxu Renchen year (1892), Wu Bazhen of Peitian Village, Liancheng, western Fujian, passed the military jinshi exam, appointed Blue-Feather Guard, imperial attendant. In rural areas this was a great clan-glorifying event; Wu's residence Wuben Hall received the "进士第" (Jinshi Residence) plaque. After Wu retired and returned home, he lived in Wuben Hall; after his death, descendants held the "ascending the hall, dotting the spirit tablet" ceremony, enshrined his tablet in the upper hall, and converted Wuben Hall's incense hall into a dedicated hall for him.

In Qing Qianlong 29 (1764), someone named Ling recorded in 《江西视臬记事》 that the province had over 9,000 ancestral halls. Daoguang Jiangxi 《宁都直隶州志》 records: inside and outside the prefectural city, "three to four tenths are halls, six to seven tenths are residences"—halls accounting for roughly one-third of all buildings. Longmen Town, Fuyang, Zhejiang, has over 50 Sun clan halls; Zhuge Village, Lanxi, Zhejiang, has 46 Zhuge clan halls. Fenglin Town, Yongjia, had 36 Ye clan halls; Japanese invaders burned 9, including the Song-dynasty Ye main hall. Many of these halls have origins similar to Liukeng's.

In Qing southern China, halls were not only numerous but large and magnificent. In Shunde, Guangdong: "Custom values ancestral halls; great clans have 20–30 hall districts, the most magnificent costing thousands of taels." (《同治广州府志·vol.1》 quoting 《顺德志》) "In village hall-building, every timber and stone is carefully selected; founders strive for magnificence, to express filial piety and solemnity." (《佛山忠义乡志·乡俗》) These halls are grand in scale, ornate in decoration, with bells on the left and drums on the right, and flanking stages—the most important buildings in the village. The Ye main hall in Qukou Village, Yongjia—"rudimentary" in Ming—was "rebuilt in Kangxi Guihai (1683)... expanded to over 20 bu, with two wings and two layers, scale roughly complete. Rebuilt gatehouse in Qianlong Renchen (1772)... front to back three layers, spacious and deep—a truly grand structure!" (《渠川叶氏宗谱》)

sections.name: 宗祠与村子管理
sections.content_zh:
四、宗祠与礼法

清世祖雍正皇帝在《圣谕广训》里给宗族定的四项任务中第一项就是"立家庙以荐丞尝"，也就是说，要造个宗祠来定期祭祀祖先。祭祀祖先，是团结宗族最重要的活动，也是宗祠最基本的功能，这是早在《礼记》里就写清楚了的：宗族稳定发展了，就能天下太平。

祭祖，向上看就是崇奉祖先，向下看就是确定每一个人在宗法社会里的血缘归属，总起来简单地说，就是"认宗归祖"。生活在同一片土地上，确认共同的血缘，崇奉共同的祖先，这是宗族的根本。

秋尝冬烝，一族的成年男子一起聚在宗祠里，行庄严肃穆的礼拜，赋予他们之间的血缘关系以神圣的意义，使他们牢牢记住，他们之间有义务团结互助，遇到困难，也可以有些依靠。宗祠于是便成了宗族的象征，宗族凝聚力的标志。明代天启年间（1621—1627）岭南凌氏立祠规，第一条就是"保守宗祧"，说"宗祠、祖墓、尝产，为立族根本，"其中以宗祠为首。所以，同族村民，说到相互间的亲密关系，常用的话是"一个祠堂里祭祖"。

祭祖时作为祖先表征的是"神主"，便是写着祖先名讳的木牌。神主陈放在宗祠后进的"寝室"里，它的当心间放开基祖的神主，比较大而且华丽。它两侧是历代"功宗德祖"的神主，受特别的崇敬。当心间里也有只供奉前五代祖先的，其他的神主按照昭穆顺序放在次间及以下。

神主代表祖先，祭祀的时候面对神主，祖先在上，正是宗族对子弟们实施教化的最佳时机。所以宗祠又是一个重要的维护宗法礼制的地方。

明代永嘉知府文林（文征明之父，成化进士）在任上颁布的《族范》规定："凡遇春秋祭祀之时，朔望参谒之日，"全族都要在宗祠里集合聚会，听朗读明太祖朱元璋的《圣训》，即《圣谕六条》。然后，再听朗诵宋人陈古灵的《劝谕文》：

为吾民者，父义，母慈，兄友，弟恭，子孝；夫妇有恩，男女有别，子弟有学，乡闾有礼；贫穷患难亲戚相救，婚姻死丧邻里相助；毋惰农业，毋作盗贼，毋学赌博，毋好争讼，毋以恶凌善，毋以富骄贫；行者逊路，耕者让畔，斑白者不负载于道路，则为礼义之俗矣！

这篇写于宋代的《劝谕文》早于康熙的《上谕十六条》很多，已经把《上谕》中有关"化民成俗"部分的内容几乎全都包括了。

在清代，许多宗族在秋尝冬烝大祭时候，在宗祠里向族人宣读本族的《族规》，而《族规》基本上包容了《劝谕文》的具体化文本。《族规》的主要内容是行为规范，附有奖惩条例，犯了规的，要在宗祠里当众训斥处罚。作为血缘共同体，最重的惩罚是"不立主"，就是死后不得以神牌入祠，又叫"出族"，便是开除出族籍。如浙江省鄞县《新河周氏立主规约》里说："生前既经出族与忤逆不孝者不得立主；出家为僧者不得立主；操业卑鄙，有干功令，不得与试者，不得立主；有娶娼妓为妻者，男女均不得立主；……妇人已经改适而复来者不立主；不守阃范，行为污秽者不立主。"安徽省宣城县四安《孙氏家规》则规定，不孝者、不悌者、为盗贼者、为奴仆者、为优伶者、为皂隶者、奸淫乱伦者、妻女淫乱不制者、盗卖祭产者、盗卖荫树、坟石者，一律者要"出"，就是开除族籍。浙江省浦江县《郑氏义门宗谱》中的《郑氏义门规范》规定，"子孙出仕有以赃墨闻者，生则于谱图上削去其名，死则不许入祠堂。"死后不许入祠堂是神主不入。浙江省武义县俞源村《俞氏宗谱·族规》里也有一条："官吏而犯赃罪不书"。"不书"就是不得写入宗谱，也便是"出族"。可见古人都认为出仕当官的人最犯不得的罪便是贪污。

出族和削名，死后没有神主，且不得入谱，被拒于宗祠之外，成为孤魂野鬼，那是极为可怕的下场。

有少数宗族的族规中甚至有把犯重罪的子弟淹死的惩罚，叫"沉塘"，即在罪犯身上捆缚石磨盘丢进水塘淹死。

由于宗祠对宗法共同体的存在和发展有重要的，近于神圣的意义，所以宗族要求人们对宗祠怀有敬畏之忱。浙江省浦江县《郑氏义门规范》里说："祠堂所以报本，宗子当严洒扫扃钥之事。所有祭器、服，不许他用。……子孙入祠者，当正衣冠，即如祖考在上，不得嬉笑、对语、疾步。"广东省保安县南头村《黄氏族规》则说："祖宗祠宇乃所以妥先灵、行礼祭，宜洁净也。……吾族姓宗人，于堂寝廊庑不许堆积杂什物及系牛马，致坏垣墙、秽处所。夫然后体统尊严而先灵永安矣。"
sections.content_en:
4. Ancestral Halls and Ritual Law

Qing Shizu (Yongzheng Emperor), in 《圣谕广训》 (Expanded Sacred Edicts), set four tasks for clans—the first being "establish family temples for seasonal sacrifice"—meaning build ancestral halls to regularly sacrifice to ancestors. Ancestor sacrifice is the most important clan-unifying activity and the ancestral hall's most basic function, as written early in 《礼记》 (Book of Rites): when clans are stable and developed, the world is at peace.

Ancestor sacrifice, looking upward, means venerating ancestors; looking downward, means determining each person's blood-kin place in patriarchal society—simply put, "recognize the clan, return to the ancestors." Living on the same land, confirming shared blood, venerating shared ancestors—this is the clan's foundation.

At autumn and winter sacrifices, all adult males of a clan gather in the ancestral hall for solemn worship, sanctifying their blood ties, impressing upon them the duty of mutual solidarity and support in hardship. The ancestral hall thus becomes the clan's symbol and cohesion marker. Ming Tianqi era (1621–1627), Ling clan of Lingnan established hall rules—first rule: "preserve the clan's ancestral succession," stating "ancestral hall, ancestral graves, sacrifice fields are the foundation of the clan," with the ancestral hall first. Hence fellow clansmen, describing closeness, often say "we sacrifice in the same ancestral hall."

At sacrifice, the ancestor's representation is the "神主" (spirit tablet)—a wooden plaque inscribed with the ancestor's name. Spirit tablets are placed in the rear "寝室" (sleeping chamber) of the hall; its central bay holds the founding ancestor's tablet, larger and more ornate. On both sides are tablets of successive "meritorious and virtuous ancestors," receiving special veneration. Some central bays enshrine only the preceding five generations; other tablets are placed in side bays and below by zhao-mu (昭穆) order.

Spirit tablets represent ancestors; facing them during sacrifice, with ancestors above, is the optimal moment for clan education of the young. Hence the ancestral hall is also an important place for maintaining patriarchal ritual order.

Ming Yongjia Prefect Wen Lin (father of Wen Zhengming, Chenghua jinshi), in his promulgated 《族范》 (Clan Models), stipulated: "At spring and autumn sacrifices, on the first and fifteenth of each month for visits," the whole clan gathers in the ancestral hall to hear the reading of Ming Taizu Zhu Yuanzhang's 《圣训》 (Sacred Edict), i.e., 《圣谕六条》 (Six Sacred Edicts). Then they hear the recitation of Song scholar Chen Guling's 《劝谕文》 (Admonition):

"As our people: fathers righteous, mothers kind, brothers friendly, younger brothers respectful, sons filial; husbands and wives affectionate, men and women distinct, children educated, villages courteous; in poverty and hardship relatives rescue each other, in marriage and death neighbors help; do not be lazy in farming, do not become bandits, do not gamble, do not love lawsuits, do not bully the good with evil, do not arrogant the poor with wealth; travelers yield the road, farmers yield the field borders, gray-haired do not carry burdens on the road—then it is a ritual and righteous custom!"

This Song-era 《劝谕文》 predates Kangxi's 《上谕十六条》 by much, already encompassing nearly all of the Edicts' "transforming the people and forming custom" content.

In Qing, many clans, at major autumn/winter sacrifices, read the clan's 《族规》 (Clan Rules) in the ancestral hall—rules essentially embodying具体化 of 《劝谕文》. Rules mainly specify behavior norms with reward/punishment clauses; violators are publicly reprimanded and punished in the hall. As a blood-kin community, the heaviest punishment is "不立主" (no spirit tablet established)—the deceased may not enter the hall with a spirit tablet, also called "出族" (expulsion from the clan), i.e., stripping clan membership. For example, Zhejiang Yin County 《新河周氏立主规约》 says: "Those expelled during life and those unfilial and disobedient may not have tablets; those who become monks may not; those in base trades violating law and ineligible for exams may not; those who marry prostitutes—both men and women may not; ... women who remarry and return may not; those violating feminine norms with filthy conduct may not." Anhui Xuancheng County Si'an 《孙氏家规》 stipulates: the unfilial, unbrotherly, thieves, servants, actors, yamen runners, adulterers, those failing to control wives'/daughters' licentiousness, those selling sacrifice property, those selling shade trees or grave stones—all must be "expelled." Zhejiang Pujiang 《郑氏义门宗谱》's 《郑氏义门规范》 stipulates: "Descendants who serve as officials and are known for corruption—while alive, strike their names from the genealogy; after death, forbid entry to the ancestral hall." Forbidding hall entry means no spirit tablet. Zhejiang Wuyi Yuyuan Village 《俞氏宗谱·族规》 also has: "Officials committing corruption are not recorded." "Not recorded" means not entered in genealogy—also "expulsion." This shows ancients believed the worst crime for officials was corruption.

Expulsion and name-striking—no spirit tablet after death, excluded from genealogy, barred from the ancestral hall, becoming a wandering ghost—is a terrifying fate.

A few clans' rules even include drowning punishment for serious offenders, called "沉塘" (sinking in the pond)—tying a stone millstone to the offender and throwing into a pond to drown.

Because the ancestral hall has important, near-sacred significance for the patriarchal community's existence and development, clans demand reverence toward it. Zhejiang Pujiang 《郑氏义门规范》 says: "The ancestral hall exists to repay the root; the clan heir must strictly maintain cleaning and locking. All sacrificial vessels and garments may not be used otherwise. ... Descendants entering the hall must straighten clothes and hats, as if ancestors are present—no laughing, chatting, or hurrying." Guangdong Bao'an Nantou Village 《黄氏族规》 says: "The ancestral hall exists to settle ancestral spirits and perform rituals—it should be clean. ... Our clansmen may not pile杂物 or tie cattle/horses in halls, chambers, or corridors, damaging walls and defiling places. Only then is the system dignified and ancestral spirits at peace.""
