sections.name: 乡土生活与礼法
sections.content_zh:
五、宗祠与村子管理

雍正的《圣谕广训》里继"立家庙以荐丞尝"之后关于宗族事务的三项是"设家塾以保子弟，置族田以赡贫乏，修族谱以联疏远"。其中最基本的一项是"置族田"，即立"尝产"，这是包括立家庙、设家塾、修族谱、赡贫乏在内的宗族活动必需的物质条件，也便是团结整个宗族的经济力量。清人张永铨在《先祠记》里说："祠堂者，敬宗者也；义田者，收族者也。祖宗之神依于主，主则依于祠堂，无祠堂则无以安亡者。子孙之生依于食，食则给于田，无义田则无以保生者。故祠堂与义田并重而不可偏废者也。"（《皇朝经世文编·卷六十六》）义田又称族田，是全族公有的产业，有史料记载的最早的族田是北宋名臣范仲淹在苏州建立的"范氏义庄"。范氏义庄初有腴田千亩，是范仲淹以俸银购买的，用来"赡养宗族，无问亲疏，日有食、岁有衣、婚嫁凶葬咸有赡养。"（民国《吴县志》卷三十四）范仲淹手订《范氏义庄规条》，详细规定了各种情况下的周济标准。这个设族田的办法后来在南方各省一直沿袭下来，成为普遍采用的惯例。如清人魏源所说："廪其谷若干以周族之贫者、老废疾者、幼不能生者、寡不嫁者。粜其余谷，为钱若干缗，以佐族之女长不能嫁者、鳏不能娶者、学无养者、丧不能葬者。"（《庐江章氏义庄记》）宗祠因而有义谷、义仓，历年储备，周济族中的困难户，不得有饿殍。所以宗祠一般都拥有大量公田，或叫族田。族田大致有"祭田"（"烝尝田"，"香火田"，用于祭祀所费），"义田"（"赡养田"，用于备荒、赈贫、优老、恤孤、助婚、赙丧等等），"学田"（"子孙田"、"膏火田"，用于延师、兴学、助考、赏报、立桅等等），"墓田"（用于祖墓护理、祭扫、守墓人生活等等）。此外，旌表（"贞节"、"孝义"、"忠贤"等）、灌溉沟洫、道路、桥梁、凉亭（包括亭内施茶、药、柴、草鞋）、长明灯、舟渡、各种"会"（龙灯会、龙船会、丝竹会、唱戏的万年会、习武的关公会和读书人的文会等），都各有专置的田亩以出产充作建造和维护等等之用。总之，族田收入的施用涵盖了《上谕十六条》中所要求于家族的福利和公益事业的各个方面。

族田作为宗族的公共财产，它的各项用途，归根到底，都是为了团结宗族和发展宗族。范仲淹写道："吴中宗族甚众，于吾固有亲疏，然以吾祖宗视之，则均是子孙，固无亲疏也。苟祖宗之意无亲疏，则饥寒者吾安得不恤也。自祖宗来积德百余年，而始发于吾，得至大官，若享富贵而不恤宗族，异日何以见祖宗于地下，今何颜面入家庙乎？"（见民国《吴县志》卷三十四）安徽绩溪《华阳邵氏族谱·家规》中的"恤族"条说："族由一本而分，彼贫即吾贫，苟托祖宗之荫而富贵，正宜推祖宗之心以覆庇之，使无所失，此仁人君子之用心也。若自矜富贵，坐视族人贫困，听其寮妻质子而为人仆妾以耻先人，是奚取贫贱羞哉，即富贵亦与有责也。"

族田的来源主要靠捐献，其次是孤寡老人以捐田归公换取晚年的抚养、身后丧葬和神主入祠，以及族人若犯法则其财产籍没归公等等。如江西省乐安县流坑村，万历年间（1573—1620）修的《董氏宗谱》里有规定，凡捐田助建宗祠的，神位可列入为"功宗德祖"专设的彰义堂，于是就有人为了这项永久的荣誉而捐田。初立祠堂的时候，也有向族人分派各出其所有农田的若干分之一为族田的。有些宗族则规定兄弟析产的时候，族中要抽取一部分为族田。无后的绝户人家，所遗下的田也都籍没归族中公有，回报是给他立主享受血食。

族田的耕种也有定规，但各地不一。苏州范氏义庄的族田不许本族子弟耕种。浙江省武义县俞源村则规定由族中缺田的贫穷农户轮流佃种，各户不得连续种三年以上。因为族田租谷比较低，有缓纾贫困户的意思，所以要照顾较多的人受惠。

族田严禁出卖，出卖族田是大罪。道光年间（1821—1850）的江苏省丹徒县《京江柳氏宗谱》卷一里《宗祠条例》说：

建立宗祠、置买田产及义举（指捐献），一经入祠，即系祠中公物，本支毋视同己产，族人亦毋垂涎。倘或私典盗卖，全族当祖宗神位前责以不孝之罪，仍协力鸣官，追还祠内。

族田的设置，随宗祠的大量兴建而骤增，20世纪50年代初，浙江省江山县城关有262座祠堂，拥有田产占农田总面积33.23%。淤头村祠田占农田总数58.52%。江西省遂川县祠田占农田总数40%以上，其中城厢一些乡里祠田占85%。族田越多，宗祠倡学、扶贫、抚孤、恤寡、抗灾的力量就越大，宗族关系就越稳定，公益性事业也就越发达。

宗族掌握了如此雄厚的公有经济实力，有清一代，中国各地农村的建设规模十分可观，成绩也可称斐然。宗族要主持村落的规划和建设，在南方，有些村落顺应地势，修水渠把溪水引进村，把雨水、废水排出村，再循渠铺街巷，并把村子切割成房基地，这是村落规划建宅的基本。许多地区，村落的各种公共工程，如灌渠、池塘、堤堰、牌坊、村墙、村门、道路、凉亭、桥梁、津渡、长明灯、水碓、风水林、公墓、文昌阁、文峰塔、庵堂、水口建筑群等等，都兴建得很完善，也管理得井然有序。大小宗祠当然就更加辉煌壮观了。佛寺道观和一些杂庙虽然另有自己的田产和香火钱以供所需，但有时亦可以从宗族得到些捐献。

为了储存族田大量的收入，宗祠常附建粮仓，也有择地另建的。这里存的是宗族在遇灾害时的救命粮，通称"平安粮"或"万年粮"，产于公有的族产田。

宗族甚至规划、控制村落规模，当村子人口超过原初规划的土地容量时，会经过公议迁出一个或几个支派，另择一地建设新村。新村另建大宗祠，另立宗谱。

有些宗祠还自行立法，执行审判和刑罚，直至判定和执行死刑。

宗族往往建设学堂（义塾），和雍正皇帝《圣谕广训》中的"设家塾以保子弟"相应。在农耕时代，虽然说"农为本业"，但农民的地位却在社会的最底层，生活最艰苦。隋唐以后，朝廷有了科举制度，"开科取仕"，大多数官吏都要从考试出身，而参加考试，一般并不看家庭出身，除了少数犯法、不端的人以外，平民百姓都可以走读书干禄的路。到了明代，制度更进一步，几乎不经考试便不得担任官吏，而在考试面前又是人人平等的。于是，"朝为田舍郎，暮登天子堂"就成了农村有志青年可能实现的梦想。对宗族制度的健全、宗祠和义田的建设大有贡献的宋代名臣范仲淹便出身于贫苦的农家。

一个家族，如果有一二子弟登第，除了所谓"光宗耀祖"之外，会对整个家族有很大的实际好处。浙江省平阳县顺溪村乾隆《宜都陈氏家乘》，有写于南宋淳佑十年（1250年）的旧序，开篇就说："温之昆阳，大族为多，而门第之赫奕、子姓之繁昌，则未有加于陈氏者也。盖门第之赫奕，实由于子姓之登科者多。藉使徒繁昌而无贤哲之士，其欲门第之赫奕者，宁可得乎？陈氏自李唐迁居昆阳，其子姓登文科、武科、特科及补入太学，请漕试与夫勉解、进纳、边赏、荫叙者不啻百有余人，此门第所以赫奕而非他族所能加也。"这篇序把陈氏门第的赫奕说成是子姓登科者多的结果，应是合乎实际的。

光绪十六年（1890年）安徽省寿州《龙氏族谱·家规》有《家训劝善十二条》，其中之一是"务读书"，说的是："凡我族人，期于克振家声，宜从诗书上苦心着力。天下惟读书人不可限量，云梯千里，凤翮九霄，上为祖先增光，下为子孙创业，岂独一身荣显而已哉！切莫浮慕无实，图侥幸以获功名，庶为有志之士。"

因此，许多族谱中都规定，子弟读书有膏火费赞助。首先是舍得花大钱聘名师，待之以礼；其次是按学业等级给子弟以生活津贴；最后是参与科考由族中出旅资等各种费用；考取各级功名按等级发奖金；中榜时招待"三报"报子等人的钱由公中支付。举人和进士及第后要在家门前和宗祠门前立桅。明代，中了进士可以造功名牌坊。立桅和建造牌坊都由宗祠出钱。

科举中榜，要到宗祠拜告祖先，往墙上贴捷报。当了官，回家的时候也要先拜祖先。江西省婺源县理村，余氏宗族出过不少大官，其中有两位尚书。余氏宗祠规模很大，特地造在村口高地上，官儿们衣锦还乡的时候，轿子进了水口就先上坡去宗祠祭拜，一路有很多段台阶，轿夫根据各段台阶级数编了些吉祥词，如"连升三级"、"四进士"、"十三太保"等等，由前面的轿夫吆喝出来，通报给后面的轿夫，以便前后步子协调。从宗祠出来，一路下坡进村，居高临下，很有气势。是官的气势，也是宗族的气势。

科举是朝廷的取仕制度，但这个制度的完成并充分发挥作用，则有赖于宗族的支持。是宗族补足了科举制度的下半部。所以，科举成就比较高的地区，都是宗族制度强而有力的地区。

雍正《圣谕广训》里有一句是"修族谱以联疏远"，大宗祠里一般都设谱房。谱房是保存宗族成员档案的地方，成员的生卒、婚姻、奖惩、科举、仕途等等，都有记录在案。

在宗法社会中，谱谍的最原始意义就是一个宗族的花名册，它的重要性在于确认一个始祖之下的宗族的存在。所以大多数宗谱总要在谱序里写上一句："家之有谱，犹国之有史也。"《虬川黄氏重修家谱序》说："孝莫大于尊祖，尊祖莫先于合族。合族之道必修谱以联之。"朱熹在他所撰写的《新安朱氏族谱》里规定"三世不修谱，当以不孝论。"在实际生活中，宗谱的作用之一是赋予每个人以宗族归属感，入了谱，他就是宗族的成员，有依有靠，生前死后都不是孤身面对生活，而能享受宗族的所有亲情和公益。宗谱确认一个成员在谱系中的位置，他的房派、行辈、婚姻关系等等。行辈关乎他的身份和影响力。大多数族谱的"族规"里都有"敬重尊长"的条文，长辈在宗族事务中有较强的发言权，有的可以任族中各种职务，或主持族中的讼争、惩罚等等。行辈的另一个意义在于防止婚姻上的伦常失误，如同族的两个平辈的人不能和外族的两个不平辈的人结婚，以免叔叔成了连襟，表姐成了婶子。确定房派归属也有实际意义，一是不要进错祠堂误拜了祖宗；二是有些地方，如果一家人穷困了要出卖房基地，必须卖给本房的人，为了"败家不败族"，也为了避免房派的居住情况杂乱。宗族的人口很多的时候，房派的重要性就会大大增强，房派的归属就更加重要。

族谱里大多有家法族规，这是一个宗族共同的《基本法》。族规不但写明了个人的行为规范和相应的奖惩，也写明了族中养老扶幼、济贫救困等等公益。宗祠和祖坟的位置、型制和相关的规定也都见载于族谱。有些族谱里还记载着族中公产的数量、位置与管理方式。此外通常有一些有懿行崇德的祖先的小传，供后人作为榜样。
sections.content_en:
5. Ancestral Halls and Village Governance

Yongzheng's 《圣谕广训》 (Expanded Sacred Edicts), after "establish family temples for seasonal sacrifice," lists three clan affairs: "establish family schools to protect children, set aside clan fields to support the poor, repair genealogy to connect distant kin." The most fundamental is "set aside clan fields" (置族田)—establishing "sacrifice property" (尝产), the material prerequisite for all clan activities including temple-building, schooling, genealogy, and poor relief—i.e., the economic power to unite the whole clan. Qing scholar Zhang Yongquan wrote in 《先祠记》: "The ancestral hall honors ancestors; charitable fields (义田) unite the clan. Ancestral spirits depend on tablets, tablets depend on the hall—without a hall, the dead cannot rest. Descendants' lives depend on food, food depends on fields—without charitable fields, the living cannot be preserved. Hence hall and charitable fields are equally important, neither can be neglected." (《皇朝经世文编·vol.66》) Charitable fields, also called clan fields (族田), are clan-owned property. The earliest recorded clan fields are the "Fan Clan Charitable Estate" (范氏义庄) established by Northern Song statesman Fan Zhongyan in Suzhou. Initially with a thousand mu of fertile land, purchased with Fan's salary, to "support the clan regardless of kinship distance—daily food, yearly clothing, weddings and funerals all provided." (Republican 《吴县志》 vol.34) Fan personally drafted 《范氏义庄规条》, detailing relief standards for various situations. This clan-field method was inherited in southern provinces, becoming universal practice. As Qing scholar Wei Yuan said: "Store grain to aid the clan's poor, aged, disabled, young unable to work, and widows not remarried. Sell surplus grain for cash to aid clan daughters unable to marry, widowers unable to remarry, students without support, and families unable to bury their dead." (《庐江章氏义庄记》) Ancestral halls thus had charitable grain and granaries, stored year after year, to aid distressed clansmen—no one should starve. Hence halls generally owned large amounts of public land, or clan fields. Types include: "sacrifice fields" (祭田/烝尝田/香火田, for sacrifice expenses); "charitable fields" (义田/赡养田, for famine relief, poor aid, elder care, orphan support, marriage assistance, funeral aid); "school fields" (学田/子孙田/膏火田, for hiring teachers, founding schools, exam aid, rewards, flag-erection); "grave fields" (墓田, for tomb maintenance, sweeping, grave-keeper livelihood). Additionally, commendations (chastity, filial piety, loyalty), irrigation ditches, roads, bridges, pavilions (including tea/medicine/firewood/straw-shoe distribution), eternal lamps, ferries, and various "associations" (dragon-lantern, dragon-boat, silk-and-bamboo, opera, martial-arts, literary) all had dedicated fields for construction and maintenance. In short, clan-field income covered all welfare and public-good aspects required by the Sixteen Imperial Edicts.

As clan public property, clan fields' uses ultimately serve clan unity and development. Fan Zhongyan wrote: "There are many clans in Wu; to me they have kinship distance, but from my ancestors' view they are all descendants—no distance. If ancestors see no distance, how can I not care for the hungry and cold? For over a hundred years ancestors accumulated virtue, which began with me reaching high office. If I enjoy wealth without caring for the clan, how can I face ancestors in the afterlife, or enter the family temple with face?" (Republican 《吴县志》 vol.34) Anhui Jixi 《华阳邵氏族谱·家规》's "aid the clan" clause says: "The clan branches from one root—their poverty is my poverty. If blessed by ancestors with wealth, one should extend ancestors' heart to shelter them, letting none be lost—this is the humane gentleman's intent. To boast of wealth while watching clan poverty, letting wives and children be sold as servants, shaming ancestors—this is worse than poverty shame; wealth shares the blame."

Clan fields mainly come from donations; second, elderly childless people donate fields to the clan in exchange for old-age care, funeral, and spirit-tablet enshrinement; third, clansmen's property is confiscated if they violate rules. In Liukeng Village, Le'an, Jiangxi, Wanli-era (1573–1620) 《董氏宗谱》 stipulated: those donating fields to help build the hall may have their spirit tablets placed in the Hall of Manifesting Righteousness (彰义堂) dedicated to "meritorious and virtuous ancestors"—so some donated for this permanent honor. When first establishing a hall, clansmen sometimes each contributed a fraction of their farmland as clan fields. Some clans stipulated that when brothers divide property, a portion is extracted as clan fields. Childless households' land is also confiscated as clan public property, in return for establishing their spirit tablet and receiving sacrifices.

Clan-field cultivation has rules varying by region. Suzhou Fan Clan Charitable Estate forbade clan descendants from farming clan fields. Wuyi Yuyuan Village, Zhejiang, stipulated rotation among land-poor peasant households, no household farming continuously over three years. Because clan-field rent is low—intended to relieve poverty—more households should benefit.

Selling clan fields is strictly forbidden—a major crime. Daoguang-era (1821–1850) Jiangsu Dantu 《京江柳氏宗谱》 vol.1 《宗祠条例》 says:

"Once ancestral hall, purchased fields, and charitable donations enter the hall, they are hall public property. Branches may not treat as own property; clansmen may not covet. If privately mortgaged or stolen and sold, the whole clan shall, before ancestral spirit tablets, condemn as unfilial, and jointly report to officials to recover for the hall."

Clan fields surged with hall construction. In early 1950s, Jiangshan County town, Zhejiang, had 262 halls owning 33.23% of total farmland. Yutou Village's hall fields were 58.52% of farmland. Suichuan County, Jiangxi, hall fields exceeded 40% of farmland, some townships reaching 85%. More clan fields mean greater hall power for schooling, poverty relief, orphan care, widow support, and disaster relief—more stable clan relations, more developed public welfare.

With such strong public economic power, Qing-dynasty rural construction across China was substantial and impressive. Clans directed village planning and construction. In the south, some villages followed terrain, building canals to bring stream water in, drain rain/wastewater out, pave streets along canals, and divide the village into house plots—the basis of village planning. In many regions, public works—irrigation canals, ponds, dikes, memorial arches, village walls, gates, roads, pavilions, bridges, ferries, eternal lamps, water-powered trip hammers, feng shui forests, cemeteries, Wenyang Pavilions, Wenfeng Pagodas, temples, water-mouth building complexes—were well built and managed. Halls of all sizes became even more magnificent. Buddhist/Daoist temples and miscellaneous shrines, though with their own fields and incense money, sometimes received clan donations.

To store large clan-field income, halls often attached granaries, or built them separately. These stored disaster-relief grain, called "peace grain" (平安粮) or "ten-thousand-year grain" (万年粮), produced from public clan fields.

Clans even planned and controlled village scale: when population exceeded planned land capacity, after public discussion one or more branches would move out to build a new village elsewhere—with its own main hall and genealogy.

Some halls enacted their own laws, conducted trials and punishments, even sentencing and executing death.

Clans often built schools (义塾, charitable schools), corresponding to Yongzheng's "establish family schools to protect children." In the agrarian era, though "farming is the base occupation," peasants were at society's bottom, living hardest. After Sui-Tang, the imperial examination system selected officials—most officials came from exams, and exam participation generally ignored family background (except criminals and the immoral); commoners could pursue study for office. By Ming, almost no one could hold office without exams, and exams were equal for all. Thus "morning a farm boy, evening a court official" became an achievable dream for ambitious rural youth. Fan Zhongyan, the Song statesman who greatly contributed to clan system, hall, and charitable-field development, was himself born to a poor farming family.

A clan with one or two successful exam candidates (登第) gains, beyond "glorifying ancestors," great practical benefits. In Shunxi Village, Pingyang, Zhejiang, Qianlong-era 《宜都陈氏家乘》 contains an old preface written in Southern Song Chunyou 10 (1250), opening: "In Kunyang of Wenzhou, there are many great clans, but none surpass the Chen in illustrious status and prosperous descendants. Illustrious status truly results from many exam-passing descendants. If merely prosperous without wise men, how could status be illustrious? Since the Chen moved to Kunyang in Tang, their descendants have passed civil, military, special exams, entered the Imperial Academy, taken provincial exams, and received office through recommendation, border merit, or hereditary privilege—over a hundred people. This is why the Chen's status is unsurpassed." This preface attributes Chen clan status to many exam-passing descendants—realistic.

Guangxu 16 (1890) Anhui Shouzhou 《龙氏族谱·家规》 has 《家训劝善十二条》, one being "must study": "All our clansmen, aiming to revive family reputation, should devote heart to books. Only scholars have unlimited potential—climbing a thousand-li ladder, soaring to the nine heavens—above bringing glory to ancestors, below establishing enterprise for descendants, not merely personal honor! Do not crave empty fame or seek success by luck; be a person of ambition."

Hence many genealogies stipulate study subsidies (膏火费) for children. First, generously hire famous teachers with courtesy; second, provide living stipends by academic level; third, cover exam travel and expenses; fourth, award bonuses by exam rank; fifth, pay for "three reports" messengers upon success. Juren and jinshi graduates erect flagpoles (立桅) before home and ancestral hall. In Ming, jinshi graduates could build merit memorial arches (功名牌坊). Both flagpoles and arches were paid by the ancestral hall.

Upon exam success, one visits the ancestral hall to report to ancestors, posting success notices on walls. When officials return home, they first worship ancestors. In Licun Village, Wuyuan, Jiangxi, the Yu clan produced many high officials, including two Ministers. The Yu ancestral hall is large, specially built on high ground at the village entrance. When officials return in glory, their sedan chairs, upon entering the water mouth, first climb to the hall for worship. The path has many stair sections; bearers composed auspicious phrases based on step counts—"promoted three ranks consecutively," "four jinshi," "thirteen grand guardians"—called out by the front bearer to coordinate with the rear. Descending from the hall into the village, looking down from on high, is imposing—both the official's and the clan's imposing presence.

The examination system was the state's official-selection system, but its completion and full effectiveness relied on clan support. Clans supplied the system's "lower half." Hence regions with high exam success are regions with strong, powerful clan systems.

Yongzheng's 《圣谕广训》 includes "repair genealogy to connect distant kin." Large ancestral halls generally have a genealogy room (谱房), storing clan member records—births, deaths, marriages, rewards, punishments, exams, official careers.

In patriarchal society, genealogy's most primitive meaning is a clan roster; its importance lies in confirming the clan's existence under one founding ancestor. Hence most genealogies begin with: "A clan's genealogy is like a state's history." 《虬川黄氏重修家谱序》 says: "No filial piety exceeds honoring ancestors; honoring ancestors begins with uniting the clan. To unite the clan, one must repair genealogy to connect it." Zhu Xi, in his 《新安朱氏族谱》, stipulated: "Three generations without genealogy repair counts as unfilial." In practice, genealogy gives each person clan belonging—entered in the genealogy, one is a clan member, supported, not alone in life or death, enjoying all clan affection and welfare. Genealogy confirms one's position: branch, generation, marriage relations. Generation rank affects status and influence. Most genealogies' "clan rules" include "respect elders"—elders have stronger say in clan affairs, may hold offices, preside over disputes and punishments. Generation rank also prevents marital ethical errors—e.g., two same-generation clan members cannot marry two different-generation outsiders, avoiding uncles becoming brothers-in-law or cousins becoming aunt-in-laws. Branch affiliation has practical meaning: (1) not entering the wrong hall and worshipping wrong ancestors; (2) in some places, if a poor family sells house land, it must sell to own-branch members—"family may fail but clan must not"—and to avoid chaotic branch residence. When clan population is large, branch importance grows significantly.

Genealogies mostly contain clan laws and rules—a clan's shared "Basic Law." Rules specify personal behavior norms with rewards/punishments, and clan welfare: elder care, child support, poor relief. Ancestral hall and grave locations, types, and regulations are recorded. Some genealogies record public property quantity, location, and management. Additionally, they usually include short biographies of virtuous ancestors as models for descendants.

sections.name: 宗祠与村落
sections.content_zh:
六、乡土生活与礼法

早先康熙的《圣谕十六条》，赋予宗族的责任远远多于后来雍正的《圣谕广训》，实际上，南方血缘村落里的宗族按《圣谕十六条》的要求起的是社会基层政权的作用，当时政府机构只到县级，村子则由宗族自治。乾隆七年（1742年），张海珊在《小安乐窝·聚民论》中说："凡族必有长，而又择其齿、德之优者为之副。凡劝导风化以及户、婚、田土、争竞之事，其长与副先听之，而事之大者方诉之官。国家赋税力役之征，亦先下族长。族必有田以赡孤寡，有塾以训子弟，……惟族长之意经营。"

宗族要履行基层政府行政职能，首先是催交国课钱粮，其次负责保安、消防，夜间组织更夫巡逻、抓捕盗贼。特殊时期，更能组织称为"乡勇"、"团练"、"义兵"等的武装力量。

宗族甚至还有司法权力。南方许多村子的族规里规定，凡发生纠纷、诉讼、治安等事件，先由宗族审理，案情较大，不好办的，再移送官府衙门。湖南《洞庭严氏族谱·族规》中说："各支如有田土、钱债细故争执，不得遽行兴讼，先宜禀达族长、支长，相约谒祠理讲，毋得偏袒。如理不服，始可到官告理。"浙江省兰溪市诸葛村《高隆诸葛氏宗谱·卷之首》有《家规》，其中一条为："凡祖遗房屋、坟茔、山塘、田地等业，势豪不得侵损，其可租赁者，必须禀明族长，立礼交租，倘有恃玩者以灭祖论。"

有些家族自定的权力更大，直到可以执私刑杀人。如湖南省常德县《映雪堂孙氏家法补略》中写道："孝弟为人之本。近见我族子弟气习渐坏，竟致忤逆父母，凌辱尊长。其房长如见此等事，不待父母尊长之投诉，便自行鸣集族总、各房长等，着真处治。轻则杖责，重则捆送，太甚则驱逐去族，极甚则筑（按：即活埋）、溺（按：即沉潭）两便。……族中子弟倘有游手好闲，不务正业，流入贼匪，其房长务预为惩责，或于族内一经捉获，与外姓捆拿交族，其房长鸣集族总、各房长等，公同议处，迫令其父兄伯叔至亲人等举手，筑、溺两便。"浙江省永嘉县枫林村《徐氏宗谱·族范八条》里规定："孽深害大，素性又终不肯改移"的盗窃犯"令其全身自毙"，好像比"筑、溺"稍稍宽容一些。

最令人痛快的，是有些宗谱规定，为官而贪，可以从谱中除名甚至也"令其全身自毙"，和盗窃犯一样。

凡这类惩罚直至死刑的严酷的事，要在祠堂里祖宗牌位前进行。祠堂平日双门紧闭，这种时刻则大门洞开，以便公众知晓，可以起震慑作用。村人们凡见村里发生了"作奸犯科"的大事，就纷纷传说"要开祠堂门"了。

有些村里，宗族建"旌善亭"和"申明亭"各一座，分别用于榜示"好人好事"和"坏人坏事"。多数村子只建"申明亭"，兼有旌善的用处。

人生礼俗有不少要在宗祠里举行，但多少因各地风俗而异。结婚是大事。《礼记·婚义》说"上流社会"的婚礼："婚礼者，将合二姓之好，上以事宗庙，而下以继后世也，故君子重之。是以婚礼纳彩、问名、纳吉、纳征、请期，皆主人筵几于庙，而拜迎于门外。入，揖让而升，听命于庙，所以敬慎重、正婚礼也。"新妇来的时候，也是"主人筵几于庙而拜于门外"。更有意思的是新妇在"著代"之礼后执掌了家务，但要在祖庙里受一次训，"古者妇人先嫁三月，祖庙未毁，教于公宫；祖庙既毁，教于宗室。教以妇德、妇言、妇容、妇功。教成祭之，牲用鱼，笔之以苹藻，所以成妇顺也。"这场婚礼，从头到尾有很多仪节是在祖庙里进行的，可见古时"上流社会"的祖庙在婚礼过程中起着重要的作用，它代表一个宗族接纳新妇。不过，这种作用后来在平民百姓中并没有一定的表现。有些地方的风俗，新妇进村必须先到宗祠行礼祭拜"报到"，如《东粤宝安南头黄氏族规》有一条："凡子姓婚娶者，于新迎吉夕，必先虔谒祖祠，然后归家堂拜。盖夫妇家室，人伦造端，礼莫大焉。到祠拜谒者，与花红钱二百文。"有些地方新妇于成婚次日到宗祠祭拜，也有些地方新妇根本不进宗祠拜祖宗。

丧礼一般不在宗祠举行而在住宅堂屋里做道场，但可以在祠堂里暂厝棺木。有些地方的风俗，暂厝的位置有区别，死者享年五十以上的，棺木可放在第二进院子的廊庑里，六十以上的，可放在第三进房子"寝室"的前檐下，七十以上可以进"寝室"，靠山墙。

有些地方，主要是闽、粤，生了男儿的人家，当年年末为父母者要到宗祠明间前金檩之下专设的"灯梁"上挂一盏灯笼，叫"添灯"，谐音"添丁"，向祖先报喜。孩子长到三岁，过了少儿高死亡率阶段，到祠堂里请族长在脖颈上套一个红丝线圈，拴住小命，十七岁时再到祠里请族长把线圈除去，这就算"成丁"了，可以写进族谱了，可以参加大宗祠的春秋祭祀了。

宗族重视聚落自然资源和环境的保护。祖山、朝山的树木都不许滥伐，而案山和坟山则连砍碎柴都不允许，违犯的要受到很严厉的处罚，直到"逐出祠堂"，也就是从宗谱上除名，"开除族籍"。所以在过去宗法农耕时代，农村周围大多树木蓊郁。不过，那时并不全而深地懂生态的道理，只是借树木的郁勃来象征宗族的生命力罢了。祖宗坟山上的树叫"荫树"，是祖荫的象征。浙江省余姚县万历《江南徐氏宗范》规定："祖宗坟墓栽树木所以妥安灵爽者，子孙如私自斫砍，致伤庇荫者，族长告官治之。"江西省婺源县洪村，浙江省景宁县大埔村，都有族规禁止在村前流过的溪里捕鱼。溪里的锦鲤成群地游着，确实给村子增添了不少生气。到二十世纪初，有些受过现代教育的知识分子对保护环境更有了些认识，如福建省连城县培田村的早期留法学生，回来后在《吴氏族谱·物产说》里写道，村子周围的山"于原有树者，设法严禁，于未有树者，竭力栽种，庶物产滋丰，财源不竭。"甚至规定，"学堂以种树为第一要义"。宗族对保护村落的生态是有贡献的。

宗族连村子的公共卫生都要管。如原徽州有些村子每逢初一、十五，家家户户要出人打扫各户分片负责的街巷。平日猪牛羊不得进村，以免污秽。要维护水渠洁净，鹅鸭不得近水渠，规定汲取净水和排出污水的时间，冬季组织人力挖塘泥，等等。

浙江省江山市清漾村的初修于乾隆，续补于同治的《清漾毛氏族谱·外集》有一篇《凝湖举人毛白圭先生志》，记载了毛白圭治理清漾的实绩。作者是乾隆癸卯（1783年）科钦赐举人，江山县学训导蔡英。文里说，毛白圭立则："族人年六十以上者祠中按月给米、肉，岁给棉衣一件。七十、八十、九十者递加倍给，衣亦自布至绸缎。生员乡试者每人给银五两。建文昌阁，合族生童课文于中，一月三会。设义塾教族子弟之贫乏者。每遇青黄不接，即以祠谷减价平粜。凡异姓商贾于其市者，族人或凌侮之，鸣于其祠，必严加惩罚。异姓于其地开铺肆者，每春正，祠内设席延请，申约不许有牌色戏博，犯者即行驱逐。邻村有贫家被灾者，必于祠中给赀救恤，丰俭厚薄俱有一定等次章程。祠产旧不甚丰，自德成综理，日加饶裕，得充诸项之用。"这文里写的是一个偏僻的山乡小村在乾隆年间（1736—1795）的大致情况。值得注意的是当时的宗族管理者毛白圭已经懂得保护"商贾"，也就是保护市场经济。《毛氏族谱》里又列"约戒"二十四条，其中有"毋违理取利"、"毋用银低假"、"毋收买不明"和"毋挖骗客货"四条，也都是针对市场上可能有的不良活动的。江山市位于钱塘江上游，是从杭州到福建泉州去的必经之地，南宋以来交通频繁，以致宗谱的约戒都受到影响。

现实的生活赋予宗祠浓郁的人文气息，宗祠对村人们显得亲切起来了。宗祠下设几个"会"，分别主管各种时节、各种场合的文化娱乐。甚至，早从宋代起，村人们普遍把全村最重要的娱乐设施，戏台，造在了宗祠大门门屋里，演戏的时候把院落、廊庑和拜殿（享堂）都当作了临时的观众席。不过，演出的环境和内容是有限制的。例如光绪二十七年（1901年）湖南常德《映雪堂孙氏家法补略》里写道："赌局、烟馆，坏俗之原；花鼓、灯戏，诲淫之具，……此系大奸大恶，伤风败俗之尤，诫之诫之。"这样的戒律虽有，但毕竟难以全面压制娱乐的愿望。

村人们每逢节日、喜庆，都希望热热闹闹看几场戏，但地方官多腐儒，认为演戏不免诲淫诲盗，看戏不免男女混杂，所以屡屡禁止。于是，村民们就把戏台造在宗祠或庙宇的大门门屋里，面对拜殿，辩解说，戏是演来敬祖酬神的，内容自然禁得起祖先或神明的审查，以此来争取解禁。

浙江省永嘉县渠口村《重修渠川叶氏大宗祠碑记》说：康熙年间（1662—1722）建造的大宗祠，到光绪甲辰（1904年）"旧建舞台倾圮，乃舍旧维新。越明年，乙巳（1905年）谋于众曰：台之所作，勿以戏观。族人致祭，岁时伏腊，团结一堂。演剧开场，以古为鉴，伸忠孝节义之心，枨触而油然以生。"冠冕堂皇，话说得很漂亮。只说漂亮话还不行，还要有严格的管束。湖南省会同县高椅村民国《杨氏族谱·祠堂记》严厉规定："家祠演戏敬祖，看戏男女须分，不得夹杂，小儿不许上台，并外姓痞棍亦不许上台。"

不过，平头百姓从另一面戳穿了这种道学酸腐气。浙江省兰溪市诸葛村，每年四月十四在大公堂春祭先祖诸葛亮，必定要演戏。演出时，全村男女都挤去看，年轻后生有一句俏皮话："要看大姑娘，四月十四大公堂。"族里规定，男子在院子里看戏，妇女在拜殿里看戏，殿前还搁一道木栏杆，专有几位六十岁以上的老人，提着长杆烟袋在栏杆前站岗巡逻，见到哪个儇薄后生仔回头向拜殿张望，就举起烟袋凿他的脑壳。这些趣事更渲染了祠堂的人文性。

有些村把戏台造在宗祠或庙宇前广场的对面，面对宗祠或庙宇，如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的塔湖庙。演戏的时候，妇女不能进入看场，而要在左右的湖水外侧站立着看，以免男女混杂。

总之，在一个血缘村落里，宗祠是全面的管理者，它和村子文化生活、经济生活、社会生活、政治生活的一切方面都有直接的或间接的联系，它们身上沉积着农耕文明时代的一整部乡土文化史，作用远远大于一个基层的政权机构。

宗族的管理多少有一点民主程序。族长不一定由"大宗子"担任，而由辈分高、年岁大、德高望重的人担任。但负实际管理之责的各种职务，则在一定范围里推举合适的人担任。浙江省建德市新叶村，管事的人组成一个类似委员会的机构，都以"九思公"为名。因为传说南宋理学家陆九渊的弟弟陆九思为人正直，又长于管理，对陆氏宗族的发展曾有很大的贡献，所以，这个管理全村事务的掌权集体就叫"九思公"。有些关系到全村全族利益的大事，比如要兴建大工程了，和邻村发生重要纠纷了，准备制定大家必须遵守的新规矩了等等，都要在祠堂里开全族大会，各户的家长，也就是有发言权和表决权的，都要参加。"凡有族中公务，族长传集子姓于家庙，务期公正和平，商酌妥协。"（《云阳涂氏族谱·祠堂碑记》）要修宗谱了，得在宗祠里立谱房，选合适的人参加，宗谱修成以后要分颁给各房派了，也得在祠堂里举行庄重的仪式。

6. Rural Life and Ritual Law

Kangxi's earlier 《圣谕十六条》 (Sixteen Imperial Edicts) assigned clans far more responsibility than Yongzheng's later 《圣谕广训》. In practice, clans in southern blood-kin villages, per the Sixteen Edicts, functioned as grassroots government—at the time, state administration reached only the county level; villages were self-governed by clans. In Qianlong 7 (1742), Zhang Haishan wrote in 《小安乐窝·聚民论》: "Every clan has a head, with deputies chosen for age and virtue. For moral guidance, household, marriage, land, and dispute matters, the head and deputies first hear them; only major matters go to officials. State tax and corvée collection also first goes to the clan head. Every clan must have fields to support orphans and widows, schools to train children... managed per the clan head's intent."

Clans fulfilling grassroots government functions: first, collecting state taxes and grain; second, security and fire prevention—organizing night watchmen to patrol and catch thieves. In special periods, they could organize armed forces called "乡勇" (village braves), "团练" (militia), "义兵" (righteous soldiers).

Clans even had judicial power. Many southern villages' rules stipulated: disputes, lawsuits, security incidents first tried by the clan; major, unmanageable cases then sent to official yamen. Hunan 《洞庭严氏族谱·族规》 says: "If branches have minor land or debt disputes, they may not immediately sue; first report to clan and branch heads, meet at the hall to reason, no favoritism. If unresolved, then may go to official court." Zhejiang Lanxi Zhuge Village 《高隆诸葛氏宗谱·卷之首》 《家规》 stipulates: "Ancestral houses, graves, ponds, fields may not be encroached by the powerful; leasable property must be reported to clan head, with formal rent payment; violators treated as 'destroying ancestors.'"

Some clans claimed even greater power—up to private execution. Hunan Changde 《映雪堂孙氏家法补略》 writes: "Filial piety and brotherhood are the root of humanity. Recently our clan's children have grown bad, even disobeying parents and insulting elders. If a branch head sees such acts, without waiting for parental complaint, he convenes the clan chief and branch heads for genuine punishment. Light: beating; heavy: binding and sending away; severe: expulsion from clan; extreme: either burying alive (筑) or drowning (沉潭). ... If clan children are idle, neglect proper work, become bandits—branch heads must punish in advance; if caught within the clan or handed over by outsiders, the branch head convenes clan chief and branch heads for public deliberation, forcing fathers, brothers, uncles to act—bury or drown." Zhejiang Yongjia Fenglin Village 《徐氏宗谱·族范八条》 stipulates: thieves "deeply harmful and incorrigible" are "ordered to take their own life"—slightly more lenient than burying or drowning.

Most satisfying: some genealogies stipulate that corrupt officials may be struck from the genealogy or even "ordered to take their own life," same as thieves.

Such severe punishments up to death are conducted before ancestral tablets in the hall. The hall's doors are normally closed; at such moments they swing wide open for public knowledge and deterrence. Villagers, seeing a major crime, whisper: "They're going to open the ancestral hall doors."

Some villages have a "旌善亭" (Praise-Goodness Pavilion) and "申明亭" (Declare-Clarity Pavilion), respectively for posting good and bad deeds. Most villages build only the latter, serving both purposes.

Many life rituals are held in ancestral halls, varying by local custom. Marriage is major. 《礼记·婚义》 describes upper-class weddings: "Marriage unites two surnames—above to serve the ancestral temple, below to continue posterity—hence gentlemen value it. Thus engagement rituals: betrothal gifts, name inquiry, auspice confirmation, betrothal presents, date selection—all with the host setting feast and table in the temple, welcoming with bows outside. Entering, bowing and ascending, receiving instruction in the temple—this is reverent and proper wedding ritual." The bride arrives similarly: "host sets feast in temple, bows outside." More interesting: after the bride's "assuming duties" ritual, she manages household affairs but receives training in the ancestral temple: "In antiquity, women, three months before marriage, if the ancestral temple was not yet destroyed, trained in the duke's palace; if destroyed, in the clan hall. Trained in wifely virtue, speech, appearance, and work. Upon completion, sacrificed with fish and pondweed—thus completing wifely obedience." This wedding, from start to finish, had many rituals in the ancestral temple—showing ancient upper-class temples' important role in weddings, representing the clan's acceptance of the bride. However, this role later had no fixed expression among commoners. In some customs, the bride must first visit the ancestral hall to "report" upon entering the village. 《东粤宝安南头黄氏族规》: "When clansmen marry, on the auspicious wedding eve, the bride must first devoutly visit the ancestral hall, then worship at home. Marriage is the beginning of human relations—no greater ritual. For hall worship, give 200 cash as red reward." In some places the bride visits the hall the day after wedding; in others she never enters.

Funerals are generally not held in the hall but in the residence hall with Buddhist rites; however, coffins may be temporarily placed in the hall. In some customs, placement differs by age: those dying at 50+ may have coffins in the second courtyard's corridors; 60+ in the third building's "sleeping chamber" front eaves; 70+ may enter the "sleeping chamber" against the gable wall.

In some places, mainly Fujian and Guangdong, families with newborn boys, at year's end, hang a lantern on a dedicated "lamp beam" (灯梁) under the main beam in the hall's central bay—called "添灯" (adding lamp), homophone for "添丁" (adding a son)—reporting joy to ancestors. At age three, past high infant mortality, the clan head ties a red silk thread around the child's neck in the hall to "bind the little life." At 17, the clan head removes the thread—this counts as "coming of age" (成丁), eligible for genealogy entry and major-hall spring/autumn sacrifices.

Clans valued natural resource and environmental protection. Trees on ancestral mountains (祖山) and facing mountains (朝山) may not be felled; on auxiliary mountains (案山) and grave mountains, even cutting firewood is forbidden—violators face severe punishment up to "expulsion from the hall" (struck from genealogy, clan membership revoked). Hence in patriarchal agrarian times, villages were usually surrounded by lush trees. However, people did not fully understand ecology then—they merely used tree luxuriance to symbolize clan vitality. Trees on grave mountains are called "荫树" (shade trees), symbolizing ancestral blessing. Zhejiang Yuyuan Wanli-era 《江南徐氏宗范》 stipulates: "Trees planted at ancestral graves comfort ancestral spirits; if descendants privately chop them, damaging the shade, the clan head reports to officials for punishment." Wuyuan Hong Village (Jiangxi) and Jingning Dapu Village (Zhejiang) both have rules forbidding fishing in the stream flowing before the village. Colorful carp swim in schoolsindeed adding vitality to the village. By early 20th century, some modern-educated intellectuals developed greater environmental awareness. For example, early French-returned students from Peitian Village, Liancheng, Fujian, wrote in 《吴氏族谱·物产说》: "For mountains with existing trees, strictly protect; for mountains without trees, vigorously plant—so products flourish and wealth never exhausts." They even stipulated: "The school's first duty is tree-planting." Clans contributed to village ecological protection.

Clans even managed village public health. In some Huizhou villages, on the first and fifteenth of each month, every household sent people to clean their assigned street sections. Pigs, cattle, sheep could not enter the village to avoid filth. Water canals had to be kept clean—geese and ducks could not approach; times for drawing clean water and discharging wastewater were regulated; winter saw organized pond-mud digging, etc.

In Qingyang Village, Jiangshan, Zhejiang, the Qianlong-founded, Tongzhi-supplemented 《清漾毛氏族谱·外集》 contains 《凝湖举人毛白圭先生志》, recording Mao Baigui's governance of Qingyang. The author, Cai Ying, was a Qianlong Guimao (1783) imperial-granted juren and Jiangshan County school instructor. The text says Mao Baigui established rules: "Clansmen aged 60+ receive monthly rice and meat from the hall, plus one cotton coat yearly. Ages 70, 80, 90 receive progressively more, clothing from cloth to silk. Student members taking provincial exams receive five taels each. Built Wenyang Pavilion where all clan students compose essays thrice monthly. Established charitable school for poor clan children. During grain shortages, hall grain sold at reduced price. If outsiders' merchants in the market are bullied by clansmen, reported to the hall—strictly punished. Outsiders opening shops: each New Year, hall hosts banquet, stipulating no gambling—violators expelled. Neighboring poor families hit by disaster receive hall relief, with fixed tiered standards. Hall property was originally modest; under Decheng's management it grew prosperous, funding all expenses." This describes a remote mountain village in Qianlong era (1736–1795). Notably, clan manager Mao Baigui already understood protecting "merchants"—i.e., protecting the market economy. 《毛氏族谱》 lists 24 "prohibitions," including "no unreasonable profit-taking," "no counterfeit silver," "no buying stolen goods," "no cheating customers"—all targeting possible market misconduct. Jiangshan, upper Qiantang River, was on the Hangzhou–Quanzhou route; frequent traffic since Southern Song influenced even clan rules.

Real life gave ancestral halls rich humanistic character, making them approachable to villagers. Halls established several "associations" (会) managing cultural entertainment for various seasons and occasions. Even from Song dynasty, villagers commonly built the village's most important entertainment facility—the stage—in the hall's gatehouse. During performances, courtyards, corridors, and worship halls (享堂) served as temporary audience seating. However, performance environment and content were restricted. For example, Guangxu 27 (1901) Hunan Changde 《映雪堂孙氏家法补略》 writes: "Gambling dens and opium shops are the source of bad customs; flower-drum and lantern plays are tools of licentiousness... these are great evils, the worst of moral corruption—warn, warn again." Such rules existed but could not fully suppress desire for entertainment.

Villagers, at festivals and celebrations, wanted lively plays, but local officials—often pedantic Confucians—believed plays inevitably incited lust and banditry, and viewing inevitably mixed men and women, so repeatedly banned them. Hence villagers built stages in hall or temple gatehouses, facing the worship hall, arguing: plays are performed to honor ancestors and repay gods—content naturally passes ancestral or divine scrutiny—thus争取 permission.

Yongjia Qukou Village 《重修渠川叶氏大宗祠碑记》 says: the Kangxi-era (1662–1722) main hall's old stage collapsed by Guangxu Jiachen (1904), so it was rebuilt. Next year, Yisi (1905), they proposed to all: "The stage is not for mere entertainment. Clansmen sacrifice at seasonal festivals, united in one hall. Plays open, using antiquity as mirror, arousing loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness." High-sounding words. But fine words alone were insufficient—strict controls needed. Hunan Huitong Gaoyi Village Republican-era 《杨氏族谱·祠堂记》 strictly stipulated: "Hall plays honor ancestors; viewers must be separated by gender, no mixing, children may not go on stage, nor may outsider rascals."

However, common people punctured this pedantic moralism from another angle. In Zhuge Village, Lanxi, Zhejiang, every April 14, at the Great Hall's spring sacrifice to ancestor Zhuge Liang, plays were mandatory. During performances, all villagers crowded to watch; young men had a quip: "To see pretty girls, April 14 at the Great Hall." Clan rules stipulated men watched in the courtyard, women in the worship hall, with a wooden railing between; several 60+ elders, carrying long-stemmed tobacco pipes, patrolled before the railing—if any frivolous young man turned to glance at the worship hall, they rapped his skull with the pipe. Such anecdotes enhanced the hall's humanistic character.

Some villages built stages opposite the hall or temple's front square, facing it—e.g., Tahu Temple in Yantou Village, Yongjia, Zhejiang. During plays, women could not enter the viewing area but stood outside the left and right lakesides, avoiding gender mixing.

In sum, in a blood-kin village, the ancestral hall is a comprehensive manager, directly or indirectly connected to all aspects of village cultural, economic, social, and political life. It embodies the entire rural cultural history of agrarian civilization, far exceeding a grassroots government institution in role.

Clan management had some democratic procedures. The clan head was not necessarily the "major-lineage heir" (大宗子), but someone of high generation, advanced age, and respected virtue. Actual management positions were elected within certain scope. In Xinye Village, Jiande, Zhejiang, managers formed a committee-like body all called "九思公" (Master Nine-Thoughts)—because legend says Southern Song neo-Confucian Lu Jiuyuan's brother Lu Jiusi was upright and skilled in management, greatly contributing to the Lu clan's development—so this village-governing collective was named after him. Major matters affecting whole village/clan interests—large construction projects, important disputes with neighboring villages, new rules everyone must follow—were decided at full clan assemblies in the hall, with every household head (having speech and vote) attending. "For all clan public affairs, the clan head gathers descendants in the family temple, striving for fairness and peace, deliberating to agreement." (《云阳涂氏族谱·祠堂碑记》) When repairing genealogy, a genealogy room was established in the hall with selected participants; when completed and distributed to branches, solemn ceremonies were held in the hall.

sections.name: 宗祠的建筑
sections.content_zh:
七、宗祠与村落

宗祠在血缘村落的建设里是一个结构性因素，也就是说，它对村落的结构布局起着重要的，某些方面甚至起决定性的作用。

许许多多现实的因素都是人们选择定居点的根本依据，主要包括安全、生产、交通、卫生、舒适等等的基本情况，形成聚落以后，在科学不发达的农耕时代，还需要一种超自然的信仰或者迷信来加强人们对居住地点的信心，这就是风水。风水术士编造出一些说法，使人们相信，山、水、地形等等自然因素以及它们和房屋的相互关系能够决定居住在某方土地上的人们的吉凶祸福（特别是他们的后代子孙的命运，这叫"风水看隔代"）。风水术士说服人们，经他们选择或稍稍加以调适的环境是一方"吉壤"，只要老老实实在这里居住下去，就能子孙繁昌，从而培养居民对这块土地的依赖心理甚至眷恋。迷信命运，这是无力掌握自己命运的村人们的心态，依恋土地，这是宗族的稳定、团结所需要的。因此，特别重视风水的，主要是福建、江西、广东、浙江、安徽各省以血缘村落为主的农村社会。在宗族共同体已经遭到严重破坏的北方地区，就不很重视风水了。

由于宗祠在血缘村落中的特殊作用，在南方，自然崇拜和祖先崇拜相结合，就对宗祠所在地点的风水有了许多巫术迷信的说法。宗祠，尤其是作为宗族总祠的大宗祠的风水对聚落的布局起了很大的作用。

一个村子，房子从少到多，不断变化，有的甚至会增长到一二百幢，而看风水却是要及早点出这块地方，也便是点出这个村子整体的风水的"穴"来，以"利于"整个村子家族的发展，"决定"他们的吉凶祸福。"穴"是不大的，有的人说只有雨伞尖子那么大，而且不能破坏它，万一破坏了，全村合族便会遭到不利。于是风水师唯一可行的办法便是由村子的大宗祠来标定并且保护这个"穴"。所以，一旦找到了这个风水的穴，就要在穴上造大宗祠，让这个穴正好位于大宗祠正厅的中央（或说在正厅太师壁的中央，也有个别人说位于大门中央的）。所以，为村子找风水穴就是同时为大宗祠选址，二者是同一回事。另一种说法是，大宗祠的定位由主山、朝山、左右的龙虎山"四灵守中"的风水位置确定的，所以大宗祠也要在村外才能明确这个关系。这便是一个村子的大宗祠多在村子的外缘而不在村内的主要原因之一，为的是避免它们的风水受到村子建筑的干扰。

大宗祠造在血缘村落的外缘，另一个理由是它演戏的时候会有大量外村的人来看，这是不能拒绝的。所以，为了安全，避免事故，大宗祠还是在村落外缘为好。有些小宗祠也有戏台，可以演戏，但次数和热闹程度就不如大宗祠了。而且，大宗祠是一村最辉煌的建筑，造在村口，也能使村子更有光彩。江西省和浙江省的村落，大宗祠便以位于村口的为多，如江西省婺源县汪口村、黄村，浙江省建德县新叶村、兰溪市诸葛村以及福建省福安县楼下村等等。

一个村子的大宗祠和四面自然山水的关系是很重要的。除了"四灵守中"之外，还有好多种可能。例如福建省福安县楼下村，四面群山环抱，南面有个高峰，一年四季，每天早晨第一束阳光必定先射在它的尖端上，于是村里的刘氏大宗祠，轴线就正对着这个山尖。阴阳先生说，因为朝阳、午阳、夕阳都照射在这山尖上，叫"三阳开泰"，是大吉大利的形局，所以把大宗祠造在一处山坡陡坎的上缘，坎下村口保留一片空地，前面不论再造什么村居，就都挡不住大宗祠和那山尖的联系了。

又例如浙江省建德市的新叶村，叶氏总祠为寻找最佳的风水而先后易址三次，最后建在村外东侧的小高地上，朝向为北偏东，正对着大约四公里外三峰山的主峰。主峰较高，另外两峰略矮，向主峰倾斜。风水术士说，主峰好比母亲，另两峰是儿子，身姿恭谨，很孝顺母亲。宗法制度的核心纲常是孝，祖庙的这个对景非常有利于宏扬宗法制度赖以存在的孝道。村人们相信，自从叶氏总祠落位之后，叶氏宗族就兴旺起来了。新叶村叶氏又分里宅和外宅两大支，外宅派的总祠叫有序堂，它正对着的朝山是圆锥形（金字形）的。圆锥形的山峰在风水术上比拟毛笔尖，叫"文笔峰"，因为这座山峰的东侧是元末大理学家金履祥的故里，所以地方人士又把它叫"道峰山"。

新叶村西傍玉华山，山上有巨大的崖壁，得名为"砚山"。于是，人们便在有序堂前挖了很大的一个半月形的泮池，叫"砚池"。道峰山倒映在砚池里，就成了"文笔蘸墨"的风水格局，这种格局主文运亨通。恰好从道峰山到有序堂，其间有三道小山冈，风水术士说，这是三道诰命。后来外宅派凑巧果然出了三位重要人物，都受到诰命封赠。村民们说，是他们"带动了"整个外宅派的兴旺。而里宅派的总祠雍睦堂的位置很局促，风水不好，以致里宅派终于没落，甚至可能已经没有后人，以致有序堂实际上几乎取代了叶氏总祠的地位。

圆锥形或金字形的文笔峰在风水术上又叫火形山，虽然有很大的"好处"，但也有很大的"隐患"。所以，面对着它的大宗祠，前面要有水池，池与宗祠正门之间要有隔火墙，宗祠的正门应该在侧面。新叶村的有序堂都一一做到了，江西省婺源县黄村的黄氏总祠经义堂也同样一一做到了。

叶氏总祠和有序堂的风水固然是穿凿附会，但它也带来了实际的好处。为了保持风水，族中规定，不许在"明堂"里造房子，也就是不许在道峰山和有序堂之间以及三峰山和叶氏总祠之间造房子，这样一来，就把新叶村最好的大片农田保护下来了。而且，风水之说大大增强了叶氏族人在这块土地上居住下去的决心和信心。他们开渠引水，平整丘陵，兴办书院，终于建成了在这一带比较富庶的村落。

新叶村的西北，道峰山和玉华山之间，也便是文笔峰和砚山之间，村子的水源地上有一座玉泉寺。村子的东南，低洼的巽位上，有一座文昌阁和文峰塔。有序堂的正面恰在玉泉寺和文昌阁的连线上。玉泉寺和有序堂都草创于元代，阁和塔则建于清代，可见，阁和塔的位置是由寺和祠的位置来确定的。

新叶村各个房派团块之间的边界建成了村中的主要巷子，比较宽，中央铺一道石板，曲曲折折，它们都通向外宅派总祠有序堂。房派团块内的巷子地面中央都没有石板，和主巷明显区别开来。循着中央有石板的巷子走，一定能达到大宗祠。

房派的住宅团块的中心是分祠，也就是众厅和私己厅，它们对村子的结构布局也有很大影响。分祠分布在全村，房派成员的住宅簇聚在分祠周围，形成房派的居住团块，它们依各种方式与大宗祠联系，组成聚落整体。于是，聚落就有了一个个以房祠为核心的团块式布局。

大宗祠要代表全村面对村子的朝山，不受阻挡。而且有演戏等活动时便于接受外村人来热闹，所以大宗祠大多不在村子中央而在村子的前缘。离新叶村不远的兰溪市诸葛村，它的领域分属孟、仲、季三大房，各以房祠崇信堂、雍睦堂和尚礼堂为核心形成片状结构的房派团块，作为全村核心的大宗祠丞相祠堂则处于村子南端入口的边缘。这种方式的房派团块结构布局是血缘村落的主流形态。

江西、福建和广东，不少地方，有些农村聚落在宗祠两侧各建一条顺墙的巷子，在巷子外侧再建几条横向的笔直的小巷，小巷侧边造整齐一致的标准化住宅，朝向和大宗祠相同，形成一个篦子形（蟹形）的很像兵营的村子。这种村子一般只有一个总祠，没有房派的分祠。例如江西省吉水县的双元村和广东省开平县的一些村子。它们都是近代建造的，有西方工业城市布局的影响。

江西省乐安县流坑村，因为人口增加，经过历年增建，乱了原有布局，嘉靖年间对全村布局做了一次大调整、大改造，统一规划成七条东西走的巷子和一条南北走的巷子，大体每条巷子住一个房派，在巷口建一座分祠。后来因人口增加，住户发生社会分化，而且祠堂由于各种原因大增到八十三座之多，这个布局又被突破了。大宗祠却独自在村北大约一百多米处，显然为了避开居住区可能发生的变化。

在浙江、江西、安徽诸省农村，房派的小宗祠前面多数也有个泮池，半月形，直径和宗祠的宽度相等，居民在这里浣洗、取水，但不许洗秽物，也不许家畜、家禽走近，更不许它们下水。泮池外侧，早年通常是绿地，种些花树。祠堂两旁或背后也常有绿地，甚至有精致的花园。由于房派祠堂多在房派住宅团块的核心，就带着把水池、树木或花园大致均匀地分布到全村，不但有利于防火、方便日常生活，而且给住房密集的村落以一些开阔的空间，便于晾晒衣服被褥。家制干菜、薯丝、腊肉、粉条也需要空地晾晒。它们使村落疏密有致，景观变化多，教人感到舒畅，不再憋闷难堪。宋代袁采著《袁氏世范·治家》中写道："居室不可无邻家，虑有火烛无人救应；宅之四周如无溪流，当为池井，虑有火烛无水救应。"宗祠前的水池起着救灭火灾的作用，它们也能和绿地一起缓解密集的村屋造成的热岛效应，改善小气候。

这些小空间也成了人们交往的场所。浣衣女蹲在塘岸相互聊些家常；大树下摆几块石头，老人们拄杖而来，坐下谈古论今，找老兄弟们下几盘五子棋。向阳的墙根下冬日里总挨着一帮男女老少晒太阳。巷子口上通风，则是夏夜乘凉的好地方。平日祠堂前空地里就这样充满生活气息。年时节下，演戏多在大祠堂里；龙灯，抬阁则都要巡游到每个次级祠堂，在祠堂前空地大大舞弄一番，从而把欢乐带遍大街小巷，家家户户。

空地不空，它们是村民生活的必需之地。

祠堂前也是村子建筑艺术的重点，居住团块的构图中心。祠堂大门，或者有华丽的门楼，或者有庄严的门廊，小型的也有雅致的雕砖门头。族人有了科举成绩，举人以上便可以在宗祠大门前立一对桅杆，举人桅杆上装一只斗，进士的便装两只了。大门是精雕细刻，金碧辉煌，桅杆是轻盈挺拔，喜气洋洋。它们是宗族的脸面，向人炫耀宗族的繁庶和成功，激励子孙们努力向上。诸葛村《高隆诸葛氏宗谱》里有一幅《高隆族居图》，画着四十五座各级祠堂，其中竟有十四座竖立着功名桅杆。遥想当年，这个村子的景观曾非常蓬勃生动。
sections.content_en:
7. Ancestral Halls and Villages

The ancestral hall is a structural factor in the construction of blood-kin villages—that is, it plays an important, in some respects even decisive, role in the village's structural layout.

Many practical factors are the fundamental basis for choosing a settlement: safety, production, transport, hygiene, comfort, etc. After a settlement forms, in scientifically undeveloped agrarian times, a supernatural belief or superstition was needed to strengthen people's confidence in their dwelling place—this is fengshui. Fengshui masters fabricated claims that mountains, water, terrain, and their relationship to houses determine the fortune or misfortune of people living on a given land (especially their descendants' fate—called "fengshui sees across generations"). Fengshui masters persuaded people that environments they selected or slightly adjusted were "auspicious soil" (吉壤)—that as long as they lived there honestly, descendants would flourish, cultivating dependence and even attachment to the land. Superstitious belief in fate is the mindset of villagers unable to control their own destiny; attachment to land is what clan stability and unity require. Hence, fengshui was especially valued in Fujian, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Zhejiang, and Anhui—rural societies dominated by blood-kin villages. In northern regions where clan communities had been severely damaged, fengshui was less valued.

Due to the ancestral hall's special role in blood-kin villages, in the south, nature worship combined with ancestor worship produced many superstitious claims about the fengshui of hall locations. The fengshui of ancestral halls—especially the main hall (大宗祠) as the clan's central shrine—greatly influenced settlement layout.

A village's houses grow from few to many, constantly changing, sometimes reaching 100–200 buildings. Fengshui, however, requires early identification of the site's "acupoint" (穴)—the village's overall fengshui point—to "benefit" the whole clan's development and "determine" their fortune. The "acupoint" is small—some say only the size of an umbrella tip—and cannot be damaged; if damaged, the entire village and clan suffer misfortune. Hence the fengshui master's only feasible method is to have the village's main hall mark and protect this "acupoint." Once found, the main hall is built on the acupoint, placing it exactly at the center of the main hall's central hall (or at the center of the taishi wall, or some say at the gate center). Thus, finding the village's fengshui acupoint is simultaneously selecting the main hall site—they are the same thing. Another view: the main hall's position is determined by the "four spirits guarding center" (四灵守中) fengshui configuration of main mountain, facing mountain, and left/right dragon-tiger mountains—so the main hall must be outside the village to clearly establish this relationship. This is a primary reason main halls are often at the village's outer edge rather than inside: to avoid their fengshui being disturbed by village buildings.

Another reason for building the main hall at the village's outer edge: during performances, large numbers of outsiders come to watch—this cannot be refused. Hence for safety and accident prevention, the outer edge is preferable. Some smaller halls also have stages, but with fewer performances and less excitement. Moreover, the main hall is the village's most splendid building; at the village entrance it enhances the village's splendor. In Jiangxi and Zhejiang villages, main halls are often at the village entrance—e.g., Wuyuan Wangkou and Huang villages (Jiangxi), Jiande Xinye and Lanxi Zhuge villages (Zhejiang), and Fu'an Louxia Village (Fujian).

A village's main hall relationship with surrounding natural landscape is important. Beyond "four spirits guarding center," many configurations exist. For example, Louxia Village, Fu'an, Fujian, is surrounded by mountains, with a southern peak that receives the first morning sunlight year-round. The village's Liu main hall axis points directly at this peak. Yin-yang masters say: because morning, noon, and evening sun all strike the peak—it's "three yangs opening prosperity" (三阳开泰), a highly auspicious configuration—so the main hall was built on the upper edge of a steep slope, with open space below at the village entrance; no future houses could block the hall-peak connection.

Another example: Xinye Village, Jiande, Zhejiang. The Ye clan's main hall was relocated three times seeking optimal fengshui, finally built on a small high ground east of the village, facing north-by-east, directly toward the main peak of Sanfeng Mountain about 4 km away. The main peak is higher; two other peaks are slightly lower, leaning toward it. Fengshui masters say: the main peak is like a mother, the other two like sons—postures respectful, filial to mother. The core of patriarchal clan system is filial piety; this view from the ancestral hall greatly promotes the filial piety on which the clan system depends. Villagers believe that since the Ye main hall was positioned, the Ye clan has prospered. The Ye clan divides into inner-residence and outer-residence branches; the outer branch's main hall is Youxu Hall (有序堂), facing a conical (pyramid-shaped) mountain. Conical mountains in fengshui are compared to brush tips—called "writing-brush peak" (文笔峰). Because this mountain's eastern side is the hometown of late-Yuan neo-Confucian Jin Lüxiang, locals also call it "Daofeng Mountain" (道峰山).

Xinye Village borders Yuhua Mountain to the west, with huge cliffs named "inkstone mountain" (砚山). Hence, a large half-moon pond was dug before Youxu Hall—called "inkstone pond" (砚池). Daofeng Mountain reflected in the inkstone pond creates the "writing brush dipping ink" fengshui configuration, which governs literary success. Coincidentally, between Daofeng Mountain and Youxu Hall are three small hills—fengshui masters say these are three "imperial edicts" (诰命). Later, the outer branch indeed produced three important figures, all receiving imperial edict honors. Villagers say they "drove" the entire outer branch's prosperity. The inner branch's main hall, Yongmu Hall (雍睦堂), was cramped with poor fengshui—leading to the inner branch's decline, possibly no descendants left—so Youxu Hall practically replaced the Ye main hall's status.

Conical or pyramid-shaped writing-brush peaks are also called "fire-form mountains" in fengshui—with great "benefits" but also great "hidden dangers." Hence, main halls facing them need a pond in front, a fire-separation wall between pond and main gate, and the main gate should be on the side. Xinye's Youxu Hall achieved all these; Wuyuan Huang Village's Huang main hall, Jingyi Hall (经义堂), also achieved all.

The fengshui of Ye main hall and Youxu Hall may be far-fetched, but it brought practical benefits. To maintain fengshui, clan rules forbade building houses in the "bright hall" (明堂)—i.e., between Daofeng Mountain and Youxu Hall, and between Sanfeng Mountain and Ye main hall—thus protecting Xinye's best farmland. Moreover, fengshui beliefs greatly strengthened Ye clansmen's determination and confidence to live on this land. They dug canals, leveled hills, established academies, finally building a relatively prosperous village in the region.

Northwest of Xinye, between Daofeng and Yuhua mountains (between writing-brush peak and inkstone mountain), at the village's water source, stands Yuquan Temple (玉泉寺). Southeast of the village, in the low-lying xun position (巽位), stand Wenchang Pavilion (文昌阁) and Wenfeng Pagoda (文峰塔). Youxu Hall's front lies exactly on the line connecting Yuquan Temple and Wenchang Pavilion. Both temple and hall were founded in Yuan; pavilion and pagoda built in Qing—showing pavilion and pagoda positions were determined by temple and hall positions.

Boundaries between Xinye's branch residential blocks form the village's main lanes—relatively wide, with a central stone slab path, winding, all leading to the outer branch's main hall Youxu Hall. Lanes within branch blocks lack central stone slabs, clearly distinguishing them from main lanes. Following the stone-slab lane always leads to the main hall.

The center of each branch's residential block is the branch hall (分祠)—also called zhongting (众厅) or siji ting (私己厅)—which greatly influences village layout. Branch halls are distributed throughout the village; branch members' houses cluster around them, forming branch residential blocks connected to the main hall in various ways, composing the settlement whole. Thus, settlements have a block-style layout with branch halls as cores.

The main hall must represent the whole village facing the village's facing mountain, unobstructed. And for performances and other activities, it should conveniently welcome outsiders—hence main halls are mostly not at the village center but at the village's front edge. Near Xinye, Lanxi Zhuge Village's territory belongs to three major branches (Meng, Zhong, Ji), each forming a片状 branch block centered on branch halls Chongxin, Yongmu, and Shangli; the village-core main hall, Prime Minister Hall (丞相祠堂), sits at the southern entrance edge. This branch-block layout is the mainstream form of blood-kin villages.

In Jiangxi, Fujian, and Guangdong, some rural settlements build two lanes along the hall's side walls, with several straight transverse lanes outside, lined with uniform standardized houses facing the same direction as the main hall—forming a comb-shaped (crab-shaped) village resembling a military camp. Such villages generally have only one main hall, no branch halls. Examples: Jishui Shuangyuan Village (Jiangxi) and some Kaiping villages (Guangdong). They were built in modern times, influenced by Western industrial city layouts.

Le'an Liukeng Village (Jiangxi), due to population growth and years of additions, disrupted its original layout. During Jiajing era, a major reorganization unified the village into seven east-west lanes and one north-south lane, roughly each lane housing one branch with a branch hall at the lane entrance. Later population growth and social differentiation, plus halls increasing to 83 for various reasons, broke this layout again. The main hall stands alone about 100+ meters north of the village—apparently to avoid changes in the residential area.

In Zhejiang, Jiangxi, and Anhui rural areas, branch halls' fronts mostly have a half-moon pond (泮池), diameter equal to hall width. Residents wash and draw water here, but may not wash filthy things, nor let livestock/poultry approach or enter. Outside the pond was usually green space with flowering trees. Hall sides or backs often had green space, even refined gardens. Since branch halls are at branch-block cores, they distribute ponds, trees, and gardens fairly evenly across the village—not only aiding fire prevention and daily life, but also giving dense settlements open space for drying clothes and bedding. Homemade dried vegetables, sweet potato shreds, cured meat, and noodles also need open drying space. They make villages疏密有致, with varied landscapes, comfortable rather than oppressive. Song dynasty Yuan Cai wrote in 《袁氏世范·治家》: "A dwelling cannot lack neighbors—fear fire without rescue; if no streams around the house, build ponds and wells—fear fire without water." Ponds before halls serve fire-fighting; together with green space they mitigate the heat-island effect of dense village houses and improve microclimate.

These small spaces also became social venues. Laundry women squat by pond banks chatting; stones under big trees where elders lean on canes, sit and discuss past and present, play chess with old brothers. Sunny wall bases in winter are crowded with people sunbathing. Ventilated lane mouths are good summer evening cooling spots. Hall-front open spaces are thus full of daily life. At festivals, performances mostly in the main hall; dragon lanterns and sedan-chair processions tour every secondary hall, performing vigorously in hall-front open spaces—spreading joy through every street and household.

Open spaces are not empty—they are essential to villagers' lives.

Hall fronts are also the focus of village architectural art, the compositional center of residential blocks. Hall gates may have ornate gate towers, solemn gate porches, or small ones with elegant carved-brick doorheads. Clansmen with exam success—juren and above—may erect a pair of flagpoles (桅杆) before the hall gate; juren flagpoles have one dou (斗), jinshi have two. Gates are exquisitely carved and gilded; flagpoles are light and upright, festive. They are the clan's face—showing off clan prosperity and success, inspiring descendants to strive. Zhuge Village's 《高隆诸葛氏宗谱》 contains a 《高隆族居图》 depicting 45 halls of various levels, 14 of which erect merit flagpoles. Imagine the village's vibrant landscape in its prime.

sections.name: 宗祠里的祭祀
sections.content_zh:
八、宗祠的建筑

宗祠是一种严肃的礼制建筑。它核心部分的型制从住宅演化而来，住宅在生活中由于种种条件而千变万化，同样，作为崇祀建筑，有些庙宇在山区，在水边，都有极丰富的形体变化。宗祠虽然也有变化，但变化不大，保持着一副由于功能而程式化的主要空间组合和一种庄重、整齐的格调。

宗祠是举行祭祀的场所，祠祭要严格按照《朱文正公家礼》规定的程序进行，以致宗祠建筑本身，尤其是它的中央主体部分，是有一定程式的。大多数宗祠，主要有三部分，从前到后，一是大门门屋；二是拜殿，或者叫享堂，是举行祭拜仪式的地方；三是寝室，是从《礼记·王制》里说的那个"庶人祭于寝"的"寝"字引发出来的名称，专为供奉祖先神位。《光绪合肥邢氏家谱》道："家庙者，祖宗之宫室也，制度即隘，亦少不得三进两庑：前门户，中厅事，后寝室。"江西省婺源县黄村的经义堂和汪口村的仁本堂以及安徽、浙江大量的宗祠都是很标准的这种格局。

局面小一点的宗祠，不另建寝室，而把神牌就供奉在拜殿后墙前的神龛里。如不够，便在山墙前也设神龛；再不够，则合并神主，在一方神主牌上写一二十个祖先名讳，这合并的措施叫"祧"。四川《云阳涂氏族谱·祠堂碑记》清楚地说："上建龛堂，所以安神主而序昭穆也；中树厅事，所以齐子孙而肃跪拜也；前列回楼，所以接宾朋而讲圣旨也；左右两庑，所以进子弟而习诗书也。"它把各部分的功用都说齐了，左右两庑的使用很有历史的特色。龛堂就是寝室，它的地坪往往比享堂的高出不少，回楼即倒座门楼。这说的是一般规模的祠堂，稍大一点的则在这里建戏台。

三进房子之间是两个院落，院落左右有廊庑。有的把后院廊庑发展成厢房，也用作"寝室"，分"左昭右穆"，恭奉先人牌位，前院廊庑分隔成小间，或作宗族办事用房，如谱房、账房或长老们的议事室。而《云阳涂氏族谱》里则规定它的用途为书塾。凡大宗祠和房祠，都必需有一个宽敞的厨房，以烹制祭祀用的各种食品，如胙肉。

大而富的宗族，宗祠有多种公共功能，因而宗祠便也比较复杂。除了核心部分之外，附属于宗祠建筑的常有后花园、书塾、义仓、义厝等等，少数的如浙江省武义县俞源村的俞氏宗祠甚至更附有孤儿院、养老院等等。

最简单的氏级别祠堂，只有大门和拜殿，把祖先神位供奉在拜殿里紧贴后墙的神橱里，免去专门的寝室，甚至没有前进和两庑。广东省珠江三角洲各地的宗族分支很早，所以宗祠多是这种小型的。

规模较大一点的宗祠，在门屋里造一个戏台，面对拜殿，前院和它两侧的廊庑成了看戏人的所在位置，甚至设楼，楼上为女眷的观戏厅。楼下在演戏时由小贩摆各种食品摊。

江西省乐安县流坑村，相传为汉儒董仲舒后人的聚落，董氏大宗祠是一座少有的大型祠堂，建于村北的陌兰洲，距村落住宅区约二百米。坐北朝南，面对村落，背靠自南而北再向西转弯的乌江。从大宗祠入村要通过寨墙上的拱宸门。大宗祠建于村外，背对村落的朝山，任乌江在后面流过，这种布局不合堪舆术常见的教条，在非常重视堪舆之说的江西省（杨筠松即江西人），流坑董氏大宗祠的这个位置可能有一些说法，但没有留下记载。

董氏大宗祠和一左一右的另外两座房祠形成建筑群，三幢建筑并列，东西宽九十米，南北纵深七十多米，共占地七千平方米。大宗祠位于中央，东侧是桂林祠，祀董氏十六世祖董季敏。西为桂岩祠（后改为文馆，祀孔子和文昌帝君）。有子弟备考科举的小小读书室。三祠前有一个共有的公共空间，形成宽敞的横向院落。院中央有一口长方形的"墨池"。院子东西端均有三开间砖坊一座，西坊书"优入贤关"（外）和"簪缨世第"（内），东坊书"理学名贤"（内）和"科甲联芳"（外）。这两座砖坊初建于康熙年间（1662—1722）。大宗祠前为三间牌坊式砖门，重檐，中央一匾正面书"厚德流光"，背面匾上书"文献世家"。次间各有石狮子一座。门前有墨池，池南有坊名"追远"，表示对祖先的怀念。池东西各有一座木坊相对，和外墙上"优入贤关"、"科甲联芳"两座砖坊在一条直线上。东木坊书"累朝师保"，西木坊书"奕世科名"，炫耀仕宦和功名的成就。院正面南墙有影壁，书"累朝世家"四个大字。

进入"厚德流光"门，在前院的左右还有钟、鼓楼各一座。

大宗祠共三进，第一进为"育贤楼"大厅，三开间重檐，中央一间额"宋赠大司徒董公大宗祠"，东间额"祖孙台部"，西间额"三世尚书"。第二进大厅为"敦睦堂"，三开间重檐，匾额书"万殊一本"。第三进为五开间，中央三开间为两层，上层额"敕书阁"。下层明间有匾额书"孝敬堂"，左右按昭穆次序为"彰义堂"、"报功堂"、"宗原堂"、"道原堂"，均有额。育贤楼和敦睦堂两侧有厢房，东侧祀"忠"、"廉"，西侧祀"孝"、"节"。按昭穆次序应是忠、孝、廉、节。宗祠犹如一座家族忠臣义士节妇贞女的纪念馆。孝敬、彰义、报功三堂先落成于嘉靖四十年（1565年）。明人董燧写《彰义堂记》说，"中题曰孝敬堂，所以祀爵也；左题曰彰义堂，所以祀义也；右题曰报功堂，所以祀功也。三堂之外，总题曰敦睦堂，所以序昭穆也。"孝敬堂祀仕宦，报功堂祀堪舆家杨筠松、曾文辿和廖瑀。董氏宗族一直认为本族的发达全由于这几位风水"大师"给祖坟和聚落寻了好风水。"彰义堂"是专祀那些捐钱捐田助建宗祠和助祭的族人的，标准是十两银子一位，钱多就有好位置。敦睦堂祀合族历代祖先。宗原堂和道原堂后建，万历九年（1581年）董燧在《宗原道原两堂簿引》中写道："道原堂特祀仲舒公，溯吾董道学之原也。……宗原堂特祀清然公列祖……重其始也。"仲舒公是汉代的董仲舒，被尊为董姓始祖；清然公是董姓迁江西省宜黄县的始祖。大宗祠因此又是一座家族传统教育的展览厅，纪念和教育，都与流坑的历史特点相符合。敦睦堂有一副对联：

以祖宗之心为心，自求多福；
若先王之法不法，入此何颜。

更揭示出宗祠的教化作用。

但特别值得注意的是"彰义堂"，它所说的"义"，就是向宗族捐款，捐田。彰义堂里供奉的就是些这样的大商人或大地主，就像不必读书应考，靠捐纳便得到什么"大夫"、"司马"的虚衔一样，靠捐纳也可以进入专祠，永享殊荣。这情况反映着明代晚期长江中下游地区商业经济发达的历史性变化，这变化在意识形态上的表现之一，便是这样突破了封建宗法制度的伦理观念。明代晚期，流坑村不少人就因经营漕运和木材而致大富。

宗祠作为庄严的礼仪建筑，格局变化少，但也有些变体。广州市的陈氏宗祠除中轴上的一路五开间厅堂和院落以外，左右还各有一路院落和厅堂，每路三进，一共九厅六院。三路之间只以敞廊相隔，最外侧处才有厢间。厅堂、厢房和斋房一共十八座，总面积竟达一万三千二百平米，这座宗祠的空阔开敞是少有其匹。

浙江省永嘉县岩头村的桂林公祠，由书院改成，享堂前有大水池，中央立方亭一座，由一道桥从仪门经方亭再到享堂。仪门外又是一座水池，进大门后，绕水池方得抵仪门。这布局很有个性。

华北地区历来多战乱，稳定有力的宗族少，所以村落多为杂性，有些人口不多的小宗族。因此也就少宗祠，尤其少大型宗祠。村落的管理多由地缘性或行业性的"社"担当。公共活动在庙宇里举行。最小的宗祠无非是仅能容身的小屋一间，四周墙上写满了祖先名讳就罢了，屋中央立一个小小的香火架，例如河北省蔚县宋家庄的苏氏宗祠，只有小小一间。

大宗祠门屋里一般都有戏台。有些富裕村落，房祠和支祠也有戏台。门屋里的戏台主要有三种，一种全部都在门屋的明间里面；一种有一半向祠内凸出于明间之外；第三种则是全部凸出，前面高高翘起一对翼角，而后台则在门屋明间里。第三种做法，观众可从戏台三面看戏，台上台下的隔阂比较小。第一种做法，戏台挡住了宗祠的大门，平日，包括演戏的日子，只开左右次间的侧门，特殊的日子，例如祭祖，例如奉安神主，便把戏台中央一溜活动台板移开，空出一条通道来。第二、第三种做法，在中央正门进入门屋，分左右绕过戏台再向拜殿。

化妆室通常设在门屋次间的夹层里，有小木楼梯从戏台太师壁后的候场处上下。

候场处与前台之间设一道板壁，太师壁，叫"守旧"，正面大多画一幅《唐明皇游月宫》图。唐明皇就是唐玄宗，他精通音律，好歌舞，曾亲自在宫中梨园里训练戏班子，所以被戏剧行业奉为祖师爷，叫"老郎神"。唐明皇游月宫是一则很浪漫的故事，白居易有诗叙述明皇因"安史之乱"仓皇出逃四川，中途杨贵妃在六军逼迫下自尽，"君王掩面救不得，回首血泪相和流"。乱平返都，明皇日夜思念贵妃。道士叶法善便作法引导明皇到月宫里去，和已经升仙住在月宫里的杨贵妃会面。二人相誓"在天愿作比翼鸟，在地愿为连理枝"。明皇游月宫的情节极富戏剧性，所以经常用来画在这个"守旧"板壁上。

"守旧"的上方挂一块横匾，大都是赞扬演出的，不出"金声玉振"、"作古振今"、"翻风弄月"之类，以套话为多。

"守旧"的两侧是上场门和下场门，门额上大多各写"出将"、"入相"两个字。也有的写得花巧些，但意思不变。台子左右和前沿，有纤小的高仅盈尺的栏杆，保护演员。栏杆小柱头上蹲着木雕的麒麟等等瑞兽。有些宗祠，如浙江省永嘉县芙蓉村的"陈氏宗祠"，在戏台左后侧附一个小小的台子，给乐队专用。

戏台往往是小木作、木雕和彩画作的精品。首先是戏台上方为拔音（或称拢音）而多用深藻井，藻井的样式极多，木工师傅们争奇斗巧，别出心裁地进行创作，频出精品。如浙江省永嘉县各村宗祠的戏台常用八角覆斗形藻井，溜金斗拱沿八个阴角线和八面中线层层上挑，长拱如流云，如灵芝，宛转曲伸，非常生动。浙江省宁海县农村，戏台的藻井各式各样，变化很多，最生动的叫"百鸟朝凤"（民间叫"鸡笼顶"），图案呈螺旋形上腾，蓬勃的动势和戏剧的热烈相呼应，珠联璧合。有些藻井整个覆满鲜艳的彩画，"开光盒子"里的戏剧场景画得很精致逼真。其次是戏台台面前沿，大木枋子前贴着一条通长的木雕，雕刻的题材都是戏剧情节。这幅雕刻是雕花匠大展身手的地方。四川省各地把这幅长长的雕花板叫做"照面枋"，意思就是说它面对观众。照面枋专供大家品评，所以制作格外精心。

江西省乐平县，村村祠堂有戏台，甚至有些村几个祠堂都有戏台，全县在"文化大革命"后保存下来的戏台还有三百多座。乐平戏台的型制大多有些特殊，而且雕梁画栋，穷极艳丽，几乎是无处不雕，无雕不贴金箔，一派耀眼的灿灿金光。

戏台前檐的一对柱子，叫"台柱"，台柱上必挂楹联，有一些是即景而写的，比较浅显直露，如"看去俨然如是，想来或者有之"；有一些带有感慨，如：

一曲商音，演成千古兴亡胜负；
数声越调，点出百年离合悲欢。

又如：

移步换形，漫说炎凉都是假；
描眉画角，须知喜怒皆成真。

台口上方也有横匾，大多书"普天同庆"、"盛世纶音"之类的喜兴话。

看戏的观众，按祠堂里规矩，一般是男的在院子里，女的在拜殿前檐下，自带凳子。院子两侧的廊庑里也是妇女们看戏的场所。山西、江西和四川等诸省有些祠堂，厢廊上有看楼，左为"男居楼"，右为"女居楼"，专为"有身份人家"使用。

明清两代有些道学腐儒，认为演戏有伤风化，如明代劳宜斋在《瓯江逸志》里批评道：每逢演戏，"十余日昼夜游观，男女杂乱"。清代道光、咸丰年间（1821—1861）永嘉县令汤成烈在《县志稿》里也写道："报赛侈鬼神之会……士女游观，靓妆华服，阗城溢郭，有司莫之能禁。"想禁又禁不住，很不满意。社会上层的这种保守意识，当然会影响到村子里的主事人物，所以祠堂里演戏要划分男女观众的位置，并且有几个六十岁以上的老人家在观众群里巡视，用长长的旱烟杆敲打眼光不老实的小后生。

一般村落，戏台大多只建在大宗祠（总祠）门屋里，面对享堂。但也有一些村落把戏台造在宗祠大门外的广场上，面对宗祠。有些村落，如福建省连城培田村，戏台的位置和朝向就不很规矩。其实是连大门的位置都不很规矩。每逢演戏，邻村的人都会来看，而且四方小贩，卖小吃食的、卖零杂货的，也都会赶来在祠堂前或戏台前两侧廊庑里摆摊，形成临时的闹市。为了保护村落内部的安全和宁静，是大多村落把总祠建在村边而不建在村子核心区的原因之一。

也有少数宗祠门厅里的戏台是可以拆卸的，如江西省婺源县黄村的总祠经义堂。浙江省建德县新叶村智字房的崇仁堂，它的戏台也是可拆卸的，木架构件平时收在祠堂里，用时取出搭在大门前泮池的水面上。这种活动戏台叫"雨台"或"露台"。号称水乡的浙江省绍兴市有一种戏台，搭在宗祠前的水面上，距岸比较远，四乡的人驾船来看戏，船就停在戏台前。从开戏到戏散，一直乱而不清，但"看戏"的乡民倒更增添不少趣味。冬烘先生们认为，妇女坐在自家的小船里看戏有利于保护风化。

山西省有些县里，庙内并肩建两三座戏台，且相距不远，看戏大受干扰，但很得村民欢喜。看戏其实以热闹为第一。

南方多雨，有些戏台前建大堂或敞厅为观众遮雨。如江西省抚州市的万寿宫，一座大堂占满了院子。浙江省宁海县有些宗祠，戏台前的院子里建高大的敞厅，沿院子中央纵向延长，少的两间，多的三间，每间顶上做一个藻井，非常精致细巧。

祠堂的第二进是拜殿，或者叫享堂。庶民的祠堂，拜殿一般遵制是三开间，但五开间的也有。特殊人物如列入朝廷祀典的诸葛亮的祠堂为五开间。安徽省歙县呈坎村东舒祠的享堂也是五开间，总面宽26.5米，进深22.5米，非常宏敞。在南方地区，拜殿的前檐完全敞开。这里是举行祭祀仪式的地方，也是最要壮观的地方。大堂高爽，木构架都很粗大，而且以雕刻装饰。

拜殿其实是宗族历史成就和荣誉的陈列室，是促成宗族团结和发展的纪念堂。它的梁枋上挂满了大匾，内容都是歌颂族人的功名、德行、寿考等等的。如"贡元"、"进士"、"叙伦"、"乡贤"、"父子柱史"、"宗德流芳"、"厚德载福"、"承天宠锡"、"耆英厚望"、"祖泽缉熙"等等，都是炫显可以"光宗耀祖"的人物或事件的，色彩灿烂辉煌，引得來祭祀的族人十分振奋。

柱身上都有楹联，内容比较驳杂。凡家世显赫的宗姓，必有一副长联，上联统叙历祖历宗的功业、懿德、声名，下联颂扬从始祖播迁以来到落根本地的经过等等。如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村大公堂的楹联：

溯汉室以来，祀文庙，祀乡贤，祀名宦，祀忠孝义烈，不少传人，自有史书标姓氏；
迁浙江而后，历绍兴，历寿昌，历常村，历南塘水阁，于兹启宇，可从谱谍证渊源。

浙江省永嘉县鹤垟村谢灵运后人宗祠叙伦堂的楹联：

江左溯家声、淝水捷书，勋绩于今照史册；
瓯东绵世泽，池塘春草，诗才亘古重儒林。

没有显赫的历史人物的宗姓，便写些颂扬宗族搬迁过程，如今的繁荣、富足，村子祥和、有序等等的闲话，如浙江省建德市新叶村有序堂的楹联：

迁移自杭睦寿而来，氏族清嘉，斯地奠安称梓里；
裔嗣绳宋元明以后，诗书启绍，先人腾达颂玉华。

又如湖南省会同县高椅村大宗祠的主联：

祖德启鸿图，念先人伯仲营迁分两甲；
孙谋贻燕翼，裕后嗣子孙螽羽绍千秋。

享堂明间的后金柱之间大多有樘板，可以启闭如门扉，在恭请祖先神主或奉安祖先神主的时候因为要出入后院的寝室，就把樘板打开。每逢祭祀则关闭樘板，在樘板上悬挂始祖和杰出祖先的画像，有些地方称为"祖容"，北方则称为"图"。樘板上方多挂祠堂的堂号匾，如"敦睦堂"、"崇恩堂"、"德馨堂"之类。那副主题性的长联便悬挂在樘板左右的后金柱上。那里光线暗淡，联、匾以黑色打底，文字贴了金箔，闪闪发亮，非常庄重肃穆。

浙江省和江西省有些大宗祠拜殿明间的前后两对金柱分别用柏、梓、桐、椿四种木材制作，谐音"百子同春"，讨个子孙繁衍发达的吉祥，这是被供奉着的祖先最关心的事。江西省婺源县黄村黄氏大宗祠明间左右前金柱下分别用青石和白石做磉墩，象征"左青龙、右白虎"，这做法殊不多见，但也并非孤例。

拜殿的两个次间，前金柱和前檐柱之间的轩顶下，架着钟鼓。左钟右鼓，在祭祀时应仪式而敲响。也有些祠堂，如江西省婺源县汪口村的俞氏宗祠，把拜殿两侧次间前檐局部向前扩大一点，分别悬挂钟、鼓，再向前便与廊庑相接，有一只檐角向侧前方挑出。浙江省兰溪市诸葛村"敕建"的名臣诸葛亮的祠堂则在寝殿左右末间前各建敞开的一小间为钟鼓楼，上覆卷棚顶，外侧面用拉弓式硬山封火墙。江西省乐安县流坑村的董氏大宗祠在大门内两侧分别建造了独立的钟鼓楼。这种独立的钟鼓楼有些重在祠内观赏，有的则为宗祠的外观增添了极强的表情，但实例很少。

浙江省旧兰溪市境内，流行一种很独特的拜殿型制，叫"中庭"，专建于村内宗族的总祠（大宗祠）内。这就是把大宗祠的拜殿建成一个面阔、进深都是三开间的近于正方的建筑，几乎满满地塞在大院子里，四面却与其他建筑如前面的门屋、后面的寝室以及两侧的廊庑都没有连接，而且不置樘板，开敞如亭。例如诸葛村的丞相祠堂，里叶村、新叶村的叶氏大宗祠（西山祠堂），上唐村的李氏大宗祠，洞源村的赵氏大宗祠，西姜村的姜氏大宗祠等。这种中庭式的拜殿只供举行隆重的祭祀仪式，不设神橱，所以必有第三进寝室，正所谓"前庭后寝"。

通用的拜殿后檐墙为砖砌，中央明间设后门。从拜殿樘板两端下金柱后面的"耳门"可以达到樘板后面，再从后门出去通向后院。后院的正面是"寝室"，专供祖先神主。为了保护神主的绝对安全，有些宗祠在后院中央砌一道高高的横墙，隔开前后，为的是防火。例如江西婺源黄村的经义堂，它的寝室与拜殿之间相距有十一米左右，并隔一道高而且厚的砖墙。放神主的神橱往往是小木作的精品，花格细巧，雕刻生动。神橱的上方正中经常挂匾额，写"彝伦攸叙"、"祖德流芳"之类的颂词，金光灿烂。神橱前置香案，上陈烛台、香炉。香案前放些拜垫在地上，气氛肃穆庄严。神橱有门或无门，正中坐始迁祖的大神主牌，上雕二龙戏珠，左右雕升降龙镶边。在它左右，恭陈历代功宗德祖的神主。两个次间有几层台子供历代祖先神位，有时也建神橱加以装饰。神主多了，就在两侧的山墙前建台。再多，则把前院两厢都改做寝室，如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的大宗祠。一个宗族在一处定居很久，历代人丁兴旺，就会有许多神主，这种情况下每隔若干年就要把晚近几代的神主改写，合并十位左右先人在一块神主牌上，以减少神主牌总数。这个仪式叫做"祧"，和各家各户把高祖以上的神主送进宗祠合并统祭一样。

绝大多数的大宗祠，始迁祖神主左右合族祖先的神主都按昭穆次序排列。少数大宗祠，如福建省福安县楼下村的刘氏大宗，则沿两边山墙按房派分建神橱安置各房祖先神主，一房一个，不另外建房祠。福建连城县培田村的吴氏宗祠报德堂和敬承堂等，始祖神主右侧供奉"杨公先师"即江西派风水祖师杨筠松的神主。更特殊的是江西省乐安县流坑村，董氏大宗祠五间正寝里竟以西次间为"报功堂"，专门用来设龛奉祀杨筠松、曾文辿和廖瑀三位风水祖师的神主，地位在一般本族祖先之上。按照万历年间（1573—1620）董氏宗谱的记载，流坑村董氏的发达，首先是因为杨、曾二人给老祖宗选了上好坟地和上好村址。对风水师的礼敬感恩，这可能是规格最高的了。

神主多了，寝室容不下时，除了采用"祧"的办法外，还有些宗祠建两层楼的寝室，如江西省婺源县黄村的黄氏大宗祠"经义堂"，安徽歙县呈坎村东舒祠的宝纶阁。有的在两侧附建小院，如浙江省兰溪市桐山后金村的仁山书院（原为金氏大宗祠），跨院门上分别嵌石匾阴刻"左昭"、"右穆"额。

江西省乐安县流坑村，董氏大宗祠寝室楼上有"敕书阁"，恭存皇帝御书。董氏在宋代出过三十名进士，并有一名状元，御赐敕书当不在少数。

小一点的宗祠，例如普通的房祠、支祠，大都不建寝室，而在第二进拜殿里建神橱。不足时再扩大到厢间里。最小的宗祠则整个只有堂屋一间而已。

有极少数宗祠，在拜殿和寝室间沿中轴建一个宽宽的廊厅，使二者连接呈工字形。如浙江省建德市新叶村的崇仁堂和相距不远的永康县的一些宗祠。距新叶村数里的桐山后金村有两座金氏房祠型制极特别，拜殿和寝室连接成一个纵向的大厅，梁架和中轴线相垂直，完全与中国建筑内部为横向空间的传统相异，连村里《金氏宗谱》都写上一笔，表示不理解。

大宗祠大多在拜殿或寝室一侧有宽敞的厨房以便春秋大祭时烹煮祭品。厨房近才能保持祭品的洁净。

在南方各省，宗祠是村落里建筑艺术的亮点。就正立面说，比较简单的一种是三开间的明柱门屋，平稳而深沉。脊檩下设樘板，当心间开门，门枕石上立抱鼓石一对。前檐廊简洁明快，平脊明柱，也有一些在前檐柱间设签子门和签子栏杆，如江西省婺源县洪村的洪氏大宗祠。又一种是砖牌楼式，有单开间的，也有三间三楼式的。用水磨砖贴在大门正面的砖墙上，大多仿木构做法，如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的雍睦堂和"乡会两魁"祠。不但梁枋齐全，而且节点上麻叶头、雀替之类也一个不缺。柱子上部、枋子、垫板等处都布满浅浮雕，图案基本上仿彩画，把彩画浮雕化。檐下做细巧的砖雕斗拱或者多层镂空的细线脚，简单一点的做冰盘线，也有用四十五度斜出的砖砌成"狼牙"线脚的。江西省抚州地区，这种狼牙线可重叠三四层，有些门上，"狼牙"变形为曲面饱满的莲瓣形，显得很丰满。在江西省乐安县湖坪村和流坑村，有些砖牌楼用木材做斗拱，工艺上比较简易合理。复杂的纯装饰性斗拱大多交叉如网状，村人爱说，这种砖仿木式牌楼的祠堂大门是族里出了有大功名的人物的标志，所以中央有"恩荣"二字竖匾，上下枋之间书"荷宠凝庥"之类的谀辞。不过大多其实并没有这种"圣眷"的荣耀，为虚荣而假冒，反正也没有人来查处。

更加华丽辉煌的一种是木牌楼式的大门，一般为三间三楼或五楼式，也有更复杂的。木牌楼形式上是独立的，其实却和门屋连成一体。比较复杂的有江西省婺源县汪口村俞氏宗祠的牌楼式大门，三重屋顶，上两重为歇山式，最下一层为硬山式。它的网式斗拱斜出五跳。木构架上布满了浮雕和彩画，大多用说部或戏剧中的慈孝忠义情节为题材。檐柱间也设签子栏杆。婺源县黄村黄氏宗祠经义堂则正门柱子为石质，以上全部为木料，比例非常清秀。安徽省黟县南屏村叶氏宗祠有一个三间三楼式的木构牌楼门。门道左右有抱鼓石一对，门扉上绘全身屹立的武门神。浙江省兰溪市诸葛村诸葛亮的专祠"大公堂"的门屋，在明间由两棵柱子架起一个歇山顶和两只翼角，檐牙高啄，非常生动。更庄重古朴的木牌楼式的大门是浙江省永嘉县花坦村朱氏雍睦堂（即"乌府"）的大门，三开间，五楼式木架，斗拱十分雄健，真昂真拱，做法与宋代《营造法式》的相似。

小型祠堂，如广东省东莞市南社村的一些，它们只有门屋和正堂。三开间门屋的前檐大多用石质的明柱和梁架，但明间没有随梁。又有一些小型祠堂的大门，是个随墙门，上面略加一道砖门楣罢了，不过雕饰极为华丽，尤其在正脊上。进了随墙门，里面有个木架雨篷。这是当地气候的表现。

宗族里每出一位举人、进士，就在大宗祠大门前立一对木杆，叫做"桅"。桅杆上装"斗"，举人每杆一只，进士每杆两只。有些宗祠大门前隔不宽的前院有长长的照壁，这种情况下，桅杆会靠照壁内侧而立，如江西省婺源县洪村洪氏大宗祠光裕堂有七对桅杆，六对贴照壁，一对在前院西门前。不过它们的夹杆石上刻的多是奉政大夫、朝议大夫之类靠捐纳得来的虚衔，只有一对是恩科进士的，地位也不高。

有些大宗祠大门前布局十分辉煌。如江西省乐安县流坑村董氏大宗祠，在重檐歇山顶的三开间门屋之前有一个长方形的水池，叫墨池，池对岸有三间三楼式砖照壁（坊）一座。池的左右岸各有一座三间三楼式木牌楼。它们的外侧又各有一座三楼式砖牌坊。门屋和这五座牌楼（坊）形成大宗祠前的广场，排满了将近一百对桅杆，仅进士的便有三十对出头，读书郎真正是"光宗耀祖"了。门屋内侧又有钟鼓楼一对。这个大门建筑群层次多，轮廓丰富，彩色灿烂，形体变化大而和谐，在农村中极少见。浙江省青田县南田镇的明代开国功臣刘伯温专祠"文成庙"，庙门正对一座很长的影壁，形成一个横长的、略略封闭的小广场，广场左右作为入口各有一座三间三楼式木牌楼，东边的嵌《帝师》额，西边的嵌《王佐》额，牌楼高大，出檐深远，风格很凝重生严，显耀刘伯温的身份地位。
