8. Architecture of Ancestral Halls

The ancestral hall is a solemn ritual building. Its core typology evolved from residences. Residences vary endlessly due to living conditions; similarly, temples in mountains or by water have rich formal variation. Ancestral halls, while varying, change little—maintaining a functional, formulaic spatial composition and a dignified, orderly character.

Ancestral halls are venues for sacrifice. Hall rituals strictly follow procedures in 《朱文正公家礼》 (Zhu Wenzheng's Family Rituals), so the building itself—especially its central main part—follows a formula. Most halls have three parts, front to back: (1) gatehouse (大门门屋); (2) worship hall (拜殿/享堂), where sacrifice rituals occur; (3) sleeping chamber (寝室), named from "commoners sacrifice in the chamber" in 《礼记·王制》, dedicated to ancestral spirit tablets. 《光绪合肥邢氏家谱》 says: "The family temple is the ancestors' palace; even if modest, it must have three bays and two side wings: front gate, middle hall, rear chamber." Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall and Wangkou Village's Renben Hall, plus many Anhui/Zhejiang halls, follow this standard layout.

Smaller halls skip a separate chamber, placing spirit tablets in a shrine against the worship hall's rear wall. If insufficient, shrines are added before gable walls; if still insufficient, spirit tablets are merged—writing 10–20 ancestor names on one tablet, called "祧" (tiao). Sichuan 《云阳涂氏族谱·祠堂碑记》 clearly states: "Above, shrine hall for spirit tablets and zhao-mu order; middle, hall for descendants' reverent kneeling; front, reversed tower for receiving guests and reading imperial edicts; left/right wings for children studying." It enumerates all parts' functions. The shrine hall is the chamber, often with floor higher than the worship hall; the reversed tower is the gatehouse. This describes average-sized halls; larger ones build stages here.

Between the three bays are two courtyards with side corridors (廊庑). Some develop rear corridors into wing rooms also used as "chambers," divided into "left zhao, right mu" (左昭右穆) for ancestral tablets. Front corridors are partitioned into small rooms for clan administration—genealogy room, account room, elders' meeting room. 《云阳涂氏族谱》 stipulates their use as schools. All main and branch halls need a spacious kitchen for sacrificial food like sacrificial meat (胙肉).

Large, wealthy clans have halls with multiple public functions, making them complex. Beyond the core, attached buildings often include rear gardens, schools, charitable granaries (义仓), charitable mortuaries (义厝). A few, like Wuyi Yu源 Village's Yu clan hall, even attach orphanages and old-age homes.

The simplest branch-level halls have only gate and worship hall, with ancestral tablets in a shrine against the rear wall—no separate chamber, no front bay or side wings. Guangdong Pearl River Delta clans branched early, so halls are often this small type.

Larger halls build a stage in the gatehouse facing the worship hall; the front courtyard and side corridors become audience seating, sometimes with upper floors for women's viewing. Below, vendors set up food stalls during performances.

Le'an Liukeng Village (Jiangxi), said to be descendants of Han Confucian Dong Zhongshu, has the Dong main hall—a rare large hall built on Molan Isle north of the village, about 200m from the residential area. Facing south toward the village, backed by the Wujiang River flowing south-to-north then west. Entering the village from the hall passes through the Gongchen Gate on the village wall. Built outside the village,背对 the village's facing mountain with the river behind—this layout violates common fengshui doctrine. In fengshui-venerating Jiangxi (Yang Yunsong was Jiangxi native), the Dong hall's position may have had explanations, but none were recorded.

The Dong main hall plus two branch halls (left/right) form a complex: three buildings side by side, 90m east-west, 70+m north-south, 7,000 sqm total. The main hall is central; east is Guilin Hall (worshiping 16th-generation ancestor Dong Jimin); west is Guiyan Hall (later converted to literary school worshiping Confucius and Wenchang Emperor), with small study rooms for exam-preparing children. Before the three halls is shared public space forming a wide transverse courtyard. Center has a rectangular "ink pond" (墨池). East/west ends each have a three-bay brick archway: west arch "优入贤关" (outer) / "簪缨世第" (inner); east arch "理学名贤" (inner) / "科甲联芳" (outer). Both built in Kangxi era (1662–1722). Before the main hall is a three-bay archway-style brick gate with double eaves; central plaque front "厚德流光", back "文献世家". Side bays each have stone lions. Before the gate is the ink pond; south of pond is "追远" arch (commemorating ancestors). East/west of pond each have a wooden arch aligned with the brick arches: east "累朝师保", west "奕世科名"—showing off official and exam success. South wall has a screen wall with "累朝世家" in large characters.

Entering the "厚德流光" gate, left/right front courtyard have bell and drum towers.

The main hall has three bays: first "育贤楼" hall (three-bay double-eave), central plaque "宋赠大司徒董公大宗祠", east "祖孙台部", west "三世尚书". Second "敦睦堂" (three-bay double-eave), plaque "万殊一本". Third five-bay: central three bays two-story, upper "敕书阁"; lower central "孝敬堂", left/right by zhao-mu order "彰义堂", "报功堂", "宗原堂", "道原堂"—all with plaques. Yuxian and Dunmu halls have side wings: east worshiping "loyalty" (忠), "integrity" (廉); west "filial piety" (孝), "chastity" (节). By zhao-mu order: loyalty, filial piety, integrity, chastity. The hall is like a memorial to loyal ministers, righteous scholars, chaste women. Xiaojing, Zhangyi, Baogong halls first completed in Jiajing 40 (1565). Ming Dong Sui wrote 《彰义堂记》: "Central Xiaojing Hall worships official rank; left Zhangyi Hall worships righteousness; right Baogong Hall worships merit. Beyond these three, overall Dunmu Hall orders zhao-mu." Xiaojing worships officials; Baogong worships fengshui masters Yang Yunsong, Zeng Wenchan, Liao Yu. The Dong clan believed its prosperity came from these fengshui "masters" finding good grave and village sites. Zhangyi Hall specially worships clansmen who donated money/land for hall construction and sacrifices—standard: 10 taels per person, more money = better position. Dunmu worships all clan ancestors. Zongyuan and Daoyuan halls built later; Wanli 9 (1581) Dong Sui wrote: "Daoyuan Hall specially worships Dong Zhongshu, tracing our Dong clan's Confucian origin... Zongyuan Hall specially worships Qingran-gong ancestors... honoring the beginning." Dong Zhongshu (Han dynasty) is revered as Dong surname ancestor; Qingran-gong is the ancestor who moved to Yihuang, Jiangxi. Thus the main hall is also a clan tradition education exhibition hall—commemoration and education matching Liukeng's historical character. Dunmu Hall has a couplet:

With ancestors' heart as heart, seek fortune yourself;
If not following ancient kings' laws, what face to enter here.

This reveals the hall's educational function.

Notably, "righteousness" in Zhangyi Hall means donating money/land to the clan. Those worshiped are large merchants or landlords—just as one can obtain empty titles like "大夫" or "司马" through donation without exams, one can enter a special hall through donation and enjoy eternal honor. This reflects late-Ming commercial economic development in the middle-lower Yangtze; one ideological manifestation was breaking through feudal clan ethics. Late Ming, many Liukeng villagers grew wealthy through grain transport and timber.

As solemn ritual buildings, halls have little layout variation, but variants exist. Guangzhou Chen clan hall: beyond the central axis's five-bay halls and courtyards, left/right each have a courtyard-hall route, three bays each—total nine halls, six courtyards. Three routes separated only by open corridors; outermost have side rooms. Eighteen buildings total (halls, wings, study rooms), 13,200 sqm—rarely matched in spacious openness.

Yongjia Yantou Village's Guilin Gong Hall, converted from an academy, has a large pond before the worship hall with a central square pavilion; a bridge from the ceremonial gate (仪门) through the pavilion to the worship hall. Outside the ceremonial gate is another pond; after entering the main gate, one circles the pond to reach the ceremonial gate. Very individual layout.

North China historically had frequent warfare, few stable powerful clans—so villages are mostly mixed-surname, some small clans with few people. Hence few ancestral halls, especially large ones. Village management often by geographic or trade-based "associations" (社). Public activities held in temples. The smallest halls are merely one small room with ancestor names written on walls and a small incense stand in the center—e.g., Yu County Songjiazhuang's Su clan hall, just one tiny room.

Main hall gatehouses generally have stages. Wealthy villages' branch and sub-branch halls also have stages. Gatehouse stages have three main types: (1) entirely within the gatehouse's central bay; (2) half protruding into the hall beyond the central bay; (3) fully protruding with high upturned wing corners in front, backstage in the gatehouse central bay. Type 3 allows viewing from three sides, less stage-audience separation. Type 1 blocks the main gate—on ordinary days and performance days, only side doors open; on special days (ancestor worship, spirit tablet installation), the central movable stage planks are removed for passage. Types 2 and 3: enter through central main gate, go left/right around the stage to the worship hall.

Dressing rooms usually in the gatehouse side bays' mezzanine, with small wooden stairs from the waiting area behind the stage's taishi wall.

Between waiting area and front stage is a board wall (taishi wall) called "守旧" (shoujiu), usually painted with 《唐明皇游月宫》 (Emperor Minghuang Visiting the Moon Palace). Emperor Minghuang (Tang Xuanzong) mastered music, loved song and dance, personally trained opera troupes in the palace Pear Garden—hence revered as opera's patron god, "老郎神" (Old Master God). The Moon Palace story is romantic: Bai Juyi's poem recounts Minghuang fleeing Sichuan during An Lushan rebellion; Yang Guifei forced to suicide by the army—"the emperor covered his face, could not save, turned back, tears and blood flowing together." After peace, Minghuang missed her day and night. Daoist Ye Fashan conjured him to the Moon Palace to meet the immortalized Yang Guifei. They vowed: "In heaven,愿 be birds flying wing to wing; on earth,愿 be trees with branches intertwined." Highly dramatic, hence often painted on the "守旧" wall.

Above "守旧" hangs a horizontal plaque praising performances—usually "金声玉振", "作古振今", "翻风弄月"—formulaic.

"守旧" sides are entrance and exit doors, plaques usually "出将" (generals emerge) and "入相" (ministers enter). Some more ornate but same meaning. Stage sides and front edge have tiny one-foot-high railings protecting actors; railing post tops have carved qilin and other auspicious beasts. Some halls, e.g., Yongjia Furong Village's Chen clan hall, attach a small platform left-rear of the stage for the orchestra.

Stages are often masterpieces of small woodwork, carving, and painting. First, above the stage, deep caissons (藻井) for acoustics (拔音/拢音)—caisson styles abound, carpenters competing in creativity. Yongjia village halls often use octagonal inverted-pyramid caissons with golden-flowing bracket sets (溜金斗拱) rising along eight internal corners and eight center lines—long brackets like flowing clouds, lingzhi mushrooms, gracefully curving. Ninghai rural stages have varied caissons; most vivid is "百鸟朝凤" (folk: "鸡笼顶"/chicken-cage top), spiral upward pattern—vital momentum echoing theatrical excitement. Some caissons fully covered in bright paintings, "开光盒子" theatrical scenes exquisitely realistic. Second, stage front edge: a long wood carving on the main beam, themes all theatrical plots—this carving is where master carvers shine. Sichuan calls this long carved board "照面枋" (face-facing beam)—facing the audience, hence specially crafted for public appraisal.

Leping County (Jiangxi): every village hall has a stage, some villages several; over 300 stages survived the Cultural Revolution. Leping stages have distinctive typologies, carved beams and painted pillars, extremely ornate—almost everywhere carved, every carving gilded—dazzling golden light.

Stage front-eave pillars, "台柱" (stage pillars), always bear couplets. Some situational and plain: "Watching, it seems so; thinking, perhaps so." Some reflective:

One tune of Shang music, performing millennia of rise and fall;
Several notes of Yue melody, revealing a century of parting and reunion.

Another:

Steps change form, don't say favor and disgrace are all false;
Brows painted, corners drawn—know joy and anger are all real.

Above the stage mouth, horizontal plaques usually "普天同庆" (universal celebration), "盛世纶音" (prosperous era's edict)—festive phrases.

Audience positions per hall rules: men in courtyard, women under worship hall front eaves, bringing stools. Side corridors also women's viewing. Some Shanxi/Jiangxi/Sichuan halls have viewing towers on side corridors: left "men's tower", right "women's tower"—for "respectable families."

Ming-Qing pedantic Confucians considered performances harmful to morals. Ming Lao Yizhai in 《瓯江逸志》 criticized: during performances, "ten+ days day/night viewing, men and women mixed." Qing Daoguang-Xianfeng (1821–1861) Yongjia magistrate Tang Chenglie in 《县志稿》: "festivals lavish on gods... men and women viewing, ornate dress, filling city and suburbs, officials cannot ban." Wanting to ban but unable, dissatisfied. This elite conservatism influenced village leaders—hence gender-segregated viewing, with 60+ elders patrolling the audience, rapping disrespectful young men with long tobacco pipes.

Most villages build stages only in main hall gatehouses facing the worship hall. But some build stages in the square outside the hall gate, facing the hall. Some villages, e.g., Liancheng Peitian (Fujian), stage position/orientation are irregular—even the gate position is irregular. During performances, neighboring villagers come; vendors of snacks and sundries set up stalls before the hall or stage side corridors, forming a temporary market. Protecting village internal safety and tranquility is one reason most villages build the main hall at the village edge rather than the core.

A few halls have detachable stages—e.g., Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall. Jiande Xinye Village's Chongren Hall (Zhi-zi branch) also has a detachable stage; wooden components stored in the hall, assembled on the pond surface before the gate when needed. Called "雨台" (rain stage) or "露台" (open terrace). Water-town Shaoxing (Zhejiang) has stages built on water before the hall, far from shore; villagers arrive by boat, boats moored before the stage. From start to end, chaotic but lively—villagers enjoy it more. Pedantic scholars believed women watching from their own boats helped protect morals.

Some Shanxi counties build 2–3 stages side by side in temples, close together—viewing greatly interfered, but villagers love it. Viewing is ultimately about excitement.

South is rainy; some stages have large halls or open pavilions for audience rain shelter. E.g., Fuzhou Wanshou Palace (Jiangxi): one large hall fills the courtyard. Some Ninghai halls build tall open pavilions in the stage-front courtyard, extending longitudinally along the center—2 to 3 bays, each with a caisson on top, exquisitely detailed.

The hall's second bay is the worship hall (拜殿/享堂). Commoners' halls: worship hall generally three bays per regulation, but five-bay exists. Special figures like Zhuge Liang (in state sacrificial canon) have five-bay halls. Shexian Chengkan Village's Dongshu Hall worship hall is also five-bay: 26.5m wide, 22.5m deep—very spacious. In the south, the worship hall's front eaves are fully open. This is where sacrifice rituals occur—the most spectacular space. High and bright, with massive timber frames and carved decoration.

The worship hall is actually a display room of clan historical achievements and honors, a memorial hall promoting clan unity and development. Its beams are covered with large plaques praising clansmen's exam success, virtue, longevity—e.g., "贡元", "进士", "叙伦", "乡贤", "父子柱史", "宗德流芳", "厚德载福", "承天宠锡", "耆英厚望", "祖泽缉熙"—all showing off "glorifying ancestors" figures/events, brilliant colors inspiring worshiping clansmen.

Pillars bear couplets of varied content. Illustrious clans always have a long couplet: upper line recounts ancestors' merits, virtue, fame; lower line praises migration from founding ancestor to settlement. E.g., Lanxi Zhuge Village's Dagong Hall:

Since Han dynasty, worshiped in Confucian temple, as village worthy, as famous official, as loyal/filial/righteous/chaste—many transmitters, history records our surname;
After moving to Zhejiang, through Shaoxing, Shouchang, Changcun, Nantang Water Pavilion—here established, genealogy proves our origin.

Yongjia Heyang Village (Xie Lingyun descendants) Xulun Hall:

Jiangzuo traces family fame, Feishui victory, achievements still illuminate history;
Oudong continues generation grace, pond spring grass, poetic talent eternally valued in Confucian circles.

Clans without illustrious historical figures write about migration process, current prosperity, village harmony/order—e.g., Jiande Xinye Village's Youxu Hall:

Migrated from Hangzhou/Muzhou/Shouchou, clan pure and auspicious, this land settled as homeland;
Descendants through Song/Yuan/Ming, books and poetry continue, ancestors' success praised at Yuhua.

Hunan Huitong Gaoyi Village main hall main couplet:

Ancestor virtue opens grand plan, recalling ancestors' brothers migrating to two districts;
Descendants' plans bless, future generations multiply through millennia.

The worship hall's central bay rear golden pillars usually have a "tang board" (樘板) that opens/closes like doors. When inviting or installing ancestral spirit tablets (needing access to the rear chamber), the board is opened. During sacrifice, it's closed; on it hang portraits of the founding ancestor and distinguished ancestors—called "祖容" (ancestor countenance) in some places, "图" (picture) in the north. Above the tang board usually hangs the hall name plaque—"敦睦堂", "崇恩堂", "德馨堂", etc. The thematic long couplet hangs on the rear golden pillars flanking the tang board. There, light is dim; couplets and plaques have black backgrounds with gold-leaf text, gleaming—very solemn.

Some Zhejiang/Jiangxi main halls use four wood types for the worship hall's front/rear golden pillar pairs: cypress (柏), catalpa (梓), tung (桐), toon (椿)—homophone "百子同春" (hundreds of children, same spring), auspicious for descendant prosperity—what worshiped ancestors care most about. Wuyuan Huang Village's Huang main hall uses bluestone and white stone plinths under left/right front golden pillars, symbolizing "left azure dragon, right white tiger"—rare but not unique.

In the worship hall's two side bays, under the xu ceiling between front golden and front eave pillars, hang bell and drum. Left bell, right drum—struck during sacrifice rituals. Some halls, e.g., Wuyuan Wangkou Yu clan hall, slightly extend the side-bay front eaves forward to hang bell/drum, then connect to corridors with one eave corner projecting side-forward. Lanxi Zhuge Village's "imperially built" Zhuge Liang hall builds open small rooms as bell/drum towers before the寝殿's end bays, with curved-roof (卷棚顶) tops and bow-style gable fire walls on outer sides. Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall builds independent bell/drum towers inside the gate's two sides. Some independent towers focus on interior viewing; others strongly enhance the hall's exterior appearance—but examples are few.

Old Lanxi (Zhejiang) area has a unique worship hall typology called "中庭" (central courtyard), built only in village main halls. The worship hall is built as a near-square building (three bays wide × three bays deep), almost filling the large courtyard, but disconnected from all other buildings (front gatehouse, rear chamber, side corridors)—no tang board, open like a pavilion. Examples: Zhuge Village's Prime Minister Hall, Liye/Xinye Ye main hall (Xishan Hall), Shangtang Li main hall, Dongyuan Zhao main hall, Xijiang Jiang main hall. This "central-courtyard" worship hall only hosts grand sacrifice rituals, no shrine—hence must have a third-bay chamber, so-called "front court, rear chamber."

The standard worship hall's rear eave wall is brick, central bay has rear door. From "ear doors" behind the tang board's lower golden pillars, one reaches behind the tang board, exits through the rear door to the back courtyard. The courtyard's front is the "chamber" (寝室) for ancestral spirit tablets. To protect tablets' absolute safety, some halls build a high transverse wall in the back courtyard separating front/rear—for fire prevention. E.g., Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall: chamber and worship hall ~11m apart, separated by a high thick brick wall. Spirit tablet shrines (神橱) are often small-woodwork masterpieces—delicate lattice, vivid carving. Above the shrine center usually hangs a plaque: "彝伦攸叙", "祖德流芳"—golden and brilliant. Before the shrine: incense table with candlesticks and incense burner. Before the table: kneeling cushions on the floor—solemn atmosphere. Shrines may have doors or not; center holds the founding ancestor's large spirit tablet, carved with two dragons playing a pearl, flanked by ascending/descending dragon borders. Beside it: reverently placed tablets of meritorious ancestors. Two side bays have tiered platforms for ancestral tablets, sometimes with shrines. More tablets → platforms before side gable walls. Even more → convert front courtyard's two wings to chambers, e.g., Lanxi Zhuge Village's main hall. A clan settled long with prosperous generations accumulates many tablets; every several years, recent generations' tablets are rewritten, merging ~10 ancestors per tablet to reduce total. This ritual is "祧" (tiao)—same as households sending great-great-grandfather+ tablets to the hall for merged collective worship.

Most main halls arrange founding ancestor and all clan ancestors' tablets by zhao-mu order. A few, e.g., Fu'an Louxia Village's Liu main hall, build separate shrines along both gable walls by branch—one per branch, no separate branch halls. Liancheng Peitian Village's Wu clan halls (Baode, Jingcheng) place "Yang Gong Xianshi" (Jiangxi fengshui founder Yang Yunsong) tablet to the right of the founding ancestor. Most special: Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall's five-bay chamber uses the west side bay as "报功堂" (Merit-Reporting Hall), with shrines worshiping fengshui founders Yang Yunsong, Zeng Wenchan, Liao Yu—status above ordinary clan ancestors. Per Wanli-era (1573–1620) Dong genealogy: Liukeng Dong's prosperity first came from Yang and Zeng selecting excellent grave and village sites for ancestors. Reverence and gratitude to fengshui masters—possibly the highest规格.

When tablets exceed chamber capacity, besides "祧", some halls build two-story chambers—e.g., Wuyuan Huang Village's "经义堂", Shexian Chengkan Dongshu Hall's Baolun Pavilion. Some attach side courtyards—e.g., Lanxi Tongshan Houjin Village's Renshan Academy (formerly Jin main hall), with stone plaques "左昭" and "右穆" on cross-courtyard gates.

Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall's chamber upper floor has "敕书阁" (Imperial Edict Pavilion) storing imperial documents. The Dong clan produced 30 jinshi and one zhuangyuan in Song—imperial edicts certainly numerous.

Smaller halls (ordinary branch/sub-branch) mostly skip the chamber, building shrines in the second-bay worship hall. If insufficient, expand to side rooms. Smallest halls are just one hall room.

Very few halls build a wide corridor hall along the central axis between worship hall and chamber, connecting them in an I-shape (工字形). E.g., Jiande Xinye Village's Chongren Hall and some Yongkang halls. Several kilometers from Xinye, Tongshan Houjin Village has two Jin branch halls with extremely special typology: worship hall and chamber connected into one longitudinal hall, with beam frames perpendicular to the central axis—completely contrary to Chinese architecture's traditional transverse interior space. Even the village 《金氏宗谱》 notes it with incomprehension.

Main halls usually have a spacious kitchen beside the worship hall or chamber for cooking sacrifices during spring/autumn grand rituals. Proximity keeps sacrificial food clean.

In southern provinces, ancestral halls are the highlight of village architectural art. Regarding the front facade: simplest is three-bay exposed-pillar gatehouse—steady and deep. Under the ridge purlin: tang board; central bay has door; door sill stones have a pair of drum-shaped stones (抱鼓石). Front eave corridor simple and bright, flat ridge, exposed pillars; some have lattice doors and railings between front eave pillars—e.g., Wuyuan Hong Village's Hong main hall. Another type: brick archway (砖牌楼)—single-bay or three-bay three-story. Water-polished bricks applied to the gate's front brick wall, mostly imitating wood structure—e.g., Lanxi Zhuge Village's Yongmu Hall and "乡会两魁" Hall. Not only complete beams and brackets, but also node details like hemp-leaf heads (麻叶头) and sparrow brackets (雀替). Pillar tops, beams, backing boards covered in low-relief carving, patterns basically imitating painted decoration (浮雕化彩画). Under eaves: delicate brick-carved bracket sets or multi-layer openwork line moldings; simpler ones do ice-disk lines; some use 45-degree斜出 bricks forming "wolf-tooth" (狼牙) moldings. Fuzhou area: wolf-tooth moldings can stack 3–4 layers; some gates transform "wolf teeth" into full curved lotus-petal shapes, very plump. Le'an Huping and Liukeng villages: some brick archways use wooden bracket sets—simpler and more reasonable工艺. Complex purely decorative bracket sets mostly cross like nets; villagers say this brick-imitating-wood archway gate marks a clan with highly successful exam candidates—hence central "恩荣" (imperial grace) vertical plaque, between upper/lower beams text like "荷宠凝庥". But most actually lacked such "imperial favor" glory—faking for vanity, anyway no one investigates.

More ornate: wooden archway gate (木牌楼)—usually three-bay three-story or five-story, sometimes more complex. Formally independent, actually integrated with the gatehouse. Complex example: Wuyuan Wangkou Yu clan hall's archway gate—three roof tiers, upper two xieshan (歇山) style, lowest hard-gable (硬山) style. Net-style bracket sets project five tiers diagonally. Timber frame covered in relief and painting, mostly themes of filial piety, loyalty, righteousness from novels or drama. Eave pillars also have lattice railings. Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall: gate pillars stone, above all wood—very elegant proportions. Yixian Nanping Village's Ye clan hall has a three-bay three-story wooden archway gate. Gate sides have drum stones; doors painted with full-body standing warrior door gods. Lanxi Zhuge Village's Zhuge Liang专祠 "Dagong Hall" gatehouse: central bay two pillars support a xieshan roof and two wing corners, eaves high and vivid—very lively. More solemn and ancient: Yongjia Huatan Village's Zhu clan Yongmu Hall ("乌府") gate—three-bay five-story wooden frame, bracket sets very robust, true ang (真昂) and true arch (真拱), construction similar to Song 《营造法式》.

Small halls, e.g., some in Dongguan Nanshe Village, have only gatehouse and main hall. Three-bay gatehouse front eaves mostly use stone exposed pillars and beams, but central bay has no following beam. Some small halls' gates are wall-attached doors (随墙门) with a slight brick lintel above—but carving extremely ornate, especially on the main ridge. Inside the wall door: a wooden-frame awning. This reflects local climate.

Each time a clan produces a juren or jinshi, a pair of wooden poles is erected before the main hall gate—called "桅" (mast). Masts carry "斗" (dou): juren one per pole, jinshi two per pole. Some halls with long screen walls in a narrow front courtyard have masts leaning against the screen wall's inner side—e.g., Wuyuan Hong Village's Hong main hall Guangyu Hall has seven mast pairs: six against the screen wall, one before the front courtyard's west gate. However, their mast-holding stones mostly刻 empty titles like "奉政大夫", "朝议大夫" obtained through donation; only one pair is from a special-exam jinshi, status not high.

Some main halls have brilliant front layouts. E.g., Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall: before the double-eave xieshan three-bay gatehouse is a rectangular pond (ink pond); opposite the pond, a three-bay three-story brick screen wall (archway). Pond's left/right banks each have a three-bay three-story wooden archway. Outside those, each has a three-story brick archway. The gatehouse plus these five archways form a square before the main hall, lined with nearly 100 mast pairs—over 30 for jinshi alone. Scholars truly "glorify ancestors." Inside the gatehouse: a pair of bell/drum towers. This gate complex has many layers, rich silhouette, brilliant colors, large yet harmonious formal variation—rare in rural areas. Qingtian Nantian Town's Liu Bowen (Ming founding minister)专祠 "Wencheng Temple": temple gate faces a long screen wall, forming a long, slightly enclosed small square; left/right entrances each have a three-bay three-story wooden archway—east with 《帝师》 (Imperial Tutor) plaque, west with 《王佐》 (Royal Assistant) plaque. Archways tall, deep eaves, style solemn and dignified—showing Liu Bowen's status.

sections.name: 文教建筑与科举
sections.content_zh:
一、文教建筑与科举

中国人热爱读书。无分南北，也无分城乡，稍稍整齐一点的人家，大门门扇上最常见的一副对联是"忠孝传家久，诗书继世长"，堂屋里最常见的两副对联则是"数百年旧家无非积德，第一等好事还是读书"和"一等人忠臣孝子，两件事耕田读书"。条案中央供着一块朱漆描金的神牌，上面写的是"天地君亲师"，香火四季不断。天地撇开不论，现实世界上，"师"仅居"君、亲"之后，地位很高了。

其实，激发中国人读书热情的，主要是科举制度，就是隋唐以后"学而优则仕"这一条大家都可以走一走的道路；其次是商业的发展。主要不是由于要积德济世，也不是要格物致知。

乡土社会中，村里的文教建筑大多和科举有关。一类是教学用的，如社学、义塾、家塾、书馆之类，主要用于基础教育。又有文馆，是上了年纪的读书人淡出功名，以文会友，切磋学问的场所，也是他们定期考核本村子弟为功名而学习的情况的场所。另一类是旌表科考成就用的，明代以往，考中了进士可以立牌坊、竖"桅"、造"进士第"。后来举人也有竖桅甚至立牌坊的了。又一类是崇祀用的，如文昌阁（魁星楼）、文峰塔、文笔、焚帛炉，用来祈求宗族和个人的文运。此外，稍大一点的庙宇多有几间房子、一所别院给读书人住下来安心准备考试。少数村子还有文庙，文庙和宗祠就可能有房子给少年人读书。一些村落有藏书楼、书斋之类，往往是科名有成，当了几年官，晚年致仕退食的人们造来读书作画待客用的。有些没有功名的商人，老来也会造一所小院幽斋做书屋，以颐养天年。宋元时期，个别地区，如江西，有书院供学者聚徒讲学，探究义理，但对乡土社会影响不大。

文教建筑多的地方，大多就是科举成绩比较突出的地方，所谓文风鼎盛之乡，领头的是苏南、浙江，后面有江西、福建、皖南、广东、两湖。这些地区，一来是商业经济发达，经济既是科举成就的背后支柱，也是文教建筑得以普及的依靠；二来是宗族的结构和管理制度稳固有力，子弟读书已经成了传统。

科举主要是朝廷的取士制度，所以民间启蒙诗里有句："天子重英豪，文章教儿曹"，它始于隋代，明代以后，措施已经十分完备，但科举同时也是平民百姓进仕的制度，为了扶掖和激励本族子弟读书以登上青云之路，宗族用公产兴学、助读、贴补赴考的费用，高低中了个功名，就给以很高的荣誉和实际的奖励。是宗族接续和完成了朝廷的科举制度，助它普及，产生巨大的影响。乡土社会中的文教建筑，绝大部分是宗族兴建的。凡宗族结构破坏的地方，科举成就便很差，文教建筑也必寥寥。

然而，经济发达和宗族关系稳定的地方未必就一定有比较高的科举成绩，如晋中和皖南，从明代起，到清代出了一大批长袖善舞、经营四方的商人，但那里的科举成绩并不很好。到了清末，每况愈下，以致清·刘大鹏《退想斋日记》说山西太谷风气，"视读书甚轻，视商业为甚重，才华秀美之子弟，率皆出门为商，而读书者寥寥无几，甚且有既游庠序竟弃儒就商者，亦谓读书之士，多受饥寒，曷若为商之多得银钱，俾家道之丰裕也。"浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的《高隆诸葛氏宗谱》里给一个商人立传，这位商人有话说："与其读万卷之书，孰若积千金之产。"千余年的价值观被颠倒过来了。经商有了钱还可以不经十年寒窗而花钱买个虚衔爵位，清代朝廷为了敛钱，"大夫"、"司马"之类的衔头，都有明码标价。

科举就是通过定期考试，从读书人中选拔各级文职官员的制度。

隋代之前，两汉和魏晋南北朝时期，官员的选任完全由强宗豪门把持，弊端丛生；世袭的豪强更有势力威胁最高统治者的地位，有碍真正人才的发现和提拔，形成社会阶级分野的僵化以致容易发生动乱。

为了克服这些弊端，隋代开始试行由地方官员荐举人才经中央考试之后从中选拔官员的办法。以后历代都有改进，形成了影响重大的科举制度。

科举制度的特点，也便是它的优点，就是把进仕的途径向全社会开放，公平竞争，避免了强势阶层对官职的垄断，而给弱势阶层以平等的机会。除了极少数"贱民"（如浙江的堕民，广东的疍民）、操"贱业"的人（如娼、优、皂隶、乐户）、犯了罪的人、居父母丧的人、罢闲官吏等之外，只要户籍有据，学历合格，原则上人人可以应试，而且考试的方法和管理很严密，防范了不公平的事情发生。

进仕途径向全社会开放，对专制统治者来说，第一个好处是虽然不能做到"野无遗贤"，朝廷毕竟得以网罗一些杰出人才担任各级官员，加强政府效能。隋唐以后，历代名臣贤相都自科举出身，所以唐代贞观初年（627—632），太宗李世民在进士放榜之日于皇宫的端门上观望，见新科进士陆续出来，对侍臣们说："天下英雄入吾彀中矣！"非常高兴。

向庶民开放的科举制度大大促进了全中国文化教育的普及。读书成为一种社会风尚。"为父兄者以其子与弟不文为咎，为母妻者以其子与夫不学为辱"，甚至有人提出了"读书人人有份"的主张。科举制度大盛之时，正逢中国雕版印刷普及。雕版印刷从唐末成熟，宋代达于完美，有了这一项技术，书籍得来比较容易，比较廉价，更为科举制度推波助澜。

科举考试吸引了大批社会精英，使他们埋头于官方设定的知识范围中"皓首穷经"，"两耳不闻窗外事，一心只读圣贤书，"以致整个社会都专注于科考，社会"科举化"了。北宋真宗皇帝写了一首著名的《劝学诗》，影响久远。诗道：

富家不用买良田，书中自有千钟粟。安房不用架高梁，书中自有黄金屋。娶妻莫恨无良媒，书中有女颜如玉。出门莫恨无人随，书中车马多如簇。男儿欲遂平生志，六经勤向窗前读。

汉武帝时候董仲舒建议的"罢黜百家，独尊儒术"，经过一千年左右，直到科举时代才在"粟"、"屋"、"玉"、"车"的引诱下真正落实到全社会。孙承泽说："夫科目之设，天下之士群趋而奔向之。上意所向，风俗随之，人才之高下，士风之醇漓，率由是出。"通过科考，"上意"引领了风俗，影响了士子们的知识范围和眼界。

科举成功首先是个人可以获得许多好处。明末清初的学者计六奇在《明季北略》中写道："常见青衿子，朝不谋夕，一叨乡荐便无穷举人，及登甲科，遂钟鸣鼎食，肥马轻裘，非数百万则数十万，……彼且身无赋，产无徭，田无粮，物无税，且庇护奸民之赋、徭、粮、税，其入之正未艾也。"

明、清时期，举人就是正途出身，已经有资格做官了，一般做个县里的官学教习之类，也有机会被"大挑"为知县。一旦中了进士，就脱离了"百姓"阶层，享有许多政治经济特权，例如全家可免赋税、徭役。进士有可能任高官，明清时期，进士大多先被选入翰林院，翰林院是高官的储备处，凡任中枢机构高官的，必出自翰林。清代，大学士都从翰林中选任，另一部分翰林到各部当主事，小部分下放地方任知县，不须候补，并有比较多的机会升迁。

明、清两代，科第高中者还更有一种长远意义的荣耀，这就是可以在家乡建牌坊、立桅杆，祠堂里挂匾。明初洪武二十一年（1388年），任亨泰中了状元，太祖朱元璋下令用官帑在任亨泰家乡湖北襄阳起造一座牌坊以旌表他的成就。这大约是第一座科名牌坊，从此以后，科名牌坊和桅杆就渐渐在各地流行起来，并且下及于举人。明中叶成化、弘治朝，甚至还给以前没有建牌坊的进士补建。后来，进士们的父亲和祖父可以在获得皇帝诰封和驰封之后也造相同式样的牌坊。这些牌坊大多造在州县城里，以致到了明代晚期万历朝（1573—1620）时候，许多州县城里已经是科第牌坊林立了。由于造牌坊的费用很大，从清代嘉庆朝（1796—1820）起不再用公帑建造，但科名牌坊数量并不见少，因为宗族情愿出钱建造。

沈德符在《万历野获编》里说：万历初年申时入阁，吴县地方官府给他竖立"状元宰辅"大旗，高高悬在他家门上。此后迅速传了开来，连"诸生出贡，皆高竿大旗，飘摇云汉，每入城市，弥望不绝"，而"鼎甲及得选庶常（入选翰林）者，复另植黄竿，另张大旗，比乡、会更加数倍。"

一个"田舍郎"，经过刻苦攻读，取得考试的成功，便能登上"天子堂"，达到如此辉煌的境地，这是对每一个有读书可能性的人的极大诱惑，激发了平头白丁奔向举业。

宗族为了全族的共同利益，支持有志的青少年读书，纷纷创办学塾，造成文化在农村的大普及。以致很穷困的小山村也有些有学塾，如浙江永嘉一个很小的村子叫林坑，村的西南角山坡上有一个小小的"学堂"，它的楼板之下是牛棚。山西省吕梁市山区有一个非常偏僻的窑洞村叫陈家塄，很小，但是一进村门，就有一幢挂着乾隆时期老匾的三合院，曾是书塾。散布在黄土峭壁之上的另一个窑洞村彩家庄，竟有两间小小的平房，它们是村子的学塾。那是在一次地震引起黄土峭壁崩塌的全村大灾难之后，重建村落时选了最安全的地点造起来的，时间大约在清代中叶。

科举制度也对少数民族开放，促进了他们文化的普及。例如，湖南省西南角上汉、侗、苗多民族杂居的会同县高椅村《杨氏族谱·八景诗》中有两首诗是写学馆的，其一是："一村几个读书堂，起凤腾蛟各有光，附近教人眠不得，五更犹听诵文章。"诗写得很真切。

科举制度大大提高了普遍的文化水平，意义就不仅仅限于个人或者宗族的成败了。

一个人中了举人进士，能给整个宗族带来很大的利益，所以，在科举时代，宗族总是鼓励和支持子弟们读书的。宗族鼓励和支持子弟读书应试，是接续和完成了朝廷创设的科举制度，是科举制度得以成功的重要条件，它几乎是这个制度的组成部分。

南宋淳佑十年（1250年），浙江省温州昆阳凤凰山的《宜都陈氏家乘序》一开头就写道：

温之昆阳，大族为多，而门第之赫奕，子姓之繁昌，则未有加于陈氏者也。盖门第之赫奕实由于子姓之繁昌。藉使徒繁昌而无贤哲之士，其欲门第之赫奕者，宁可得乎？陈氏自李唐迁居昆阳，其子姓登文科、武科、特科及补入太学、请漕试，与夫勉解、进纳、边赏、荫叙者不啻百有余人，此门第所以赫奕而非他族所能加也。

这个陈氏宗族之所以"赫奕"，重要原因之一是有子姓登科。所以，清代光绪十六年（1890年）安徽《寿州龙氏宗谱·家规》里有一项《务读书》：

士农与工商，读书为第一。勿偷闲，勿贪嬉，愤发以前在勉力。俸禄享千钟，黄金收万镒，皆从读书苦中来，一寸光阴宜自惜。

凡我族人，期于克振家声，宜从诗书上苦心著力。天下惟读书人不可限量！云梯千里，凤翮九霄，上为父祖增光，下为子孙创业，岂独一身荣显已哉！切莫浮慕无实，图侥幸以获功名，庶为有志之士。

这一项不但讲了许多读书人可能获得的好处，还从宗族的整体利益上着眼来衡量子弟读书的好处，许许多多的宗谱都有类似的教训和规定。安徽黟县关麓村汪氏支祠有一副楹联，写的是："一水护田，常看秋敛春耕，俾小子先知稼穑；五经堆案，更喜夏萤冬雪，助后人永守诗书。"这便是耕读社会中宗族对子弟的期望。

除了一般的鼓励，宗族采取了许多具体实在的措施，以支持子弟读书并参加科考。这些措施中最普遍的有：设村塾和义塾，聘明师，资助贫寒而有志的子弟学习，建文馆，定期举办文会，提供学子参加科举考试的费用，给科考成功的子弟以物质的和荣誉的奖励，等等。一切费用都由族中公有的膏火田（即学田）的收入来支出。这是民间对科举制度的呼应、补充和完成。

清代同治十一年（1872年），浙江省镇海县方氏族内一些比较富裕而"家有余赀"的人，"慨然有志于赡族之举"，他们采取的赡族办法是创办一所义塾。创办之初，订立了一篇《义塾规则》，写得非常具体详尽，比较重要的有：

本堂设立义塾，为族内无力延师者陶教子弟。其师由本堂聘请，修金即由本堂送奉。凡来就学者，概无须出赀。

塾中有才质迈众，学可造就而其家或无力卒业者，本堂自当另行筹酌助给书资。

无力之家或并笔墨书纸等不能自具，先行告明登册，本堂备给。

义塾是宗族为贫寒子弟开设的，少数由富裕人家捐田创办。有钱人家自办"专馆"，就是一家人家延师设馆，专教家里的子弟。这些"专馆"的师资会好一点，多是在乡里有名气的老塾师。还有一种"散馆"，由几家人合资聘师教习子弟。还有"家塾"和"私塾"，或叫"座馆"，是老师在自己家里设馆，各家送子弟来学习，老师酌情收取学资。

有些村子，出公积建造很好的学堂，如山西省临县孙家沟村，位置很偏僻，地势很局促，农田不多，却在村口最美的高地上建了一座很漂亮的学塾。村民在极窘迫的情况下，把摆脱穷困的希望都寄托在孩子的读书成绩上了。

凡参加科考的，宗族继续予以鼓励支持。例如同治十三年（1874年）本《东粤宝安南头黄氏族谱·族规》里有详细规定：

童生有县名应府试者，每名给花银二两。
童生有府名应院试者，每名给花银三元。
生员有志科考等第，每名给花银二元。
文武生员及贡、监考遗才者，每名给花银二元。

以上是资助科考费用的。赴考乡试、会试的，往往在府县的"宾兴馆"（聚贤馆）会合之后集体出发，由府县出资补助。但大多数宗族仍旧自行出资补助，数额也写在《族规》里。

考试成功的，宗族有奖励。例如，这个《东粤宝安南头黄氏族谱·族规》接着写：

游泮（即中了秀才）谒祖，每一名花红银伍拾元，真银花一对，重伍钱，马花红绸一匹。至是日，祠中酒席费用众出，花银四十大元，依每房一人同办。

廪贡谒祖，每一名花红银捌拾两；真银花一对，重五钱；马花红绸一匹。凡所有买桅、竖桅及酒席费用，俱是祠出。（桅即旗杆）

文武举人谒祖，每一名花红银二百两，真银花一对，重七钱；马花红绸一匹。买桅、竖桅及酒席费用俱祠出。京费花银一百两。

文武进士谒祖，每一名花红银三百两，真银花一对，重一两。写花红绸一匹。买桅、竖桅及酒席费用俱祠办。翰林、部属、侍卫谒祖，加花红银三百两，余与进士同。鼎甲谒祖，加花红银五百两，余与进士同。

买桅、竖桅就是立一对大木杆，杆上有"斗"。每杆之上，举人一只斗，进士两只斗。这个族规是清代同治年间的，所以没有提建进士牌坊的事。顺治十五年（1658年），还曾"赐进士彩花、牌坊银三十两，一甲三名各再加五十两。"嘉庆朝（1796—1820）起，朝廷不出钱建进士牌坊了，虽然宗族中还有建造的，但已不便于写进宗谱族规。有些旺族便建"世科坊"，便是造一座石坊，把本族历届的进士甚至举人，陆续刻上去。

有奖便也有罚。明代初年，浙江省浦江郑氏义门立《郑氏规范》，有一条是："子弟未冠者，学业未成，不听食肉。古有是法，非惟有资于勤苦，抑欲其识齑盐之味。"康熙三十五年（1696年）毗陵《长沟朱氏宗谱·族范·祠规》里有一条："立义学。族中贫不能延师者，俱送子入祠读书。如幼童品质颖秀，其父甘于废弃，不送读书，罚银一两。有从旁谤议阻挠，不肯成人之美，定责二十板。"受罚的是为父者和谤议者。

只要中一个秀才，虽然没有官职，在乡土社会中就是头面人物。村里的公共事务，都要他们出头露面，俨然缙绅。宗祠大祭的时候，秀才可以不顾"在朝以爵，在乡以齿"的常例，大摇大摆位于前辈尊长之上，受到各种礼遇。清代道光五年（1825年）《京江柳氏宗谱·宗祠条例》里规定，每逢宗祠大祭：

祭毕，管年者分胙，议定进士、举人猪胙三斤、羊胙二斤，生员、贡、监猪胙三斤、羊胙一斤，无职者猪羊各一斤。妇人及未成丁者不分，惟孀妇虽子未成丁，亦送猪羊胙各一斤，重节也。

事实上，进士一般都外出当官，举人也大多出任公职而不再在乡，村子里就只有秀才（生员、贡、监）或致仕的官员是"博学能文"之士了。多分胙肉更重要的是一种身份，一种荣誉，也便是一种鼓励。

明代进士可以在州县建牌坊，后来举人也有建的，清代嘉庆朝取消了这种"恩荣"，但仍有人在村里建造。至于"进士第"则几乎是必建的。进士和举人的"桅"，初时只建于宗祠门前，后来连住宅门前也建了起来。

总之，唐人牛希济在《贡士论》里写的登科的荣耀，"秋风八月，鞍马九衢，神气扬扬，行者避路。取富贵若咳唾，视州县如奴仆。"这份神气，在乡土社会中都会一一落到实处，不论是唐朝还是清朝。

从兴学、资助到给予荣耀，这便是宗族对科举制度的回应、支持和最后完成。因为朝廷眼里的取士制度在宗族看来是一个"进仕制度"，出于自身的利益考虑，它有巨大的热情去实现这个制度。正是宗族组织，成就了科举制度一千多年的作为。

科举制度本来是帝王择优取士的制度，也是乡社可以利用来培养人才改善宗族地位和生活的制度。但这制度又毫无疑问有利于普遍提高民众的文化水平和行为教养。中国早期商品经济的发展，起初大多在科举成绩比较好的地区。后来，如山西中、南部和安徽南部，商品经济又夺走了人才，以致当地科举成绩下降。不过，这仅仅是社会文化重点的转移而不是它的退步。

科举取仕不能杜绝官员们的贪墨，"三年清知府，十万雪花银"不是极少数的现象，但是，"两袖清风"毕竟成了官吏们的道德标准，并非毫无影响。浙江省浦江郑氏义门立《郑氏规范》里写道："子孙出仕，有以赃墨闻者，生则于谱图上削去其名，死则不许入祠堂。"也就是读书当官而贪污就得开除出家门了，族谱里也会除名。可见古人已经懂得对当了官的人更应该严加管束。

"读圣贤书，所学何事？"这是民族英雄文天祥的"天问"，他以最忠诚的操守和战斗，回答了这个问题。几百年后的史可法和张苍水，在经历了极其艰苦的又一场斗争后也忠诚地献出了生命。张苍水在战斗时期到过杭州，写下了一首诗：

国亡家破复何之？西子湖头有我师。
日月双悬于氏墓，乾坤半壁岳家祠。

不少家训、族规之类，谆谆教戒子弟读书首先为了做人，而不是为了做官。又如《训俗遗规》引《昆山朱氏家训》里朱用纯写的一篇《劝言》说："圣贤之书，不为后人中举人进士而设，是教千万世做好人。"《训俗遗规》里又收了王士晋写的一篇《宗规》，里面说：教育子弟"将正经书史严加训迪，务使变化气质，陶熔德性。他日若做秀才、做官，固为良士、为廉吏，就是为农为工为商，亦不失为醇谨君子"。

这些思想，都已经跳出了科举求仕狭隘的功利性束缚，提高了读书的意义。

因此一些清廉为民，守土卫国的历史人物便得到了人民的尊重，永远纪念。乡土环境中就有了一种纪念这些人物的建筑，有祠庙，有牌楼，有故居。这是些很有历史价值和教育意义的建筑物，例如，浙江省永康市方岩村的方岩山上，便有一座规模不小，香火很旺的胡公庙，纪念宋代的胡则，他曾经在灾荒之年为遭难百姓申请了免税。永康的邻县东阳，在北宋时出过一位朝廷重臣李纲，他在金兵南下入侵的时候力主抵抗，高呼"渡河"，吐血而亡，百姓为他建造了专祠。赣东、浙东、皖南农村里还有大量的汪公庙，是祭祀越国公汪华的，他是隋、唐间义军领袖，曾占有宣、杭、睦、婺、饶五州，在天下大乱的形势下保护了五州人民，所以深得百姓感恩。

这些庙虽然在当时的大环境中也不免染了些迷信色彩，但受祭祀的确实是真正的历史人物，做过利国利民的好事。

这些人做好事，老百姓礼拜这些人，多少也受到社会文化程度提高的影响。所以提倡读圣贤书也并非只着眼于升官发财，而有重大的社会历史意义。

1. Cultural-Educational Architecture and Imperial Examinations

Chinese people love reading. North or south, city or village, reasonably well-off households most commonly display on their main gate the couplet: "Loyalty and filial piety pass down the family long; poetry and books continue generations." In the main hall, the two most common couplets are: "A centuries-old family is nothing but accumulated virtue; the first and best good deed is still reading" and "First-class people: loyal ministers and filial sons; two occupations: farming and reading." At the center of the long altar table stands a red-lacquered, gold-painted spirit tablet inscribed "Heaven-Earth-Sovereign-Parent-Teacher" (天地君亲师), with incense burning year-round. Setting aside Heaven and Earth, in the real world "Teacher" ranks only after "Sovereign" and "Parent"—very high status indeed.

Actually, what primarily激发 Chinese reading enthusiasm was the imperial examination system (科举)—the Sui-Tang path of "those who excel in study become officials" (学而优则仕), a road anyone could try; second was commercial development. It was not primarily about accumulating virtue to help the world, nor about investigating things to attain knowledge (格物致知).

In rural society, village cultural-educational buildings mostly relate to the examinations. One category is for teaching: community schools (社学), charitable schools (义塾), family schools (家塾), study halls (书馆)—mainly basic education. Then there are literary halls (文馆): older scholars who have stepped back from official ambition, gathering friends through literature, discussing learning, and periodically assessing village children's exam-preparation progress. Another category commemorates exam success: from Ming onward, jinshi graduates could erect memorial archways (牌坊), flagpoles (桅), and build "jinshi mansions" (进士第). Later, juren graduates also erected flagpoles and even archways. Another category is for worship: Wenchang pavilions (文昌阁/魁星楼), Wenfeng pagodas (文峰塔), writing brushes (文笔), paper-burning furnaces (焚帛炉)—praying for clan and individual literary fortune. Additionally, larger temples often have rooms or a separate courtyard for scholars to live and prepare for exams. A few villages have Confucian temples (文庙), which along with ancestral halls may house young students. Some villages have library towers and studios—often built by successful exam candidates who served as officials, then retired in old age to read, paint, and receive guests. Some merchants without official titles, in old age, also build small quiet courtyards as study retreats. In Song-Yuan, a few regions like Jiangxi had academies (书院) where scholars taught disciples and explored philosophical principles, but these had little impact on rural society.

Places with many cultural-educational buildings are mostly places with strong exam performance—so-called "lands of flourishing literary culture," led by southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang, followed by Jiangxi, Fujian, southern Anhui, Guangdong, and the two Hubei/Hunan regions. These areas: first, had developed commercial economies—economy was both the backer of exam success and the basis for widespread educational buildings; second, had stable, powerful clan structures and management systems, where children's reading had become tradition.

The examination system was primarily the state's official-selection system—hence folk启蒙 verse: "The Son of Heaven values heroes; articles teach children." It began in Sui, became fully developed after Ming. But it was also a system for commoners to enter officialdom. To support and激励 clan children to study and climb the "blue cloud path," clans used public property to found schools, assist reading, subsidize exam travel, and upon obtaining any degree, grant high honor and tangible rewards. Clans接续 and completed the state's examination system, helping it spread and产生巨大影响. Rural cultural-educational buildings were overwhelmingly built by clans. Where clan structures were destroyed, exam performance was poor and educational buildings few.

However, economically developed and clan-stable regions did not necessarily have high exam performance. Central Shanxi and southern Anhui, from Ming through Qing, produced many skilled merchants operating across the country, but their exam performance was not strong. By late Qing, it declined further. Liu Dapeng's 《退想斋日记》 describes Taigu (Shanxi)风气: "Reading is viewed lightly, commerce heavily; talented children all go into trade, few study; some even abandon Confucian study for commerce after entering school—saying scholars suffer hunger, while merchants gain silver and family prosperity." Lanxi Zhuge Village's 《高隆诸葛氏宗谱》 includes a merchant biography with his words: "Rather than reading ten thousand books,不如 accumulating a thousand gold in property." A thousand-year value system was inverted. With money from commerce, one could buy empty titles without ten years of hard study—Qing court, to raise revenue, had fixed prices for titles like "大夫" and "司马".

The examination system selected civil officials through periodic exams from among the educated.

Before Sui, in Han, Wei-Jin, and Northern-Southern Dynasties, official selection was entirely controlled by powerful clans—rampant abuse. Hereditary strongmen threatened the supreme ruler, hindered true talent discovery, and caused rigid class stratification leading to instability.

To overcome these abuses, Sui began trial-recommending talent by local officials, then selecting through central exams. Subsequent dynasties refined this into the hugely influential examination system.

The system's feature—and advantage—was opening official careers to all society, fair competition, avoiding powerful class monopoly and giving weaker classes equal opportunity. Except for极少数 "base people" (e.g., Zhejiang's duomin 堕民, Guangdong's danmin 疍民), those in "base occupations" (prostitutes, actors, yamen runners, musician households), criminals, those in parental mourning, and dismissed officials—anyone with registered household and qualified education could, in principle, take the exams. Exam methods and administration were rigorous, preventing unfairness.

For autocratic rulers, opening official careers to all society's first benefit: though not achieving "no talent left in the wild," the court could网罗 outstanding talent for official positions, strengthening governance. After Sui-Tang, all famous ministers and chancellors came from the exams. Hence in early Zhenguan (627–632), Emperor Taizong, watching new jinshi graduates emerge on announcement day at the palace gate, told attendants: "All heroes under heaven have entered my trap!" (天下英雄入吾彀中矣)—very pleased.

The exam system, open to commoners, greatly promoted cultural-educational普及 across China. Reading became a social custom. "Fathers and older brothers blame sons/younger brothers for not being literary; mothers and wives are ashamed if sons/husbands do not study." Some even proposed "everyone has a share in reading." The exam system's peak coincided with woodblock printing普及. Woodblock printing matured in late Tang, perfected in Song—making books easier and cheaper, further fueling the exam system.

Exams attracted大批 social elites, burying them in officially set knowledge—"white-haired from studying classics" (皓首穷经), "ears deaf to outside matters, heart only on sage books"—so that whole society focused on exams; society became "examination-ized." Northern Song Emperor Zhenzong wrote a famous 《劝学诗》 (Poem Encouraging Study), long influential:

The rich need not buy good fields—books hold a thousand bushels of grain.
Building a house need not raise high beams—books hold a house of gold.
Marrying need not lament no good matchmaker—books hold a beauty like jade.
Going out need not lament no retinue—books hold crowds of carriages and horses.
If a man would fulfill his life's ambition, diligently study the Six Classics before the window.

Dong Zhongshu's Han-dynasty proposal "reject all schools, honor only Confucianism" (罢黜百家，独尊儒术), after about a thousand years, only truly reached all society in the exam era—lured by "grain, house, jade, carriage." Sun Chengze said: "Once the exam system was established, scholars everywhere flocked to it. What the upper intent favors, custom follows; the quality of talent and the purity of scholar ethos all derive from this." Through exams, "upper intent" led custom, shaping scholars' knowledge scope and horizons.

Exam success first brought个人 many benefits. Late Ming-early Qing scholar Ji Liuqi wrote in 《明季北略》: "I often see blue-gowned youths (students) unable to plan from morning to evening; once they pass the provincial exam, they become endless juren; once they pass the palace exam, they dine to bells and eat from tripods, ride fat horses in light furs—worth not millions but hundreds of thousands... they pay no personal tax, no labor service, no grain tax, no commodity tax, and even shelter wicked people from taxes and labor—their income is just beginning."

In Ming-Qing, juren were "proper-path" graduates, already qualified for office—usually county school instructors, with chance of being "great selection" (大挑) as county magistrate. Once jinshi, one left the "commoner" class, enjoying many political-economic privileges—e.g., whole family exempt from taxes and labor. Jinshi could hold high office; in Ming-Qing, most jinshi first entered the Hanlin Academy (翰林院)—the reserve for high officials; all central-government high officials came from Hanlin. In Qing, grand secretaries (大学士) were selected from Hanlin; other Hanlin became department directors, a few became county magistrates without waiting, with more promotion opportunities.

In Ming-Qing, high exam graduates also had a longer-term glory: building archways and flagpoles in hometown, hanging plaques in ancestral halls. In early Ming Hongwu 21 (1388), Ren Hengtai became zhuangyuan (first-place jinshi); Emperor Taizu ordered official funds to build an archway in his hometown Xiangyang (Hubei) to honor him. This was likely the first exam-success archway. Thereafter, exam archways and flagpoles gradually spread everywhere, extending to juren. Mid-Ming Chenghua-Hongzhi era, even earlier jinshi without archways got them built retroactively. Later, jinshi fathers and grandfathers, after receiving imperial titles, could build same-style archways. These archways were mostly built in county seats—so by late Ming Wanli (1573–1620), many county seats were dense with exam archways. Due to high cost, from Qing Jiaqing (1796–1820) the state stopped funding them, but numbers did not decrease—clans willingly paid.

Shen Defu wrote in 《万历野获编》: In early Wanli, when Shen Shixing entered the grand secretariat, Wuxian local officials erected a "Zhuangyuan Grand Secretary" great flag high at his gate. This quickly spread—even "students becoming tribute students all raise high poles and great flags, fluttering in the clouds; entering cities, they fill the view." And "top-three graduates and those selected as Hanlin scholars raise yellow poles and great flags separately, several times more than provincial and metropolitan exam graduates."

A "farm boy" (田舍郎), through diligent study and exam success, could ascend to the "Son of Heaven's hall" (天子堂)—such brilliance was a tremendous temptation to anyone capable of reading,激发 commoners to pursue the exams.

Clans, for collective benefit, supported ambitious youth to study, founding schools everywhere—causing widespread literacy in rural areas. Even very poor mountain villages had schools: e.g., a tiny Yongjia village called Linkeng had a small "school" on its southwest hillside, with a cattle shed below its floor. In Shanxi's Lüliang mountains, a very remote cave village called Chenjialeng—small, but upon entering the village gate, a three-courtyard house with a Qianlong-era old plaque, once a school. Another cave village, Caijiazhuang, scattered on loess cliffs, had two small single-story houses serving as the village school—built after an earthquake caused loess cliff collapse and village disaster, rebuilt at the safest location in mid-Qing.

The exam system was also open to ethnic minorities, promoting their cultural普及. E.g., in Hunan's southwest corner, multi-ethnic Gaoyi Village (Han, Dong, Miao) 《杨氏族谱·八景诗》 has two poems about study halls; one: "A village has several reading halls, each shining with rising phoenixes and leaping dragons; nearby people cannot sleep—at the fifth watch still hear reciting articles." Very vivid.

The exam system greatly raised general cultural level—meaning beyond individual or clan success/failure.

One person becoming juren or jinshi brought great benefit to the whole clan—hence in the exam era, clans always encouraged and supported children's study. Clan encouragement and support of children's exam study接续 and completed the state-founded exam system, a key condition for its success—almost part of the system itself.

In Southern Song Chunyou 10 (1250), Wenzhou Kunyang Fenghuang Mountain's 《宜都陈氏家乘序》 opens:

In Kunyang of Wenzhou, there are many great clans, but none surpass the Chen in illustrious status and prosperous descendants. Illustrious status truly results from prosperous descendants. If merely prosperous without wise men, how could status be illustrious? Since Tang, the Chen's descendants passed civil, military, special exams, entered the Imperial Academy, took provincial exams, and received office through recommendation, border merit, or hereditary privilege—over a hundred people. This is why the Chen's status is unsurpassed.

This Chen clan's "illustriousness" importantly came from descendants passing exams. Hence Qing Guangxu 16 (1890) Anhui 《寿州龙氏宗谱·家规》 has a "Must Study" section:

Scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants—reading is first. Do not idle, do not play, strive diligently. Salary of a thousand bushels, gold of ten thousand taels—all come from the bitterness of study; cherish every inch of time.

All our clansmen, aiming to revive family reputation, should devote heart to books. Only scholars have unlimited potential! Climbing a thousand-li ladder, soaring to the nine heavens—above bringing glory to fathers and ancestors, below establishing enterprise for descendants—not merely personal honor! Do not crave empty fame, seek success by luck; be a person of ambition.

This not only lists benefits of reading but measures children's study from the clan's overall interest. Many genealogies have similar teachings and rules. Shexian Guanlu Village's Wang branch hall has a couplet: "One stream protects fields, watching autumn harvest and spring plowing, so children first know farming; Five Classics piled on desks, delighting in summer fireflies and winter snow, helping descendants forever keep books." This is the clan's expectation for children in a farming-reading society.

Beyond general encouragement, clans took many concrete measures to support children's study and exams. Most common: establish village and charitable schools, hire good teachers, subsidize poor but ambitious children, build literary halls, hold regular literary gatherings, provide exam travel expenses, give material and honor rewards to successful candidates—all expenses from clan-owned "study-field" (膏火田/学田) income. This was the民间 response, supplement, and completion of the exam system.

In Qing Tongzhi 11 (1872), wealthy members of Zhenhai Fang clan (Zhejiang), "generously aspiring to clan-support," founded a charitable school. At founding, they established detailed 《义塾规则》; key points:

This hall establishes a charitable school to educate children of clan members unable to hire teachers. Teachers are hired by the hall, salaries paid by the hall. All students pay nothing.

For students of outstanding talent whose families cannot support completion, the hall will separately provide book funds.

For families unable to provide even brush, ink, paper, books—register in advance, the hall provides them.

Charitable schools were founded by clans for poor children; a few by wealthy families donating land. Rich families ran "private exclusive schools" (专馆)—one family hiring a teacher exclusively for its children, with better teachers (respected village old teachers). There were "joint schools" (散馆)—several families jointly hiring a teacher. And "family schools" (家塾) / "private schools" (私塾) / "seat schools" (座馆)—teachers running schools in their own homes, families sending children, teachers charging modest fees.

Some villages built excellent schools from public funds: e.g., Linxian Sunjiagou Village (Shanxi)—remote, cramped, little farmland, yet built a beautiful school on the most beautiful high ground at the village entrance. Villagers, in dire poverty, pinned their escape-from-poverty hope on children's exam success.

For those taking exams, clans continued support. E.g., Tongzhi 13 (1874) 《东粤宝安南头黄氏族谱·族规》 detailed:

Students with county qualification for prefectural exam: 2 taels silver each.
Students with prefectural qualification for academy exam: 3 yuan silver each.
Students aspiring to exam ranking: 2 yuan silver each.
Military/civil students and tribute/imperial exam candidates: 2 yuan silver each.

These subsidized exam expenses. Those taking provincial and metropolitan exams often gathered at the prefecture/county's "Binxing Hall" (宾兴馆) for collective departure, subsidized by prefecture/county. But most clans still subsidized independently, amounts written in clan rules.

Successful candidates received clan rewards. The same Huang clan rules continue:

Youcai (passing xiucai) visiting ancestors: 50 yuan silver each, pair of real silver flowers (5 qian), one bolt of red silk. That day, hall banquet expenses shared by all, 40 yuan silver, one person per branch.

Lin-gong (tribute student) visiting ancestors: 80 taels silver; pair of real silver flowers (5 qian); one bolt red silk. All flagpole purchase/erection and banquet expenses paid by hall.

Military/civil juren visiting ancestors: 200 taels silver; pair real silver flowers (7 qian); one bolt red silk. Flagpole and banquet expenses paid by hall. Capital exam expense: 100 taels.

Military/civil jinshi visiting ancestors: 300 taels silver; pair real silver flowers (1 tael); one bolt red silk. Flagpole and banquet expenses paid by hall. Hanlin, department officials, imperial guards visiting ancestors: additional 300 taels, rest same as jinshi. Top-three graduates: additional 500 taels, rest same as jinshi.

Buying/erecting flagpoles means raising a pair of large wooden poles with "dou" (斗) on top. Juren: one dou per pole; jinshi: two dou. This clan rule is Tongzhi-era, so does not mention jinshi archways. In Shunzhi 15 (1658), the court "awarded jinshi colored flowers and 30 taels archway silver, top three an additional 50 taels each." From Jiaqing (1796–1820), the court stopped funding jinshi archways—though clans still built them, it was no longer convenient to write into clan rules. Some prosperous clans built "generation-exam archways" (世科坊)—a stone archway刻上 successive clan jinshi and even juren names.

Rewards had corresponding punishments. Early Ming, Pujiang Zheng clan's 《郑氏规范》: "Uncapped children with unfinished studies may not eat meat. This is ancient law—not only aiding diligence, but让 them know the taste of hardship." Kangxi 35 (1696) Piling 《长沟朱氏宗谱·族范·祠规》: "Establish charitable school. Poor clan members unable to hire teachers must send children to study in the hall. If a talented child's father willingly wastes him, not sending to study—fine 1 tael. Those who gossip and obstruct, refusing to help others—20 strokes." Punished are fathers and gossipers.

Even passing xiucai (student), though no official position, made one a prominent figure in rural society. Village public affairs required their presence—like gentry. At grand ancestral sacrifices, xiucai could ignore the rule "at court by rank, in village by age" (在朝以爵，在乡以齿), boldly positioning above elders, receiving various courtesies. Qing Daoguang 5 (1825) 《京江柳氏宗谱·宗祠条例》 stipulates at grand sacrifices:

After sacrifice, the manager distributes sacrificial meat: jinshi/juren get 3 jin pork, 2 jin mutton; students/tribute/imperial students get 3 jin pork, 1 jin mutton; those without office get 1 jin each of pork and mutton. Women and minors get none; but widows, even if sons are minors, get 1 jin each of pork and mutton—valuing chastity.

In fact, jinshi generally served as officials away from home, juren also mostly took public office and left—only xiucai (students, tribute, imperial students) or retired officials remained as "learned" men in the village. More sacrificial meat importantly meant status, honor, and encouragement.

Ming jinshi could build archways in counties; later juren too. Qing Jiaqing取消 this "imperial grace," but some still built in villages. As for "jinshi mansions" (进士第), they were almost always built. Jinshi and juren "flagpoles" initially only before ancestral halls, later also before residences.

In sum, Tang Niu Xiji wrote in 《贡士论》 of exam glory: "Autumn wind, eighth month, saddle and horse on nine avenues, spirit soaring, passersby making way. Gaining wealth like spitting, viewing counties like servants." This swagger, in rural society, all became real—whether Tang or Qing.

From founding schools, subsidizing, to granting honor—this was the clan's response, support, and final completion of the exam system. Because the state's official-selection system, in clans' view, was an "official-entry system"—out of self-interest, they had tremendous enthusiasm to implement it. It was clan organization that achieved the exam system's thousand-year success.

The exam system was originally the emperor's system for selecting talent, and also a system rural communities could use to培养 talent and improve clan status and life. But it undoubtedly helped raise general cultural level and behavioral cultivation. China's early commercial economy initially developed mostly in regions with strong exam performance. Later, in central/southern Shanxi and southern Anhui, commercial economy drew away talent, causing local exam performance to decline. But this was merely a shift in social-cultural focus, not its decline.

The exam system could not eliminate official corruption—"three years as an honest prefect, ten thousand snowflake silver" was not rare—but "two sleeves full of breeze" (两袖清风, honest) became officials' moral standard, not without influence. Pujiang Zheng clan's 《郑氏规范》: "Descendants serving as officials, if known for corruption—while alive, strike their name from the genealogy; when dead, forbid entry to the ancestral hall." That is: studying to become an official but corrupting means expulsion from the family and genealogy. Shows ancients understood officials needed stricter discipline.

"What does reading sage books teach?" This was national hero Wen Tianxiang's "heavenly question"—he answered with the most loyal conduct and battle. Centuries later, Shi Kefa and Zhang Cangshui, after extremely hard struggle, also loyally gave their lives. Zhang Cangshang, visiting Hangzhou during battle, wrote:

Nation fallen, family broken—where to go? By West Lake's shore I have my teachers.
Sun and moon hang together at Yu's tomb; heaven and earth half-supported at Yue's shrine.

Many family instructions and clan rules earnestly taught children to read first to become good people, not to become officials. E.g., 《训俗遗规》 quotes 《昆山朱氏家训》 Zhu Yongchun's 《劝言》: "Sage books were not written for later people to become juren/jinshi—they teach countless generations to be good people." 《训俗遗规》 also includes Wang Shijin's 《宗规》: educating children "strictly teach proper classics and histories, transforming their temperament and cultivating virtue. If they later become students or officials, they will be good scholars and honest officials; even if farmers, artisans, or merchants, they will still be prudent gentlemen."

These thoughts transcended the narrow utilitarian束缚 of exam-seeking officialdom, elevating reading's meaning.

Hence honest, people-serving, territory-defending historical figures gained people's respect and eternal commemoration. Rural environments had buildings commemorating them: temples, archways, former residences. These are historically valuable and educational buildings. E.g., Yongkang Fangyan Village's Fangyan Mountain has a sizable, incense-rich Hu Gong Temple commemorating Song dynasty Hu Ze, who secured tax exemption for disaster-stricken people. Yongkang's neighboring Dongyang produced Northern Song important official Li Gang, who advocated resistance when Jin troops invaded south, shouting "Cross the river!" (渡河), vomiting blood and dying—people built a dedicated temple. In eastern Jiangxi, eastern Zhejiang, southern Anhui rural areas, many Wang Gong Temples worship Duke of Yue Wang Hua—a Sui-Tang rebel leader who controlled Xuan, Hang, Mu, Wu, Rao prefectures, protecting five prefectures' people in chaos—hence deeply grateful.

These temples, though inevitably tinged with superstition in their era, worshiped real historical figures who did beneficial deeds for nation and people.

These people did good; commoners worshiped them—influenced in part by raised social-cultural level. Hence advocating reading sage books was not merely about official promotion and wealth, but had major social-historical significance.

sections.name: 耕读生活一例——楠溪江诸村
sections.content_zh:
二、耕读生活一例——楠溪江诸村

用科举取士制度代替门阀世袭制度，对乡土社会来说，至少促进了文化教育的大普及、大提高，并进而提高了乡土社会的整体建设。一方面是平民百姓都有了比较公平的进仕机会，激发了青少年为争取进入社会上层而努力读书习文；另一方面是当官没有终身制，到了年限，便要卸职致仕，其中不少人要回归田园，从而把知识和阅历带回农村，对农村建设和文化教育甚至经济发展作出贡献。

中国农耕时代乡土社会里的文化教育状态，可以用浙江省永嘉县楠溪江中游的村落群作为实例来考察。这是一个普普通通的山区，向来默默无闻，但在我国广大的农村里，很有典型意义。楠溪江主流长145公里，流域面积2429平方公里，村落260余座。村民从事的主要是稻作农业，由于自然条件很好，衣食无虑，但只靠日出而作，日入而息，经济难以发达。一直到20世纪90年代初，绝大多数村子里还没有小店，买点针头线脑、火柴蜡烛，都靠偶或一来的货郎担。然而在"五日一风、十日一雨，帝力于我何有哉"的悠然生活之中，却不忘读书明理，也撇不开"朝为田舍郎，暮登天子堂"的科名追求。

永嘉开发很晚，西晋末年，中原大乱，南渡的中原士族用先进的文化改造了瓯越文化，楠溪江中游开始了新的历史。东晋时设永嘉郡，楠溪江流域是它的辖区。由于一时人文荟萃江右，初建的永嘉郡，六朝时竟有幸得中国文化史上几颗灿烂夺目的星辰来任郡守，先后有东晋大文学家、大书法家王羲之，注《三国志》的刘宋史学家裴松之，玄言诗人、赋家孙绰，诗人、骈文家、文论家颜延之，中国第一位山水诗人谢灵运，萧梁文学家、骈文高手丘迟。这些当时中国文化的精英，以"助人伦，成教化"为从政的最高理想。乾隆《永嘉县志》转引《旧志》说："晋立郡城，生齿日繁，王右军导之以文教，谢康乐继之，乃知向方，自是家务为学，至宋遂为小邹鲁。"又说"王羲之治尚慈惠，谢灵运招士进学，由是人知向学，民风一变。"王谢风流，培养出楠溪江浓郁的人文气息。明末清初诗人梅调元有永嘉《王谢祠》诗，写的是：

前守推王谢，荒祠倚郡城，
千秋传墨妙，六代擅诗名。
沼古鹅还浴，塘春草自生，
风流今古事，俯仰一含情。

楠溪江最灿烂的文化高峰在南宋，中原衣冠又一次大规模南渡，像东晋一样，偏安之地人文荟萃，来任温州"一把手"的如张九成、王十朋、楼钥和杨简，都是一时俊彦。张九成在《咨目》里写道："永嘉道德之乡，贤哲相踵，前辈虽往，风流犹存。"他们也都以礼乐教化为从政的第一要务。这对于提高永嘉的文化水平，起了很大作用。乾隆《永嘉县志·学校》说："永嘉于宋，名贤辈出，登洛闽之堂者，后先相望，郁郁彬彬，至称为小邹鲁，何其盛哉！"永嘉在北宋有程门弟子十三人，在南宋有朱门弟子十六人。在国学里，先后有永嘉籍的元丰九先生和淳熙六君子，"俱以道德性命传程朱之学"。（见乾隆《永嘉县志·风俗》）南宋时形成的理学中的"永嘉学派"，以薛季宣、陈傅良、郑伯熊和叶适为代表，其中郑、叶为楠溪江人。郑伯熊原籍塘湾村，叶适童年时代在岩头村由金姓抚养并读书（见《岩头金氏宗谱》）。

溪口村戴氏家族，北宋时有戴述[元符三年（1100年）进士]、戴迅两兄弟从二程学。到南宋，有戴述子戴栩（嘉定进士），是叶适的学生，著作《五经说》、《诸子辩论》、《东都要略》等。戴迅子戴溪[淳熙五年（1178年）进士]，据嘉靖《温州府志·人物》说他"由礼部郎中凡六转为太子詹事，兼秘书监。景献太子命类《易》、《诗》、《书》、《春秋》、《语》、《孟》、《资治通鉴》各为说以进。权工部尚书，除文华阁学士，卒赠端明殿学士，谥文端。太子亲书"明经"匾其堂，有《岷隐集》。宁宗称他为"诸儒之宗"。叶适评戴溪说，"少望天下奇才，于今世不过数人"。戴溪的亲侄子戴蒙[绍熙庚戌（1190年）进士]曾从学朱熹于武夷，著作有《易、书、四书家说》，《六书故》等；戴蒙长子戴仔，不乐仕进，著有《诸经补义》、《通鉴补纪》、《说林文集》等。蒙次子侗[淳佑辛丑（1241年）进士]，著有《六书设》和一些杂著文集。这戴氏一门，学术成就不同寻常，溪口戴氏大宗祠里有一副楹联写道：

入程朱门迭奏埙篪理学渊源双接绪；
历南北宋并称邹鲁春官第甲六登墀。

塘湾村郑伯熊三兄弟都是南宋进士。郑伯熊"德行夙成，尤邃经学，登绍兴第，历官国子司业，宗正少卿。乞外，以龙图阁知宁国府。卒谥文肃，绍兴末，伊洛之学稍息，复于伯熊得之。弟伯英、（从弟）伯海皆知名，由是永嘉之学宗郑氏。有《郑景望集》"。（嘉靖《温州府志·人物》）伯英是隆兴癸未年（1163年）进士，著有《归愚集》。从弟伯海是绍兴辛未年（1151年）进士，设帐授徒，生徒常达五百人。全祖望《宋元学案》说："乾淳之间，永嘉学者联袂成帷，然无不以先生兄弟为渠率。"伯熊弟子枫林人木待问为隆兴状元。

此外，岙底上湾村有陈揆，登绍兴癸丑陈亮榜进士，与叶适相善，有诗集二十余卷、文集五卷传世。芙蓉村陈宝之，绍兴进士，从吕祖谦学，与陈亮为诗友，宗谱存"送陈同父"和"挽吕东莱"诗各一首。同村又有陈虞之，咸淳元年（1265年）进士，响应文天祥号召，起兵勤王，率全村义士八百多人据守芙蓉峰抗元，全部殉难。

乾隆《永嘉县志》记载，朱熹任两浙路常平盐茶公事的时候，曾到楠溪江来访问当地的理学家，先到岩头村访问门人"以理学鸣于世"的刘愈，说："过楠溪不识刘进之，如过洞庭不识桔。"不巧没有见到，又去谢岙访问门人谢复经，再访溪口戴蒙、戴侗及蓬溪村李时靖，并在蓬溪留下了墨迹。

楠溪江地区所处荒僻，却与当时的主流文化保持着这样密切的关系，达到这样的水平。

学术带动了科举和仕进。从唐代到清代，历代进士中可以确认为楠溪江村子中人的总计至少有五十多位。溪口村戴氏，豫章村胡氏，塘湾村郑氏，花坦村朱氏，苍坡村李氏，芙蓉村陈氏，都是"簪缨鹊起，甲第蝉联"的名门望族。田父野老引以为乡土光荣的，是宋代豫章村一门三代五进士，溪口村戴氏一门四代六进士，花坦村朱氏和塘湾村郑氏的兄弟进士，枫林村有南宋隆兴元年（1163年）状元木待问。

科甲盛，当官的自然多。光绪《永嘉县志·人物》统计：永嘉县"自宋以来，位宰执者六人，侍从台谏五十余人，监司郡守百十余人，可谓盛矣。"其中芙蓉村在南宋就有过"十八金带"，便是有十八个人在临安当过朝中高官。

宋代楠溪江科甲之盛，虽然和当时朝廷扩大科举录取名额有关，但晋、宋两次中原大乱，衣冠望族大量来到楠溪江流域安居更有不少的关系。

宋元、元明和明清三次易代都在楠溪江发生过战争，破坏严重，明代嘉靖之后，又遭倭寇侵扰。不过，元、明、清三朝，楠溪江文风依然尚有可观。元明之间，鹤垟村出了个谢德瑀，他"博通经史，为时名儒"，著有《狂斐集》、《家礼会通》等。同时的花坦村朱谧，著有《四书述义》、《四书补注》、《太极图说》、《西铭集》等，从祀郡庠。豫章胡氏、鹤垟谢氏、岩头金氏、花坦朱氏、溪口戴氏这些望族，在明清两代还有过一些科举功名的成就。明代，胡氏出过一位中书舍人，戴氏出过一位御史，谢氏则出过一位锦衣卫指挥佥事。清代，豫章村《胡氏宗谱》康熙三十四年（1695年）的"旧序"说："至清鼎革，变起沧桑，兵燹之余，世家右族不无徙迁，集泽哀鸣，未能常聚。"在这种情况下，学术和科名成绩大大落后了。整个清代将近三百年，值得一书的学术著述几乎没有。道光三十年（1850年）的《重修鹤垟谢氏宗谱序》夸耀谢氏在普遍衰落的情况下又出了两名进士道："至今犹想见谢家之门第，即为溪山之生色者，历久弗衰矣！"

楠溪江中游的岩头村有一条大约三百米长的遮雨廊，沿河而建，叫丽水街。中段有一副楹联："萍风碧漾观鱼栏，柳浪翠泠闻莺廊"，很美。

耕读生活培养出来的乡村知识分子，科场得意走上仕途的是少数，成为理学家的更是寥寥。他们大多留在村子里生活，自然成为上层文化的代表，与郡县官吏如明代的郡守何文渊和文林、清代的县令汤成烈一起，在乡里担起了"化民成俗"的责任。文林制定了《族范》，作为各姓宗谱里必有的家法族规的范本。汤成烈在咸丰《县志》稿里写道："永嘉在宋有邹鲁之风，维时士大夫先达者多从二程朱子游，居乡恒以讲学为业，故能诱掖后进，式化乡闾，薰为善良，浸成风俗。户有弦诵，邑无巫觋，人怀忠信，女行贞洁，冠昏丧祭，厚薄适中，奢俭当礼。疾病不祷祈，婚配不听星命。岁时娱乐，弛张合宜，其于养生送死之制，盖秩如也。自元而明，去古渐远，风尚亦漓，轨物废而邪说行，儒术衰而异端起，奁资盛而女溺，宴食腆而讼繁。疾病薄骨肉之亲，报赛侈鬼神之会。婚丧之仪非复曩制。至于上元灯火，端午竞渡，争奇炫彩，靡财奢费，略不顾惜。士女游观，靓妆华服，阗城溢郭，有司莫之能禁。"（见光绪《永嘉县志·风土》）他把过去风俗之好，归功于读书人向理学家学习，回家之后居乡讲学；把当时风俗之漓，归咎于"轨物废而儒术衰"。他寄希望于"士大夫"，也便是盼在乡知识分子来挽世风于既颓。

这时候，楠溪江中游古来文化比较领先的村落，已经有人从商，有些人"权子母，量出入，铢积寸累，握算持筹"。但是，许多乡贤士绅，还是保持了引领读书风气的传统。例如《棠川郑氏宗谱》记载，乡绅郑公谔"旷达多才，好稽古，善词赋，筑美室，置图书，列古画玩物以供清赏。读诵之暇，惟以弹琴栽花为乐。遇风日晴和，则汲泉煮茗，拂席开樽，与二三知己，啸傲于烟霞泉石间，不复知有人世荣辱事。且课子有程，义方之外，更以诗书陶镕其气质。"明代嘉靖朝（1796—1820）岩头村的金九峰，"性闲静，每日闲坐一室，凡经史以及诸子百家书无不娴，而尤究心于星学，陶情音律。至于制艺歌词，皆其余事耳。……设绛帐以诲生徒，春风四座，化雨一庭，询是师儒领袖。"（《岩头金氏宗谱·九峰先生五旬寿序》）明代花坦村的朱伯清，"丰神秀逸，嗜学有文，不乐仕进，志存林壑……家事付之诸子，惟以文墨自娱。凡石、树、虫、鱼、水泉、花药之会心寓目者，咸属吟咏。其间，遇风和日暖，角巾鹿裘，从以弟子，徘徊乎水光山色，拂云坐石，手挥丝桐，目送飞鸿，逍遥自乐。"（《珍川朱氏宗谱·伯清公珍川十咏序》）同村的朱谧，"读书好古，淳朴自持，利欲不能移其心，荣禄不足夺其志，孝以事亲，友以处弟"。（《珍川朱氏宗谱·明义堂处士墓志铭》）以致《珍川朱氏宗谱》夸赞花坦村"秀士成群，多含英咀华之彦；古怀如晤，有庄襟老带之风，可谓文质彬彬，野处多秀者已。"

各村各姓的宗谱里所推崇的贤士们虽然都不求仕进而嗜学乐道，但这都是儒者"退则独善其身"的生活，而他们并没有忘记"达则既济天下"的抱负。他们都关怀族中年轻人的仕途，不但自己设帐授徒，而且运用他们的影响力，促进宗族大兴办学之风。楠溪江大小血缘村落的族谱，都在《家训》或《族规》里规定子弟务必要读书。《岩头金氏宗谱·家规》写道："每岁延敦厚博学之士以教子弟，须重以学俸，隆以礼文，无失故家轨度。子弟有质士堪上进而无力从学者，众当资以祠租曲成之。"在当时，读书的目的首先科考直取功名。《茗川胡氏大宗谱·田川胡氏义塾规》说："是以愿人文蔚起，高拔五桂之芳；门第常新，足兆三槐之瑞。……愿沼芹叠采，云路同登。"和各地一样，宗祠对子弟读书，赴考，中式之后各方打点等都由义田所出予以资助。凡科举有成绩的，都能得到表彰。

读书主要为了进仕，但不专为进仕。《珍川朱氏合族副谱》里有一篇《如在堂记》写道："使我拥书万卷，何减积粟千钟，然则后之子若孙，苟不忘此意，必将奋志诗书，骧首云逵，上以绳其祖武，下以贻厥孙谋，无忝先世科甲之荣，不振前朝理学之绪，则不惟有光于近祖，亦且善述乎大宗矣！"既要有科甲之荣，又要振理学之绪，目标比较宽阔。

除了科甲和理学，读书还有更大的目的。又是这个花坦村朱氏，在《珍川朱氏宗谱·族范盟辞》里写得明白："不学则夷乎物，学则可以立，故学不亦大乎。学者尽人事所以助乎天也。天设其伦，非学莫能敦；人有恒纪，非学莫能叙。贤者由学以明，不贤者废学以昏。大匠成室，材木盈前，程度去取而不乱者，由绳墨之素定。君子临事而不骇，制度而不扰者，非学安能定其心哉。是故学者君子之绳墨也。"乾隆《永嘉县志·学校》说到教育："此吏治所首重，民风所视以转移也。"对文化教育的这种既深又宽的理解和热烈追求，给楠溪江的村子笼罩了一层浓浓的高远的生活理念。

所以，楠溪江各村落对教育事业和子弟的要求很高。《鹤垟谢氏宗谱·义学条规》说："义学之设，原为国家树人至计，非以为后生习浮艳、取青紫而已也。凡系生徒，务须以《白鹿洞规》身体力行……凡肄业弟子，必须一举足疾徐，一语言进止，事事雍容审详，安雅冲和。"义学是专为贫寒子弟办的公费学校，仍然强调取青紫之外还要讲究操守品行。要求身体力行的《白鹿洞规》，是南宋理学家朱熹于淳熙六年（1179年）为白鹿洞书院订下的学行规范。淳佑元年（1241年），宋理宗亲笔书写赐给太学生作为教规，于是通行天下，直至穷乡僻壤的农村义塾。它的纲领性内容是：

父子有亲，君臣有义，夫妇有别，长幼有序，朋友有信（右五教之目）。博学之，审问之，慎思之，明辨之，笃行之（右为学之序）。言忠信，行笃敬，惩忿窒欲，迁善改过（右修身之要）。正其义不谋其利，明其道不计其功（右处事之要）。己所不欲，勿施于人，行有不得，反求诸己（右接物之要）。

这个规范完全是关于修身养性的。和这个《白鹿洞书院规》相似而更详细且严格的，是明太祖给国子监建的"卧碑"，后来顺治九年（1653年）又补充了一部分，在全国官学推行。所补充的有一条是："军民一切利病，不许生员上书陈言，如有一言建白，以违制论，黜革治罪。"贤才是不许论政的，只要议论过一句，便是有罪，要开除学籍。

所以，农村的初级书塾具有两重性，一方面为求得科考成就，一方面为铸造未来知识分子的思想品格。这种教育的影响及于普通农民，乾隆《永嘉县志》记载，县丞何森为了平定民风强悍的楠溪江地区的动乱，措施之一是在枫林村办了一所"楠溪义学"。宗族在《族规》里立的育人目标，和朝廷是完全一致的。

乾隆《永嘉县志·学校》说，永嘉"乡闾社学，本古党庠术序，亦较他州为多"。楠溪江村落的学校，最基础的是社学和义塾，几乎村村都有，有些村且不止一处。社学、义塾以学习识字、计数为主，读些初级启蒙教材准备升学。有些学行高卓的人，如明代岩头村的金九峰和花坦村的朱伯清，他们办的可能是私塾，既然以弟子从游于山光水色，并且"春风四座、化雨一庭，询是师儒领袖，"显然所教的已经不是蒙童。家塾、私塾所在往往是住宅的一部分，通常为一个别院，如芙蓉村西端的司马第，家塾在大宅前北侧独立的小花园里。

比较高级的教育则由书院来承担。楠溪江最早的书院之一，溪口村的东山书院，是南宋进士、曾任太子讲读的著名理学家戴蒙辞官之后办的，由于成绩斐然，皇上赐额"明文"。明代主持朱垟村白岩书院的朱广文和主持花坦村凤南书院的朱墨臞，都是当地著名的学者，颇有著述。墨臞的学生王瓒于弘治九年（1496年）中进士一甲二名，曾任两京国子祭酒、礼部侍郎，也有著作问世。明孝宗因此亲书"溪山第一"匾赐给朱墨臞。豫章村明代的石马书院也得退休还乡的中书公胡宗韫来论学题诗。此外，花坦村还有西园书院，芙蓉村中心有芙蓉书院，等等。书院都有自己专用的独立的建筑。

这些书院的水平，大都以主持的山长而变，一旦任山长的学者不再能教学，后继乏人，便会沦落为普通的学塾。在康熙《温州府志》里，竟已将溪口村的明文书院称为菰田塾，"所以启童蒙也"。

楠溪江中游芙蓉村的中心芙蓉池，它边上的芙蓉书院，面向东。它的大门开在北侧墙的前端，靠村子的主街如意街。进门小院里左手有"半亩方塘"，右手有一道棂星门式的仪门，门前有桅杆一对。进仪门，隔院子是明伦堂，堂前有杏坛，仿孔子讲学处，坛宽3.2米，长6.4米，略高于周边地面。明伦堂的后院有一座讲堂。明伦堂和讲堂都是三开间的。这一路通长52米，宽12.8米，布局很规矩。讲堂前檐廊右（南）端开腰门通花园，山长的三间住宅在花园里，面东。花园很大，有水渠、有土丘、有石假山，树木和翠竹长得郁郁葱葱。

由宗族公建而规模比较大或者层次比较高的书院，一般都选址在风景最佳的地方。豫章村的石马书院，位于"渠口寨山之麓，后枕高岳石壁，下临溪流深渊"。塘湾村的栳甡甡书院造在屏风岩侧，"岩后百武许有小瀑布，……下有重磨岩。"因此，各地的"十景"、"八景"，大多有一景甚至两景和书院有关系。

书塾的建设和管理一般由宗族负责，乡绅们常常是主持人。《茗川胡氏大宗谱·东山书塾记》生动地记述了这种情况："茗屿胡氏旧有读书楼，在居之东，极其幽静……尝延师以诲子弟，由是族属衣冠济济，咸知以礼律身……（后读书楼废，文运遂衰）嘉靖癸丑仲至冬日，源泉、乔西二公谋于众曰：……今宜续建精舍，以陶后进，庶几书香不泯，愿克肖者听。皆曰善。于是改卜地于东山之屏……期年而舍成……望之岿然，名之曰东山书塾。量出田租若干石，以为累岁延师教育之费。"

楠溪江村落另三类比较重要的文教建筑是文昌阁、文峰塔和牌楼。它们虽然和科举制度有关，但已经远远超脱了科举之上了。

文昌阁祭祀文昌帝君，文昌帝君主管人间功名，因此受到普遍祭祀。在楠溪江的廊下、花坦、岩头、水云各村，都曾有过文昌阁。它们通常和书塾、书院相呼应或内有堂庑作为书塾、书院的讲堂。

因为关系到科举成就，也就是关系到宗族的兴衰，所以宗族都以兴建文昌阁为大事，也成为乡绅们的善举之一。《珍川朱氏合谱·慎轩公传》记载朱光润捐赀在花坦村"创建文阁……经营结构，鸟革翚飞。"主体是一幢两层楼阁，两庑用作书院讲堂，"珍川之胜，于此称第一焉"。

文昌阁大多造于村外的"水口"，即村子所在的小盆地内地表水聚合后流出盆地的隘口。由于风水师简单地认为中国的地势是西北高而东南低，"此天地之大势也"，所以村子的选址多在隘口的西北，以致水口大多在村子的东南方，即巽方。水口往往山丘夹岸，树木茂盛，风景美好。如岩头村的文昌阁，创建于乾隆庚申年（1740年），位于全楠溪江流域最大的乡土园林的南端、汤山的北麓，在园林主体建筑塔湖庙（孝祐庙）的西侧，前临智水湖，左傍一条水量丰沛的小溪。阁背后较高处有一座文峰塔。

由于环境优美，所以楠溪江两岸村子的"十景"、"八景"里常有一景是文昌阁或书院，为文人们吟咏的对象。

鹤垟村的书院叫"环翠楼"，"八景"里有"环翠书声"："幽阁崚嶒碧树荣，琅琅中有读书声，半空掷地金钱解，五岳朝天玉佩鸣。"花坦村的《十景诗》里有《文昌登眺》二首，其一："杰阁凌云起，溪山入眼奇……游身图画里，俯仰展须眉。"其二："……竹疏风弄影，花暗鸟鸣阴，古树浮波静，空潭落月深……"

文峰塔起源于风水迷信，认为科甲不利的村子，在甲、巽、丙、丁的方位上造一座塔或立一支文笔，便可以振兴文运。一般以造在巽位上的为多，因为水口建筑群也大多在村外的巽位上，文峰塔和水口建筑群相表里，更为生色。楠溪江流域层峦起伏，都是火山流纹岩，经过亿万年的侵蚀，有不少圆锥形的山峰。风水术数上可以认它们为"文笔"，所以这里人造的文峰塔不多，仅岩头村和塘湾村各有一座。岩头村的文峰塔是明代桂林公（金氏）于嘉靖年间（1522—1566）建造的，和水亭书院、森秀轩同时。它位于村子东南端文昌阁后面的山坡上，全用灰白色大理石筑成，从残石看，塔可能为七层楼阁式，高仅四米左右。

村子里的文人们常在风景佳丽之地造幽斋读书。岩头村的金氏桂林公便把塔湖庙的斋堂改建成了书斋森秀轩，背对右军池，面向镇南湖。桂林公诗《题森秀轩·其二》中有两联：

门植垂堤陶公柳，院开洗砚右军池；
谈棋石磴风频至，烹茗松轩月上时。

斋里的文化生活品味很高。

水亭书院、森秀轩、文峰塔、文昌阁、戏台和右军池等一起形成了岩头村的文化建筑群落。

塘湾村的《十景诗》之一咏"巽吉山"云："耸然特立一高峰，恰位东南秀气钟；巽吉更加崇宝塔，文风焕发笔游龙。"这座文峰塔是造在山上的，山便在村子的巽方，即东南方。

有些文士乡绅则在住宅里营造书香气。明代初年洪武、永乐间（1368—1424），鹤垟村有一位谢德玹，家里有一间书斋，濒临澄江。他自制《临水书斋》诗：

碧流湛湛涵长天，小斋横枕清堪怜，
牙签插架三万轴，灯火照窗二十年。
长日尘埃飞不到，常时风月闲无边，
已知圣道犹如此，乐处寻来即自然。

同村同宗谢廷循，宣德年间（1426—1435）曾供职于锦衣卫，晚年在故乡旧宅里造了一幢静乐轩，宗谱写道："士大夫与之游者，皆为赋静乐之诗"。连宣宗皇帝也写了一首《静乐诗》赠他："暮色动前轩，重城欲闭门。残霞收赤气，新月破黄昏。已觉乾坤静，都无市井喧。阴阳有恒理，斯与达人论。"

谢廷循的朋友，豫章村的胡宗韫，明代宣德时任中书舍人，归田时同僚赠诗送行，有句："诛茆今日野，把钓旧时溪。晒药晴檐短，安书夜榻低。"（陈斌）以及"烟霞三亩宅，霜露百年心，黄菊陶潜兴，清风梁父吟。"（陈中）胡宗韫回乡后在故宅"中翰第"造了一座紫微楼作为颐养之所。《豫章胡氏宗谱》写他："植竹种花，终日坐卧其间，时临墨迹，随兴吟诗，优游自乐，或与密友笑谈、围棋、饮酒，如是二十余年"。

这些乡间知识分子所标榜、所追求的生活方式，"超脱于物，求之在心"的态度，对乡土文化生活不可能不产生引领的作用。

楠溪江流域的文教建筑里，还有一种比较重要的，是牌楼。光绪《永嘉县志·古迹》里写到坊表，说："古人志厥宅里，树之风声，可法可传，政教攸系。"楠溪江人对牌楼的教化作用是很重视的，一般造得很讲究，位置在宗祠或村门近旁，成为村落礼制中心的一部分。

花坦村的牌楼最多也最壮美。明代英宗正统年间（1436—1449），在大宗祠敦睦堂正门前左右侧为兵科给事中朱良暹各建了一座牌楼，相对而立，东边一座额"乌府"，西边一座额"黄门"。面对着敦睦堂，又有一座牌楼，题额"奕世簪缨"，为明代嘉靖（1522—1566）进士朱腆立。它和"乌府"、"黄门"两座牌楼形成品字，在敦睦堂前围出一个小小空场，给大宗祠增添了气色。这种品字形的布局多流行于城乡之文风较盛者。"黄门"牌楼西侧，沿大路又有"乡贤"牌楼，明代正德朝（1506—1521）温州知府何文渊为学政朱思宁立。再西侧为"钟秀"牌楼，是明代嘉靖朝朱腆中举人时所立。再西为嘉靖丙寅（1566年）冬永嘉知县程文著为朱双溪立，题额"公直谆良"。再西为"翕和"牌楼，是乡绅西华王公为朱莲溪立，大约也在明代晚期。大路上最后一座牌楼是"溪山第一"牌楼，为乡进士知凤阳县令朱义川立，朱腆书匾。这座牌楼就是花坦村的西门。另外还有一座"宪台"牌楼，在村中央宪台祠堂大门前正中，是明代弘治乙丑年（1505年）温州知府李端、永嘉知县刘经为工部给事中朱良以立的。在西园书院里又有"鸢飞鱼跃"牌楼，是中书舍人周令为朱幽独建的。以上这些牌楼，都是为表彰一些读书中了科甲又当了官的人，目的在于荣耀宗族，激励后人。另有邑令伍公为朱小山立的"为公宣力"牌楼（朱小山的身份、事绩不见记载）和明末崇祯已巳（1629年）巡按使徐吉公为节妇邵孺人立的"松柏寒贞"牌楼，只见于宗谱，已在"文化大革命"中拆毁，不知位置何在。

岩头村有一座牌楼，是明世宗赐给大理寺左寺右寺副、后来迁任瑞州知府金昭的。这座牌楼和花坦村的宪台牌楼风格近似，都是四柱四楼式，斗拱雄大，制度近于宋式，实在很难得。

楠溪江流域两千多平方公里的范围，文教如此发达，却又长期不闻于世，它提供了一个很典型的江南纯农业地区乡土社会文教状态的实例，也很典型地叙说了乡土社会文教建筑兴建的背景、动力、追求、环境和风貌。
