2. Farming-Reading Life: Nanxi River Villages

Replacing the hereditary aristocratic system with the imperial examination system, for rural society, at least promoted the widespread普及 and great improvement of cultural education, and further enhanced overall rural construction. On one hand, common people gained relatively fair opportunities to enter officialdom,激发 youth to study diligently to enter the upper social stratum; on the other hand, official positions were not lifelong—after their term, officials had to retire, and many returned to the countryside, bringing knowledge and experience back to rural areas, contributing to rural construction, cultural education, and even economic development.

The cultural-educational state of rural society in China's agrarian era can be examined through the village cluster in the middle reaches of Nanxi River, Yongjia County, Zhejiang Province. This is an ordinary mountainous region, long unknown to the world, but highly typical of China's vast countryside. The Nanxi River main stream is 145 km long, with a drainage area of 2,429 sq km and over 260 villages. Villagers mainly practice rice agriculture; due to favorable natural conditions, they have no worries about food and clothing, but relying solely on "rising at sunrise, resting at sunset," the economy could not develop. Until the early 1990s, most villages had no shops—buying needles, thread, matches, candles depended on occasional peddlers. Yet in this leisurely life of "wind every five days, rain every ten, what has the emperor's power to do with me?" they never forgot reading to understand principle, nor could they let go of the exam ambition of "morning a farm boy, evening ascending the Son of Heaven's hall."

Yongjia was developed late. In late Western Jin, central China was in chaos; migrating central plains aristocrats transformed Ou-Yue culture with advanced culture, and the middle Nanxi River began a new history. In Eastern Jin, Yongjia Commandery was established, with the Nanxi River basin under its jurisdiction. Due to the concentration of cultural figures on the right bank of the Yangtze, the newly established Yongjia Commandery, during the Six Dynasties, was fortunate to have several brilliant stars of Chinese cultural history serve as commandery governors: Eastern Jin great writer and calligrapher Wang Xizhi; Liu-Song historian Pei Songzhi (annotator of Records of the Three Kingdoms); metaphysical poet and rhapsodist Sun Chuo; poet, parallel prose writer, and literary theorist Yan Yanzhi; China's first landscape poet Xie Lingyun; and Xiao-Liang writer and parallel prose master Qiu Chi. These cultural elites of the time took "assisting human relations, completing moral transformation" (助人伦，成教化) as the highest ideal of governance. Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer quotes the Old Gazetteer: "When Jin established the commandery city, population grew; Wang Youjun (Wang Xizhi) guided with culture and education, Xie Kangle (Xie Lingyun) continued—people then knew the right direction; from then on every family pursued learning, and by Song it became a 'little Zou-Lu' (hometown of Confucius and Mencius)." It also says: "Wang Xizhi governed with kindness and benevolence; Xie Lingyun recruited scholars to advance learning—hence people knew to study, and local customs changed." Wang-Xie elegance cultivated Nanxi River's rich humanistic atmosphere. Late Ming-early Qing poet Mei Diaoyuan wrote a poem "Wang-Xie Shrine" in Yongjia:

Former governors Wang and Xie, their desolate shrine leans by the commandery city;
Through a thousand years their calligraphy's wonder passed, six dynasties excelled in poetic fame.
The ancient pond still has geese bathing, spring grass grows by the pond;
Elegance is an ancient and modern matter, looking up and down one feels emotion.

Nanxi River's most brilliant cultural peak was in Southern Song. Central plains aristocrats again migrated south on a large scale; like Eastern Jin, the refuge region became culturally rich. Those serving as Wenzhou's "top officials"—Zhang Jiucheng, Wang Shipeng, Lou Yue, Yang Jian—were all outstanding talents of the time. Zhang Jiucheng wrote in his "Memorandum": "Yongjia is a land of morality, sages follow one after another; though predecessors have passed, their elegance remains." They all took ritual-music education as the first priority of governance, greatly raising Yongjia's cultural level. Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Schools says: "Yongjia in Song produced famous worthies one after another; those entering the halls of Luo (Cheng Hao/Cheng Yi) and Min (Zhu Xi) followed one after another, lush and refined—called 'little Zou-Lu,' how prosperous!" Yongjia had 13 Cheng-school disciples in Northern Song, 16 Zhu-school disciples in Southern Song. In the Imperial Academy, Yongjia natives successively included the "Nine Yuanfeng Gentlemen" and "Six Chunxi Gentlemen," "all transmitting Cheng-Zhu learning through moral nature." (See Qianlong Yongjia County Gazetteer · Customs) The "Yongjia School" of Neo-Confucianism formed in Southern Song, represented by Xue Jixuan, Chen Fuliang, Zheng Boxiong, and Ye Shi—Zheng and Ye were Nanxi River natives. Zheng Boxiong was originally from Tangwan Village; Ye Shi was raised and studied by the Jin clan in Yantou Village in childhood (see Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy).

Xikou Village's Dai clan: in Northern Song, Dai Shu [jinshi of Yuanfu 3 (1100)] and Dai Xun brothers studied under the Two Chengs. In Southern Song, Dai Shu's son Dai Xu (Jiading jinshi), a student of Ye Shi, authored Five Classics Commentary, Disputations of Masters, Essentials of the Eastern Capital, etc. Dai Xun's son Dai Xi [jinshi of Chunxi 5 (1178)], according to Jiajing Wenzhou Prefecture Gazetteer · Figures, "from Ministry of Rites director, through six promotions became Crown Prince's Supervisor, concurrently Imperial Library Director. The Crown Prince Jingxian ordered him to compile commentaries on Changes, Poetry, Documents, Spring and Autumn, Analects, Mencius, Comprehensive Mirror for Governance. Acting Minister of Works, appointed Wenge Academician; posthumously granted Duanming Palace Academician, posthumous name Wenduan. The Crown Prince personally wrote 'Understanding Classics' plaque for his hall; he has Muyin Collection. Emperor Ningzong called him 'the patriarch of all Confucians.'" Ye Shi evaluated Dai Xi: "A rare talent under heaven from youth, in this age no more than a few." Dai Xi's nephew Dai Meng [jinshi of Shaoxing Gengxu (1190)] studied under Zhu Xi at Wuyi, authored Family Commentaries on Changes, Documents, Four Books, and Six Books Explained, etc. Dai Meng's eldest son Dai Zai, not seeking office, authored Supplements to Classics, Supplements to Comprehensive Mirror, Saying Forest Collection, etc. Meng's second son Dai Tong [jinshi of Chunyou Xinchou (1241)] authored Six Books and various miscellaneous collections. This Dai clan's scholarly achievements were extraordinary; Xikou Dai's main ancestral hall has a couplet:

Entering Cheng-Zhu's gate, playing xun and chi in succession, Neo-Confucian origins doubly connected;
Through Northern and Southern Song, called Zou-Lu together, six times topped the spring official examination.

Tangwan Village's Zheng Boxiong three brothers were all Southern Song jinshi. Zheng Boxiong "virtue formed early, especially deep in classical learning; passed Shaoxing exam, served as Imperial Academy Director, Imperial Clan Court Vice Minister. Requested external post, served as Ningguo Prefect with Longtuge rank. Posthumous name Wensu. In late Shaoxing, Yi-Luo learning had somewhat declined, revived through Boxiong. Brother Boying and (cousin) Bohai were both famous—hence Yongjia learning followed the Zheng clan. Has Zheng Jingwang Collection." (Jiajing Wenzhou Prefecture Gazetteer · Figures) Boying was jinshi of Longxing Guiwei (1163), authored Guiyu Collection. Cousin Bohai was jinshi of Shaoxing Xinwei (1151), taught disciples, often reaching 500 students. Quan Zuwang's Song-Yuan Learning Cases says: "During Qianchun period, Yongjia scholars lined up like curtains, yet all followed these brothers as leaders." Boxiong's disciple, Fenglin native Mu Daiwen, became Longxing zhuangyuan (first-place jinshi).

Additionally, Aodi Shangwan Village had Chen Kui, jinshi of Shaoxing Guichou (Chen Liang's list), friendly with Ye Shi, with over 20 volumes of poetry and 5 volumes of prose surviving. Furong Village's Chen Baozhi, Shaoxing jinshi, studied under Lü Zuqian, was a poetry friend of Chen Liang; genealogy preserves poems "Sending Chen Tongfu" and "Mourning Lü Donglai." Same village had Chen Yuzhi, jinshi of Xianchun 1 (1265), responding to Wen Tianxiang's call, raised troops to aid the throne, led over 800 village righteous men to defend Furong Peak against Yuan, all died martyrs.

Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer records that when Zhu Xi served as Liangzhe Circuit salt-tea commissioner, he visited Nanxi River to consult local Neo-Confucians: first to Yantou Village to visit disciple Liu Yu, "renowned for Neo-Confucian learning," saying: "Passing Nanxi without knowing Liu Jinzhi is like passing Dongting without knowing oranges." Unfortunately not meeting him, he went to Xie'ao to visit disciple Xie Fujing, then visited Xikou's Dai Meng, Dai Tong, and Pengxi Village's Li Shijing, leaving calligraphy in Pengxi.

Nanxi River region, though remote, maintained such close relations with mainstream culture and reached such a level.

Scholarship drove examinations and official careers. From Tang to Qing, at least 50+ jinshi can be confirmed as Nanxi River village natives. Xikou Dai, Yuzhang Hu, Tangwan Zheng, Huatan Zhu, Cangpo Li, Furong Chen—all were "official hats rising like magpies, top degrees following one after another" prominent clans. What farmers and elders took as local glory: Song-era Yuzhang Village had three generations of five jinshi in one clan; Xikou Dai had four generations of six jinshi; Huatan Zhu and Tangwan Zheng had brother jinshi; Fenglin Village had Southern Song Longxing 1 (1163) zhuangyuan Mu Daiwen.

With prosperous exams, many became officials. Guangxu's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Figures statistics: Yongjia County "since Song, six served as grand councilors, over 50 as attendants/censors, over 100 as circuit supervisors/prefects—how prosperous!" Among them, Furong Village in Southern Song had "Eighteen Gold Belts"—eighteen people served as high court officials in Lin'an.

Song-era Nanxi River's exam prosperity, though related to the court expanding exam quotas, was more related to the two great central plains chaos (Jin and Song) bringing aristocratic clans to settle in the Nanxi River basin.

Three dynastic changes (Song-Yuan, Yuan-Ming, Ming-Qing) all brought war to Nanxi River, causing severe destruction; after Ming Jiajing, it also suffered wokou raids. Nevertheless, in Yuan, Ming, Qing, Nanxi River's literary culture remained notable. Between Yuan and Ming, Heyang Village produced Xie Deyu, "broadly versed in classics and history, a famous Confucian of the time," authoring Kuangfei Collection, Family Rituals Compendium, etc. Contemporary Huatan Village's Zhu Mi authored Four Books Expounded, Four Books Supplements, Taiji Diagram Commentary, Western Inscription Collection, etc., enshrined in the prefectural school. Yuzhang Hu, Heyang Xie, Yantou Jin, Huatan Zhu, Xikou Dai—these prominent clans still had some exam success in Ming-Qing. In Ming, Hu produced a Zhongshu Sheren (palace secretary), Dai produced a censor, Xie produced a Brocade Guard commander. In Qing, Yuzhang Village's Hu Clan Genealogy (Kangxi 34, 1695) "old preface" says: "To the Qing dynastic change, chaos arose; after war's destruction, prominent clans migrated, gathered in sorrow, unable to always gather." Under these conditions, scholarly and exam achievement greatly declined. In nearly 300 years of Qing, almost no scholarly works worth recording. Daoguang 30 (1850) "Preface to Rebuilding Heyang Xie Clan Genealogy" boasted that Xie, amid general decline, produced two more jinshi: "To this day one can still imagine the Xie clan's status, bringing color to the streams and mountains, enduring without decline!"

Yantou Village in middle Nanxi River has a ~300m rain corridor along the river, called Lishui Street. Its middle section has a couplet: "Duckweed wind green ripples viewing fish railings; willow waves green cold hearing orioles corridor"—very beautiful.

Rural intellectuals cultivated by farming-reading life: few succeeded in exams and entered official careers, even fewer became Neo-Confucians. Most stayed in villages, naturally becoming representatives of upper culture, and together with county officials—like Ming prefects He Wenyuan and Wen Lin, Qing magistrate Tang Chenglie—shouldered the responsibility of "transforming people and forming customs" (化民成俗) in the countryside. Wen Lin established Clan Norms as a model for family rules in all clan genealogies. Tang Chenglie wrote in Xianfeng's Gazetteer draft: "Yongjia in Song had Zou-Lu ethos; then scholar-official pioneers mostly studied with Two Chengs and Zhu Xi, living in villages always engaged in teaching—hence they could guide later generations, transform villages, cultivate goodness, form customs. Every household had stringed recitation, no shamans in the county; people cherished loyalty and trust, women practiced chastity; capping, marriage, funeral, sacrifice—moderate in thickness, appropriate in luxury and frugality. Illness not prayed for, marriage not guided by astrology. Seasonal entertainment, relaxation and tension appropriate; systems for nurturing the living and sending off the dead were orderly. From Yuan to Ming, farther from antiquity, customs also declined; norms abandoned and heterodoxies spread, Confucianism declined and异端 arose; dowry wealth increased and female infanticide, banquets lavish and lawsuits numerous. Illness estranged flesh-and-blood, sacrifices extravagantly honored spirits. Marriage and funeral rituals no longer followed old systems. As for Lantern Festival lights, Dragon Boat boat races—competing in splendor, wasting wealth, no regard. Men and women sightseeing, in makeup and fine clothes, filling cities—officials could not prohibit." (See Guangxu Yongjia County Gazetteer · Local Conditions) He attributed past good customs to scholars studying Neo-Confucianism and returning to teach in villages; attributed current decline to "norms abandoned and Confucianism declined." He placed hope in "scholar-officials"—expecting village intellectuals to reverse declining customs.

At this time, villages in middle Nanxi River with historically leading culture already had some people going into commerce, some "weighing principal and interest, measuring income and expenditure, accumulating penny by penny, holding abacus and tallies." But many local worthies and gentry still maintained the tradition of leading reading culture. E.g., Tangchuan Zheng Clan Genealogy records local gentleman Zheng Gong'e: "Broad and talented, fond of antiquity, skilled in rhapsody; built a fine house, placed books, displayed ancient paintings and curios for refined appreciation. Between reading, only took joy in playing qin and planting flowers. On fine days, drew spring water to brew tea, opened mats and wine cups, with two or three close friends, proudly roaming among mist, clouds, springs and rocks, no longer knowing worldly honor or shame. And teaching sons with schedule, beyond proper guidance, further refined their temperament with poetry and books." Ming Jiajing era (1796–1820) Yantou Village's Jin Jiufeng: "By nature quiet and still, daily sitting alone in a room; all classics, histories, and masters' hundred schools books none not familiar, especially devoted to astrology, finding joy in music. As for examination essays and lyrics—all mere side matters... Set up a red curtain to teach students, spring breeze filling four seats, transforming rain filling one courtyard—truly a leader among teacher-Confucians." (Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy · Preface to Mr. Jiufeng's Fiftieth Birthday) Ming Huatan Village's Zhu Boqing: "Handsome and elegant, fond of learning with literary talent, not seeking official advancement, ambition in forests and ravines... family affairs entrusted to sons, only amusing himself with writing and ink. All rocks, trees, insects, fish, springs, flowers that caught heart and eye—all became subjects of chanting. Among these, on warm sunny days, in square scarf and deerskin robe, with disciples following, wandering among water-light and mountain-color, brushing clouds, sitting on rocks, waving silk tong, watching flying geese—carefree and self-content." (Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy · Preface to Boqing's Ten Chants of Zhenchuan) Same village's Zhu Mi: "Reading and loving antiquity, simple and self-sustaining, profit and desire could not move his heart, glory and salary could not seize his will; filial to parents, friendly to brothers." (Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy · Epitaph of Mingyi Hall Gentleman) Hence Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy praises Huatan Village: "Talented scholars in groups, many with refined beauty; ancient spirit as if meeting, with dignified bearing and old-style grace—truly cultured and refined, the countryside abounds in worthy men."

Worthies praised in various clan genealogies, though not seeking official advancement but loving learning and the Way, all lived the Confucian "in retirement, cultivate oneself" (退则独善其身) life—but they never forgot the ambition of "in success, benefit all under heaven" (达则济天下). They all cared for young clansmen's official careers: not only teaching disciples themselves, but using their influence to promote clans' vigorous school-founding. All Nanxi River blood-relation village genealogies stipulate in Family Instructions or Clan Rules that children must study. Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy · Clan Rules writes: "Each year hire honest and learned scholars to teach children; must pay generous salaries, honor with ritual and culture, not losing old family standards. Children of talent capable of advancement but lacking means to study—all should support with ancestral hall rents to help them succeed." At the time, reading's primary purpose was exam success and official rank. Mingchuan Hu Main Clan Genealogy · Tianchuan Hu Charitable School Rules says: "Hence we wish for literary talent to rise, highly plucking the fragrance of five cassias; family gates ever new, foretelling the auspiciousness of three locusts... May the marsh celery be repeatedly gathered, cloud paths ascended together." Like everywhere, ancestral halls funded children's study, exam travel, and post-success expenses from charitable fields; all with exam success received commendation.

Reading mainly for official advancement, but not exclusively for it. Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Combined Genealogy has "Record of Ruzai Hall": "If I hold ten thousand books, how is that less than storing a thousand bushels of grain? Then later descendants, if not forgetting this intent, will surely strive in poetry and books, gallop to cloud paths—above continuing ancestors' footsteps, below leaving plans for grandchildren; not disgracing ancestors' exam glory, reviving former dynasty's Neo-Confucian legacy—then not only bringing glory to recent ancestors, but also well continuing the great clan!" Both exam glory and Neo-Confucian revival—broader goals.

Beyond exams and Neo-Confucianism, reading had an even greater purpose. Again this Huatan Zhu clan, in Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy · Clan Norms Oath, writes clearly: "Without learning, one is like a thing; with learning, one can stand—so is learning not great? The learner exhausts human affairs to assist heaven. Heaven established human relations—without learning none can be earnest; people have constant order—without learning none can arrange. The wise become clear through learning; the unwise become dull through abandoning learning. A great master building a house, timber filling the front, measuring and selecting without confusion—because the ink-line was set beforehand. The gentleman facing affairs without alarm, managing systems without disturbance—without learning how could his heart be settled? Hence learning is the gentleman's ink-line." Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Schools says of education: "This is the first priority of governance, what local customs look to for transformation." This deep and broad understanding and passionate pursuit of cultural education enveloped Nanxi River villages in a lofty life philosophy.

Hence Nanxi River villages had high demands for education and children. Heyang Xie Clan Genealogy · Charitable School Regulations says: "Charitable schools were established for the nation's utmost plan of nurturing people—not merely for youth to learn flowery style and gain official rank. All students must practice the White Deer Grotto Rules personally... All studying disciples must have measured steps, measured speech and conduct—everything dignified and careful, peaceful and refined." Charitable schools were public schools for poor children, yet still emphasized character beyond official rank. The White Deer Grotto Rules, required personal practice, were established by Southern Song Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi in Chunxi 6 (1179) for White Deer Grotto Academy. In Chunyou 1 (1241), Emperor Lizong personally wrote them and granted to Imperial Academy students as teaching regulations—hence they spread nationwide, even to remote rural charitable schools. Their纲领 content:

Father and son have affection; sovereign and minister have righteousness; husband and wife have distinction; elder and younger have order; friends have trust (right: five teachings' aims).
Learn broadly, inquire carefully, think cautiously, distinguish clearly, practice earnestly (right: learning's sequence).
Speak with loyalty and trust, act with earnestness and respect; restrain anger and curb desire; move toward good and correct faults (right: self-cultivation's essentials).
Uphold righteousness without seeking profit; clarify the Way without counting merit (right: handling affairs' essentials).
Do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself; when actions fail, seek within yourself (right: interacting with things' essentials).

This regulation is entirely about self-cultivation. Similar but more detailed and strict than White Deer Grotto Academy Rules was the "Lying Stele" (卧碑) established by Ming Taizu for the Imperial Academy; later Shunzhi 9 (1653) supplemented part,推行 nationwide in official schools. One supplemented clause: "All military and civilian advantages and harms—students are forbidden to submit written opinions; if one word of proposal is made, treated as violating regulations, expelled and punished." Talents were forbidden from discussing politics—even one word of discussion was a crime, expulsion from school.

Hence rural elementary schools had a dual nature: on one hand for exam achievement, on one hand for shaping future intellectuals' ideological character. This education's influence reached ordinary farmers. Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer records that county assistant He Sen, to pacify unrest in the tough-customed Nanxi River region, one measure was founding a "Nanxi Charitable School" in Fenglin Village. Clans' educational goals in Clan Rules were完全 consistent with the court.

Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Schools says Yongjia "village community schools, following ancient village and district schools, are also more than other prefectures." Nanxi River village schools: most basic are community schools and charitable schools, almost every village has them, some villages more than one. Community and charitable schools mainly teach literacy and counting, reading elementary primers to prepare for advancement. Some people of high learning and conduct, like Ming Yantou Village's Jin Jiufeng and Huatan Village's Zhu Boqing, may have run private schools—since disciples wandered with them amid mountain and water scenery, and "spring breeze filling four seats, transforming rain filling one courtyard, truly teacher-Confucian leaders"—clearly they taught beyond young children. Family and private schools were often part of a residence, usually a separate courtyard—e.g., Furong Village's western Sima Mansion, family school in an independent small garden north of the main house.

Higher-level education was undertaken by academies. One of Nanxi River's earliest academies, Xikou Village's Dongshan Academy, was founded after Southern Song jinshi and famous Neo-Confucian Dai Meng (former Crown Prince lecturer) resigned from office; due to outstanding results, the emperor granted the plaque "Mingwen" (Clear Literature). Ming-era Zhu Guangwen, heading Zhuyang Village's Baiyan Academy, and Zhu Moqu, heading Huatan Village's Fengnan Academy, were both famous local scholars with writings. Moqu's student Wang Zan became jinshi first-rank second place in Hongzhi 9 (1496), served as both capitals' Imperial Academy director and Ministry of Rites vice minister, also with writings. Emperor Xiaozong hence personally wrote "Xishan First" (溪山第一) plaque for Zhu Moqu. Yuzhang Village's Ming-era Shima Academy also had retired Zhongshu Sheren Hu Zongyun come to discuss learning and compose poetry. Additionally, Huatan Village had Xiyuan Academy, Furong Village center had Furong Academy, etc. Academies all had their own dedicated independent buildings.

These academies' levels mostly varied with their presiding shanzhang (academy head); once the presiding scholar could no longer teach, with no successor, they declined to ordinary schools. In Kangxi's Wenzhou Prefecture Gazetteer, Xikou Village's Mingwen Academy was already called Gutian School, "for enlightening young children."

Furong Academy, beside Furong Pool at the center of Furong Village in middle Nanxi River, faces east. Its main gate opens at the front of the north wall, by the village's main street Ruyi Street. Entering the small courtyard: left has "Half-Mu Square Pond" (半亩方塘), right has a Lingxing Gate-style ceremonial gate, with a pair of flagpoles before it. Entering the ceremonial gate, across the courtyard is Minglun Hall (明伦堂); before it is an Apricot Altar (杏坛), imitating Confucius's teaching place—altar 3.2m wide, 6.4m long, slightly higher than surrounding ground. Minglun Hall's rear courtyard has a lecture hall. Both Minglun Hall and lecture hall are three-bay. This entire axis is 52m long, 12.8m wide, layout very regular. The lecture hall's front eave corridor right (south) end opens a side door to the garden; the shanzhang's three-bay residence is in the garden, facing east. The garden is large, with water channels, earthen mounds, rockery, trees and bamboo growing lushly.

Academies publicly built by clans, of larger scale or higher level, were generally sited in the most scenic locations. Yuzhang Village's Shima Academy is located "at the foot of Qukou Zhai Mountain, backed by high cliff, overlooking deep stream abyss." Tangwan Village's Laoshengshen Academy was built beside Pingfeng Rock: "behind the rock about a hundred paces there is a small waterfall... below there is Chongmo Rock." Hence various places' "Ten Scenes," "Eight Scenes" mostly have one or even two scenes related to academies.

School construction and management were generally the clan's responsibility, with local gentry often as directors. Mingchuan Hu Main Clan Genealogy · Record of Dongshan School vividly records this: "Mingyu Hu clan formerly had a Reading Tower, east of the residences, extremely quiet... once hired teachers to teach children, hence clan members dressed as officials, all knowing to discipline themselves with ritual... (later Reading Tower fell into disuse, literary fortune declined) Jiajing Guichou mid-winter day, Yuanquan and Qiaoxi two gentlemen proposed to all: ... now we should continue building a refined lodge to cultivate later generations, so that book fragrance does not die out—those willing to follow may listen. All said good. Hence chose land at Dongshan's screen... after a year the lodge was completed... looking majestic, named Dongshan School. Set aside several shi of field rent as annual teacher-hiring and education expenses."

Three other important types of cultural-educational buildings in Nanxi River villages are Wenchang Pavilions (文昌阁), Wenfeng Pagodas (文峰塔), and memorial archways (牌楼). Though related to the exam system, they have far transcended it.

Wenchang Pavilions worship Wenchang Emperor (文昌帝君), who governs human worldly fame and success—hence widely worshipped. In Nanxi River's Langxia, Huatan, Yantou, Shuiyun villages, all once had Wenchang Pavilions. They usually echoed schools/academies or had halls serving as school/academy lecture rooms.

Because related to exam success—i.e., clan prosperity—clans regarded building Wenchang Pavilions as a major event, also one of local gentry's good deeds. Zhenchuan Zhu Combined Genealogy · Biography of Shenxuan Gentleman records Zhu Guangrun donating funds in Huatan Village to "build a literary pavilion... structure and construction, birds soaring and wings flying." The main body is a two-story pavilion, with two side wings serving as academy lecture rooms—"Zhenchuan's scenery, here ranks first."

Wenchang Pavilions were mostly built at the village's "water mouth" (水口)—the narrow outlet where surface water from the village's small basin gathers and flows out. Since fengshui masters simply believed China's terrain is northwest high and southeast low, "this is the great tendency of heaven and earth," villages were mostly sited northwest of the outlet, so water mouths were mostly southeast of the village—the xun (巽) direction. Water mouths often have hills on both banks, lush trees, beautiful scenery. E.g., Yantou Village's Wenchang Pavilion, founded in Qianlong Gengshen (1740), is located at the southern end of the entire Nanxi River basin's largest rural garden, at the northern foot of Tang Mountain, west of the garden's main building Tahu Temple (Xiaoyou Temple), facing Zhishui Lake in front, beside a stream with abundant water on the left. Behind the pavilion, at a higher point, stands a Wenfeng Pagoda.

Due to beautiful surroundings, Nanxi River两岸 villages' "Ten Scenes," "Eight Scenes" often include a scene of Wenchang Pavilion or academy, as objects for scholars' chanting.

Heyang Village's academy is called "Huancui Tower" (环翠楼); its "Eight Scenes" includes "Huancui Reading Sound": "Secluded pavilion steep among green trees, inside resounds reading sound; mid-air throwing to earth gold coins解, five mountains facing heaven jade pendants鸣." Huatan Village's Ten Scenes Poems includes two poems "Wenchang Ascent and Gaze": first: "Outstanding pavilion rises to the clouds, streams and mountains enter the eye wondrously... body wandering in painting, looking up and down spreading beard and brows." Second: "... bamboo sparse wind playing shadows, flowers dark birds singing shade, ancient trees floating waves still, empty pool setting moon deep..."

Wenchang Pagodas originated from fengshui superstition: believing villages with poor exam luck could build a pagoda or erect a writing brush in the jia, xun, bing, ding directions to revive literary fortune. Most were built in the xun direction, since water-mouth building complexes were also mostly outside the village in xun direction—Wenchang Pagoda and water-mouth complex complement each other, more vivid. Nanxi River basin has rolling mountains, all volcanic rhyolite, after hundreds of millions of years of erosion, with many conical peaks. In fengshui numerology these could be recognized as "writing brushes"—hence few man-made Wenfeng Pagodas here, only one each in Yantou and Tangwan villages. Yantou Village's Wenfeng Pagoda was built by Ming Guilin Gentleman (Jin clan) in Jiajing era (1522–1566), contemporaneous with Shuiting Academy and Senxiu Studio. It is located on the hillside behind the Wenchang Pavilion at the village's southeast end, entirely built of gray-white marble; from remnants, the pagoda was likely seven-story pavilion style, only about 4m high.

Village scholars often built quiet studios in scenic spots for reading. Yantou Village's Jin Guilin Gentleman converted Tahu Temple's vegetarian hall into study Senxiu Studio, backed by Youjun Pond, facing Zhennan Lake. Guilin Gentleman's poem "Inscription on Senxiu Studio · Second" has two couplets:

Door planted with embankment Tao Gong willows; courtyard opened with ink-washing Youjun pond;
Playing chess on stone steps wind frequently arrives; brewing tea in pine studio moon rises at the time.

The studio's cultural life taste was very high.

Shuiting Academy, Senxiu Studio, Wenfeng Pagoda, Wenchang Pavilion, stage, and Youjun Pond together formed Yantou Village's cultural building complex.

Tangwan Village's Ten Scenes Poems, one chanting "Xunji Mountain": "Solemnly standing alone a high peak, precisely positioned southeast gathering elegant air; xun auspicious further adding a precious pagoda, literary style flourishing brush roaming dragons." This Wenfeng Pagoda was built on the mountain—the mountain is in the village's xun direction, i.e., southeast.

Some scholar-gentry created bookish atmosphere within their residences. Early Ming Hongwu-Yongle era (1368–1424), Heyang Village had Xie Dexuan, with a study overlooking the clear river. He composed his own "Waterside Study" poem:

Green currents vast contain long sky; small study横枕 clear and pitiable;
Toothpicks holding thirty thousand scrolls; lamp light illuminating windows twenty years.
Long days dust cannot fly in; constant wind and moon leisure boundless;
Already knowing the sage Way is like this; joy found comes naturally.

Same village same clan Xie Tingxun, Xuande era (1426–1435) served in Brocade Guard, in old age built a "Jingle Xuan" (静乐轩) in his hometown old residence; genealogy writes: "Scholar-officials who visited him all composed Jingle poems." Even Emperor Xuanzong wrote a "Jingle Poem" to gift him: "Twilight moves the front pavilion, heavy city about to close gates. Remaining sunset gathers red air, new moon breaks dusk. Already feel heaven and earth still, no market noise. Yin and yang have constant principle, this discussed with the free man."

Xie Tingxun's friend, Yuzhang Village's Hu Zongyun, Ming Xuande era Zhongshu Sheren, when returning to farm had colleagues present farewell poems: lines: "Cutting thatch today in the wild, fishing old stream as before. Drying medicine sunny eaves short, arranging books night bed low." (Chen Bin) and "Mist and clouds three- mu residence, frost and dew hundred-year heart; yellow chrysanthemum Tao Qian's delight, clear wind Liangfu's chant." (Chen Zhong) After returning, Hu Zongyun built a Ziwei Tower in his old residence "Zhonghan Di" as a retirement place. Yuzhang Hu Clan Genealogy writes of him: "Planting bamboo and flowers, daily sitting and lying among them, at times touching ink, composing poems as inspired, carefree and self-content, or laughing and talking with close friends, playing go, drinking wine—like this for over twenty years."

These rural intellectuals' advocated and pursued lifestyle, the attitude of "transcending things, seeking within the heart," inevitably had a leading influence on rural cultural life.

Among Nanxi River basin's cultural-educational buildings, another important type is memorial archways (牌楼). Guangxu's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Ancient Sites writes about archway tablets: "Ancients marked their residences and villages, establishing their reputation—worthy of emulation and transmission, related to governance and education." Nanxi River people valued archways' educational role highly, generally building them exquisitely, positioned near ancestral halls or village gates, becoming part of the village's ritual center.

Huatan Village has the most and most magnificent archways. Ming Yingzong Zhengtong era (1436–1449), at the left and right of the main ancestral hall Dunmutang's front gate, for War Section Secretariat Zhu Liangxian, two archways were built facing each other: east one inscribed "Wu Fu" (Black Office, censorate), west one inscribed "Huang Men" (Yellow Gate, palace secretariat). Facing Dunmutang, another archway inscribed "Yishi Zanying" (Generations of Official Hats), erected for Ming Jiajing (1522–1566) jinshi Zhu Tian. It and "Wu Fu," "Huang Men" archways form a pin (品) character shape, enclosing a small open space before Dunmutang, adding spirit to the main ancestral hall. This pin-character layout was popular in culturally prosperous urban and rural areas. West of "Huang Men" archway, along the main road, is "Xiangxian" (Local Worthy) archway, Ming Zhengde era (1506–1521) Wenzhou Prefect He Wenyuan erected for education official Zhu Sining. Further west is "Zhongxiu" (Gathered Excellence) archway, erected when Zhu Tian passed juren in Ming Jiajing. Further west, Jiajing Bingyin (1566) winter Yongjia Magistrate Cheng Wenzhu erected for Zhu Shuangxi, inscribed "Gongzhi Chunliang" (Public, Upright, Sincere, Good). Further west is "Xihe" (Harmony) archway, local gentleman Xihua Wang erected for Zhu Lianxi, roughly late Ming. The last archway on the main road is "Xishan First" archway, erected for local jinshi and Fengyang Magistrate Zhu Yichuan, plaque written by Zhu Tian. This archway is Huatan Village's west gate. Additionally, "Xiantai" (Censorate) archway, at the center before Xiantai Ancestral Hall's main gate, Ming Hongzhi Yichou (1505) Wenzhou Prefect Li Duan and Yongjia Magistrate Liu Jing erected for Works Section Secretariat Zhu Liangyi. In Xiyuan Academy, there is "Yuanfei Yuyue" (Kites Flying, Fish Leaping) archway, Zhongshu Sheren Zhou Ling built for Zhu Youdu. All these archways honored people who studied, passed exams, and became officials—purpose: glorify the clan,激励 later generations. Additionally, county magistrate Wu Gong erected "Wei Gong Xuanli" (Serving the Public with Strength) archway for Zhu Xiaoshan (Zhu Xiaoshan's identity and deeds unrecorded), and late Ming Chongzhen Jisi (1629) Surveillance Commissioner Xu Jigong erected "Songbai Hanzhen" (Pine and Cypress Cold Chastity) archway for chaste widow Shao—only recorded in genealogy, demolished during the Cultural Revolution, location unknown.

Yantou Village has an archway, granted by Ming Shizong to Jin Zhao, left/right assistant of the Court of Judicial Review, later promoted to Ruizhou Prefect. This archway and Huatan Village's Xiantai archway are similar in style—both four-pillar four-story, with grand bracket sets, system close to Song style—truly rare.

The Nanxi River basin, over 2,000 sq km, with such developed culture and education yet long unknown to the world, provides a very typical example of rural society's cultural-educational state in a purely agricultural region of Jiangnan, and also typically narrates the background, motivation, pursuit, environment, and style of rural cultural-educational building construction.

sections.name: 学塾、书院
sections.content_zh:
三、学塾、书院

在乡土社会里，书院和学塾两种称谓的区别并不很确定。层次较低的学塾有称为书院的，而层次较高的书院却没有称为学塾的。有的私人书院自称为"精舍"、"山房"、"斋"之类，求其雅而脱俗，元代的理学家吴澄便命名自己的书院为"草庐"。

书院和学塾的建筑型制变化很大，没有一定的规例。不过一般都有课读的书房和山长或塾师的住房而已。浙江省兰溪市的诸葛村、武义市的俞源村、江西省乐安县的流坑村，村里的学塾内部模仿科考场所的布局。

老夫子坐馆授徒的私塾，大都很小，通常在住宅的"别厅"即小跨院里。江南诸省，有些小康人家的家塾，也设在别厅里。别厅面向正院的侧墙，堂屋居中，供朱子像，一个次间为课室，容量不大；另一次间为塾师卧室兼书房。有个小小的吸壁天井，贴正房侧墙建水池，池取朱熹"半亩方塘一鉴开，天光云影共徘徊，问渠那得清如许，为有源头活水来"的诗意。池边陈列几盆幽兰、茉莉之类。书声伴花香，小小别厅也很清雅。这样的别厅书塾，在浙江、江西、安徽、福建等地很普遍。

在经济发达，文风丕盛的地区，学塾和初级书院很多。江西省乐安县流坑村，据明代万历年间（1573—1620）董氏宗谱，有学堂二十六座，清代道光年宗谱记录有二十八座。福建省连城县培田村，以竹木生意而繁荣，有乡谚说它："十户一祠堂，五户一书院，三户一店铺"，看似夸张，其实并不夸张。旧皖南徽州六邑，村村有很多私家独门独户的"学堂屋"，其中黟县关麓村，只有四十三座住宅，却有十七座精致典雅的独立的学堂屋，既可作为退休商人高朋雅集、过琴棋书画休闲生活的场所，也可用作子弟课读的家塾，聘来的塾师也住在里面。学堂屋尺度比住宅小一点，布局比较自由，空间有变化，讲究情趣，装修和装饰很精致典雅，处处显得玲珑，大多带一个小园。关麓村还有多座书屋，多为独院式小楼，三间两层，有花园式的前院、环廊，点缀些仿形门，如蕉叶形、画卷形等。门额和两侧的白粉墙上镶匾和联，所题的字多为清水砖刻，或髹石绿、石青色。室内天花上满布鱼藻之类的彩画，色泽和谐清雅。

婺源县（今属江西省）理坑村也有一些学堂屋，与住宅完全分离，独立于村前小河的对岸，参差比肩而建，形成一个小区，它们各自有前后两幢屋，三开间，中为小院。前后屋的明间有曲廊连接。廊一侧从河里引水进院成小池，凭槛可数池鱼，另一侧植花木。前进两次间可为学童读书处，后进一个次间为塾师书斋，明间及另一个次间合而为敞厅，布置很潇洒。

这类学堂屋大都留意于园林趣味，福建省永安县吉山的萃园和稍小一点的西洋福庄的问渠书屋，远离村舍，建筑和家具都十分精致。萃园规模很大，正屋三开间，前后厅。左右都有跨院，花木扶疏，园前有个宽阔的大水池。它名为书院，实际功能已远远超出。又如，江西省婺源县李坑村的智仁书屋，面南，三间两层，前檐通面阔为玲珑桶扇花窗。西边另贴一间卧室。不宽的前院，满铺卵石，图案极为精致。书屋前墙外是一条水量丰沛的五米左右宽的小溪，溪对岸的小山上竹木荫翳茂盛。书屋之北为一所大花园，宽十二米多，长约二十三米。东侧又是一座花园，宽十五米多，长约十米，中央挖一个直径略小于十五米的半圆形水池，叫月池。书屋西侧小院是主人的读书厅，叫新轩，轩前一所花园，中央凿七米见方的莲池，一面贴新轩南墙，三面围以石栏，池中锦鳞出没于莲叶之下。再西侧，围墙外，又有一个约五米见方的水池，叫日池。

广东省河源市南园村有一座柳溪书院，规模不大，布局很紧凑，又很复杂。它面南有正方形两圈建筑，内圈正厅一大间，是低班学子的课堂，它明间门前有一座亭子式的方形敞轩，叫"杏坛"，仿孔子讲学的场所。宽与正厅相等的一圈方形围墙围住杏坛。围墙左右开洞门。墙的外侧，三面有狭窄的天井，东面为大门，南、西两面隔天井有房子，南面的房子是两层的，底层分为小间，给高班学子读书。楼上住塾师，西端一间是他的书房，塾师坐在书房里，可以俯视正厅和杏坛里的情况。书院的内院常植玉兰花和金桂花各一株，寄意"兰桂齐芳"。

宗祠举办的义塾经费由公共财产的义田中划出若干"学田"来提供，建筑质量稍平常一点。这种义塾的型制虽然还是没有定规，但有为科考而建的功利性特点。比较简单的，如浙江省武义县俞源村的义塾培英书屋，是一个横长的院落，大门在西端，北边一排大房间，给低班学童用，南边一排四个很小的房间，是给高班学童用的。东端地势高，上七步台阶之后有几间居住用房，是塾师的卧室和书斋。南边小房间有一扇窗花上刻着四个字，是"读圣贤书"，所以村人把这书屋叫"家训阁"。浙江省兰溪市诸葛村有一所义塾，叫笔耘轩，也是横长的院子，大门在南房正中，门两侧各有四间，划分为很小的房间。门厅正对北房正中的香火堂，它左右各为两大间教室。浙江省建德市新叶村的义塾、福建省南靖县石桥村步云斋书屋，也都类似这样。这种横排小间的布局是仿科考的场屋，让高班的学童习惯它们。北房正中文昌帝君的香火堂也祭朱子（即朱熹）。

义塾也有少数是富裕的"善人"捐出田亩来创办的。浙江省永嘉县芙蓉村的近邻岩头村，有一座桂林公专祠，叫水亭祠，面朝北。它本来是金氏桂林公在明代晚期建造的水亭书院。《岩头金氏宗谱·宗祠》说，嘉靖年间（1522—1566）桂林公"原创水亭为子孙课业计，自兹文学振兴，叨膺科第，至今胶序蝉联，绳绳不绝"。进三楼式砖砌大门之后，先见一方大水池（24.5米×21.4米），绕过这池水，中轴线上是仪门，进门，眼前又是一方大水池（25.0米×21.4米），池正中一道平平的石板桥，可达池中央的方亭（4米×4米）。穿亭而过，再经桥引向后面的讲堂。讲堂面阔7开间，左右侧还有廊子。这座书院的布局构思奇特，极为少见。桂林公对岩头村的建设作出过全面的贡献，殁后族人把书院改为他的专祠。

较大的私塾也有住宅型的，如徽州六邑之一婺源县延村西南角的一座私塾，是两个两层的三合院并肩而成的，其中一座因地形所限平面不很规则。学生是住读的，有七小间宿舍，教师也有两间卧室。另有食堂和厨房，突出在它东南角。楼上有外廊，正对着院子里的金桂、银桂各一株。桂树是学业有成，科考得捷的象征，考中了就叫"折桂"。

婺源县的甲路村也有一座楼房，楼上三间通开为学塾，前后檐均辟大窗，内部空间敞朗。楼梯十分宽阔平缓，以免拥挤。后檐大窗外的底层屋面上还有疏散措施，保障学童的安全。这学塾的功能推敲很周到。

婺源县汪口镇上深巷里有一座小小的院落，院门额上篆"掩翠"二字，正屋完全与住宅相同，三间两层。院前有短墙，左前方小门上方嵌"养源书院"额。前院里，四季香溢的月月桂下，侧墙上镶着一方青石碑，刊刻的是光绪十年（1884年）婺源县正堂吴的告示，公布了"汪口封职俞光銮"的一则呈文，并明确予以批准和支持。呈文的主要内容是："职少孤贫，成童后贸易江西，辛勤积累，随置田亩。因思承先裕后，励学为先。而励学则储田为要，除存祀田慰先灵、微派田亩为六子分析外，仍余之田另立户册完课，存为后人膏火之资。……唯恐日后弊生，或有不肖之子孙举此田而私废之，则励学将堕于半途，而砚田莫贞于悠远，为此，吁叩恩赏给示，以禁私废而杜私受。"这座养源书院是一所真正意义上的义塾，用俞光銮捐出的田亩收益创办并维持。

和浙江省楠溪江流域的村子相同，各地都有些村落在风景佳丽之地建造书院，甚至形成一个"景点"。

福建省连城县培田村有好几个书院，其中"南山书院"创建于清代乾隆三十年（1765年）。它位于卧虎山北麓，创始人吴锦江取陶渊明"采菊东篱下，悠然见南山"诗意，命名为"南山书院"。"南山书院"是培田新八景之一，吴受仁有诗：

步上南山境僻幽，琅玕诵读韵悠悠，
蕉窗雨冷偏逢夜，竹院风凉又报秋。
金石一声天地震，简编万卷古今搜，
朝晴早起人倾听，鸟语书声乐唱酬。

南山书院由三座院落相聚组成。东院大门居中，为牌坊式，清人曾瑞春《南山书院记》说："书'德造庐'于门之外，'培兰植桂'于门之内，'朱子读书乐诗'于东西壁"。现在所见略有不同，大门内侧门额以上书"南山书院"四字，门外两侧门柱上是裴应章尚书题的对联"距汀城郭虽百里，入孔门墙第一家"。门内墙上书朱子语录："观古者圣贤所以教人为学之要，莫不使之讲明义理，以修其身，然后推己及后。"正房五开间，两层，底层当心间正厅供孔子牌位，其余各间为学生教室。西院比东院低七步台阶，是一所两层楼的四合院，西、南两面有前檐廊和美人靠，是当年塾师居住、读书的地方。东、西两院之间夹着一个狭长的小院，有小门向南通院外。书院前有一个半月形水塘，作为泮池，又叫"砚池"，与书院的朝山文笔峰相映成"文笔蘸墨"的风水。

浙江省兰溪市诸葛村，村北有南阳书舍，为"高隆八景"之首。明代正德年间（1506—1521），陆凤仪写《南阳书舍》诗：

花竹绕庭除，图书万卷余，
云藏扬子宅，人识卧龙居。
景物随游惬，江山入望舒，
悠然栖息者，谁羡武陵墟。

这座书院不但藏书丰富，而且环境优美，江山景物望之舒而游之惬。在这样的场合读书，"坛杏飞红铺砌畔，泮芹分翠入轩中。春风绛帐频施教，夜雨青灯好课功"（清人王以璋诗二、三联），真是人生快事。

距诸葛村不远，今建德市铜山后金村是元代最大的学者金履祥（字仁山）的故里，村口外，有一座仁山书院，格局完全与中等宗祠相同，疑为后人所筑。

浙江省宁海县跃麟庵为方孝孺读书处，前童村有方孝孺讲学的鹿山书院。方孝孺少年时曾在宁海南谷草堂读书，中年时作《草堂歌》纪事：

草堂坐对陵南谷，勤把诗书向窗读。
学门长掩寂无人，惟有白云相伴宿。
昨日溪头罢钓归，花笑莺啼芳草绿。
猿鹤嘹嘹哀怨啼，萧瑟自理山家曲。

当年这书院环境风光也是十分秀丽的。

除了学塾、书院之外，江南较大的村子里又常有一座"文馆"，北方也有但少见。文馆是"文会"的活动场所，文会的成员主要是村子里的文化人、读书人，包括致仕退食的官员和困顿场屋但也曾熟读经书的人，等等。他们形成村子的舆论集体，有威信、有影响，宗族的大事常要请他们参议，族人有犯过失甚至涉罪的，先由他们问审，决定是否送官。不过他们日常的活动是到文馆里交谊，谈诗论文，拨弦吹竹，品茶斗棋。村里的童生、秀才，每月两度到文馆，或携卷呈交，或受题当场作文，由文会中前辈评审、指点。同治安徽《黟县三志·艺文》有康熙庚寅（1710年）知县李登龙写的《聚奎文会序》，其中说："黟县各都之设有文会，一以敦气谊，一以广观摩，诚美举也……余所望会中诸子，正其谊不谋其利，明其道不计其功。日有课，月有会……经旨有未晰者折衷而商订之，文义有未善者讲论而开导之……有过必折，有善必规。"浙江省兰溪市诸葛村，在乾隆年间（1736—1795）由族人殷实者捐田、捐银，建立了一个"登瀛文会"，诸葛氏宗谱里的《重整登瀛文会记》说："月数聚士子课制艺，优者给以膏火之费，乡会试赠以宾兴之资，从无间断。"说的就是文会提携后生搏科举的事。

文馆的建筑都很精致。江西省乐安县流坑村董氏大宗祠的右侧，广东省始兴县东湖坪村的曾氏大宗祠左侧，都有文馆。它们的型制几乎和宗祠相同，三进两院，宏堂高轩，常用的功能空间都在两厢里。有些文馆的建筑则别有深意，如江西省广昌县驿前村的文馆，紧贴抚江左岸，厅堂馆屋不作纵深排列而是横向沿江展开，并依江岸而微曲，只有大厅三间是以轴线向江的。从江上望去，长长一带粉墙上悬出几间敞廊，跌宕有致，典雅而洒脱。它的前院有一座小屋，从内部来看，形式完全仿船舱，拱顶，内部墙面都处理成船篷编织形状。安徽省黟县关麓村有一座双桂书屋，村人就叫它"船屋"，它的一个突出墙外的厅，平面呈弧形三角形，有尖，宛如船的前端。另有一座住宅里的暖阁就叫"船厅"，厅左右均有敞廊，廊外侧为水池。江西省乐安县流坑村有两座船形住宅，一座是明经巷的"董步汀仙舫"，一座是上巷的"董演四仙舫"，都建于光绪年间（1875—1908），悬"仙舫"匾额。村人叫它们为"船屋"。舫体"前舱"为甲板，"中舱"为客厅，"后舱"为卧室，屋后有"泮池"。江西省、安徽省和福建省，还有些村里的大宅，正房前檐的平面呈弧形，酷似船舷。关于这种特殊形状的文馆和书屋，如今有多种解说，但大约以象征"学海无涯苦作舟"的俚语或者"为学如逆水行舟，不进则退"这类的教导为近似。
sections.content_en:
3. Schools and Academies

In rural society, the distinction between the terms "academy" (书院) and "school" (学塾) was not firmly fixed. Lower-level schools were sometimes called academies, while higher-level academies were never called schools. Some private academies called themselves "refined lodges" (精舍), "mountain chambers" (山房), "studies" (斋), and the like—seeking elegance and refinement. Yuan dynasty Neo-Confucian Wu Cheng named his own academy "Thatched Hut" (草庐).

The architectural forms of academies and schools varied greatly, with no fixed rules. Generally, however, they had reading rooms for classes and residences for the academy head (shanzhang) or schoolmaster. In Zhuge Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang), Yuyuan Village (Wuyi, Zhejiang), and Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi), village schools internally imitated the layout of examination halls.

Private schools where old masters taught were mostly small, usually located in a residence's "separate hall" (别厅), i.e., a small side courtyard. In Jiangnan provinces, some moderately well-off families' family schools were also in separate halls. The separate hall faces the main courtyard's side wall; the central hall houses a Zhu Xi statue; one secondary room is a classroom of modest capacity; the other secondary room is the schoolmaster's bedroom cum study. There is a small attached light well (吸壁天井), with a water pool built against the main house's side wall—the pool evoking Zhu Xi's poem: "Half-mu square pond opens like a mirror; sky light and cloud shadows wander together. Ask how the canal stays so clear? Because flowing water comes from the source." By the pool stand several pots of orchids, jasmine, and the like. Reading sound accompanied by flower fragrance—the small separate hall is quite elegant. Such separate-hall schools were common in Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Anhui, Fujian, and elsewhere.

In economically developed, culturally flourishing regions, schools and elementary academies were numerous. Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi), according to Ming Wanli-era (1573–1620) Dong clan genealogy, had 26 school buildings; Qing Daoguang-era genealogy records 28. Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian), prosperous from bamboo and timber trade, has a local saying: "One ancestral hall per ten households, one academy per five households, one shop per three households"—seemingly exaggerated, actually not. In old Huizhou's six counties, every village had many private, independent "school houses" (学堂屋); among them, Guanlu Village (Yixian) had only 43 residences but 17 exquisitely elegant independent school houses—serving both as venues for retired merchants' elegant gatherings (qin, chess, calligraphy, painting leisure) and as family schools for children's study, with hired schoolmasters living inside. School houses were slightly smaller than residences, with freer layout, varied spaces, attention to charm, refined decoration, everywhere delicate—most with a small garden. Guanlu Village also had multiple study houses, mostly independent-courtyard small buildings, three-bay two-story, with garden-style front courtyards, surrounding corridors, and decorative shaped doors (banana-leaf form, painting-scroll form, etc.). Door lintels and side white-plaster walls bore plaques and couplets, mostly in clear-water brick carving or painted stone-green/stone-blue. Interior ceilings were covered with colorful paintings of fish and water plants, harmonious and elegant in color.

Likeng Village (Wuyuan, now Jiangxi) also had school houses, completely separated from residences, independently built across the small river in front of the village, arranged unevenly side by side forming a small district. Each had front and rear buildings, three-bay, with a small courtyard between. The central bays of front and rear buildings were connected by a winding corridor. On one side of the corridor, water was channeled from the river into a small pool—leaning on the railing one could count the fish; on the other side, flowers and trees were planted. The front building's two secondary rooms could serve as children's reading spaces; the rear building's one secondary room was the schoolmaster's study; the central bay and another secondary room combined into an open hall—layout very free and easy.

Such school houses mostly paid attention to garden charm. Cuiyuan (萃园) at Jishan (Yong'an, Fujian) and the slightly smaller Wenqu Study House (问渠书屋) at Xiyang Fuzhuang, far from village houses, had both buildings and furniture very refined. Cuiyuan was large-scale: main house three-bay, front and rear halls. Both sides had side courtyards with lush flowers and trees; before the garden was a broad large pool. Called an academy, its actual functions far exceeded that. Another example: Zhiren Study House (智仁书屋) at Likeng Village (Wuyuan), facing south, three-bay two-story, front eave full width of exquisite lattice flower windows. West side attached a bedroom. The modest front courtyard was fully paved with pebbles in extremely refined patterns. Outside the study house's front wall was a stream about 5m wide with abundant water; on the opposite bank's small hill, bamboo and trees were lush. North of the study house was a large garden, over 12m wide, ~23m long. East side was another garden, over 15m wide, ~10m long, with a semicircular pool slightly under 15m diameter in the center, called Moon Pool (月池). The study house's west side small courtyard was the owner's reading hall, called Xin Xuan (新轩); before it was a garden with a 7m-square lotus pool in the center, one side against Xin Xuan's south wall, three sides fenced with stone railings—carp appeared and disappeared among lotus leaves. Further west, outside the wall, another ~5m-square pool, called Sun Pool (日池).

Liuxi Academy (柳溪书院) at Nanyuan Village (Heyuan, Guangdong) was modest in scale, compact yet complex in layout. Facing south, it had two square rings of buildings: the inner ring's main hall was one large room, the classroom for lower-level students; before its central bay was a pavilion-style square open veranda called "Apricot Altar" (杏坛), imitating Confucius's teaching place. A square enclosing wall equal in width to the main hall surrounded the Apricot Altar. The wall had arched doors on left and right. Outside the wall, three sides had narrow light wells; east side was the main gate; south and west sides had buildings across light wells—the south building was two-story, ground floor divided into small rooms for higher-level students. Upstairs lived the schoolmaster; the west-end room was his study—sitting in his study, the schoolmaster could overlook the main hall and Apricot Altar. The academy's inner courtyard often planted one magnolia and one osmanthus, symbolizing "orchid and osmanthus together fragrant" (兰桂齐芳).

Charitable schools (义塾) run by ancestral halls were funded by setting aside "study fields" (学田) from public charitable fields; building quality was somewhat ordinary. Though their form had no fixed rule, they had the utilitarian characteristic of being built for examinations. Simpler examples: Peiying Study House (培英书屋), the charitable school at Yuyuan Village (Wuyi, Zhejiang), was a horizontally long courtyard—main gate at west end; north side a row of large rooms for lower-level students; south side a row of four very small rooms for higher-level students. East end was higher; after seven steps up were several residential rooms—the schoolmaster's bedroom and study. One south small room's window lattice was carved with four characters "Read Sage Books" (读圣贤书), hence villagers called it "Family Instruction Pavilion" (家训阁). Zhuge Village (Lanxi) had a charitable school called Biyun Xuan (笔耘轩), also a horizontally long courtyard—main gate in the center of the south building, four rooms on each side divided into very small rooms. The entrance hall faced the central incense hall of the north building; its left and right were each two large classrooms. The charitable school at Xinye Village (Jiande, Zhejiang) and Buyun Zhai Study House (步云斋) at Shiqiao Village (Nanjing, Fujian) were similar. This horizontal-row small-room layout imitated examination halls, letting higher-level students get used to them. The north building's central Wenchang Emperor incense hall also worshipped Zhu Xi.

A few charitable schools were founded by wealthy "good people" donating fields. Near Furong Village (Yongjia, Zhejiang), Yantou Village had a Guilin Gong dedicated shrine called Shuiting Shrine (水亭祠), facing north. It was originally the Shuiting Academy (水亭书院) built by Jin clan's Guilin Gong in late Ming. Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy · Ancestral Halls says that in Jiajing era (1522–1566), Guilin Gong "originally created Shuiting for descendants' study; from then literature flourished, received examination degrees, to this day schools continue unbroken." Entering the three-story brick main gate, first one saw a large pool (24.5m × 21.4m);绕过 the pool, on the central axis was the ceremonial gate; entering, before one was another large pool (25.0m × 21.4m); in the pool's center a flat stone bridge led to a square pavilion (4m × 4m). Passing through the pavilion, another bridge led to the rear lecture hall. The lecture hall was 7-bay wide, with corridors on both sides. This academy's layout was ingenious and extremely rare. Guilin Gong made comprehensive contributions to Yantou Village's construction; after his death, clansmen converted the academy into his dedicated shrine.

Larger private schools could also be residence-type. E.g., a private school at the southwest corner of Yancun Village (Wuyuan, one of Huizhou's six counties) was two two-story three-courtyard compounds side by side—one had an irregular plan due to terrain. Students boarded: seven small dormitory rooms; teachers had two bedrooms. Additionally a dining hall and kitchen protruded at the southeast corner. Upstairs had an outer corridor facing one golden osmanthus and one silver osmanthus in the courtyard. Osmanthus was a symbol of academic success and examination victory—passing was called "plucking osmanthus" (折桂).

Jialu Village (Wuyuan) also had a building: upstairs three bays opened through as a school, front and rear eaves both had large windows, interior space open and bright. The staircase was very wide and gentle to avoid crowding. Outside the rear-eave large window, on the ground-floor roof, there were evacuation measures ensuring children's safety. This school's functional design was very thorough.

In a deep alley of Wangkou Town (Wuyuan), a small courtyard had a gate lintel with seal-script "Concealed Green" (掩翠); the main house was exactly like a residence, three-bay two-story. Before the courtyard was a low wall; above the small gate at left front was embedded "Yangyuan Academy" (养源书院) plaque. In the front courtyard, under the fragrant monthly osmanthus, the side wall bore a blue stone stele engraved with a Guangxu 10 (1884) Wuyuan County Magistrate Wu's proclamation—publicizing a petition by "Wangkou titled official Yu Guangluan" and explicitly granting approval and support. The petition's main content: "I was orphaned and poor in youth; after coming of age I traded in Jiangxi, diligently accumulating, purchasing fields. Thinking of honoring ancestors and benefiting descendants, encouraging learning is first. And encouraging learning requires storing fields as essential—besides keeping sacrificial fields to comfort ancestral spirits and allocating small fields for six sons' division, the remaining fields I register under a separate household to pay taxes, kept as later generations' study-fund resources. ... Fearing future abuses, or unworthy descendants privately abolishing these fields, then learning encouragement would fall halfway, and the 'inkstone field' would not endure long—hence I humbly request your honor's proclamation to forbid private abolition and prevent private misappropriation." This Yangyuan Academy was a true charitable school, founded and maintained by Yu Guangluan's donated field income.

Like villages in Zhejiang's Nanxi River basin, various places had villages building academies in scenic spots, even forming a "scenic spot."

Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian) had several academies; among them "Nanshan Academy" (南山书院) was founded in Qing Qianlong 30 (1765). Located at the northern foot of Wohu Mountain, founder Wu Jinjiang took Tao Yuanming's poem "Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern fence, calmly seeing the southern mountain" to name it "Nanshan Academy." It was one of Peitian's New Eight Scenes; Wu Shouren wrote a poem:

Stepping up Nanshan, realm secluded and quiet, bamboo reading rhymes lingering;
Banana-window rain cold偏偏 meets night, bamboo-courtyard wind cool again reports autumn.
Metal-stone one sound heaven and earth shake, bamboo-slips ten thousand volumes ancient and modern search;
Morning clear early rise people listen, bird songs and reading sound joyfully respond.

Nanshan Academy consisted of three courtyards clustered together. The east courtyard's main gate was centered, archway-style; Qing person Zeng Ruichun's Record of Nanshan Academy says: "Inscribed 'Virtue-Built Lodge' outside the gate, 'Cultivating Orchid and Osmanthus' inside the gate, 'Zhu Xi's Reading Joy Poem' on east and west walls." What remains differs slightly: inside the gate, above the lintel, "Nanshan Academy" four characters; outside the gate, on both side pillars, a couplet by Minister Pei Yingzhang: "Though a hundred li from Ting city wall, the first family entering Confucius's gate." Inside the gate wall was Zhu Xi's quotation: "Observe how ancient sages taught the essentials of learning—none did not make them clarify moral principle, cultivate themselves, then extend to others." The main house was five-bay, two-story; ground floor central bay main hall enshrined Confucius's tablet; remaining bays were student classrooms. The west courtyard was seven steps lower than the east, a two-story quadrangle with front-eave corridors and "beauty rests" (美人靠) on west and south sides—where schoolmasters lived and studied. Between east and west courtyards was a narrow small courtyard with a small gate leading south outside. Before the academy was a crescent-shaped pond serving as the Pan Pool (泮池), also called "Inkstone Pool" (砚池), echoing the academy's facing mountain Writing-Brush Peak in the fengshui of "writing brush dipping ink."

Zhuge Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang), north of the village, had Nanyang Study House (南阳书舍), first of "Gaolong Eight Scenes." Ming Zhengde era (1506–1521), Lu Fengyi wrote a poem Nanyang Study House:

Flowers and bamboo surround the courtyard, books and pictures over ten thousand scrolls;
Clouds hide Yangzi's residence, people recognize Wolong's dwelling.
Scenery follows wandering content, rivers and mountains enter gaze comfortably;
Carefree dweller here, who would envy Wuling's paradise?

This academy not only had rich book collections but beautiful environment—rivers and mountains comfortable to gaze and wander. Reading in such a setting: "Altar apricot blossoms red paving the courtyard edge, Pan celery green entering the veranda. Spring breeze red curtain frequently teaches, night rain green lamp good for lessons" (Qing poet Wang Yizhang's poem, second and third couplets)—truly a joy of life.

Not far from Zhuge Village, today's Tongshan Houjin Village (Jiande) was the hometown of Yuan dynasty's greatest scholar Jin Lüxiang (courtesy name Renshan); outside the village entrance was Renshan Academy (仁山书院), its layout exactly like a medium ancestral hall—suspected to be built by later generations.

Yuelin Nunnery (跃麟庵) at Ninghai (Zhejiang) was Fang Xiaoru's reading place; Qiantong Village had Lushan Academy where Fang Xiaoru lectured. Fang Xiaoru studied at Nangu Thatched Cottage (南谷草堂) in youth; in middle age he wrote Thatched Cottage Song to record:

Thatched cottage facing Lingnan Valley, diligently reading poetry and books by the window;
School gate long closed silent no one, only white clouds accompanying lodging.
Yesterday returned from fishing at the stream head, flowers smiling orioles singing fragrant grass green;
Apes and cranes sadly calling, bleakly playing the mountain family tune.

That academy's environment and scenery were also very beautiful back then.

Beyond schools and academies, larger Jiangnan villages often had a "Literary Hall" (文馆), rare in the north. The Literary Hall was the activity venue for "Literary Societies" (文会)—members mainly village cultural figures and readers, including retired officials and those who struggled in examinations but had thoroughly studied the classics. They formed the village's opinion collective, with prestige and influence; clan major affairs often required their consultation; clansmen committing faults or even crimes were first interrogated by them, deciding whether to send to officials. But their daily activities were gathering at the Literary Hall for friendship, discussing poetry and prose, playing string and wind instruments, tasting tea and playing chess. Village students and xiucai (秀才) came twice monthly to the Literary Hall—either submitting essays or composing on assigned topics on the spot, reviewed and guided by senior society members. Tongzhi-era Anhui Yixian Three Gazetteers · Literature has a Preface to Jukui Literary Society (聚奎文会序) by Kangxi Gengyin (1710) County Magistrate Li Denglong: "Yixian's each district has literary societies—one to cultivate friendship, one to broaden observation and emulation, truly a fine endeavor... What I hope of society members: uphold righteousness without seeking profit, clarify the Way without counting merit. Daily lessons, monthly gatherings... classical meanings not yet clear—compromise and discuss; literary meanings not yet good—lecture and guide... faults must be corrected, goodness must be encouraged." Zhuge Village (Lanxi), in Qianlong era (1736–1795), had clansmen of means donate fields and silver to establish "Dengying Literary Society" (登瀛文会); Zhuge clan genealogy's Record of Reorganizing Dengying Literary Society says: "Monthly gather scholars several times to test examination essays; excellent ones given study-fund expenses; provincial and metropolitan exams given travel funds—never interrupted." This describes literary societies guiding later generations in examination pursuit.

Literary Hall buildings were all refined. Right of Dong clan's main ancestral hall at Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi), and left of Zeng clan's main ancestral hall at Donghuping Village (Shixing, Guangdong), both had Literary Halls. Their form was almost identical to ancestral halls—three entries, two courtyards, grand halls and high pavilions, with functional spaces in the two side wings. Some Literary Hall buildings had deeper meaning: e.g., the Literary Hall at Yiqian Village (Guangchang, Jiangxi), tightly against the left bank of the Fu River—halls and rooms not arranged in depth but horizontally along the river, slightly curving with the bank; only the three-bay main hall had its axis toward the river. Viewed from the river, a long stretch of white plaster wall with several open verandas cantilevered out—rhythmic, elegant and free. Its front courtyard had a small building that, internally, was entirely shaped like a ship's cabin—vaulted ceiling, interior walls treated as woven ship-canopy form. Guanlu Village (Yixian, Anhui) had Shuanggui Study House, villagers called it "Ship House" (船屋)—one hall protruding beyond the wall had an arc-triangular plan with a point, like a ship's bow. Another residence's warm pavilion was called "Ship Hall" (船厅), with open corridors on both sides and a pool outside the corridors. Liukeng Village had two ship-shaped residences: one "Dong Buting Immortal Boat" (董步汀仙舫) in Mingjing Alley, one "Dong Yansi Immortal Boat" (董演四仙舫) in Shang Alley—both built in Guangxu era (1875–1908), with "Immortal Boat" plaques. Villagers called them "Ship Houses." The boat body's "front cabin" was a deck, "middle cabin" a living room, "rear cabin" a bedroom; behind the house was a "Pan Pool." In Jiangxi, Anhui, and Fujian, some village large residences had curved front-eave plans, exactly like a ship's side. About these specially shaped Literary Halls and study houses, there are various interpretations today—but most likely they symbolize the saying "the sea of learning is boundless, diligence is the boat" (学海无涯苦作舟) or teachings like "learning is like rowing upstream—not advancing means retreating" (为学如逆水行舟，不进则退).

sections.name: 孔庙、科名牌坊、桅
sections.content_zh:
四、孔庙、科名牌坊、桅

孔庙又称文庙，按例，只有县以上建置方可建文庙，但极少数村子经曲阜衍圣公府批准也建了文庙。山西省阳城县郭峪村和不远的沁水县西文兴村各有一座，浙江省永嘉县的芙蓉村也有。文庙的地位高过于文昌阁，按规定，它的"典籍官"也要由衍圣公府正式任命。

郭峪村的文庙位于村内西城墙根。明代成化六年（1470年），在这里的古代公用建筑废墟上复建了一座"里馆"，"选老人以掌乡之政令教化"，大约相当于一个村政府。万历初，因张居正掌朝政改制被毁。遗址于"崇祯时始赎归里，焕宇王君（即王重新）议诸绅士而据馆废墟建庙焉"，这便是孔子庙，后来叫文庙。到清代乾隆十二年（1747年）重修时，将庙址扩大，等级提高，成为当地最壮观的建筑物之一。文庙后期有庙产地十余亩，都是乡人捐献。

郭峪村所在的"里"，从唐代到清初，出了一百多位"乡贤"，本村在清代初年又出了文渊阁大学士、《康熙字典》总裁官之一陈廷敬。

清代所建郭峪村文庙坐北面南，四合院，占地面积大约四千平方米。地势北高南低，大门前要上十几级台阶。大门五开间，中央三间为明柱厦廊，正殿为大成殿，面阔五开间，正中供孔子坐像，两侧按昭穆分列颜回、曾子等孔门七十二贤人的牌位。大成殿结构用斗拱，前檐有格扇门窗，殿前有月台，便是"杏坛"。大殿左右各有耳房两间，供储存祭仪用品，管理人员也住在这里。

东西配殿各八间，为乡贤祠，殿内供郭峪及附近各村（属郭峪里）的乡贤牌位一百多个，并有名贤碑七座，其中两座刻着自唐代至清代一千多年郭峪里考取功名的人的姓名，有八十八位之多。乡谚说，"金谷十里长，才子出郭峪"。金谷是郭峪村所在的山谷的名称。

郭峪文庙内另有各种纪事石碑一百余块，并有文昌阁一座。

文庙大门的厦廊是科考张榜的地方，平日里孩子不得在这里玩耍，闲杂人等不得在这里喧哗，颇有严肃之气。

每年春秋二季有隆重的祭祀，生员以上的文化人才有资格参加。参加祭祀的人必须长袍马褂、衣冠整齐、形象端庄，并且事先要洗脸剃头。参祭的人按品级年龄先在大门外排队，然后徐徐鱼贯进入庙内，在杏坛上举行隆重的典礼。杏坛上布陈祭品，人们焚香跪拜，行三献礼，燃放鞭炮。祭毕孔子，再祭拜乡贤。"大社"（乡间的行政组织，高于"社"一级）出资做嫩豆腐，祭礼完毕，分给社中儿童吃掉，相信可以补脑，读书聪明，将来登科进仕。

山西省沁水县西文兴村的文庙也是附近西乡各村共祀。民国十年（1921年）的西文兴村《重修文昌阁、文庙碑记》写道："春秋祀期，往之邑侯下临，或遣学官为代表，率西乡士子习礼讲学于其中，渐摩以诗、书、礼、乐之化，故当时科举联翩，民俗亦为之敦厚。……自前清道光年间殿宇倾圮，呈请移此圣木主于县城文庙，嗣后父老子弟不复睹衣冠文物之盛，习礼讲学之风遂以中辍，文风亦因之不振，迄今百有余年。"

这座文庙在村子正门之内，正门之上为奎星阁。文庙北邻为圣庙，内祀历代帝王圣贤的牌位。圣庙之北为文昌阁，文昌阁恰位于村内正街东口，街内有进士牌楼两座。文庙的西侧有敬惜字纸的焚帛炉两座。这一组文教建筑占了全村不小的面积。

福建省连城县培田村有"文武庙"，建成于清代乾隆己亥年（1779年）。两层楼阁，上层祀孔子，下层祀关羽。文圣、武圣共处一楼。《吴氏宗谱》里写道："每修皆大发，诚敬必高升。"

中了科举功名，不但仕途通畅，而且光宗耀祖，自己更可以得到一份永久的纪念。明初洪武二十一年（1388年），太祖朱元璋下诏用公帑给新科状元任亨泰建造一座牌坊。从此进士牌坊便流行起来，到了明代中叶成化、弘治朝，还给以前没有建牌坊的进士补建，不久，州府和一些乡村都可以看到壮观的进士牌坊了。清代虽然自嘉庆朝起停止用官帑给进士造牌坊，但听宗族自建。"自建"引发有些举人也造起了牌坊，不过数量不多。清初的雍正皇帝说过，"四民以士为长，农次之，工商其下"，光绪年间（1875—1908）编就的《大清会典》说："崇本抑末，载诸会典，若为常经，由来已久。"这些仕进牌坊，把"士"的首要地位形象地告示于天下。对牛角挂书的田舍郎，这又是一个有力的激励。

因为纪念性建筑求耐久，早在元末明初，仕进牌坊就有用石材的或木、石并用的了，多雨潮湿的南方诸省以石柱的为多，也有大量整体都为石材的。但石质构件的式样和做法等仍仿木构。北方诸省因干燥而仍多全身木质的。牌坊式样有两大类，一类由古代"衡门"发展而来，大约在宋代开始用作纪念性的牌坊；另一类由古代"乌头门"（或称"棂星门"）发展而来，用冲天柱。乌头门式的牌坊大约出现于明代弘治、正德年间（1488—1521），明末盛行，到清代成为主要的型制。这两类牌坊都可以跨街巷而建，作为地标，引人注意。（但贞节牌坊不许人在下面穿过，所以多贴墙而建，并在柱间密列栏杆，处理得很严肃。）

牌坊的规格有双柱单楼或三楼、四柱三间三楼或五楼几种。"楼"，指的是一段狭窄的双坡的小屋顶。

双柱单楼式牌坊是最简单的一种，它可以用山西省沁水县西文兴村的一对全石质乡进士牌坊为代表作。它们是为炫耀明代成化十六年（1480年）乡进士柳騄和明代嘉靖二十五年（1546年）乡进士柳遇春的科举成就而立的，分别造于1544年和1550年。二者式样和尺寸一模一样，结构和比例完全模仿木结构，左右对称地竖立在村子居住区主门永庆门前的横向主街上。柳騄的牌坊刻"丹桂传芳"四字，柳遇春的刻"青云接武"。它们相距大约二十五米，和永庆门一起组成了全村建筑的核心。

三间五楼式牌坊是仕进（进士）牌坊中最华丽有气派的，只有衡门式而不可能有冲天柱式，因为三间而有五楼，便是在中央一对柱顶正上方支一小段双坡式顶子。例子之一是安徽省绩溪县冯村的冯瑢进士牌坊。冯瑢于明代成化十四年（1478年）考中进士，屡任福州推官，北京兵部车驾司主事，弘治二年（1489年）致仕。这座牌坊建于成化十五年（1479年），即中进士的次年。它四根柱子都是石质的，前后都有抱鼓形的"靠背石"，增加牌楼的稳定性和厚重感。明间和次间之上的木质歇山式楼顶各有两攒斗拱，夹在中间的两个楼顶只各有一攒斗拱。斗拱出三跳，并有斜出的拱，很轻巧华丽。脊上的吻和宝瓶的尺度都很夸张，以致轮廓跳动而有喜庆的气息。明间的下枋上雕一对狮子滚绣球，这是民间抒写欢快而热烈心情常用的题材。次间的下枋上雕的是鹿，谐音"禄"，读书考进士为的是当官，也便是求禄。明间上下枋之间的"字牌"上镌刻"进士第"三字，它上方，有竖向匾额刻"恩荣"二字。恩荣二字表示牌坊的建造是由皇上恩准了的。也有些牌坊在这块匾额上刻"圣旨"或"敕建"等字，是同样的意思。

类似的四柱三间五楼式进士牌坊还有浙江省遂昌县独山村的进士牌坊和福建省连城县培田村武进士吴拔祯的牌坊。吴拔祯护卫慈禧太后西狩有功，所以牌坊上刊刻对联：

世有凤毛迭荷宸慈颁紫綍；
身随豹尾曾陪仙仗列黄麾。

浙江省永嘉县楠溪江中游岩头村幸存的进士牌坊，是明世宗嘉靖年间（1522—1566）为进士金昭造的，四柱三间三楼，但中央明间两根柱子是石质的，断面为方形。每根柱子也都是前后有抱鼓石式的靠背石夹住。这座牌坊的特点是结构近似宋式，斗拱雄大而且用真昂，最上面两层昂的后尾合力托住脊檩，它们下面一层昂的后尾又在中段托住它们。整个牌坊的造型非常刚健有力。它通面宽8.46米，柱高4.40米，总高7.63米，前后各出檐1.65米，很飘洒。瓦脊的曲线十分柔和轻巧。虽然斗拱复杂但整体很简洁，没有装饰，然而比例和谐。永嘉县花坦村的宪台牌楼和朱氏大宗祠（敦睦祠）的大门以及苍坡村的大门，结构和风格都与这座进士牌楼相似。

三开间进士牌坊也有全部用石料建造的，不过数量少。实例之一是浙江省兰溪市长乐村的进士牌坊。它三开间，正贴村门，几乎成了村门的主体。可惜在文化大革命时遭到了严重的破坏。

除了为个别的进士建造牌坊之外，宗族或大家族还出资造一种"世科牌坊"，就是造一座牌坊，它的明间的上部横着石板或木板，把本宗族或家族历届举人以上的科名陆陆续续都刻在上面，集体荣耀。例如山西省阳城县黄城村和郭峪村都有几座这种家族性的"世科牌坊"，其中有陈氏家族相同的一对分别在黄城村村口和郭峪村陈昌言老宅门口先后建造，它们都是清初《康熙字典》总裁官之一陈廷敬家族的。因为黄城村和郭峪村都属同一个陈氏家族。陈昌言是陈廷敬的伯父，也有功名。郭峪村还有张好古一门三进士、张鹏云"祖孙兄弟科甲"等的世科牌坊。与郭峪村相邻的上庄、中庄和下庄也都有。江西省乐安县流坑村则有"五桂坊"，纪念董氏三代五人于宋仁宗明道二年（1033年）同榜中了进士。

又有一种和科举有很大关系的牌坊，就是揄扬一个家族的仕途成就的，如"四世一品"、"同胞翰林"、"父子尚书"等等。这些牌坊的形式和进士牌坊没有差别，而且常常造在一起，形成牌坊群。

另有一种"集体性"的进士牌坊，如山西省阳城县城里的"九凤朝阳"和"十凤齐鸣"坊，两坊都是纪念同一位老师的十名弟子于清代顺治丙戌年（1646年）同榜高中进士。这种牌坊数量当然很少。这两座牌坊的重复是因为中榜的进士里有一位的喜报迟到了些日子。这教后人看到弟子们中进士之后老师和乡亲们急切地炫耀的心情。

进士牌坊和牌坊群在村子里并没有一定的位置。常见的为：第一，在大宗祠门前附近，如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的进士金昭牌坊；第二，在村子的主街上，如山西省沁水县西文兴村的"丹桂传芳"和"青云接武"两座牌坊，于明代嘉靖年间（1522—1566）分别为柳騄、柳遇春两位乡进士建立的。牌坊因为形式特殊，又有炫耀公众的意义，所以对村子的景观起很大的作用。当若干个牌坊组合在一起的时候，很能形成一幅壮丽的图景。例如，安徽省歙县棠樾村村口大路上一溜七座石牌坊，浙江省永嘉县花坦村大宗祠前大道上的八座牌坊。可惜后者经"文化大革命"的摧残，已经只剩下三座了。总之，牌坊的建造目的在于表彰个人、荣耀宗族、教化大众，所以总要选择在容易被乡人们见到的位置，以充分发挥它们的作用。

有一些地方，不少牌坊和宗祠的正立面相结合，就是牌坊贴到宗祠正面，而以当心间框住宗祠正门的门洞。例如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的房派宗祠行原堂的正面，以"乡会两魁"为主题做三间贴墙牌坊。单间的有雍睦堂。

还有一种牌坊和纪念性建筑物结合的方式，便是用牌坊作为主建物正门前小广场的门，例如浙江省青田县南田镇的明代开国元勋刘基（伯温）庙前，小广场左侧牌坊门书"帝师"，右侧牌坊门书"王佐"，正前方为一道矮墙。它们既形成了庄严华丽的庙前空间，又写出了庙主的历史地位。

类似于牌坊的旌表科名成就的建筑，还有独立的楼、门等等，如江西省乐安县流坑村的西主门"状元楼"，追纪南宋绍兴十八年（1148年）董德元得中状元。楼的下部为一座砖石高台，中央有门洞穿过，很像一段城门。高台上为木构的方形两层楼式建筑。同村还有东主门"翰林门"，是为被荐为翰林院编修参与编纂《永乐大典》的举人董琰造的，门洞两侧有大学士杨士奇题的联：

国史总裁，望重一时锁闼；
英才乐育，名高天下崇师。

除了牌坊，浙江、江西、福建诸省，凡得了举人以上功名的还可以立"桅"。桅是一根长长的笔直的木杆或石杆，高高竖立在祠堂大门前，或门前广场周边。它下端有大石座或者一对夹杆石把它稳住。它上段，近杆顶处，装着木板做的"斗"，凡进士的，上下两只斗，举人的，仅有一只斗。它们向外村人炫耀着一个家族的成就和光荣，对本家族的后裔则是强有力的鞭策和推动。它们的高度，大约在十米左右，通常是超过宗祠门楼的檐口。这些垂直竖立的桅，和华丽的祠堂正门相辉映，使整个画面十分活泼。

也有些宗祠把这些桅集中立在门前小广场上或者广场周边。功名成绩较好的宗姓，它们形成了一大片桅的丛簇，例如，江西省新建县程氏"汪山土库"之前，三十余座桅杆密拥如林。

福建省西部不少村落，功名桅杆全身用整块巨石雕凿而成，秀气又挺拔，如永安县西洋福庄邢氏宗祠前空场三面立着六根石桅杆，为环境增加不少活气。

桅和牌坊除了基本的旌表作用外，对装饰和活跃村落的景观起了很大的作用。
