4. Confucian Temples, Examination Archways, and Flagpoles

Confucian temples (孔庙), also called Culture Temples (文庙), by regulation could only be built at county level or above—but a very few villages, with approval from the Duke of Yansheng's office in Qufu, also built them. Guoyu Village (Yangcheng, Shanxi) and nearby Xiwenxing Village (Qinshui, Shanxi) each have one; Furong Village (Yongjia, Zhejiang) also has one. Culture Temples ranked higher than Wenchang Pavilions; by regulation, their "Classics Officer" (典籍官) had to be formally appointed by the Duke of Yansheng's office.

Guoyu Village's Culture Temple stands at the base of the west city wall inside the village. In Ming Chenghua 6 (1470), on the ruins of an ancient public building here, a "Village Hall" (里馆) was rebuilt—"selecting elders to manage village governance and moral transformation," roughly equivalent to a village government. In early Wanli, due to Zhang Juzheng's political reforms, it was destroyed. The site was "redeemed by the village in Chongzhen era; Wang Huanyu (i.e., Wang Chongxin) discussed with gentlemen and built a temple on the hall's ruins"—this was the Confucius Temple, later called Culture Temple. In Qing Qianlong 12 (1747), during reconstruction, the temple site was expanded and its rank raised, becoming one of the area's most spectacular buildings. The temple later had over ten mu of temple land, all donated by villagers.

The "village district" (里) where Guoyu Village is located produced over a hundred "local worthies" (乡贤) from Tang to early Qing; the village itself, in early Qing, produced Chen Tingjing—Wenyuan Pavilion Grand Secretary and one of the chief editors of the Kangxi Dictionary.

The Qing-built Guoyu Culture Temple faces south, a quadrangle covering ~4,000 sq m. Terrain is high north, low south—over ten steps up before the main gate. Main gate is five-bay, central three bays with exposed-pillar eave corridors. The main hall is Dacheng Hall (大成殿), five-bay wide; center enshrines a seated Confucius statue; both sides, by zhaomu order, display tablets of Yan Hui, Zengzi, and the other seventy-two disciples. Dacheng Hall uses bracket sets (斗拱), front eave has lattice doors and windows; before the hall is a moon terrace (月台), which is the "Apricot Altar" (杏坛). On both sides of the main hall are two side rooms each, storing ritual supplies; management staff also live there.

East and west side halls are eight bays each, serving as Local Worthy Shrines (乡贤祠)—inside enshrine over 100 local worthy tablets from Guoyu and nearby villages (belonging to Guoyu district), with seven famous-worthy stelae, two of which刻 names of those who obtained examination degrees in Guoyu district over a thousand years from Tang to Qing—88 people. A local saying: "Jingu Valley ten li long, talents come from Guoyu." Jingu is the name of the valley where Guoyu Village lies.

Guoyu Culture Temple also has over 100 various commemorative stone stelae, and one Wenchang Pavilion.

The Culture Temple main gate's eave corridor was where examination results were posted. On ordinary days, children were forbidden to play there, idlers forbidden to make noise—quite a solemn atmosphere.

Each year, in spring and autumn, there were grand sacrifices. Only educated people at student (生员) level or above qualified to participate. Participants had to wear long gowns and mandarin jackets, dress neatly and dignified, and wash their faces and shave beforehand. Participants, by rank and age, first lined up outside the main gate, then slowly entered in single file, holding grand ceremony at the Apricot Altar. On the altar, sacrificial offerings were laid out; people burned incense, knelt, performed the three-offering ritual (三献礼), and set off firecrackers. After sacrificing to Confucius, they worshipped local worthies. The "Great Society" (大社—rural administrative organization, one level above "society") funded tender tofu; after the ritual, it was distributed to village children to eat—believed to nourish the brain, make them read smartly, and pass examinations in the future.

Xiwenxing Village's (Qinshui, Shanxi) Culture Temple was also jointly worshipped by nearby West Township villages. The 1921 Xiwenxing Village "Record of Rebuilding Wenchang Pavilion and Culture Temple" writes: "At spring and autumn sacrifice periods, the county magistrate would come in person, or send a school official as representative, leading West Township scholars to practice ritual and lecture there—gradually transformed by poetry, books, ritual, and music; hence at that time examinations were continuously successful, and local customs became honest and generous. ... Since late Qing Daoguang era, halls collapsed; petitioned to move the sacred tablet to the county city Culture Temple; thereafter fathers, sons, and elders no longer saw the splendor of dress and artifacts; the custom of ritual practice and lecturing ceased, and literary style declined—now over a hundred years."

This Culture Temple is inside the village's main gate; above the main gate is Kuixing Pavilion (奎星阁). North of the Culture Temple is Sage Temple (圣庙), enshrining tablets of successive emperors and sages. North of Sage Temple is Wenchang Pavilion, precisely at the east end of the village's main street; inside the street are two jinshi archways. West of the Culture Temple are two paper-burning furnaces (焚帛炉) for respectfully disposing of written paper. This group of cultural-educational buildings occupies a significant area of the village.

Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian) has a "Civil-Military Temple" (文武庙), built in Qing Qianlong Jihai (1779). Two-story pavilion: upper floor enshrines Confucius, lower floor enshrines Guan Yu. Civil sage and military sage share one building. The Wu Clan Genealogy writes: "Every restoration brings great fortune; sincere reverence must bring promotion."

Obtaining examination degrees not only smoothed official careers and brought glory to ancestors and clan, but also gave oneself a permanent memorial. In early Ming Hongwu 21 (1388), Emperor Taizu Zhu Yuanzhang decreed using public funds to build an archway for new zhuangyuan Ren Hengtai. From then on jinshi archways became popular; by mid-Ming Chenghua-Hongzhi era, archways were even retroactively built for earlier jinshi; soon, prefectures, counties, and some villages could see spectacular jinshi archways. In Qing, though from Jiaqing era public funds for jinshi archways stopped, clans were allowed to build them themselves. "Self-building" led some juren to also build archways, though in smaller numbers. Early Qing Yongzheng Emperor said: "Among the four peoples, scholars rank first, farmers second, artisans and merchants below." The Guangxu-era (1875–1908) Collected Regulations of the Great Qing says: "Honoring the root and suppressing the branches, recorded in the Collected Regulations, as constant principle, from long ago." These official-advancement archways visually proclaimed the scholar's primary status to all under heaven. For farm boys with books hanging from ox horns, this was another powerful激励.

Because commemorative buildings sought durability, as early as late Yuan-early Ming, official-advancement archways used stone or wood-stone combinations. In rainy, humid southern provinces, stone-pillar archways were common, with many entirely stone. But stone components' forms and methods still imitated wooden construction. Northern provinces, due to dryness, still had many entirely wooden archways. Archway styles fall into two major categories: one developed from ancient "Heng Gate" (衡门), beginning to be used as commemorative archways around Song dynasty; the other developed from ancient "Black-Head Gate" (乌头门, also called Lattice-Star Gate 棂星门), using soaring pillars. Black-Head Gate style archways appeared around Ming Hongzhi-Zhengde era (1488–1521), flourished in late Ming, and became the dominant form in Qing. Both types could be built across streets as landmarks, drawing attention. (But chastity archways forbade people passing underneath—hence mostly built against walls, with dense railings between pillars, treated very solemnly.)

Archway specifications include: two-pillar single-roof or three-roof; four-pillar three-bay three-roof or five-roof. "Roof" (楼) refers to a narrow gabled small roof section.

The two-pillar single-roof archway is the simplest type, represented by a pair of entirely stone local-jinshi archways at Xiwenxing Village (Qinshui, Shanxi). They were built to炫耀 the examination achievements of local jinshi Liu Lu (Ming Chenghua 16, 1480) and Liu Yuchun (Ming Jiajing 25, 1546), built in 1544 and 1550 respectively. Both are identical in style and dimensions, structure and proportion entirely imitating wooden construction, symmetrically erected on the horizontal main street before the village residential area's main gate Yongqing Gate. Liu Lu's archway is刻 "Cassia Fragrance Passed On" (丹桂传芳); Liu Yuchun's is刻 "Blue Clouds Following Martial Steps" (青云接武). They stand ~25m apart, and together with Yongqing Gate form the core of the village's architecture.

The three-bay five-roof archway is the most ornate and imposing of official-advancement (jinshi) archways—only Heng-Gate style, never soaring-pillar style, because three bays with five roofs means a small gabled roof section directly above the central pair of pillar tops. One example is the Feng Rong jinshi archway at Feng Village (Jixi, Anhui). Feng Rong passed jinshi in Ming Chenghua 14 (1478), served successively as Fuzhou judicial official, Beijing Ministry of War carriage-office director, and retired in Hongzhi 2 (1489). This archway was built in Chenghua 15 (1479), the year after passing jinshi. Its four pillars are all stone, with drum-shaped "back-rest stones" (靠背石) front and back, increasing stability and massiveness. Above the central and side bays, wooden hip-and-gable roofs each have two cluster bracket sets; the two middle roofs each have one cluster. Bracket sets project three tiers, with diagonal brackets—light and ornate. Ridge ornaments and treasure vases are exaggerated in scale, making the silhouette lively and festive. The central bay's lower lintel is carved with a pair of lions playing with embroidered balls—a common folk motif for joyful, warm feeling. The side bays' lower lintels are carved with deer, homophone for "salary" (禄)—reading to pass jinshi was to become an official, i.e., seek salary. Between the central bay's upper and lower lintels, the "name plaque" (字牌) is engraved "Jinshi Mansion" (进士第); above it, a vertical plaque is刻 "Imperial Grace" (恩荣). "Enrong" indicates the archway's construction was approved by the emperor. Some archways刻 "Imperial Edict" (圣旨) or "Imperially Built" (敕建) on this plaque—same meaning.

Similar four-pillar three-bay five-roof jinshi archways include the Dushan Village (Suichang, Zhejiang) jinshi archway and the military-jinshi Wu Bazhen archway at Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian). Wu Bazhen meritoriously escorted Empress Dowager Cixi's western flight, hence the archway bears a couplet:

The world has phoenix feathers, repeatedly receiving imperial grace issuing purple edicts;
Body followed leopard tails, once accompanied immortal retinue in yellow banners.

The surviving jinshi archway at Yantou Village (middle Nanxi River, Yongjia, Zhejiang), built for jinshi Jin Zhao in Ming Jiajing era (1522–1566), is four-pillar three-bay three-roof—but the central bay's two pillars are stone, square in section. Each pillar is also clamped front and back by drum-stone back-rest stones. This archway's特点 is structure approximating Song style: bracket sets grand and using true ang (真昂); the rearmost tails of the top two ang tiers jointly support the ridge purlin, and the ang tier below them supports them at mid-section. The entire archway's form is very robust and powerful. It is 8.46m wide overall, pillars 4.40m high, total height 7.63m, eaves projecting 1.65m front and back—very graceful. Tile ridge curves are soft and light. Though bracket sets are complex, the whole is simple, without decoration, yet proportions harmonious. Huatan Village's Xiantai Archway, the Zhu Clan Main Ancestral Hall (Dunmu Hall) gate, and Cangpo Village's gate—all similar in structure and style to this jinshi archway.

Three-bay jinshi archways also exist entirely built of stone, though fewer. One example is the Changle Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang) jinshi archway. It is three-bay, directly attached to the village gate, almost becoming the village gate's main body. Unfortunately severely damaged during the Cultural Revolution.

Beyond building archways for individual jinshi, clans or large families also funded "Generation-Examination Archways" (世科牌坊)—one archway whose central bay's upper part has a horizontal stone or wooden plank, on which successive juren-and-above examination names of the clan or family are刻 one after another—collective glory. E.g., Huangcheng Village and Guoyu Village (Yangcheng, Shanxi) each have several such family "generation-examination archways"; among them, an identical pair of the Chen family was built successively at Huangcheng Village entrance and at Guoyu Village's Chen Changyan old residence gate—both belonging to early Qing Kangxi Dictionary chief editor Chen Tingjing's family. Because Huangcheng and Guoyu both belong to the same Chen family. Chen Changyan was Chen Tingjing's uncle, also with examination degrees. Guoyu Village also has generation-examination archways for Zhang Haogu's "one family three jinshi" and Zhang Pengyun's "grandfather-grandson-brother examination degrees." Neighboring Shangzhuang, Zhongzhuang, Xiazhuang also have them. Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi) has "Five Cassia Archway" (五桂坊), commemorating five Dong family members across three generations who passed jinshi on the same list in Song Renzong Mingdao 2 (1033).

Another type of archway closely related to examinations praises a family's official-career achievements—e.g., "Four Generations First Rank" (四世一品), "Brother Hanlin Scholars" (同胞翰林), "Father-Son Ministers" (父子尚书), etc. These archways' form is no different from jinshi archways, and they are often built together, forming archway groups.

Another "collective" jinshi archway: in Yangcheng city (Shanxi), "Nine Phoenixes Facing the Sun" (九凤朝阳) and "Ten Phoenixes Singing Together" (十凤齐鸣) archways—both commemorate ten disciples of the same teacher who passed jinshi on the same list in Qing Shunzhi Bingxu (1646). Such archways are naturally very few. The duplication of these two archways occurred because one of the passing jinshi's good news arrived a few days late. This teaches later generations of the eager炫耀 mood of teachers and villagers after disciples passed jinshi.

Jinshi archways and archway groups have no fixed position in villages. Common positions: first, near the main ancestral hall's front gate—e.g., Yantou Village's jinshi Jin Zhao archway; second, on the village's main street—e.g., Xiwenxing Village's "Cassia Fragrance Passed On" and "Blue Clouds Following Martial Steps" archways, built in Ming Jiajing era (1522–1566) for local jinshi Liu Lu and Liu Yuchun respectively. Because archways have special form and public炫耀 significance, they greatly affect the village's landscape. When several archways combine, they can form a magnificent scene. E.g., seven stone archways in a row along the entrance road at Tangyue Village (Shexian, Anhui); eight archways along the avenue before Huatan Village's main ancestral hall (Yongjia, Zhejiang)—unfortunately the latter, after Cultural Revolution destruction, only three remain. In short, archways' purpose is to commend individuals, glorify clans, and educate the public—hence always positioned where villagers can easily see them, to fully发挥 their role.

In some places, many archways combine with the ancestral hall's front facade—the archway is贴 to the ancestral hall's front, with the central bay framing the ancestral hall's main gate opening. E.g., the branch ancestral hall Xingyuan Hall at Zhuge Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang) has, on its front, a three-bay wall-attached archway themed "Two Champions in Township and Provincial Examinations" (乡会两魁). Single-bay examples include Yongmu Hall.

Another way archways combine with commemorative buildings: using archways as gates of the small square before a main building's front entrance. E.g., before the temple of Ming founding merit official Liu Ji (Bowen) at Nantian Town (Qingtian, Zhejiang), the small square's left archway gate is inscribed "Imperial Teacher" (帝师), right archway gate "Royal Assistant" (王佐), with a low wall straight ahead. They both form a solemn, ornate temple-front space and express the temple patron's historical status.

Buildings similar to archways in commemorating examination achievements include independent towers and gates. E.g., Liukeng Village's west main gate "Zhuangyuan Tower" (状元楼), commemorating Southern Song Shaoxing 18 (1148) Dong Deyuan becoming zhuangyuan. The tower's lower part is a brick-stone high platform with a gate opening through the center, much like a section of city gate. On the platform is a wooden square two-story tower building. The same village has east main gate "Hanlin Gate" (翰林门), built for juren Dong Yan, who was recommended as Hanlin Academy compiler and participated in compiling the Yongle Encyclopedia; on both sides of the gate opening is a couplet by Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi:

National history chief editor, prestige heavy in one era's palace gates;
Outstanding talents happily nurtured, name high under heaven revering teachers.

Beyond archways, in Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian provinces, those obtaining juren-and-above degrees could also erect "flagpoles" (桅). A flagpole is a long, straight wooden or stone pole, erected high before an ancestral hall's main gate or around the front square. Its lower end is stabilized by a large stone base or a pair of pole-clamping stones. Its upper section, near the top, has wooden "dou" (斗, bracket-like blocks): jinshi graduates have two dou (upper and lower), juren only one. They炫耀 to outsiders a family's achievements and glory, and to the family's descendants are a powerful鞭策 and推动. Their height is about 10m, usually exceeding the ancestral hall gate tower's eave line. These vertically erected flagpoles, echoing the ornate ancestral hall main gate, make the whole scene very lively.

Some ancestral halls集中 erect these flagpoles on the front small square or around it. Clans with better examination records form a large cluster of flagpoles—e.g., before the Cheng clan's "Wangshan Earth Warehouse" (汪山土库) at Xinjian County (Jiangxi), over 30 flagpoles stand dense as a forest.

In many villages of western Fujian, merit flagpoles are entirely carved from single massive stone blocks—elegant and upright. E.g., before the Xing clan ancestral hall at Xiyang Fuzhuang (Yong'an, Fujian), six stone flagpoles stand on three sides of the open square, adding much vitality to the environment.

Flagpoles and archways, beyond their basic commemorative role, greatly contribute to decorating and enlivening the village landscape.

sections.name: 文峰塔、文昌阁、奎星楼
sections.content_zh:
五、文峰塔、文昌阁、奎星楼

书院、学塾、文馆之外，最重要的文教建筑就数文昌阁、文峰塔、功名牌坊、惜字亭等等了。村办的学堂，有些就和村口的文昌阁和文峰塔一起。

文峰塔是风水术的一种道具，以迷信的方式改变村落原来的自然环境，使它"有利于"大发科甲。风水典籍《相宅经纂》说：

"凡都、省、州、县、乡村，文人不利，不发科甲者，可于甲、巽、丙、丁四字方位择其吉地，立一文笔尖峰，只要高过别山，即发科甲。或于山上立文笔，或于平地建高塔，皆为文笔峰。"

"文笔"是一个垂直的实心的圆柱或四方抹角的石柱，顶上尖尖如笔端，很简单，一般也不高，五米上下而已。"高塔"指的就是文峰塔，多层，木构、砖构或二者合构均有，以纯砖构的为多，纯木构的较少。内为砖砌多边形筒构，外围木构架檐廊的也有而少见。造型以楼阁式为多。大的可以登临，小的多为实心的。通常有七层，二三十米高。

《相宅经纂》虽说文笔可建在四个方位，但实建的大多在巽位，即村子的东南方。这是因为村子一着手选址的时候，就要把村子和水口的关系定下来。水口就是村子所在地一定范围之内的地表水汇合后流出这个范围去的口子。风水术上把水比作财，所以不希望水流直泻而去，而希望"去水有情"，于是，就一来要求溪河在水口处曲折。二来要求水口两侧有一对小山丘，一个峻峭一点，为"狮"；一个平缓一点，为"象"，二者对峙，叫做"狮象把门"。三来最好再有一些亭阁之类的建筑物点缀一下，加强对水口的闭锁，文峰塔就是很合适的闭锁水口的建筑。中国的大地势，照风水术的说法，是西北高而东南低，宋代王洙等撰的风水典籍《地理新书》说道："西北高，东南低，水流出巽，为天地之势也。"于是，村子的选址就常使水口处在村子的巽位上，并常在水口造些风雨桥、亭阁、庙宇之类形体自由而很美的建筑。水口既是众水的出口，地势当然就低，那就更希望在那里造一座塔"高过别山"了。但这"高"其实是象征性的，大多数的塔并不真的能够"高过别山"，风水术士诡称，这类风水塔高度的计算法是一寸等于一丈。或者造在村边山峰上，那就另编一套风水说法。

因为造价很高，文峰塔并非村村都有，只有富而大且重文教的村子才造。

浙江省建德市新叶村在东南方（巽方）水口上有一座抟云塔，通高约三十余米，砖砌楼阁式，正六边形，七层，每层有叠涩砖檐，并有券窗三个，错层而开。塔内有楼板，以木梯上下。建于明代隆庆、万历年间（1567年始建，1574年落成）。《玉华叶氏宗谱》里有主持建塔的白崖山人写的《抟云塔记》，记下了当年一位风水师的建议："凡通都大邑，巨聚伟集，于山川赳缺之处，每每借此（按：指塔）以充填挽之助。虽假人之力以俾天之功，而萃然巍然，凌霄耸兀，实壮厥观"。于是，"友松翁暨弟侄辈拟于所居之东，叠级而层垣焉，使天柱之高标与玉华、道峰相鼎峙，以补巽方之不足也"。这其实就是《相宅经纂》里的话。但塔的体量当然远远比不上玉华山和道峰山，所谓均衡，不过是风水术上的一种象征性的安慰而已。《抟云塔记》又说：初建的塔"凡高一百四十尺有奇，围得高之三一，外辟通明之户者三，内为升梯者六，下作周廊，视其周倍之"。"是役也，虽曰仿浮屠之制万一，堪舆之左券可执，则将来之题名纪捷者当籍籍乎其蝉联而骥附也。如是则古所称雁塔者岂得专其美于前耶？故兹之名抟云者亦曰于方为巽，取象则风，当夫秋飙迅发、彼鹍鹏起者负乘天之云抟扶摇而上九万里，将拭目俟之矣！"可惜，乐观的预言没有实现，新叶村的后人渐渐转向商业，文运反不如前。不过，文峰塔确实给村落风光增色不少。

原徽州六邑之一的婺源县碧山村的文峰塔就在大学者俞正燮居停过的碧山书院一侧。山西介休焦家堡村的奎星塔，楼阁式，砖砌实心，六边七层，高二十三米，底层壶门塑奎星像，第七层有"文光射斗"匾，塔顶为葫芦宝瓶式琉璃塔刹。它立在河岸边，确实为大环境生色不少。

州县的文峰塔在南方诸省多见，以"官办"代替"民办"来祈一方的文运，也算是为官者的"德政"。因为州县辖区大，塔址不见得都限于巽位，这种州县的文峰塔的选址便甲、巽、丙、丁四方都有，多在小山巅上，如婺源县城的就造在丁峰上，而塔形仍旧与村中的相类，是"仿浮屠之制"。

山西省介休县的文峰塔，建于城东南（巽方）二十公里外的天峻山顶端，是一个石砌实心的平顶圆柱形建筑，有收分，形式很别致，高二十三点五米，始建于明代万历年间，由知县史某主持建造。广州市小水口的赤岗塔也是一座文峰塔。广州位于东南海滨，堪舆家素来把中华全国地形简化为西北高而东南低的"天地之大势"，所以，清代屈大均在所著《广东新语》里记录："形家者以为中原气力至岭南而薄，岭南地最卑下"，而广州"其东水口空虚，灵气不属，法宜以人力补之。补之莫如塔，于是以赤岗为巽而塔其上，觚棱峻起，凡九级，特立江干，以为人文之英锷"。这座塔不但是为了振兴广州的文运而建，且是关锁水口的重要建筑物之一。

用塔来促文运，这风俗也普及到西南各地的兄弟民族中去。贵州省都匀市剑江岸边的文峰塔，"为明代万历年间一位姓桂的总兵率领乡人所建。原为五层木塔，后因年久失修而倒塌。道光十九年（1839年），都匀籍（布依族）的甘肃按察使陶廷杰致书乡里，并捐银一千两，资助重建此塔。"这座塔重建后为石质，六边形，七层楼阁式，高三十一米。

多民族杂居的湖南会同县高椅村，村前有巫水流过，通航，陆上有驿道，水陆交会，于是造了一座文峰塔。嘉庆二十年（1815年）《杨氏族谱》有诗赞曰："斜阳翘首塔流光，照耀全村景运昌，况是巽峰偏得玄，子孙代代姓名香。"有些村落财力弱，而又盼望文风大兴，便借用略近笔尖形的天然山峰而称文笔峰。

又因为州县的辖区大，自然环境的选择范围宽，所以州县的文峰塔多能造在风景很优美的地方，点缀风景的作用很大。有一部分文峰塔占据地势，远迎水陆交通线，成了州县的地标，给人以此地居民奋发有为的印象。例如浙江省江山县于宋代在城边山上造了百祐和凝秀两座塔，前者七级六面，高二十四米，后者九级六面，高三十米，均为楼阁式砖塔。从江上放舟而下，遥望双塔，小城充满了生气。

以塔象征文风、文运的起因，可能是唐代新科进士都要到长安大雁塔上留名的缘故。

科举时代另一种标志性文教建筑是文昌阁。文昌阁祭祀文昌帝君。《史记·天官书》里说："北斗之上有六星，合称为文昌宫，掌人间文运。"

文昌帝君主文运，就是主科举应考者的成败，而科考的成败又不仅关系到每一个读书人本身，甚至关系到一个宗族的命运，因此，文昌阁的兴建就和村落的兴衰息息相关。《道园学古录》作者宋元间人虞集所撰《四川顺庆路蓬州相如县大文昌万寿宫记》里说："宋亡蜀残，民无孑遗，鬼神之祀消歇。自科举废而文昌之灵异亦寂然者四十年余，延祐初，元天子特出睿断，明诏天下以科举取士，而蜀人稍复治文昌之祠焉。"相如县清泉乡慕蔺里抢先造了一座文昌宫。虞集叹道："于戏，圣天子赫然兴科举，未及期月，万里之外，岩绝之邑，已有闻风而兴起者，信乎其神矣。"

到了明代，朝廷诏"天下学宫皆立文昌祠"，而且从学宫又普及到几乎所有村落。清代嘉庆六年（1801年）仁宗颁上谕："文昌帝君君着海内崇奉与关圣大帝相同，宜列入祀典，同光文治。"每年农历二月三日文昌帝君圣诞，都要派官员祭拜。

文昌阁的型制，大体是一所合院，前后两堂，左右有厢房或无厢房而有厢廊，甚至连厢廊都没有。前堂之上有楼阁，供文昌帝君像。后堂常用为学塾的讲堂。由于楼阁居前堂之上，又多用翼角翻飞的歇山顶，所以文昌阁的外形高耸而轮廓参差，正脊两端吻饰则塑为变形的鲤鱼，以首向下。因为民间以"鲤跃龙门而化龙"比喻平民在科考中一举成功而改变身份，所以鱼尾变形为细细的龙身形状，轻快而灵活，几经大弯大曲向上冲腾，动感极强。这是象征"青云直上"，也是科场成功的常用比喻。浙江省建德市新叶村和相邻的上吴方村的文昌阁吻饰为这种型制的典型。

浙江省江山市廿八都村是仙霞关戍兵退役以后留居而成的大杂姓村落，有一百四十多个姓氏，几十种乡音，所以没有宗祠，却有两座文昌阁。都是三进两院，楼阁在第二进，三层楼阁，三开间，歇山顶，有腰檐，气势很盛。这两座文昌阁成了全村最宏丽的公共建筑。它们两侧安静整洁的跨院为讲堂和山长住所。

小型的文昌阁则是一个独立的两层阁子。前徽州六邑之一的婺源县西武乡黄村造在水口上的文昌阁只有方方的一大间加一圈廊步，两层，四坡顶，像一座玲珑轻巧的亭子。

古人深知，为学不可有市井气，所以文昌阁常和比较高层次的书院等组合在一起形成一个建筑群。可作为代表的是安徽歙县雄村的竹山书院，由曹氏宗族初创于清代乾隆年间（1736—1795）。书院主体厅堂有前后两进，上堂三间，太师壁左右悬蓝底金字板联一副：

竹解心虚，学然后知不足；
山由篑进，为则必要其成。

右厢房一侧有门通向内院。院内布局活泼，药畦花圃之间，有学生上课的教室和山长的书斋、住房。一条游廊引向一座花园，内有"清旷轩"，悬书法家郑莱小篆"所得乃清旷"匾。厅内有屏风，上书乾隆时诗人曹学诗的"清旷赋"。曹氏宗族立下了一条规矩，凡科举得了功名的子弟，可以在园里种一棵桂花树，以应读书人"蟾宫折桂"的故事，这个清旷轩因此俗名"桂花厅"。桂花厅东北方有文昌阁，筑于高台上，呈八角形，俗称"八角亭"。这座竹山书院和文昌阁很清新脱俗，给求学的和教书的一个高雅的环境。

文昌阁与书院一样，园林化是一个极普遍的现象。外借天然山色水光，内则种花栽草，如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的文昌阁，据1947年《高隆诸葛氏宗谱·重建文昌阁碑记》里描写："为堂三楹，架以杰阁，而奉帝座于其巅。……启窗则岩峦之秀出者咸若蜿蜒盘曲而环拱于其前，俯槛则桃李竹桂之属缤纷掩映于其下。"可惜"文化大革命"时阁被拆毁，竹木也被伐尽。

为了远避市井气，乡村士绅知识分子很重视文昌阁的选址。浙江省永嘉县珍溪《朱氏合族副谱·改建文昌阁记》里记载，清初雍正年间（1723—1735），廊下村乡绅们集资建了一座文昌阁。"然其地卑下，树木蔽障"，邑庠生朱闻轩觉得不满意，遂邀朋友们登上桂松岭，到了"广可亩余"的一处山阿，"见潭水漈洄而涵影，秀峰耸拔以连云；文笔插其右，斗山踞其左；山川环绕，若绣若绮。因喜不胜曰：此真文昌阁基地，可以安神灵而聚风气矣！"于是在乾隆二年（1737年）将原来的文昌阁拆迁到这块新址重建。新阁"门临水曲，地耸云端，拱群峰之突屹，面万木之郁葱，珍川之胜，于此称第一焉。登斯阁者，晨夕之赏心各异，四时之兴趣不穷，文思秀发，颖悟宏开。"（《珍川朱氏合谱·慎轩公传》）它"右文笔、左斗山"，借堪舆风水之术以求科考兴盛，未能脱俗。

一般情况下，水口也都是村子近处风景最好的地方，流水在这里弯曲，两岸山丘对峙，林木葱茏，数百年不伐。而且水口又是文峰塔、庙宇、水碓、亭桥等等的聚集之所。这些建筑形体活泼而变化丰富，没有住宅之类的干扰，所以很容易形成优美的建筑群，于是，文昌阁也常常会侧身其间。文昌阁不但按风水术的要求参与了"关锁去水"，并且以它耸拔活泼的轮廓、华丽的装饰，大大使水口建筑群生色。所以水口建筑群常常成为村子的"八景"或"十景"之一。福建省连城县培田村水口的文昌阁为"新八景"之首，有《杰阁吟风》诗：

一望云霄势欲冲，巍巍高阁插空中，披襟快我开怀抱，琢句惊人夺化工。檐际抑扬鸣铁马，天边往复送霜鸿。凭栏益壮凌云志，直拟扶摇万里风。

浙江省建德市新叶村的水口，文昌阁和名为抟云塔的文峰塔、观音堂以及五谷祠（即土地庙）一起组成的建筑群在柏树林的衬托下非常生动。文昌阁、文峰塔、观音堂和五谷祠的组合，是中国千年"耕读文化"的绝妙诠释。

文昌阁是村子里的公共建筑，营造费用一般是宗祠的公款，但也有私人乐捐的。前徽州六邑之一婺源县的延村（今在江西）有一方关于建造文昌阁的碑记，全文是："本村水口关帝庙左首，金霁坪自愿输租八秤，与众换田，独建文昌阁，为合里肇开文运，颇当大观。楼上恭奉神像四座，楼下恭奉神位二尊，计用费二千金。子孙笃志诗书，世守勿替也。嘉庆八年秋月霁坪金盖亮记"。个人有了钱，给全村造一座文昌阁作为公益事业，祈求文运肇开，不论文昌帝君是否灵验，也确是善举。

类似的记载在婺源各村还有不少。

和文昌阁相似的是奎星楼或魁星楼。奎星和魁星都是天上星宿，都被认为"主文运"，因奎与魁二字同音，民间把它们混同了，以致奎（魁）星楼和文昌阁也有混同现象，反正是科举时代祈求考试得意的地方罢了。山西省沁水县西文兴村既有文昌阁也有魁星阁。文昌阁在村里街口，街上有两座进士牌坊。魁星阁就造在村子正门门洞之上，它的右侧是关帝庙，进了洞门，里面便是文庙。关帝是武圣人，文武二圣在一起，也是常见的组合。清代嘉庆辛未年（1811年）西文兴村建魁星阁，《魁星阁新建记》碑里说道："文庙功成而魁星阁未建，建章公曰：村之东南（按即巽方）地势渐下，将欲修一阁以补之，祀魁星神。"它的选址完全符合风水术的要求，如《相宅经纂》所说，只消在聚落的甲、巽、丙、丁四个方位之一上造个高耸的建筑物便可以变"不发科甲"的地形为"即发科甲"。这座魁星阁造在巽位的村门之上，显然就是为了增加高度。阁两层，三开间，上层为歇山顶，下层有腰檐。它加强了村门的表现力，使进入村子所在的小盆地的人抬眼便见它耸立于一个台地的边缘，魁星阁成了村子的标志。
sections.content_en:
5. Wenfeng Pagodas, Wenchang Pavilions, and Kuixing Towers

Beyond academies, schools, and literary halls, the most important cultural-educational buildings include Wenchang Pavilions (文昌阁), Wenfeng Pagodas (文峰塔), merit archways, and character-respecting pavilions (惜字亭). Village-run schools were sometimes located together with the village entrance's Wenchang Pavilion and Wenfeng Pagoda.

Wenfeng Pagodas are a tool of fengshui, using superstitious means to alter a village's original natural environment to make it "favorable" for abundant examination success. The fengshui classic Xiangzhai Jingzuan (相宅经纂) says:

"All capitals, provinces, prefectures, counties, and villages where scholars are disadvantaged and examinations do not flourish—one may choose an auspicious site in the jia, xun, bing, or ding directions, erect a writing-brush pointed peak; as long as it rises higher than other mountains, examinations will flourish. Or erect a writing brush on a mountain, or build a tall tower on flat ground—both are writing-brush peaks."

A "writing brush" (文笔) is a vertical solid cylindrical or square-chamfered stone pillar, pointed at the top like a brush tip—very simple, generally not tall, around 5m. A "tall tower" refers to Wenfeng Pagoda: multi-story, wooden, brick, or composite construction—mostly pure brick, rarely pure wood. Interior is brick polygonal cylinder; exterior wooden-frame eave corridors exist but are rare. Form is mostly pavilion-style (楼阁式). Large ones can be climbed; small ones are mostly solid. Usually seven stories, 20–30m high.

Though Xiangzhai Jingzuan says writing brushes may be built in four directions, actual construction was mostly in the xun direction—the village's southeast. This is because when village site selection began, the relationship between village and water mouth (水口) had to be determined. The water mouth is the outlet where surface water within the village's defined area gathers and flows out. In fengshui, water is compared to wealth—hence one does not wish water to flow straight away, but hopes "outgoing water has feeling" (去水有情). Thus: first, require streams to bend at the water mouth. Second, require a pair of small hills on both sides of the water mouth—one steep, called "lion" (狮); one gentle, called "elephant" (象)—facing each other, called "lion and elephant guarding the gate" (狮象把门). Third, ideally some pavilions and towers decorate the spot, strengthening the water mouth's closure—Wenfeng Pagodas are very suitable buildings for closing water mouths. China's great terrain, per fengshui, is northwest high and southeast low; Song dynasty Wang Zhu's fengshui classic Dili Xinshu (地理新书) says: "Northwest high, southeast low, water flows out through xun—this is the tendency of heaven and earth." Hence village sites often place the water mouth in the village's xun direction, and often build wind-rain bridges, pavilions, temples—free-form, beautiful buildings—at the water mouth. Since the water mouth is the outlet of all waters, terrain is naturally low—hence one more hopes to build a tower there "higher than other mountains." But this "height" is actually symbolic; most towers cannot truly be "higher than other mountains." Fengshui masters诡称 that for such fengshui towers, the height calculation is one cun (inch) equals one zhang (ten feet). Or built on a village-edge mountain peak—then another set of fengshui explanations is invented.

Because construction cost was high, Wenfeng Pagodas were not in every village—only wealthy, large, culture-valuing villages built them.

Xinye Village (Jiande, Zhejiang) has Tuanyun Pagoda (抟云塔) at its southeast (xun) water mouth, ~30m+ total height, brick pavilion-style, regular hexagon, seven stories, each story with corbelled brick eaves and three arched windows opening on alternate stories. Inside has floors, with wooden ladders. Built in Ming Longqing-Wanli era (founded 1567, completed 1574). The Yuhua Ye Clan Genealogy contains "Record of Tuanyun Pagoda" by Baiya Shanren, who presided over construction, recording a fengshui master's suggestion: "All great cities and large gatherings, where mountains and streams are deficient, often use this [pagoda] to fill and supplement. Though using human power to assist heaven's work, yet gathered and majestic, soaring to the clouds, truly strengthening the scene." Hence "Yousong Weng and brothers/nephews planned, east of their residences, to build tiered walls, making the pillar of heaven's height stand tripod-like with Yuhua and Daofeng mountains, to supplement the xun direction's deficiency." This is essentially what Xiangzhai Jingzuan says. But the pagoda's mass is of course far less than Yuhua and Daofeng mountains—so-called balance is merely a symbolic comfort in fengshui. The Record further says: the initially built pagoda "over 140 chi high, circumference one-third of height, outside three bright windows, inside six ladders, below a surrounding corridor twice the circumference." "This work, though imitating one ten-thousandth of stupa form, the fengshui guarantee can be held—then future names recorded in success will abundantly follow in succession. Thus the ancient so-called Wild Goose Pagoda could not monopolize beauty before? Hence this name Tuanyun also means: in direction it is xun, in image it is wind; when autumn winds swiftly rise, that great bird rises, carrying heaven's clouds, whirling upward ninety thousand li—we will watch and wait!" Unfortunately, the optimistic prophecy did not come true; Xinye Village's descendants gradually turned to commerce, and literary fortune declined. Nevertheless, Wenfeng Pagoda truly added much to the village's scenery.

The Wenfeng Pagoda at Bishan Village (Wuyuan, one of old Huizhou's six counties) stands beside Bishan Academy where great scholar Yu Zhengxie once stayed. The Kuixing Pagoda at Jiaojiabao Village (Jiexiu, Shanxi) is pavilion-style, solid brick, hexagonal seven-story, 23m high; ground floor arched door has a Kuixing statue; seventh floor has "Literary Light Shoots the Dipper" (文光射斗) plaque; top is gourd-vase-style glazed tile finial. Standing by the river, it truly adds much to the larger environment.

Prefecture/county Wenfeng Pagodas are common in southern provinces—using "official construction" instead of "private construction" to pray for a region's literary fortune,也算 an official's "virtuous governance." Because prefectures/counties have large jurisdictions, pagoda sites are not limited to xun direction—these pagodas' sites can be in jia, xun, bing, ding all four directions, mostly on small mountain peaks. E.g., Wuyuan county town's is built on Ding Peak; pagoda form still resembles village ones, "imitating stupa form."

Jiexiu County's (Shanxi) Wenfeng Pagoda, built at the top of Tianjun Mountain 20km southeast (xun) of the city, is a solid stone flat-top cylindrical building with entasis, distinctive form, 23.5m high, founded in Ming Wanli era, presided over by Magistrate Shi. Guangzhou's Chigang Pagoda at the small water mouth is also a Wenfeng Pagoda. Guangzhou lies on the southeast coast; fengshui masters have long simplified China's terrain as "northwest high, southeast low—the great tendency of heaven and earth." Hence Qing Qu Dajun's Guangdong Xinyu (广东新语) records: "Shape-masters believe central plains' energy thins at Lingnan, Lingnan land is lowest"; and Guangzhou "its east water mouth is empty, spiritual energy does not belong—by principle should supplement with human power. Nothing supplements like a pagoda—hence using Chigang as xun and building a pagoda on it, angular and soaring, nine levels, standing alone by the river, as the cutting edge of human culture." This pagoda was built not only to revive Guangzhou's literary fortune, but also as one of the important buildings closing the water mouth.

The custom of using pagodas to promote literary fortune also spread to fraternal ethnic groups in the southwest. The Wenfeng Pagoda by the Jian River in Duyun (Guizhou) "was built by a General Gui leading villagers in Ming Wanli era. Originally a five-story wooden pagoda, later collapsed from long neglect. In Daoguang 19 (1839), Duyun-native (Buyei) Gansu Surveillance Commissioner Tao Tingjie wrote to his hometown and donated 1,000 taels to fund reconstruction." Rebuilt as stone, hexagonal, seven-story pavilion-style, 31m high.

Gaoyi Village (Huitong, Hunan), multi-ethnic mixed, has Wu River flowing before the village (navigable), land post road, water-land junction—hence built a Wenfeng Pagoda. Jiaqing 20 (1815) Yang Clan Genealogy has a praising poem: "Setting sun raises head, pagoda flows light, illuminating whole village's prosperous fortune; moreover xun peak especially obtains mystery, descendants' names fragrant generation after generation." Some villages with weak finances, yet hoping for literary flourishing, borrow natural mountain peaks slightly brush-tip-shaped and call them writing-brush peaks.

Because prefectures/counties have large jurisdictions and wide natural-environment choice, their Wenfeng Pagodas can mostly be built in very scenic places, with great landscape-decoration role. Some Wenfeng Pagodas occupy terrain, facing water-land transportation lines from afar, becoming prefecture/county landmarks—giving the impression that local residents are ambitious and accomplished. E.g., Jiangshan County (Zhejiang) in Song built two pagodas, Baiyou and Ningxiu, on mountains by the city: former seven-level six-sided 24m high, latter nine-level six-sided 30m high, both pavilion-style brick pagodas. Boating down the river, viewing the twin pagodas from afar, the small city is full of vitality.

The origin of using pagodas to symbolize literary style and fortune may be that Tang new jinshi graduates all went to Chang'an's Great Wild Goose Pagoda to inscribe their names.

Another landmark cultural-educational building of the exam era is the Wenchang Pavilion. Wenchang Pavilions worship Wenchang Emperor (文昌帝君). Records of the Grand Historian · Heavenly Officials says: "Above the Northern Dipper are six stars, collectively called Wenchang Palace, governing human literary fortune."

Wenchang Emperor governs literary fortune—i.e., governs the success or failure of exam candidates; exam success or failure relates not only to each reader himself, but even to a clan's destiny—hence Wenchang Pavilion construction is closely tied to village prosperity. Song-Yuan scholar Yu Ji, author of Daoyuan Xuegu Lu, wrote in "Record of the Great Wenchang Longevity Palace at Xiangru County, Pengzhou, Shunqing Circuit, Sichuan": "Song fell, Shu was devastated, people had no survivors, spirit worship ceased. Since exams were abolished, Wenchang's spiritual efficacy was also silent for over forty years; in early Yanyou, the Yuan emperor with exceptional judgment clearly decreed the empire to select officials through exams, and Shu people gradually resumed Wenchang temple worship." Xiangru County's Qingquan Township Mulin Village rushed to build a Wenchang Palace. Yu Ji sighed: "Alas, the sage emperor vigorously revived exams; before a month passed, beyond ten thousand li, in remote cliff counties, there were already those who rose upon hearing the wind—truly its spirit is efficacious!"

In Ming, the court decreed "all empire's schools establish Wenchang shrines"—and from schools this spread to almost all villages. Qing Jiaqing 6 (1801), Emperor Renzong issued an edict: "Wenchang Emperor is worshipped throughout the empire same as Guan Yu the Great; should be列入 sacrificial canon, equally illuminating civil governance." Each year on lunar 2/3, Wenchang Emperor's birthday, officials were sent to worship.

Wenchang Pavilion form: generally a courtyard compound, front and rear halls, left and right with side rooms or no side rooms but side corridors, sometimes even no side corridors. Above the front hall is a pavilion housing the Wenchang Emperor statue. The rear hall often serves as a school's lecture hall. Because the pavilion sits above the front hall and often uses hip-and-gable roofs with flying wing corners, Wenchang Pavilion's exterior is tall with varied silhouette; the main ridge's end ornaments are molded as transformed carp, heads downward. Because folk use "carp leaping the dragon gate to become dragon" to metaphor commoners' one-shot exam success and identity change, the carp tail transforms into a thin dragon-body shape—light and flexible, after several great bends surging upward, very dynamic. This symbolizes "soaring straight to the blue clouds" (青云直上), also a common metaphor for exam success. Xinye Village and neighboring Shangwufang Village's Wenchang Pavilion ridge ornaments are typical of this form.

Nianbadu Village (Jiangshan, Zhejiang), a large mixed-surname village formed by retired Xianxia Pass garrison soldiers, has over 140 surnames and dozens of dialects—hence no ancestral hall, but two Wenchang Pavilions. Both are three-entry two-courtyard, pavilion at second entry, three-story pavilion, three-bay, hip-and-gable roof with waist eaves—very imposing. These two Wenchang Pavilions became the village's most magnificent public buildings. Their两侧 quiet, tidy side courtyards serve as lecture halls and shanzhang residences.

Small Wenchang Pavilions are independent two-story pavilions. The one at Huang Village, Xiwu Township (Wuyuan, old Huizhou), built at the water mouth, is only one large square room plus a surrounding corridor, two-story, four-slope roof—like an exquisite, light pavilion.

Ancients well understood that learning must not have marketplace atmosphere—hence Wenchang Pavilions often combine with higher-level academies to form building complexes. A representative is Zhushan Academy (竹山书院) at Xiongcun Village (Shexian, Anhui), founded by Cao clan in Qing Qianlong era (1736–1795). The academy's main halls have front and rear entries; upper hall three-bay, with a blue-background gold-character board couplet on both sides of the master's wall:

Bamboo understands hollow heart, learning then knows insufficiency;
Mountain advances by basketfuls, acting then requires completion.

The right side room has a door to the inner courtyard. Inner courtyard layout is lively: among herb beds and flower gardens are student classrooms and shanzhang's study/residence. A covered corridor leads to a garden containing "Qingkuang Xuan" (清旷轩), with calligrapher Zheng Lai's seal-script plaque "What is obtained is clear and broad." Inside the hall is a screen with Qianlong-era poet Cao Xueshi's "Qingkuang Rhapsody." The Cao clan established a rule: any clan member obtaining exam degrees may plant an osmanthus tree in the garden, corresponding to the scholar's story "plucking osmanthus in the toad palace" (蟾宫折桂)—hence Qingkuang Xuan is commonly called "Osmanthus Hall." Northeast of Osmanthus Hall is a Wenchang Pavilion, built on a high platform, octagonal, commonly called "Octagonal Pavilion." This Zhushan Academy and Wenchang Pavilion are fresh and refined, giving learners and teachers an elegant environment.

Like academies, Wenchang Pavilions' gardenization is extremely common. Borrowing natural mountain/water scenery outside, planting flowers and grass inside—e.g., Zhuge Village's (Lanxi, Zhejiang) Wenchang Pavilion, per 1947 Gaolong Zhuge Clan Genealogy · Record of Rebuilding Wenchang Pavilion: "Three-bay hall, topped by a great pavilion, enshrining the emperor's seat at its peak. ... Opening windows, the graceful peaks all seem to wind and curve, surrounding before it; leaning on rails, peaches, plums, bamboo, osmanthus all colorfully shade below it." Unfortunately during the Cultural Revolution the pavilion was demolished, trees and bamboo also cut down.

To avoid marketplace atmosphere, rural gentry intellectuals valued Wenchang Pavilion site selection highly. Yongjia Zhenxi Zhu Clan Combined Genealogy · Record of Rebuilding Wenchang Pavilion records: in early Qing Yongzheng era (1723–1735), Langxia Village gentry pooled funds to build a Wenchang Pavilion. "But its site was low, trees blocked it"—county student Zhu Wenxuan was dissatisfied, so invited friends up Guisong Ridge to a mountain hollow "over one mu wide," where they "saw pool water swirling and reflecting images, graceful peaks soaring to clouds; writing brush pierces its right, Dipper Mountain sits its left; mountains and streams surround, like embroidery and brocade. Delighted, they said: This is truly Wenchang Pavilion site, can settle spirits and gather atmosphere!" Hence in Qianlong 2 (1737), the original Wenchang Pavilion was dismantled and rebuilt at this new site. The new pavilion "gate by winding water, ground soaring to clouds, arching sudden peaks, facing lush ten-thousand trees—Zhenchuan's scenery, here ranks first. Those ascending this pavilion find morning/evening delights different, four seasons' interests endless, literary thoughts luxuriant, understanding broad." It has "right writing brush, left Dipper Mountain"—using fengshui to seek exam prosperity, not escaping convention.

Generally, the water mouth is also the best scenery near the village: water bends here, hills on both banks face each other, trees lush, uncut for centuries. And the water mouth is also the gathering place of Wenfeng Pagodas, temples, water-powered trip hammers, pavilion bridges, etc. These buildings have lively, varied forms, without residence interference—hence easily form beautiful building complexes, and Wenchang Pavilions often join them. Wenchang Pavilions not only participate in "closing outgoing water" per fengshui requirements, but with their tall lively silhouettes and ornate decoration greatly enhance the water-mouth building complex. Hence water-mouth building complexes often become one of the village's "Eight Scenes" or "Ten Scenes." Peitian Village's water-mouth Wenchang Pavilion ranks first of "New Eight Scenes," with a poem "Outstanding Pavilion Chanting Wind":

One look at clouds, momentum about to soar; towering high pavilion pierces the sky;
Opening robes, I joyfully open my embrace; crafting verses, astonishingly surpassing nature's craft.
At eaves, iron horses rise and fall; at horizon, frost geese come and go.
Leaning on rails, strengthens soaring-to-clouds ambition; straightly planning to whirl ten thousand li in wind.

Xinye Village's water mouth—Wenchang Pavilion, Tuanyun Pagoda (Wenfeng Pagoda), Guanyin Hall, and Wugu Shrine (i.e., Earth God Temple)—together form a building complex, very vivid against cypress forest. The combination of Wenchang Pavilion, Wenfeng Pagoda, Guanyin Hall, and Wugu Shrine is a wonderful interpretation of China's thousand-year "farming-reading culture."

Wenchang Pavilion is a village public building; construction cost generally from ancestral hall public funds, but also private donations. Yancun Village (Wuyuan, old Huizhou, now Jiangxi) has a stele about building a Wenchang Pavilion, full text: "At the left of Guandi Temple at this village's water mouth, Jin Jiping voluntarily donated eight cheng of rent, exchanged land with others, solely built Wenchang Pavilion, to inaugurate literary fortune for the whole community, quite a grand sight. Upstairs respectfully enshrine four deity statues; downstairs respectfully enshrine two deity seats; total cost 2,000 gold. Descendants devoted to poetry and books, generations preserve without replacement. Jiaqing 8 autumn, Jiping Jin Gailiang inscribed." An individual with money building a Wenchang Pavilion for the whole village as public welfare, praying for literary fortune—whether Wenchang Emperor is efficacious or not, it is truly a good deed. Similar records exist in many Wuyuan villages.

Similar to Wenchang Pavilions are Kuixing Towers (奎星楼) or Kuixing Towers (魁星楼). Kuixing and Kuixing are both celestial constellations, both believed to "govern literary fortune"; because "kui" and "kui" are homophones, folk confused them—hence Kui (Kui) Star Towers and Wenchang Pavilions also show confusion phenomena—anyway they are places praying for exam success in the exam era. Xiwenxing Village (Qinshui, Shanxi) has both Wenchang Pavilion and Kuixing Pavilion. Wenchang Pavilion is at the village street intersection; the street has two jinshi archways. Kuixing Pavilion is built above the village main gate's gate opening; its right side is Guandi Temple; entering the gate opening, inside is the Culture Temple. Guandi is the military sage—civil and military sages together, also a common combination. In Qing Jiaqing Xinwei (1811), Xiwenxing Village built Kuixing Pavilion; the "Record of Newly Building Kuixing Pavilion" stele says: "Culture Temple completed but Kuixing Pavilion not built; Jianzhang Gong said: village's southeast (i.e., xun direction) terrain gradually lowers, wish to build a pavilion to supplement it, worship Kuixing deity." Its site完全符合 fengshui requirements—as Xiangzhai Jingzuan says, merely building a tall building in one of the settlement's jia, xun, bing, ding four directions can transform "no exam success" terrain into "immediate exam success." This Kuixing Pavilion built above the xun-direction village gate is clearly to increase height. Pavilion two-story, three-bay, upper floor hip-and-gable roof, lower floor with waist eaves. It strengthens the village gate's expressiveness, making anyone entering the village's small basin look up and see it standing on a terrace edge—Kuixing Pavilion became the village's landmark.

sections.name: 惜字亭
sections.content_zh:
六、惜字亭

乡土社会中还有一种重要的文教建筑，便是"惜字亭"，或者叫"焚帛炉"、"苍颉亭"，是用来焚烧有字迹的废纸的。

文字是人类最伟大的创造。人类的智慧来自信息的积累和传递，而积累和传递信息的最有效的工具是文字。四川省民间流行的传单《敬惜字纸文》说："千里之遥，付数言可以相通；万古产业，皆赖字迹为据。"说的便是文字信息的传递可以突破空间和时间的限制。百姓把社会强势群体叫"识文断字"的人，说弱势群体"西瓜大的字识不了一箩筐"。是不是识字，识多少字，能决定一个人在社会中的地位。

文字既然有这样大的威力，人们采取的上策是努力学会识字，摆脱"睁眼瞎"，同时，又不禁油然而生对文字的敬畏之忱，甚至带一点神秘色彩。几乎普及于全中国的一种巫咒说：凡脚踩了有字迹的纸张，必会瞎眼，更不用说拿来做污秽的用途了。四川省同治《合江县志》有清代乾隆年间（1736—1795）当地解元罗文思写的《惜字引》，说："赤文绿字，无非天地精灵；鸟迹龙章，尽是圣贤心血。"于是有诗道：

世间字纸藏经同，见者须当付火中，
灰送长流埋净土，后世子孙必昌荣。

把敬重成文的字，扩大到敬重零星的字迹，为了避免亵渎文字，就得把有字的废纸烧掉，把灰送进河流中去或者掩埋于土中，以免被糟踏。

民间广泛成立"惜字会"或"惜字社"，起名为"崇文"、"广善"、"德文"、"拾遗"等等。会员自己身体力行，或出资雇人，背个篓子到处捡拾有字迹的纸；同时，向住户、商店、学校等处散发传单，呼吁敬惜字纸以积阴德。他们把收集到的字纸集中焚烧，为此募款建造专门的焚烧炉。焚烧炉通常叫"惜字亭"，也有叫"焚帛亭"的，因为古人在纸张发明之前在帛上写字；也有些地方叫"苍颉亭"，因为传说苍颉是中国文字的发明人，是"字祖"。四川县合江县《同治旧志》有一篇罗允猷写的《惜字炉碑文》说："苍颉作书，功侔造化，启文明而有象，衍圣教于无穷，字之功用大矣！"有些惜字亭就造在文昌宫边上，把苍颉和文昌帝君并列。书塾大门两侧墙上经常有焚字纸的壁炉。

台湾《噶玛兰志略·卷十一》记载："兰中字纸，虽村氓童妇皆知敬惜。士人于文昌宫左筑有敬字亭，立为惜字会，雇丁搜觅，洗净焚化。每年以二月三日文昌帝君诞辰，通属士庶齐集宫中，演剧设筵，结彩张灯，推年长者为主祭，配以仓颉神位。三献礼毕，即奉仓颉牌于彩亭，将一年所焚字灰，装以巨匣。凡启蒙诸童子皆具衣冠，与衿耆护送至北门外渡船头，然后装入小船。用彩旗鼓吹，沉之大海而回。"这段资料很生动地记载了捡字纸、洗净、焚化、积灰，并以隆重的仪式将字纸灰最后送入大海的过程。

惜字亭遍及全国城乡，一个村子往往不止有一座惜字亭，立在人们常到的地方。惜字亭的形状，是建筑式的，多是小小一座歇山顶或者攒尖顶的砖砌小方亭子，只有一米来高，下面再垫着一米来高的座子。另一种是瓶式的，圆腹，四面开圆孔，上面或者是攒尖式的建筑屋顶，或者叠几个连珠、莲花，总高也不过两米左右。这两种都做得很精致。

四川省合江县许多村里都有一座石砌的惜字亭，为五层至七层楼阁式的塔，六边形，高度在六米至八米之间，有一些在塔身上安两个小龛用来祭仓颉和文昌帝君的像。它们或者起着文峰塔的作用。建造年代从明至清，以清代为多。有些塔身上刻一篇《序》或《记》，有些只刻"增福禄"或"天开文运"之类的吉祥话。合江县福宝场的惜字塔，在字纸入口处有额书"字库"二字，左右一副对联：

双笔归杜库，
一画入曹仓。

塔身上还刻着清代中叶嘉庆年间重庆府训导邑人赵予际撰的一篇序文，是研究福宝场历史的重要文献。

台湾桃园县龙潭乡凌云村竹窗子段的圣迹亭，是一座惜字亭，初建于光绪元年（1875年），经光绪十八年（1892年）和民国十四年（1925年）的两度扩建，成了一个规模不小的建筑群，占地南北长46.7米，东西宽21.7米。它坐北面南，圣迹亭居于北端，它从下而上有正方形台基、八边形亭座、正方形炉身、六边形的上段和壶芦攒尖顶几部分，总高6.92米。圣迹亭的核心是炉身，它正面的炉门口，有两副对联，外侧比较大的一副刻的是"鸟喙笔峰光射斗，龙潭墨浪锦成文"，内侧一副小的是"文章到十分火候，笔墨走百丈银澜"。横批分别为"文运宏开"和"过化存神"。

亭前面向南伸出中轴上的石板路，两侧铺草地。中轴路的北端，圣迹亭的台基前，有供台，南端有祭台。祭台之外是中门，门两侧有弧形云墙一段。云墙尽端各立一根石质的"文笔"。再往南为头门，是比较简单的一对砖质方柱体。头门之外是1979年扩展的外院，它的轴线为东西向，东侧建四柱三间三楼式高大的砖质仿木构牌楼门，面向东，体量远大于圣迹亭本身，西侧则建三开间冲天式石质牌楼一座，它的又西侧建一座大照壁，上面书写圣迹亭建造的经过。这一个圣迹亭建筑群的规模之大是全国少见的。

惜字亭日常管理和祭祀仪典由村里的民间组织"文会"负责。

书院、学塾一般都有自己焚字纸的炉子，常见到的是嵌在墙上，像个壁龛，多为葫芦形，都很精致。龛口镶一圈砖浮雕花边，上方再加一些如意云头或者昆卢帽式的装饰。福建省连城县培田村南山书院的化纸炉有联："赐火曾传汉；遗灰尚憾秦"，气概很大。

对字纸的珍惜甚至敬畏，其实是对文化的珍惜和敬畏，更现实的考虑则是惜字纸者会有好报应，而最好的报应便是后人中科名。四川省合江县人罗文思在《惜字引》里说：

杨全善埋字而世掇巍科，实为盛事；
王沂公捡废而子登鼎甲，最是美谈。

对文化的珍惜和敬畏，其实也是很功利的。
sections.content_en:
6. Character-Respecting Pavilions (Xizi Ting)

Another important cultural-educational building in rural society is the "character-respecting pavilion" (惜字亭), also called "silk-burning furnace" (焚帛炉) or "Cangjie pavilion" (苍颉亭)—used to burn waste paper bearing writing.

Writing is humanity's greatest creation. Human wisdom comes from accumulation and transmission of information, and the most effective tool for accumulating and transmitting information is writing. A popular Sichuan flyer "Text Respecting Written Paper" says: "A thousand li away, a few words can communicate; ten-thousand-generation property all relies on written records as evidence." This means written information transmission can break through spatial and temporal limits. Common people called the socially powerful "those who know writing and judge characters" (识文断字), and called the weak "can't recognize a watermelon-sized character in a whole basket." Whether one can read, how many characters one knows, determines one's social position.

Since writing has such great power, people's best strategy was to strive to learn to read, escape "blind eyes" (睁眼瞎)—while at the same time spontaneously feeling reverence for writing, even with a touch of mystery. A curse spread almost throughout all China: anyone stepping on paper bearing writing will surely go blind, let alone using it for filthy purposes. Sichuan Tongzhi "Hejiang County Gazetteer" contains a "Preface to Character Respecting" by local juren Luo Wensi from Qing Qianlong era (1736–1795), saying: "Red writing and green characters are nothing but heaven and earth's spirits; bird-trace and dragon-seal are all sages' heart's blood." Hence a poem says:

Worldly written paper is same as sutras, those who see must put into fire,
Ash sent to flowing river buried in pure earth, later descendants will surely prosper.

Extending respect for finished writing to respect for scattered traces—to avoid blaspheming writing, one must burn waste paper with writing, send the ash into rivers or bury it in soil, to prevent it from being trampled.

Folk widely established "character-respecting societies" (惜字会) or "character-respecting associations" (惜字社), named "Revering Culture" (崇文), "Broad Goodness" (广善), "Virtuous Culture" (德文), "Gathering the Lost" (拾遗), etc. Members practiced themselves, or funded hired workers carrying baskets to collect paper with writing everywhere; simultaneously distributed flyers to households, shops, schools, calling for respecting written paper to accumulate hidden virtue. They centrally burned collected paper, and for this raised funds to build dedicated furnaces. Burning furnaces are usually called "character-respecting pavilions," also called "silk-burning pavilions"—because ancients wrote on silk before paper was invented; some places call them "Cangjie pavilions," because legend says Cangjie invented Chinese writing, the "character ancestor." Sichuan Hejiang County "Tongzhi Old Gazetteer" contains a "Character-Respecting Furnace Stele Inscription" by Luo Yunyou: "Cangjie made writing, merit equal to creation, inaugurating civilization with images, extending sage teaching infinitely—writing's function is great!" Some character-respecting pavilions were built beside Wenchang Palaces, placing Cangjie and Wenchang Emperor side by side. School gate's two side walls often had wall furnaces for burning written paper.

Taiwan "Kavalan Gazetteer Brief · Volume 11" records: "In Lan, written paper, even village women and children know to respect. Scholars built a character-respecting pavilion left of Wenchang Palace, established a character-respecting society, hired workers to search, wash clean and burn. Each year on 2/3 Wenchang Emperor's birthday, all scholars and commoners gather in the palace, perform drama and banquets, hang colored lanterns, elect eldest as chief officiant, paired with Cangjie deity seat. After three-offering ceremony, carry Cangjie tablet in colored pavilion, put one year's burned character ash in large box. All newly enlightened children wear official clothes, with elders escort to north gate ferry head, then load into small boat. With colored flags and music, sink into the great sea and return." This material vividly records the process of collecting paper, washing, burning, accumulating ash, and with solemn ceremony finally sending character ash into the sea.

Character-respecting pavilions spread throughout urban and rural China; a village often had more than one, placed where people frequently go. Their shape is architectural: mostly a small brick square pavilion with hip-and-gable or pyramidal roof, only about 1m high, below padded with a ~1m high base. Another type is bottle-shaped: round belly, round holes on four sides, top either pyramidal architectural roof or stacked several pearls/lotus—total height no more than ~2m. Both types are exquisitely made.

Many villages in Hejiang County (Sichuan) have a stone character-respecting pavilion: a five-to-seven-story pavilion-style pagoda, hexagonal, 6–8m high; some have two small niches on the pagoda body for Cangjie and Wenchang Emperor statues. They may also serve as Wenfeng Pagodas. Construction dates from Ming to Qing, mostly Qing. Some pagoda bodies carve a "Preface" or "Record"; some only carve auspicious phrases like "Increase Fortune and Blessing" or "Heaven Opens Literary Fortune." Hejiang County Fubao Market's character-respecting pagoda has a horizontal plaque "Character Treasury" (字库) at the paper entrance, with a couplet on both sides:

Twin brushes return to Du's treasury,
One stroke enters Cao's granary.

The pagoda body also carves a preface by Zhao Yuji, Chongqing Prefecture instructor and local, from mid-Qing Jiaqing era—important document for studying Fubao Market history.

Shengji Pavilion (圣迹亭) at Zhuchuangzi Section, Lingyun Village, Longtan Township, Taoyuan County (Taiwan) is a character-respecting pavilion, first built in Guangxu 1 (1875), expanded twice in Guangxu 18 (1892) and Republic 14 (1925), becoming a sizable building complex: site 46.7m north-south, 21.7m east-west. It faces south, Shengji Pavilion at north end; from bottom up: square platform base, octagonal pavilion seat, square furnace body, hexagonal upper section, and gourd pyramidal roof—total height 6.92m. The core of Shengji Pavilion is the furnace body; its front furnace mouth has two couplets: the larger outer one carves "Bird-beak brush peak light shoots the dipper, Longtan ink waves brocade into writing"; the smaller inner one is "Writing reaches ten-tenths火候, brush and ink walk hundred-zhang silver waves." Horizontal inscriptions are "Literary Fortune Grandly Opens" and "Transforming and Preserving Spirit."

South of the pavilion extends a central-axis stone path, with grass on both sides. At north end of central path, before Shengji Pavilion's platform, is an offering table; south end is a sacrifice altar. Beyond sacrifice altar is middle gate, with curved cloud walls on both sides. At cloud wall ends each stands a stone "writing brush." Further south is head gate—a simpler pair of brick square pillars. Beyond head gate is the 1979-expanded outer courtyard, axis east-west: east side builds a tall four-column three-bay three-story brick imitation-wood archway gate facing east, mass far larger than Shengji Pavilion itself; west side builds a three-bay soaring stone archway; further west builds a large screen wall writing the history of Shengji Pavilion's construction. This Shengji Pavilion building complex's scale is rare nationwide.

Daily management and sacrificial rituals of character-respecting pavilions are handled by the village folk organization "Literary Society" (文会).

Academies and schools generally had their own paper-burning furnaces—commonly embedded in walls, like a wall niche, mostly gourd-shaped, all exquisite. Niche mouth镶 a circle of brick relief border, above adding ruyi cloud-heads or Kunlu-cap-style decoration. Peitian Village's (Liancheng, Fujian) Nanshan Academy's paper-transforming furnace has a couplet: "Bestowing fire once transmitted Han; remaining ash still regrets Qin"—very grand spirit.

Cherishing and even revering written paper is actually cherishing and revering culture; a more realistic consideration is that character-respecters will have good retribution, and the best retribution is descendants obtaining exam degrees. Hejiang County native Luo Wensi says in "Preface to Character Respecting":

Yang Quanshan buried characters and generations obtained high degrees, truly a grand event;
Wang Yigong gathered waste and son attained top graduate, most a fine tale.

Cherishing and revering culture is actually also quite utilitarian.

sections.name: 福建省连城县培田村
sections.content_zh:
一、福建省连城县培田村

中国封建社会的价值观是以伦理为本位，它的核心是人伦关系，家庭作为一个最基本、最重要的社会组织为此受到极大的重视。但如何使家族更具威信和凝聚力，其中最重要的是培养后代，对他们实施文化教育，提高家族子弟的整体文化素质，使他们获得能够安身立命的本领，并且有更大的发展、更多的机会，因此历史上福建省西部连城县培田村曾建有书院、私塾和文、武学堂等十八座之多，还有各种文教建筑，如文庙、武庙、字纸炉等多处。为支持在外子弟们就读，在汀州、连城、漳州等地还建有吴氏家族的学馆、书院、文昌阁、魁星阁等。除此之外，宗族还成立了一些文化组织，如孔圣会、朱子惜字社、文社等来烘托浓郁的文化氛围，培田村因此被誉为汀州、连城一带著名的"文墨之乡"。

（一）学塾初创

培田六世祖郭隆公于明代中叶主持族务时，吴氏家族已人丁兴旺，整体的经济实力堪称河源里之首。但当时整个河源里，文化教育还很薄弱，没有一个像样的学堂，只得请先生到家里来教授，也有几家孩子凑在一起请个先生的，但这种方式对家族整体教育程度的提高十分不利。祖宽公看到了这种情况，决定创办自己的家塾。

祖宽公为吴氏第七世祖，郭隆公次子，郡庠生，生于明成化十二年（1476）丙申岁，卒年不详。培田《吴氏族谱·祖宽公石头坵草堂记》载："吴君（祖宽公）少读书，有远志，十四好剑术，三十成文章，名擅当时。征士缪恭称其诗为闽海最。"但两次入闱不利，乃援例赴阙，回乡后，于明正德年间（1506—1521）在培田村北侧的石头坵创办了吴氏家族第一座学堂石头坵草堂，为讲学之所。《吴氏族谱·祖宽公石头坵草堂记》载："山川蜿蜒翚飞乎陇云之间，渤海培田也；地幽势阻若陶潜之松菊三径，则石头坵草堂也。作之者谁，有伊君子吴祖宽也。"

石头坵是村北山道边的山坎，有一块五六米高的大石头，突兀浑厚，环境静谧，这里很适宜读书，学堂便在石头坵边开工营建。后来有人说也许祖宽公当时想到了"它山之石可以攻玉"和"学要有恒，心如石坚"的道理才选择了这"石头坵"的地方造学堂的。

新学堂坐西朝东，为三开间三进的土坯草顶房，下厅为大门，中厅供奉着孔子的牌位。其他房间有供孩子读书的教室、教书先生的宿舍和厨房。上厅还有藏书房、书画间等。书院前有作为泮池的水塘，大门正对村东的文笔峰，学堂便取名为"石头坵草堂"。

石头坵草堂建成之后，招收宗族子弟，"延学士谢桃溪先生训其后昆"。谢先生题匾"草堂别墅"。为保证学堂的各项开支，祖祠衍庆堂每年支付学堂租谷百担。以后南邨公祠也承担起部分学堂租谷。

石头坵草堂使吴氏子弟有了稳定的系统学习之所，"开长（长汀）连（连城）十三坊书香之祖"。明代进士、兵部尚书、清流人裴应章来到培田，深深地被吴氏家族对教育的重视感动，题写了一副对联："距汀城郭虽百里，入孔门墙第一家"。后来南山书院替代了石头坵草堂成为家族主要的学堂，它的大门上用的还是这副对联。

（二）明末清中叶的学堂书院

北宋文人胡瑗有句名言："治天下之至者在人才，成天下之才者在教化，教化之本者在学校"。继吴祖宽创办石头坵草堂之后，明代末年至清代初年，培田吴氏陆续有上业屋的云江书院，紫阳书院，下业屋的宏江书院；十世祖在宏公办起宏公书院，十四世祖健庵公办岩子前学堂，十四世祖君健公办白学堂书馆，十五世祖配虞公办业屋学堂和伴山公馆，十五世祖锦江公办南山书院，十六世祖纯一公办清宁寨书院。这些学堂和书院分布吴氏各村，村中随处可听到学童们琅琅的读书声。

培田吴氏家族读书之风兴起，学堂、书院都为各房派自建。学堂书院的建设高潮，引发人才辈出的高潮。根据培田吴氏宗谱统计：从明成化朝到清乾隆三十年（1765年）的三百年间，培田共出了一百九十一名秀才。

上业屋的云江书院、紫阳书院，下业屋的宏江书院、宏公书院、白学堂书馆和业屋学堂等，均设在住宅内，辟一二房间作学堂，现在仅存的下业屋宏江书院，虽已空空荡荡，残破不堪，但厅堂上挂着的"渤水蜚英"大匾，仍能让人感受到一品大员纪晓岚在培田巡视时题写匾额的文韵气度。在住宅中，又有岩子前学堂和清宁寨书院，均为独立建造，规模较大。岩子前学堂建在南坑口西部，是个三间两进的小院，院前是阡陌农田，院后是古树奇岩，溪流傍院而过。清宁寨书院建在南坑口北侧高冈上，是三间两进的院落。清代中后期这些学堂和书院中有的因缺少生源、有的因经费不足而停办。一些学堂房屋长期无人管理而塌毁，有的转卖给他人改建成住宅。清光绪《培田吴氏宗谱·六学堂拾遗记》中载："石头坵之草堂，祖宽公创之，李钱塘记之，诚先人育俊首善之区也。……初更为屋，再垦为田，沧桑代易，为日久矣。……由明迄清，风霜剥尽，而古柏一株，森森蔽日，至今抚之犹想见公之手泽焉。"

但南山书院却保留了下来，一是学堂地点好，清静适读书；二是教学质量较高。村人说，清同治年间（1862—1874），南山书院就已是河源里一带有名的学堂，附近村里有钱的人的孩子都到这里读书，一年学费要四五担谷子。南山书院在清代中期以后替代了石头坵草堂，成为公认的家族书院。

（三）南山书院的崛起

南山书院由培田十五世祖锦江公于乾隆末年（1760—1770年前后）创建，它位于南坑口内卧虎山北侧的山脚下，依南山北坡而建，取陶渊明《饮酒》："采菊东篱下，悠然见南山"诗意，称南山书院。曾任教于书院的曾瑞春在碑中这样描述："岁庚申，承吴君化行昆玉召典西席，馆余于南山。嘉木葱郁，胜概清幽，鹿洞鹅湖，殆不啻也。"这不亚于白鹿洞书院和鹅湖书院的南山书院，东有一条延伸的山鼻梁，林木茂盛，隔开了村内村外，使南坑口内十分僻静，有利于学子潜心读书。它也是培田新八景之一，吴爱仁有"南院书声"诗描写这里幽雅的环境和读书的气氛：

步上南山境僻幽，琅玕诵读韵悠悠。
蕉窗雨冷偏逢夜，竹院风凉又报秋。
金石一声天地震，简编万卷古今搜。
朝晴早起人倾听，鸟语书声乐唱酬。

南山书院坐东南朝西北，由两座院落并肩排列组成，东侧院落正房为五开间，上下两层。底层当心间厅房供奉着孔子牌位，并"书'德造庐'于门之外，'培兰植桂'于门之内，朱子'读书、乐诗'于东西壁"。墙上还挂有朱子语录"观古者圣贤所以教人为学之要，莫不使之讲明义理，以修其身，然后推己及后。"次间作为学生的教室。清道光年间（1821—1850），十八世吴昌同，曾对东院建筑进行了修缮，因此东院至今保存较好。教室前有不大的院落，牌坊式大门居中，朝向西北，大门的门额上内外原都题"南山书院"四字，现外侧因几易校名，题字无存，内侧的四字依旧保存完好。门外两侧砖柱上是尚书裴应章写的门联："距汀城郭虽百里，入孔门墙第一家"。

西侧院落与东侧院落相邻。西院比东院低六七步台阶，是一个四合院式的两层建筑，南和西两侧底层是当年教书先生居住、备课的地方，前檐廊有美人靠坐凳。两院之间是一个窄长的砌有花墙的院落，有小门通向书院之外。整座书院顺山势高低错落，显得精巧秀美。书院外有一半月形水塘，象征着泮池，又是文房四宝的"砚池"，与南山书院前有如文笔的山峰，正好形成"文笔蘸墨"的风水。小门前还有一株几百年的罗汉松。传说清代纪晓岚到培田视察就曾在这里住宿了两个晚上。

宁化名儒曾瑞春出仕前在南山书院执教多年，吴氏家族不仅信任他，还为他提供了优越的条件。曾瑞春在《南山书院记》中写道："岁庚申，承吴君化行昆玉召典西席，馆余于南山。……始于厅事见'抗颜敢诩为时望；便服何妨尽日眠'句，细看旁注，知令曾祖闻翁雅意栽培，延滋九邱先生训令大父于此。先生率上杭袁南宫维丰、永定温孝廉恭同事笔砚，句其自题卧榻者也。"十年后他进京会试，金榜题名，"钦点翰林院庶吉士"。他专程回到培田南山书院，提笔书联："十年前讲贯斯庭，绿野当轩，宝树滋培齐竞发；百里外潜修此地，青云得路，玉堂清洁待相随"，并写了《南山书院记》，刻为石碑，至今保存完好。

南山书院的经费除了祖祠"衍庆堂"和"南邨公"祖祠支付外，至清光绪年间（1875—1908），五亭公吴昌凤以田42.327亩，租子731斗，建立义学仓，在家族中建立了助学和奖学基金的先例。

南山书院从清乾隆三十年（1765年）创办至清光绪三十一年（1905年）止，据《培田吴氏宗谱》统计：由此步入仕途的国学生、贡生、秀才、举人、武进士等多达一百二十多人，其中达到三品至五品衔的有九人。

（四）清末民初的培田学堂

清代末年西方教育思想不断传入中国，废科举，兴新学成为当时社会的潮流。为顺应时代的发展，南山书院改名为"培田两等小学堂（含初等、高等）"，是长汀县第一所民办完全小学。

光绪三十二年（1906年），南山书院再次更名为"长汀县南宣乡区中心国校"；以后多次更名，1950年改为"吴坊中心小学"。1956年培田村从长汀县划归连城县，校名也随之改为"连城县宣和乡培田小学"。

清末以前，南山书院的课文主要是《三字经》、《千字文》、《增广贤文》、《幼学琼林》、《中庸》、《论语》、《四书集注》及应试科举的八股和诗、对等。20世纪初改革后全部用新的课程代替，学习课程为国文、作文、修身、算术、历史、地理、英语、音乐、手工，体育课有单杠、双杠、篮球、乒乓球、赛跑、甩铁饼、铁球等活动。抗日战争时期设军事课，有段时间还有"童子军"组织。

新建校舍大楼坐西朝东，面阔为九开间，进深四开间，上下两层，四坡顶，上下均有一圈跑马廊，砖木结构。底层正中是大礼堂，两侧是教室。二层是三个教室。由于新楼又正好卡在南坑口的口上，楼左侧山坡有台阶上下，再通过一段天桥到达二层。楼的右侧从二层建起一段天桥直通到南山书院内。那时南山书院里的教室依旧使用，教师办公、寄宿生住宿、厨房都在那里。学生多了，新楼东侧又买了一片农田开辟为操场。

（五）妇女学堂——容膝居

清嘉庆年间（1796—1820）培田经济、文化的发展都处于鼎盛时期，由于汀（州）连（城）官道建成，常有文人、官宦、商贾往来，与吴姓结亲的人家也多起来。但后来却发生了一件让吴氏家族十分难堪的事。据村人传说，一位女子外嫁他姓前，听信了新婚之夜如何可怕的谗言，在出嫁时将自己的下身用夏布层层缠死，并随身藏了一把锋利的剪刀。结果没有几天，这位女子就遭休妻，退回培田。吴氏家族丢尽了脸。为了让以后嫁出去的女儿和娶进来的媳妇们能知书达理，掌握必备的知识以及与大家门户相称的风范，清嘉庆年间，吴氏十八世祖吴昌同捐资，办了一座妇女学堂。据罗兰芬老人说：昌同公办妇女学堂是专门到长汀县请督学批下来的，为此县里还派人专程来村检查过，查学员人数，教师情况，教授内容，非常认真。初建时只为吴昌同一个房派使用，不久应其他房派的要求，全家族的妇女都可以到这里学习。学堂很小，便起名叫"容膝居"。

"容膝居"，指房子很小，仅可容膝而已。借陶潜《归去来辞》曰，"倚南窗以寄傲，审容膝之易安"；又《韩诗外传》曰，"结驷连骑，所安不过容膝"。

培田的容膝居位于村落中街的中段，坐北朝南，是一座三间两厢的小院，当心间是厅堂，左右为辅助房，堂前是小天井，左右侧各有一间厢廊。全部房子敞开不做门窗扇，右侧厢廊有大门，门额上题"容膝居"，左右对联为："庭来竹友心胸阔，门对松冈眼界宽"。中厅上大匾为："玉国伟人"，道出办妇女学堂的宗旨是提高妇女的文化修养，开阔她们的心胸。

妇女学堂的学员是本族的媳妇、闺女，老师就是她们的母亲、婆婆或长嫂。1922年出生的罗兰芬老太太说："上妇女学堂的约有三十多人，最大的二十六七岁，小的十七八岁。那时学堂每天下午要学两个小时，老师是本村的寡妇，叫吴德春，当时三十多岁。"

罗兰芬说："妇女学堂学的内容很多，主要是学文化，学写字、读书，还学算术，乘除法、记账，是为了那些失去丈夫的妇女能管理起家中财产，收租等。学习女红，有绣花、剪纸、制衣、做鞋等。要学礼仪，孝敬老人，友爱兄弟。早上给老人穿衣、洗脸、梳头，冬天要把衣裤烤热；清洗裹脚布、缠裹小脚；侍奉丈夫。客人来家，女人要进房躲避。平日在家吃饭时，男人吃完，媳妇才能吃。用竹竿晾晒衣服，男衣要在上，女衣在下，等等。学作家务，洗衣做饭、养猪、养鸡、养蚕、纺线、织布，要勤俭持家等。妇女学堂还要妇女懂婚姻卫生知识和养育孩子的常识。在学习文化的同时还让妇女学些小戏来娱乐，如《小姑贤》、《孔雀东南飞》等。后来因家务事太忙，断断续续读了两年多就不再读了。"老人怀念妇女学堂真是让妇女受益很多，懂得了许多道理，认识了几百个汉字，能看能写简单的信件。

这座充满了妇女活力的小屋至今完好地保留着。

（六）锄经别墅

培田村中街中部有一座锄经别墅，初建于清末，坐西朝东，正对中街，是一幢三开间三进两院式的建筑，第二进曾经办学。第一进正中大门门额上题："锄经别墅"四字，门联为："半亩砚田余菽粟，数椽瓦屋课桑麻"。村人们据这付门联说这座学塾兼教农耕知识，并引《培田八景诗》有稚子学扶犁的记述：

溶溶秋水绕曹溪，杨柳垂垂两岸低。
罢未老农闲弄笛，补蓑稚子学扶犁。
垅云漠漠天将晓，坝草萋萋日已西。
扣角荷锄归小径，乱山深处鹧鸪啼。

也有村民说这仅仅是座启蒙学堂，教些《三字经》、《百家姓》，并没有教授农业知识。
