1. Peitian Village, Liancheng County, Fujian Province

Chinese feudal society's values were ethics-based, its core being human relationships; the family, as the most basic and important social organization, received great emphasis. But how to make a clan more prestigious and cohesive—most important was cultivating descendants, implementing cultural education, raising clan children's overall cultural quality, enabling them to gain skills for establishing themselves, and having greater development and more opportunities. Hence historically Peitian Village in western Fujian's Liancheng County built as many as eighteen academies, private schools, and civil/military schools, plus various cultural-educational buildings such as Culture Temple, Military Temple, and paper-burning furnaces. To support children studying away, in Tingzhou, Liancheng, Zhangzhou and elsewhere the Wu clan also built study halls, academies, Wenchang Pavilions, and Kuixing Pavilions. Beyond this, the clan established cultural organizations such as Confucius Sage Society, Zhu Xi Character-Respecting Society, and literary societies to foster a rich cultural atmosphere—Peitian Village thus became known as the famous "Hometown of Ink and Writing" in the Tingzhou-Liancheng area.

(1) Founding of Schools

When sixth-generation ancestor Guo Long Gong presided over clan affairs in mid-Ming, the Wu clan was already populous, overall economic strength ranking first in Heyuan Li. But at that time throughout Heyuan Li, cultural education was still weak—no decent school existed, so one had to invite a teacher to teach at home, or several families pooled children to hire one teacher—but this method was very unfavorable to raising the clan's overall education level. Ancestor Zu Kuan Gong saw this situation and decided to found his own family school.

Zu Kuan Gong was the Wu clan's seventh-generation ancestor, second son of Guo Long Gong, a county student (郡庠生), born in Ming Chenghua 12 (1476), death year unknown. Peitian "Wu Clan Genealogy · Record of Zu Kuan Gong's Shitouqiu Thatched Hall" records: "Lord Wu (Zu Kuan Gong) read from youth, had lofty ambitions; at fourteen loved swordsmanship; at thirty completed writings, fame renowned at the time. Recruited scholar Miao Gong called his poetry the best in Minhai." But twice failing the provincial exam, he followed precedent to the capital, and after returning home, in Ming Zhengde era (1506–1521) founded the Wu clan's first school, Shitouqiu Thatched Hall, at Shitouqiu north of Peitian Village, as a place for lectures. The genealogy records: "Mountains and streams wind, pheasants fly among ridge clouds—this is Bohai Peitian; place secluded, terrain obstructed, like Tao Yuanming's pine-chrysanthemum three paths—this is Shitouqiu Thatched Hall. Who made it? That gentleman Wu Zu Kuan."

Shitouqiu is a mountain ridge by the village's north mountain path, with a 5–6m high large boulder, abrupt and solid, environment quiet—very suitable for reading; the school was built beside Shitouqiu. Later some said perhaps Zu Kuan Gong thought of the principles "other mountains' stones can polish jade" and "learning requires perseverance, heart as firm as stone" when choosing this "Shitouqiu" place for the school.

The new school faced east, a three-bay three-entry adobe thatched-roof building: lower hall was the gate, middle hall enshrined Confucius's tablet. Other rooms had children's classrooms, teacher's dormitory, and kitchen. Upper hall had library and calligraphy-painting room. Before the academy was a pond serving as Pan Pond (泮池); the gate directly faced the village east's Writing-Brush Peak—hence the school was named "Shitouqiu Thatched Hall."

After completion, it recruited clan children, "invited scholar Xie Taoxi to train descendants." Mr. Xie inscribed a plaque "Thatched Hall Villa." To guarantee school expenses, ancestral hall Yanqing Tang paid 100 dan of rent grain yearly. Later Nancun Gong Ancestral Hall also bore part of the school's rent grain.

Shitouqiu Thatched Hall gave Wu clan children a stable place for systematic study—"founding the tradition of book fragrance in the thirteen villages of Changting-Liancheng." Ming jinshi, Minister of War, Qingliu native Pei Yingzhang came to Peitian, deeply moved by the Wu clan's emphasis on education, and inscribed a couplet: "Though a hundred li from Tingzhou's city walls, the first family entering Confucius's gate." Later Nanshan Academy replaced Shitouqiu Thatched Hall as the clan's main school, and its gate still used this same couplet.

(2) Schools and Academies from Late Ming to Mid-Qing

Northern Song scholar Hu Yuan famously said: "Governing the world ultimately depends on talent; forming world talent depends on education; the root of education is schools." Following Wu Zu Kuan's founding of Shitouqiu Thatched Hall, from late Ming to early Qing, Peitian Wu clan successively had: Shangye House's Yunjiang Academy and Ziyang Academy; Xiaye House's Hongjiang Academy; tenth-generation ancestor Zai Hong Gong's Hong Gong Academy; fourteenth-generation ancestor Jian'an Gong's Yanziqian School; fourteenth-generation ancestor Junjian Gong's Baixuetang Study Hall; fifteenth-generation ancestor Peiyu Gong's Yewu School and Banshan Mansion; fifteenth-generation ancestor Jinjiang Gong's Nanshan Academy; sixteenth-generation ancestor Chunyi Gong's Qingningzhai Academy. These schools and academies were distributed across Wu clan villages—children's reading sounds could be heard everywhere in the village.

Peitian Wu clan's reading tradition rose; schools and academies were all built by various branch lineages. The construction climax of schools and academies triggered a climax of talent emergence. According to Peitian Wu clan genealogy statistics: from Ming Chenghua reign to Qing Qianlong 30 (1765), over three hundred years, Peitian produced 191 xiucai (government students).

Shangye House's Yunjiang Academy, Ziyang Academy, Xiaye House's Hongjiang Academy, Hong Gong Academy, Baixuetang Study Hall, and Yewu School were all located within residences, allocating one or two rooms as schools. Now only Xiaye House's Hongjiang Academy remains—though empty and dilapidated, the large plaque "Bohui Feiying" hanging in the hall still lets one feel the literary bearing of first-rank official Ji Xiaolan when he inscribed the plaque during his Peitian inspection. Among residences, there were also Yanziqian School and Qingningzhai Academy, both independently built with larger scale. Yanziqian School was built west of Nankengkou, a three-bay two-entry small courtyard—before it were farm fields, behind it ancient trees and strange rocks, a stream flowing beside the courtyard. Qingningzhai Academy was built on the high ridge north of Nankengkou, a three-bay two-entry courtyard. In mid-late Qing, some of these schools and academies closed due to lack of students or insufficient funds. Some school buildings, long unmanaged, collapsed; some were sold to others and converted to residences. Qing Guangxu "Peitian Wu Clan Genealogy · Record of Six Schools' Remnants" records: "Shitouqiu Thatched Hall, founded by Zu Kuan Gong, recorded by Li Qiantang—truly the first place where ancestors nurtured talent. ... First converted to house, then reclaimed to field, vicissitudes of generations, long ago. ... From Ming to Qing, wind and frost stripped away all, but one ancient cypress, dense and shading the sun—today touching it one still imagines the ancestor's hand's beneficence."

But Nanshan Academy was preserved—first, its location was good, quiet and suitable for reading; second, teaching quality was higher. Villagers say that in Qing Tongzhi era (1862–1874), Nanshan Academy was already a famous school in the Heyuan Li area—children from wealthy families in nearby villages all came here to study, annual tuition four or five dan of grain. After mid-Qing, Nanshan Academy replaced Shitouqiu Thatched Hall, becoming the recognized clan academy.

(3) Rise of Nanshan Academy

Nanshan Academy was founded by Peitian's fifteenth-generation ancestor Jinjiang Gong in late Qianlong (c. 1760–1770). It lies at the foot of the north slope of Wohu Mountain inside Nankengkou, built against Nanshan's north slope—taking Tao Yuanming's "Drinking Wine" poem: "Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern fence, leisurely seeing Nanshan"—hence named Nanshan Academy. Zeng Ruichun, who once taught at the academy, described in a stele: "In gengshen year, invited by Lord Wu Huaxing and brothers to be head teacher, lodging me at Nanshan. Fine trees lush, scenery serene and secluded—Ludong and Ehu [academies] are no better." This Nanshan Academy, no inferior to White Deer Cave Academy and Ehu Academy, had an extending mountain ridge to the east with lush trees, separating inside and outside the village, making Nankengkou very secluded—conducive to students' devoted study. It was also one of Peitian's New Eight Scenes; Wu Airen's poem "South Academy Reading Sounds" describes the elegant environment and reading atmosphere:

Stepping up Nanshan, realm secluded and quiet, jade-like reading rhythms lingering.
Banana-window rain cold especially at night, bamboo-courtyard wind cool again reporting autumn.
Metal-stone one sound heaven and earth shake, bamboo slips ten thousand volumes ancient and modern searched.
Morning clear early rising people listen, bird sounds and book music joyfully exchange.

Nanshan Academy faces northwest, composed of two courtyards side by side. East courtyard's main building is five-bay, two stories. Ground floor central bay hall enshrines Confucius's tablet, and "inscribes 'Virtue-Building Hut' outside the gate, 'Cultivating Orchids and Planting Cassia' inside the gate, Zhu Xi's 'Reading, Enjoying Poetry' on east and west walls." The wall also hung Zhu Xi's sayings: "Observing ancient sages' essentials of teaching people to learn—none did not make them clarify moral principles, cultivate themselves, then extend to others." Side bays served as student classrooms. In Qing Daoguang era (1821–1850), eighteenth-generation Wu Changtong repaired the east courtyard building—hence east courtyard remains well-preserved today. Before classrooms was a small courtyard, with an archway-style gate centered facing northwest; the gate's lintel originally inscribed "Nanshan Academy" on both inside and outside—now the outside, due to several school-name changes, has no inscription; the inside four characters remain well-preserved. Outside the gate, on both brick pillars, was Minister Pei Yingzhang's gate couplet: "Though a hundred li from Tingzhou's city walls, the first family entering Confucius's gate."

West courtyard adjacent to east courtyard. West courtyard is six or seven steps lower than east, a siheyuan-style two-story building; south and west ground floors were where teachers lived and prepared lessons, with front-eave corridor having beauty-rest (美人靠) benches. Between the two courtyards was a narrow long courtyard with flower walls, with a small door leading outside the academy. The whole academy follows the mountain slope,高低错落, appearing exquisite and graceful. Outside the academy was a half-moon pond, symbolizing Pan Pond, also the "inkstone" of the four scholar's treasures—with the writing-brush-like mountain before Nanshan Academy, exactly forming the "writing brush dipping ink" fengshui. Before the small door was a several-hundred-year-old Buddhist pine (罗汉松). Legend says Qing Ji Xiaolan, during his Peitian inspection, stayed here for two nights.

Ninghua famous scholar Zeng Ruichun taught at Nanshan Academy for many years before official service; the Wu clan not only trusted him but provided excellent conditions. Zeng Ruichun wrote in "Record of Nanshan Academy": "In gengshen year, invited by Lord Wu Huaxing and brothers to be head teacher, lodging me at Nanshan. ... First in the hall saw the couplet 'Bold face dares to claim being the era's hope; casual clothes why not sleep all day'—reading marginal notes, learned that the great-grandfather Wen Weng elegantly intended cultivation, inviting Mr. Zi Jiuqiu to train grandfather here. Mr. led Shanghang Yuan Nangong Weifeng and Yongding Wen Xiaolian Gong to share writing and inkstone—this was his self-inscribed sleeping couch." Ten years later he went to the capital for the metropolitan exam, passed with distinction, "appointed Hanlin Academy bachelor." He specially returned to Peitian Nanshan Academy, writing a couplet: "Ten years ago lecturing in this hall, green fields by the window, precious trees cultivated all competing to sprout; A hundred li away secretly cultivating here, blue clouds attained the path, jade hall clean and pure awaiting companionship"—and wrote "Record of Nanshan Academy," carved as a stone stele, well-preserved to this day.

Nanshan Academy's funding, besides ancestral halls "Yanqing Tang" and "Nancun Gong" paying, by Qing Guangxu era (1875–1908), fifth-generation Wuting Gong Wu Changfeng used 42.327 mu of land, 731 dou of rent grain, to establish a Righteous Study Granary—setting a precedent for study-assistance and scholarship funds in the clan.

From Qing Qianlong 30 (1765) founding to Qing Guangxu 31 (1905), according to "Peitian Wu Clan Genealogy" statistics: over 120 people entered official careers through here—national students, tribute students, xiucai, juren, military jinshi, etc.—among whom nine reached third-to-fifth rank.

(4) Peitian Schools in Late Qing and Early Republic

In late Qing, Western educational ideas continuously entered China; abolishing imperial exams and establishing new schools became the social trend. To顺应时代 development, Nanshan Academy was renamed "Peitian Two-Grade Primary School (including elementary and higher)"—the first privately-run complete primary school in Changting County.

In Guangxu 32 (1906), Nanshan Academy was again renamed "Changting County Nanxuan Township Central National School"; later renamed multiple times, in 1950 changed to "Wufang Central Primary School." In 1956 Peitian Village was transferred from Changting County to Liancheng County, school name accordingly changed to "Liancheng County Xuanhe Township Peitian Primary School."

Before late Qing, Nanshan Academy's texts were mainly "Three Character Classic," "Thousand Character Essay," "Expanded Wise Sayings," "Children's Knowledge Garden," "Doctrine of the Mean," "Analects," "Four Books Collected Commentaries," plus eight-legged essays and poetry/couplets for imperial exams. After early 20th century reform, all replaced by new curricula: national language, composition, self-cultivation, arithmetic, history, geography, English, music, handicrafts; physical education had horizontal bar, parallel bars, basketball, table tennis, racing, discus, shot put, etc. During Anti-Japanese War, military courses were set, and for a period there was a "Boy Scouts" organization.

The new school building faced east, nine-bay wide, four-bay deep, two stories, four-slope roof, with a surrounding gallery on both floors, brick-wood structure. Ground floor center was the grand auditorium, both sides classrooms. Second floor had three classrooms. Since the new building was exactly at the mouth of Nankengkou, the building's left hillside had steps up and down, then through a sky bridge to reach the second floor. The building's right side built a sky bridge from the second floor directly into Nanshan Academy. At that time Nanshan Academy's classrooms were still in use—teacher offices, boarding student dorms, and kitchen were all there. With more students, east of the new building a piece of farmland was purchased and opened as a playground.

(5) Women's School — Rongxi Ju (Knee-Room Residence)

In Qing Jiaqing era (1796–1820), Peitian's economic and cultural development was at its peak. Due to the Tingzhou-Liancheng official road's completion, scholars, officials, and merchants frequently passed through, and families intermarrying with the Wu surname also increased. But later an event occurred that greatly embarrassed the Wu clan. According to village legend, a woman, before marrying into another surname, believed slander about how terrible the wedding night would be—at marriage she tightly wrapped her lower body with grass cloth layers, and hid a sharp pair of scissors on her person. Result: within a few days, this woman was divorced and sent back to Peitian. The Wu clan lost all face. To ensure future daughters marrying out and daughters-in-law marrying in would be educated and reasonable,掌握 necessary knowledge and bearing commensurate with a great family, in Qing Jiaqing era, eighteenth-generation ancestor Wu Changtong donated funds to run a women's school. According to elderly Luo Lanfen: Changtong Gong's running of the women's school was specially approved by the Changting County education inspector—for this the county sent people to the village to inspect, checking student numbers, teacher situation, teaching content—very serious. Initially only for Wu Changtong's own branch lineage; soon at other branches' request, all clan women could study here. The school was very small, hence named "Rongxi Ju" (Knee-Room Residence).

"Rongxi Ju" means the house is very small, only enough to accommodate one's knees. Borrowing Tao Yuanming's "Returning Home": "Leaning by the south window to express pride, examining that a knee-room is easy to find peace in"; and "Han Shi Wai Zhuan": "Four-horse carriages in succession, what one rests in is no more than a knee-room."

Peitian's Rongxi Ju is located in the middle section of the village's central street, facing south, a three-bay two-side-room small courtyard: central bay is the hall, left and right are auxiliary rooms, before the hall is a small skylight courtyard, each side has a side corridor. All rooms are open without door/window leaves. The right side corridor has a gate, lighthouse inscribed "Rongxi Ju," left-right couplet: "Courtyard welcomes bamboo friends,心胸 broad; Gate faces pine ridge,眼界 wide." The central hall's large plaque: "Jade Nation Great Person"—expressing the women's school's purpose: raising women's cultural cultivation, broadening their minds.

Women's school students were the clan's daughters-in-law and unmarried daughters; teachers were their mothers, mothers-in-law, or elder sisters-in-law. 1922-born elderly Luo Lanfen said: "About thirty-plus people attended the women's school, oldest twenty-six or twenty-seven, youngest seventeen or eighteen. At that time the school studied two hours every afternoon; the teacher was a village widow named Wu Dechun, then in her thirties."

Luo Lanfen said: "The women's school taught much content—mainly culture, learning to write and read; also arithmetic, multiplication/division, bookkeeping—so women who lost husbands could manage family property, collect rent, etc. Learned needlework: embroidery, paper-cutting, clothes-making, shoe-making. Learned etiquette: respecting elders, loving brothers. Morning dressing, washing face, combing hair for elders; in winter warming clothes; washing foot-binding cloths, binding small feet; serving husband. When guests came, women had to go inside to avoid. Daily at home eating: men finish first, then daughters-in-law can eat. Using bamboo poles to dry clothes: men's clothes above, women's below, etc. Learned housework: washing, cooking, raising pigs/chickens/silkworms, spinning, weaving—being diligent and thrifty in managing the home. The women's school also wanted women to understand marital hygiene knowledge and child-rearing common sense. While learning culture, also let women learn small plays for entertainment, such as 'Sister-in-Law Xian' and 'Peacock Flies Southeast.' Later because housework was too busy, studied on and off for over two years then stopped." The elderly misses the women's school—it truly benefited women greatly, understanding many principles, recognizing several hundred Chinese characters, able to read and write simple letters.

This small house full of women's vitality remains well-preserved to this day.

(6) Chujing Villa (Plowing-Classics Villa)

In the middle of Peitian Village's central street stands Chujing Villa, first built in late Qing, facing east, directly opposite the central street—a three-bay three-entry two-courtyard building; the second entry once ran a school. The first entry's central gate lighthouse inscribed "Chujing Villa" four characters, gate couplet: "Half-mu inkstone field leaves beans and millet; Several rafter tile-house teaches mulberry and hemp." Villagers, based on this couplet, say this school also taught farming knowledge, and cite "Peitian Eight Scenes Poem" with records of children learning to hold the plow:

Limpid autumn water winds around Cao Stream, willows drooping low on both banks.
Old farmer after work idly plays flute, mending raincoat child learns to hold plow.
Ridge clouds vast sky about to dawn, dam grass lush sun already west.
Carrying hoe on shoulder returning down small path, deep in chaotic mountains partridges cry.

Some villagers also say this was merely an elementary school, teaching "Three Character Classic" and "Hundred Family Surnames," without teaching agricultural knowledge.

sections.name: 浙江省建德市新叶村
sections.content_zh:
二、浙江省建德市新叶村

高吟只许松涛和，绝响那容野潦追。
手捧遗编心耿耿，耳旁犹觉有唔咿。
——叶一清《儒谷书声》

浙江省建德市新叶村叶一清（1517—1583）的这首七律，追忆了自己幼年时代的读书生涯。

新叶村古代虽然是一个宗族社会，但宗族的文化传统并不很封闭，在一个时期，它还相当开放过。例如，叶氏的重乐书院曾接纳四乡的子弟；明代，白崖山人叶一清游历四方，就学于王阳明门下。在新叶村所保留的一些古代文化建筑遗迹中，还能看到这个宗族的文化传统。

（一）玉华叶氏的劝学传统

像江南许多宗族世家一样，叶氏在创业之初就十分重视子弟读书，把耕和读作为宗族兴旺的两件大事。

到叶克诚（1250—1323）时代，"耕可致富"的愿望大约已基本实现，但"读可荣身"的理想并未成功。他创办书院、敦聘名儒任教，并经常与金履祥、柳贯、许谦等论理学、诗文，且有著作。

叶克诚的长子叶震（1277—1360）是玉华叶氏家族第一个通过科举步入仕途的人。宗谱载："叶震，字雷甫，治《春秋》，登元壬子（1312年）乡荐。授江西安福县县尹，课最，擢刑部郎中，升河南廉访副使。"

到明万历二年（1574年），白崖山人叶一清写了《勉族祖训》诗，有一条《读书》，其中写道：

谋生惟有读书高，试把书高训尔曹。
平地可登卿与相，翻身便作俊和髦。
能消心上如焚火，解拔胸中似织茅。
更有一言是真诀，买珠还椟剑进鞘。

为鼓励读书进阶，叶氏宗族对读书有成就者给予多种形式的奖励。赴考发给盘费，考中功名分级奖赏，并记入宗谱。叶氏宗谱《仁分祀产》中载："文武童生县试，给盘费银二钱五分，府试给盘费银二钱五分，院试给盘费银三钱正。"《义分祀产》中则记载："举人每年给谷六石，副拔岁贡每年给谷四石，进士每年给谷八石。"除此之外，还要在功名人所属支堂前设立"抱鼓石"（当地称神鼓石），"上下马石"，"竖旗立座"。每逢喜庆日，还要挂长幛于祠堂内，上面记录着中试人的姓名、等第和待任官职，以激励族中子弟。每次大祭后会馂时，读书有成就的子弟受到特殊的优待。

（二）书院和学塾

多方办学是江南乡村文化的一大特点，有私塾、宗族办的义学、官学堂以及高一级的书院。

玉华叶氏始祖叶坤（约1200—1202年出生），虽然出身牧牛的小佣工，创业艰难，仍不忘督促叶氏的子弟读书。当时，他没有条件办学，只好送孙子叶克诚到兰溪城南叶氏"宗人讳诞者所建"的灏东书院就读。后来，叶克诚的长子叶震也就读于这所书院。

到叶克诚执掌家族事务后，终于开办了属于玉华叶氏的书院——重乐精舍，后改名重乐书院。据《玉华叶氏宗谱·叶氏书院记》载："世族大家，比有书院之建，所以崇儒重道为弟子藏修游息之地，事之最有补于风教者也。……在元有重乐书院，东谷太翁所建。……今日之书院虽荒芜，而址与名则犹存焉。""在今儒源上新屋左手大麦地内，败瓦残垣依稀可辨识"，"前门三间，正堂三间，两厢共六间，缭以周垣"。

一个平民之家自己开办书院是十分不易的，因为书院一般都要有固定的学田作为经费来源，并且要聘请比较著名的学者任教授。所以，叶克诚能够创办书院，说明他事业的成功及在当地已有了不小的影响。虽然这时玉华叶氏不过50人左右。

据《玉华叶氏宗谱》载，重乐书院建在距新叶村七八里山后的儒源村。儒源村本无名，只因为有了重乐书院，聚集了几位儒者，尤其是聘请了宋末元初理学大师金履祥来会讲之后才得名。

叶氏书院不同于学堂，更不是私塾。书院特点是讲学与研究相结合，广纳四方学子而不仅为一姓子弟所用。所以，它不宜办在已被双溪所围合的新叶村内，以免受世事的干扰，以利于子弟"藏修游息"。

1. 重乐书院的衰亡

重乐书院建于元初，大约兴旺了三百年。这段时期正是玉华叶氏家族日渐发展并臻于鼎盛的时期，也是劝学、耕读之风最盛的时期。

当时政府对民间的书院没有很多的干涉，农村经济平稳，全国的书院以及与科举相连的平民文化水平有了较快的发展。但是，到明初，民办书院渐渐被朝廷视为逆流。因为书院并不以举业为教学的唯一内容，重的是聚会结社，思想风气比较活跃。玉华叶氏的重乐书院也有类似的活动。如叶氏宗谱《叶氏书院记》载：延聘金履祥先生时，"白云许先生，由庚叶先生、道传柳先生、见心徐先生辈亦曾往来于其间"。这些先生都是当时很有名气的学者，他们在研习交流学问之余，也要结社议政。金履祥先生去世后，没有人能担负起书院事务，重乐书院于明代中期颓败，一直没有再恢复。

2. 私塾、义学和官学堂

新叶村除重乐书院外，村中还有私塾、义学。私塾是教师在自己家中招几个小孩子识字读书，收学费。义学多为宗族兴办，由宗族出资聘请塾师，教授本支堂派的子弟读书识字，如有序堂、荣寿堂的书房都曾是义学的场所。教师通常只教三五个孩子。到清末，光绪三十二年（1906年），慈禧太后下诏废除科举，除京师已设大学堂外，令各直省省府与府、州、县设立学堂、作育人才。即时全国范围内官学、书院再次兴起。叶氏宗族在官方的资助下，于清末又开办了一所官学堂。学堂建在南部的村边上，即原来宗族内颐养鳏寡老人的"居敬轩"的基址上，紧靠着石塘，环境幽雅而宁静。学堂不大而型制却已经很适应学堂的功能。从现存建筑来看，为九开间对合式。每间面阔相等，均为三米。正屋每二间为一厅，一共四厅，宽敞高大，靠天井一侧开大片格扇窗，大约是讲堂，正中一间为神堂，供文昌帝君。而倒座屋却窄而矮，进深仅有一点八米，每一小间之间都有木板分隔，靠天井一侧做成不能开启的棱木方格窗，这是模仿正式科考棚舍的小间的，为的是让生员熟悉真考棚的环境。目前正厅只剩下靠中央的两间，明间中恭恭敬敬地供奉着文昌帝君的塑像。倒座仍残留着断壁残垣及部分窗棂。到民国二年（1913年）叶氏宗族又利用西山祠堂建起了华山小学。

（三）文运与抟云塔、文昌阁

抟云塔位于新叶村东南方的地势低洼处，它始建于明代隆庆元年(1567年)，落成于明万历二年(1574年)，是新叶村目前保留得年代最早、最完好的一幢古建筑。

1. 抟云塔与新叶村的文运

抟云塔又叫做"文峰塔"，是南方比较常见的一种风水塔。

古时候，耕耘大半是靠天吃饭，人们摆脱不了原始的自然崇拜，于是迷信风水。走科举道路，虽说靠悬发锥股，也不得不惴惴地盼望老天爷保佑。恰好新叶村东南角的洼地太低，"巽位不足"，《玉华叶氏宗谱》中白崖山人撰《抟云塔记》载，当时的一位堪舆师建议建塔，说："凡通都大邑，巨聚伟集，于山川赳缺之处，每每藉此（按，指塔）以充填挽之助。虽假人之力，以俾天之功，而萃然巍然，凌霄耸兀，实状厥观"。于是，"友松翁暨弟侄辈拟于所居之东，叠级而层垣焉，使天柱之高标与玉华、道峰相鼎峙，以补巽方之不足也"。抟云塔正是为这个目标而建的文笔峰，它修补了新叶村的风水，维系着玉华叶氏对文运的憧憬。

一座文峰塔毕竟还显得单薄，所以叶氏又喻道峰山为卓笔峰，喻玉华山为砚山，将有序堂前的南塘喻为墨池，来共振文运。

2. 抟云塔的建筑型制

叶氏宗谱《抟云塔记》载，明代隆庆年间（1567—1572）初建时的塔"凡高一百四十尺有奇，围得高之三一，外辟通明之户者三，内为升高之梯者六，下作周廊，视其围倍之"。"是役也，虽曰仿浮屠之制万一，堪舆之左券可执，则将来之题名纪捷者当籍籍乎其蝉联而骥附也。如是，则古所称雁塔者岂得专其美于前耶？故兹之名抟云者亦曰于方为巽，取象则风，当夫秋飚迅发，彼鹍鹏起者负乘天之云抟扶摇而上九万里，将拭目俟之也。"现存的抟云塔，除底层的周廊已不知于何时何故失去外，与明代初建时的情况大致相同。塔为砖砌，平面正六边形，七层，通高约三十余米。底层有三个券门，从二层以上每层有三个发券窗洞。为求塔体坚固，各层窗洞间相互错开排列。每层略有收分，层高逐级稍减。塔内各层原有木楼板，以固定木梯上下。这种类型的塔在浙江各县常见。由于年代久远，修缮不力，木楼板及木梯已经全部毁坏无遗。抟云塔的外立面，用砖牙叠涩作腰檐，从下层到顶层叠涩砖层分别为六、六、五、五、四、四、三。檐角微微挑起。塔刹由五个圆形石盘累叠，居中的第三个最大，往上、下均渐小，外形如枣核。一根木楮将它们串接在一起，固定在塔顶。塔的高宽之比约为十比一。自下而上逐层缩小，产生了一种向上的动势。

虽然塔身上下无任何雕饰，但建筑造型秀丽、端庄，尤其是在丘陵包围的原野上，四周衬着高低起伏的小山冈，更显得异常挺拔精神。

（四）文昌神与文昌阁

新叶村的文峰塔建成之后约三百年，清代同治年间（1862—1874），在它脚下又造了一座文昌阁。文昌阁是文峰塔的配套建筑，同样为了祈求文运。在这位置造文昌阁，也是为了加强关拦"水口"。新叶村的双溪在文峰塔前与外溪先后汇合，向东南流去，这里是全村的"水口"。据风水之说："水口关拦不重叠，而易成易败。"单单一座文峰塔，没有重叠，层次不够，又没有小山丘加强关拦，就只能用寺庙来加强。所以要再造一座文昌阁。《史记·天官书》记载："北斗之上有六星，合称为文昌宫"，主人间文运。

在中国南方各省许多旧村落都有文昌阁。除祭祀文昌帝君外还供族中子弟读书会文，起书院或义塾的作用。类似的有魁星楼(阁)，但浙江一带不常见。

据《寿昌县志》卷九《文昌祠碑记》中记载：对文昌帝君"而今祠以栋宇，祀以春秋，宜也。况神建兹地，为偃武而崇文，则神锡诸福，必转否而为泰。"

清同治年间所建的文昌阁，坐东面西，木结构楼阁式，样子像亭，因此也叫"水口亭"。四柱落地，四周开敞无墙，顶子为歇山式。

民国初年，经过五十年风雨的文昌阁部分坍塌，遂于1915年在原基地上重建。以后又经多次修缮。现存文昌阁为木结构，分为前后两进。

前进为三开间，明间宽4米，进深3.28米。前门外两侧有八字墙。明间上面建楼，重檐歇山。翼角起翘高耸，戗脊前端装饰着灰塑的鲤鱼化龙，鱼首向下，鱼身变为又细又长的龙身，摆动着将龙尾高高伸向天穹，最高点为9.50米。戗脊和正脊表现了科举制度使鱼变化成龙的重大意义。

文昌阁大门正面的木构件上都布满雕饰，尤其华丽的是"骑门梁"(即明间檐枋)和出挑用的牛腿。雕刻构图巧妙，内容丰富，人物、动物、花草的造型生动如有气息。有戏曲场面，民间传说人物，"四君子"——梅、兰、竹、菊，也有回纹卷草组成的图案。山墙面上博风之下和墀头沿边，还绘有彩色的、很写实的鸡、鱼、猪、狗等，乡土气息十足。文昌阁是全村最华丽的建筑，色彩斑斓，甚至胜过大宗祠等各级祠堂，虽然规模不及。而且，它和抟云塔是全村仅有的外向性建筑，供人观赏，成为重要的景观和村落的标志。这情况鲜明地表现出文运对宗族的重大意义。

文昌阁的后进也是三开间，尺寸与前一进相仿，无楼层。这后进又名"白云庵"。无雕饰，与前进楼阁建筑的雕梁画栋对照鲜明。后进曾用作义塾，室内至今供奉着两幅"魁星"(奎星)像。魁星一手执斗，一手执笔，形状约略如魁字。一如顾炎武《日知录·魁》所说：神像"不能像奎而改奎为魁，又不能像魁而取之字形为鬼举足而起其斗"，正是魁星像的写照。

前后进之间的天井用石条墁地。两进建筑都向天井一面敞开。

紧挨文昌阁的南侧，1915年重建时添了一组辅助用房，形成一个小三合院，(是观音堂，曾全毁，近年完全重建)，与文昌阁以角门相通。到1919年文昌阁正式建成开光时，又在北侧紧贴文昌阁高大的封火山墙建成一座土地祠，是一座独立的院落，有自己的大门。耕读之梦在文昌阁与土地祠的结合中体现了出来。

在文昌阁与抟云塔四周，曾有大片的松柏林，明、清两代的诗文中多次提到，如"密松围似砌"，可惜土地改革时这片长青的林木被砍伐得一棵不剩了。

虽然抟云塔、文昌阁与土地祠并不是建于一个时期，但它们的组合却达到了和谐统一。高耸的抟云塔的七层塔檐横向层层排列，与文昌阁的横向双重檐口相呼应。而文昌阁的翼角与正吻一起，高高刺向天穹，向上的动态很强，与塔的竖向构图互为呼应。塔和阁在建筑艺术上既对比又统一。文昌阁与土地祠共同给文峰塔一个十分稳定厚实的基座，高耸的塔刹与文昌阁的飞檐翼角又很自然地赋予这组建筑以上挺的生气。

如今，抟云塔、文昌阁这组建筑仍矗立于新叶村的田野上，很远就能见到它们，给村子以生动的轮廓，它们是村子的地标，只要看到它就会想起新叶村人们耕读的理想。

2. Xinye Village, Jiande City, Zhejiang Province

High chanting only allows pine waves to harmonize, absolute echo how can wild mud pursue;
Holding inherited books heart sincere, beside ears still seems to hear reading sounds.
— Ye Yiqing, "Reading Sounds in Confucian Valley"

This seven-character regulated verse by Ye Yiqing (1517–1583) of Xinye Village, Jiande, Zhejiang, recollects his childhood reading career.

Although ancient Xinye Village was a clan society, the clan's cultural tradition was not very closed—for a period it was quite open. For example, the Ye clan's Chongyue Academy once accepted children from four surrounding townships; in Ming, Baiya Shanren Ye Yiqing traveled everywhere and studied under Wang Yangming. In some ancient cultural building remains preserved in Xinye Village, one can still see this clan's cultural tradition.

(1) Yuhua Ye Clan's Tradition of Encouraging Study

Like many Jiangnan clan families, the Ye clan from its founding greatly valued children's reading, taking farming and reading as the two great matters for clan prosperity.

By Ye Kecheng's (1250–1323) era, the "farming can enrich" wish had basically been realized, but the "reading can honor the body" ideal had not succeeded. He founded academies, earnestly hired famous Confucian scholars to teach, and frequently discussed Neo-Confucianism and poetry with Jin Lüxiang, Liu Guan, Xu Qian, etc., and had writings.

Ye Kecheng's eldest son Ye Zhen (1277–1360) was the first person in the Yuhua Ye clan to enter officialdom through imperial exams. The clan genealogy records: "Ye Zhen, style Leifu, studied Spring and Autumn Annals, obtained provincial recommendation in Yuan Renzi (1312). Appointed magistrate of Anfu County, Jiangxi, with outstanding performance, promoted to Ministry of Justice director, then Henan surveillance vice-commissioner."

In Ming Wanli 2 (1574), Baiya Shanren Ye Yiqing wrote "Poems Exhorting Clan Ancestral Instructions," with one "Reading," which says:

For making a living, only reading is high; try using book-high to instruct you all;
On flat ground one can ascend to ministers and chancellors, turning over becomes outstanding and talented;
Can extinguish heart's burning-like fire, can unbind chest's woven-like thatch;
One more word is the true formula: buy pearl return case, sword enters sheath.

To encourage reading advancement, the Ye clan gave various forms of rewards to those with reading achievements. Going to exams received travel expenses; passing exam degrees received graded rewards, recorded in the clan genealogy. Ye clan genealogy "Ren Branch Sacrificial Properties" records: "Civil and military child students county exam: give travel expense silver 2.5 qian; prefecture exam: give 2.5 qian; academy exam: give 3 qian exactly." "Yi Branch Sacrificial Properties" records: "Juren (provincial graduate) yearly give grain 6 shi; associate/selected/tribute students yearly give 4 shi; jinshi (palace graduate) yearly give 8 shi." Beyond this, before the branch hall of degree-holders, they established "drum-holding stones" (locally called divine-drum stones), "dismounting/mounting horse stones," "erecting flags and seats." On festive days, long banners were hung in the ancestral hall, recording exam-passer names, ranks, and pending official positions, to激励 clan children. At the post-grand-sacrifice communal meal, reading-achieved children received special优待.

(2) Academies and Schools

Running schools in multiple ways is a major feature of Jiangnan rural culture: private schools, clan-run charity schools, official schools, and higher-level academies.

Yuhua Ye clan founder Ye Kun (born c.1200–1202), though from a cowherd laborer background with difficult创业, never forgot urging Ye children to read. At that time, he had no conditions to run a school, so had to send grandson Ye Kecheng to study at Haodong Academy, built by "clansman named Dan" south of Lanxi city. Later, Ye Kecheng's eldest son Ye Zhen also studied at this academy.

After Ye Kecheng took charge of clan affairs, he finally opened an academy belonging to the Yuhua Ye clan—Chongyue Retreat (重乐精舍), later renamed Chongyue Academy. According to "Yuhua Ye Clan Genealogy · Record of Ye Clan Academy": "Great clan families, all have academy construction, so as to revere Confucianism and value the Way, as a place for children to study, rest, and travel—the matter most beneficial to moral education. ... In Yuan there was Chongyue Academy, built by Great Lord Donggu. ... Today's academy though barren, its site and name still remain." "In today's Ruyuan, left of new house, in barley field, broken tiles and ruined walls faintly discernible," "front gate three bays, main hall three bays, two side wings total six bays, surrounded by walls."

A commoner family running its own academy was very difficult, because academies generally needed fixed school land as funding source, and needed to hire relatively famous scholars as teachers. Hence Ye Kecheng's ability to found an academy shows his career success and considerable local influence—though at this time Yuhua Ye clan had only about 50 people.

According to Yuhua Ye clan genealogy, Chongyue Academy was built at Ruyuan Village, seven or eight li behind the mountains from Xinye Village. Ruyuan Village originally had no name—only because of Chongyue Academy, gathering several Confucian scholars, especially after hiring late-Song early-Yuan Neo-Confucian master Jin Lüxiang to come lecture, did it gain a name.

Ye clan academies differed from schools, even more from private schools. Academy feature: combining lectures and research, broadly accepting students from all directions, not only for one surname's children. Hence it was not suitable to build inside Xinye Village, already enclosed by twin streams, to avoid worldly disturbance, facilitating children's "study, rest, and travel."

1. Decline of Chongyue Academy

Chongyue Academy was built in early Yuan, flourishing for about three hundred years. This period was exactly when the Yuhua Ye clan gradually developed and reached its peak, also when the tradition of encouraging study and farming-reading was strongest.

At that time the government did not interfere much with private academies; rural economy was stable; academies nationwide and the commoner cultural level linked to imperial exams developed relatively quickly. But by early Ming, private academies were gradually regarded by the court as countercurrent. Because academies did not take exam preparation as the sole teaching content—they valued gathering and forming associations, with relatively active intellectual atmosphere. Yuhua Ye's Chongyue Academy had similar activities. As Ye clan genealogy "Record of Ye Clan Academy" records: when hiring Jin Lüxiang, "White Cloud Mr. Xu, Yougeng Mr. Ye, Daochuan Mr. Liu, Jianxin Mr. Xu and others also came and went among it." These gentlemen were all very famous scholars of the time—besides studying and exchanging learning, they also formed associations to discuss politics. After Mr. Jin Lüxiang died, no one could take on academy affairs; Chongyue Academy declined in mid-Ming and was never restored.

2. Private Schools, Charity Schools, and Official Schools

Besides Chongyue Academy, Xinye Village also had private schools and charity schools. Private schools: teachers recruited a few young children at their own homes to learn characters and read, charging tuition. Charity schools were mostly clan-run, with clan funds hiring tutors, teaching children of their own branch to read and write—e.g., Youxu Hall and Rongshou Hall's studies were once charity school venues. Teachers usually taught only three to five children. By late Qing, Guangxu 32 (1906), Empress Dowager Cixi issued an edict abolishing imperial exams; besides the capital's already-established university, ordered all provincial, prefectural, and county governments to establish schools and cultivate talent. Immediately nationwide, official schools and academies rose again. With official funding, the Ye clan in late Qing opened an official school. The school was built at the southern village edge, on the site of "Jujing Xuan"—originally the clan's home for caring for widows and widowers—right by Stone Pond, environment elegant and quiet. The school was not large but its form already well-adapted to school functions. From surviving buildings: nine-bay paired layout. Each bay equal width, all 3m. Main building every two bays forms one hall—four halls total, spacious and tall; by the skylight courtyard side opens large lattice windows, probably lecture halls; the central bay is the divine hall, enshrining Wenchang Emperor. The reverse building, however, is narrow and low, depth only 1.8m; each small room separated by wooden boards; by the courtyard side made non-openable lattice square windows—imitating formal exam booth small rooms, so students could familiarize with the real exam booth environment. Currently the main hall only has the central two bays remaining; in the central bay, Wenchang Emperor's statue is respectfully enshrined. The reverse building still retains broken walls and部分 window lattices. By Republic 2 (1913), the Ye clan used West Mountain Ancestral Hall to build Huashan Primary School.

(3) Literary Fortune and Tuanyun Pagoda, Wenchang Pavilion

Tuanyun Pagoda lies at the low-lying southeast of Xinye Village. It was founded in Ming Longqing 1 (1567), completed in Ming Wanli 2 (1574)—the oldest and best-preserved ancient building currently remaining in Xinye Village.

1. Tuanyun Pagoda and Xinye Village's Literary Fortune

Tuanyun Pagoda is also called "Wenfeng Pagoda"—a relatively common fengshui pagoda in the south.

In ancient times, farming mostly depended on heaven for food; people could not escape primitive nature worship, hence believed in fengshui. Taking the imperial exam path, though relying on hanging hair and awl thighs, still had to anxiously hope for heaven's blessing.恰好 Xinye Village's southeast lowland was too low—"xun direction insufficient." Yuhua Ye clan genealogy, Baiya Shanren's "Record of Tuanyun Pagoda," records that a fengshui master at the time suggested building a pagoda, saying: "All great cities and large gatherings, where mountains and streams are deficient, often use this [pagoda] to fill and supplement. Though using human power to assist heaven's work, yet gathered and majestic, soaring to the clouds, truly strengthening the scene." Hence "Yousong Weng and brothers/nephews planned, east of their residences, to build tiered walls, making the pillar of heaven's height stand tripod-like with Yuhua and Daofeng mountains, to supplement the xun direction's deficiency." Tuanyun Pagoda was precisely the writing-brush peak built for this goal—it repaired Xinye Village's fengshui, sustaining the Yuhua Ye clan's longing for literary fortune.

One Wenfeng Pagoda after all still seemed thin, so the Ye clan also metaphorized Daofeng Mountain as Outstanding-Brush Peak, Yuhua Mountain as Inkstone Mountain, and the South Pond before Youxu Hall as Ink Pool, to jointly resonate literary fortune.

2. Tuanyun Pagoda's Architectural Form

Ye clan genealogy "Record of Tuanyun Pagoda" records that the pagoda initially built in Ming Longqing era (1567–1572) "over 140 chi high, circumference one-third of height, outside three bright windows, inside six ladders, below a surrounding corridor twice the circumference." "This work, though imitating one ten-thousandth of stupa form, the fengshui guarantee can be held—then future names recorded in success will abundantly follow in succession. Thus the ancient so-called Wild Goose Pagoda could not monopolize beauty before? Hence this name Tuanyun also means: in direction it is xun, in image it is wind; when autumn winds swiftly rise, that great bird rises, carrying heaven's clouds, whirling upward ninety thousand li—we will watch and wait!" The existing Tuanyun Pagoda, except the ground floor's surrounding corridor lost at unknown time and reason, is大致 same as initially built in Ming. Pagoda is brick, regular hexagon plan, seven stories, ~30m+ total height. Ground floor has three arched doors; from second story up, each story has three arched window openings. For pagoda body solidity, each story's windows are staggered. Each story slightly tapers, story height gradually decreases. Inside each story originally had wooden floors, with fixed wooden ladders. This type of pagoda is common in Zhejiang counties. Due to age and poor maintenance, wooden floors and ladders all destroyed. Tuanyun Pagoda's exterior uses brick-tooth corbelling for waist eaves; from bottom to top, corbelled brick layers are 6, 6, 5, 5, 4, 4, 3. Eave corners slightly upturned. The finial consists of five circular stone disks stacked; the central third is largest, tapering up and down,外形 like a date pit. A wooden dowel strings them together, fixed at the pagoda top. Pagoda height-width ratio about 10:1. Tapering from bottom up produces an upward momentum.

Though the pagoda body has no carving top or bottom, its architectural form is graceful and dignified—especially on the plain surrounded by hills, with undulating small hills around, it appears exceptionally tall and spirited.

(4) Wenchang Deity and Wenchang Pavilion

About three hundred years after Xinye Village's Wenfeng Pagoda was built, in Qing Tongzhi era (1862–1874), a Wenchang Pavilion was built at its foot. Wenchang Pavilion is the配套 building of Wenfeng Pagoda, similarly for praying literary fortune. Building Wenchang Pavilion at this position also strengthens "water mouth" closure. Xinye Village's twin streams converge with the outer stream before the Wenfeng Pagoda, flowing southeast—this is the whole village's "water mouth." According to fengshui: "Water mouth closure not layered, then easy come easy go." A single Wenfeng Pagoda, no layering, insufficient hierarchy, and no small hills to strengthen closure—can only use temples to strengthen. Hence another Wenchang Pavilion must be built. Records of the Grand Historian · Heavenly Officials records: "Above the Northern Dipper are six stars, collectively called Wenchang Palace," governing human literary fortune.

Many old villages in southern China provinces have Wenchang Pavilions. Besides worshipping Wenchang Emperor, they also serve clan children to gather, read, and discuss writing—acting as academy or charity school. Similar are Kuixing Towers (Pavilions), but uncommon in Zhejiang.

According to "Shouchang County Gazetteer" Volume 9 "Wenchang Shrine Stele Inscription": for Wenchang Emperor "now enshrined in buildings, worshipped in spring and autumn—appropriate. Moreover the deity established this place, to cease martial and revere culture—then the deity bestows blessings, surely turning adversity to prosperity."

The Wenchang Pavilion built in Qing Tongzhi era faces west, wooden-structure pavilion style, looking like a亭—hence also called "Water Mouth Pavilion." Four pillars to ground, open all around without walls, roof is hip-and-gable.

In early Republic, after fifty years of weather, Wenchang Pavilion partially collapsed, so in 1915 rebuilt on the original site. Later repaired multiple times. Existing Wenchang Pavilion is wooden structure, divided into front and rear entries.

Front entry: three bays, central bay 4m wide, 3.28m deep. Outside front gate both sides have splayed walls (八字墙). Above central bay builds a tower, double-eave hip-and-gable. Wing corners soar high; diagonal ridge front ends decorated with gray-plaster carp-transforming-to-dragon: carp head downward, carp body becomes thin long dragon body, swinging dragon tail high toward the sky—highest point 9.50m. Diagonal ridges and main ridge express the great significance of the imperial exam system making carp transform into dragon.

Wenchang Pavilion's front gate wooden members are all covered with carvings—especially ornate are the "gate-straddling beam" (central bay eave lintel) and corbel brackets (牛腿) used for overhang. Carving composition ingenious, content rich; figures, animals, flowers and plants modeled vividly as if alive. There are opera scenes, folk legend figures, "Four Gentlemen"—plum, orchid, bamboo, chrysanthemum—and also patterns of fretwork and scrolling grass. On gable walls below bargeboards and along gable ends, also painted colorful realistic chickens, fish, pigs, dogs, etc.—very rustic. Wenchang Pavilion is the village's most ornate building, colorful, even surpassing the great ancestral hall and various-level ancestral halls, though smaller in scale. Moreover, it and Tuanyun Pagoda are the village's only outward-facing buildings, for people to view, becoming important landscape and village landmark. This situation clearly expresses the great significance of literary fortune to the clan.

Wenchang Pavilion's rear entry is also three bays, dimensions similar to front entry, no floors. This rear entry is also named "White Cloud Nunnery" (白云庵). No carvings, contrasting sharply with front entry's carved beams and painted pillars. Rear entry once used as charity school; indoors still enshrines two "Kuixing" (Kui Star) statues. Kuixing holds a dipper in one hand, a brush in the other—shape roughly like the character 魁. As Gu Yanwu's "Daily Knowledge · Kui" says: the deity statue "cannot resemble Kui (奎) so changed Kui to 魁; cannot resemble 魁 so took its character form as a ghost raising foot and lifting its dipper"—exactly a portrayal of the Kuixing statue.

The courtyard between front and rear entries is paved with stone strips. Both entries open toward the courtyard side.

紧挨着 Wenchang Pavilion's south side, during the 1915 reconstruction, a group of auxiliary rooms was added, forming a small three-sided courtyard (Guanyin Hall, once completely destroyed, recently fully rebuilt), communicating with Wenchang Pavilion through a corner gate. By 1919 when Wenchang Pavilion was officially completed and consecrated, on the north side紧贴着 Wenchang Pavilion's tall fire-sealing gable, a Earth God Shrine was built—an independent courtyard with its own gate. The farming-reading dream is embodied in the combination of Wenchang Pavilion and Earth God Shrine.

Around Wenchang Pavilion and Tuanyun Pagoda, there were once large pine and cypress forests, mentioned many times in Ming and Qing poetry, such as "dense pines surround like masonry"—unfortunately during land reform this evergreen forest was cut down not a single tree left.

Though Tuanyun Pagoda, Wenchang Pavilion, and Earth God Shrine were not built in the same period, their combination achieved harmonious unity. The towering Tuanyun Pagoda's seven-story eaves arranged horizontally layer by layer, echoing Wenchang Pavilion's horizontal double eaves. And Wenchang Pavilion's wing corners together with main ridge ornaments, high piercing the sky, strong upward momentum, echoing the pagoda's vertical composition. Pagoda and pavilion are both contrasting and unified in architectural art. Wenchang Pavilion and Earth God Shrine together give Wenfeng Pagoda a very stable and solid base; the towering finial and Wenchang Pavilion's flying eaves and wing corners naturally endow this building group with upward vitality.

Today, the Tuanyun Pagoda and Wenchang Pavilion building group still stands on Xinye Village's fields, visible from far away, giving the village a vivid silhouette—they are the village's landmark; seeing them reminds one of Xinye Village people's farming-reading ideal.

sections.name: 关麓村
sections.content_zh:
三、关麓村

安徽省黟县关麓村的一个极其重要的特点是学堂厅的数量之多，质量之高，规制之完整。学堂厅是一幢独立的建筑，通常与住宅一起建造。关麓村现有中型住宅不过三十几幢，而学堂厅竟有十四幢。

（一）学堂厅的功能

学堂厅的建造跟徽商崇尚读书有关。商人在经济上成功之后，退休养老，仍然乐于文墨、吟诵，也不完全放弃子弟通过科举踏上仕途。子弟读了书，即使"屡试不售"，也可以"弃儒就贾"，凭文化底子在商场竞争中获得优势。于是一些殷实的经商人家，便在自己家族的住宅团组中，建起别致的书房厅，既可诗书自娱，也可设家塾，供子弟课读。没有家塾的人家，子弟可以到别人家寄读。通常从外乡外村请来人品端正、教导有方的先生。

学堂厅为退休徽商颐养天年及子弟读书而建，但科举道路狭窄而艰苦，有成就的很少，而经商则容易发家，以致徽商子弟大多十二三岁便外出学徒习商。以致后来有些塾中，除读四书五经外，便是打算盘记账。一些商人子弟把学堂当做玩乐的场所。如现存的涵远楼，屋宇高大，彩饰雕镂非常精致。它左侧靠山墙有个楼梯夹道，半高处设平台，平台旁山墙上开了一扇一米多宽、近一米高的砖雕漏花窗。这夹道是少东家的养鸽房，他们用许多时间来养鸽、放鸽，漏花窗就是鸽子出入用的。鸽子吃的粟米，附近没有，遣专人从外地买来。还雇了佣人打扫鸽房。在这种富裕环境中，有些孩子无心刻苦学习，少数甚至堕落为"皮赖"。虽然如此，家塾的普及毕竟提高了关麓村人的文化水平。生活中有很浓的书卷气。

（二）学堂厅的地位与位置

关麓村曾有大型学堂厅七座，即"吾爱吾庐"、"涵远楼"、"安雅书屋"、"问渠书屋"、"双桂书屋"、汪沛云家学堂厅和武亭山房学堂厅。小型学堂厅还有"临溪书屋"、"余屋"、汪曙绘画厅、汪高跃学堂厅、"容膝亦安"、"桂屏书屋"和"中对屋"等七座。大小学堂厅共计十四座，可见学堂厅在关麓村的重要地位。

大型学堂厅在住宅团组中的位置，多靠近花园和村边绿地，环境幽雅。如武亭山房学堂厅和问渠书屋都在园林之中。"吾爱吾庐"和"临溪书屋"紧濒峰下溪，前者又有自己不小的花园。涵远楼一侧为花园竹林，另一侧便是村外桑田。安雅书屋前面是村中央最大的一片绿地，汪沛云家学堂厅在这片绿地的北面不远，它北侧还有一座花园。学堂厅的建造是经过合理的布局考虑的。

学堂厅的风格华丽，轻盈，尺度略小。它的家具与别厅里的相似，多用红木，也是以玲珑精巧见长，且有一些特有的家具，如花几、书桌等。

（三）学堂厅的类型和型制

在家族的住宅团组中，大型学堂厅独立而建，两层，规模通常与"大廊步三间"住宅相近，质量则比住宅正房还更精致。它们的型制比较活泼，常见新意，局部有外向性的特征。上下层门窗都做得比较大，原因之一，就是女眷不进学堂厅，只有男人和孩子在里面，而且又要读书，门窗不妨大些。

小型学堂厅多附着于住宅而为旁院，以三间菱花门式为多，少量为一间菱花门式。

1. 回廊三间（大型）

这一类为三间上房，上下两层，前有回廊。上房之前是一个大庭院，开敞宽阔。回廊的做法有两种："吾爱吾庐"园中是三面环绕庭院；安雅书屋、涵远楼、汪沛云家学堂厅等则只在庭院左右侧有廊子。

上房底层明间是厅堂，太师壁前供孔子或朱子的神位，也有供"天地君亲师"神位的。"吾爱吾庐"学堂厅的朱子神位放在楼上正厅，孩子上学时要先拜朱子，然后拜先生。厅堂家具布置与住宅的厅堂相同，厅堂前金柱间装有菱花格扇十扇。厅堂两侧次间是孩子学习的课堂，需要充足的光线，因此采用菱花格扇槛窗，多为一间六扇，所以学堂厅上房前檐装修远比住宅上房华丽。次间的门开在面对厅堂的一侧，前金柱的后面。学堂厅的厅堂又是主人的重要客厅，称为"官厅"，轿子可以从大门一直抬进来。

楼上明间和次间也用菱花格扇。大廊步的，有外廊，设花格栏杆或美人靠。小廊步的没有外廊，在前金柱上安格扇。明间靠后檐墙有壁柜，架在楼梯上方。

楼上有一个次间是老师的卧室，室内大部为固定式家具，通常有单人床、书架、博古架、衣柜等。窗前设桌及椅子。沿墙装吸壁墙板。卧室山墙常开很大的窗子。如"吾爱吾庐"，装上四扇较小的菱花格扇窗。打开窗子，面对来龙山上郁郁葱葱的茂林，天高云轻，胸怀如洗。

当地一般住宅的楼上多用穿斗式草架，十分简陋。而学堂厅楼上明间则采用抬梁式屋架，彻上露明的做法，人称"明脊厅"。檩子、椽子都涂以朱漆，或有彩画，望板涂以深暗的青莲色，并仿望砖的作法绘出一条条白色灰缝。脊檩正中及金檩两端装华丽的镂花鎏金铜灯笼钩。次间室内做天棚，冬季温暖，夏季凉爽。

学堂厅内的色彩鲜亮明快，楼上楼下的厅堂均以朱红为底色。楼下厅堂太师壁两侧门口上部的花梁和垫斗上薄雕描金，和住宅中的一样。楼下厅堂及底层和二层的次间的天棚满绘彩画，题材也和住宅中的相同。次间槛墙用磨砖对缝。门窗菱花格扇外面为红色，用青莲、绿两色衬贝壳屑面饰，内面用青莲色为底，饰彩画。卧室内壁以白和青莲为底色，作大幅山水或人物画。床檐画花鸟鱼虫，十分丰富灿烂。

游廊与上房脱开建造，二者结构没有关连。游廊左右各三间，开间面阔两米多。正对上房一面的游廊也是三间，与上房对应。游廊檐柱间有花栏杆，横枋下用菱花挂落做装饰。游廊宽大约一点五米，靠上房尽端的山墙上做一个通上房檐廊的小门，右面的是"挂画"门，左面的是"秋叶"门，即门洞的形状如一幅挂画，或一片落叶。造型写实，都以水磨砖饰边。

书院的庭院里种些天竺之类的矮棵植物，"吾爱吾庐"小院里种金桂银桂各一株，寄意于"折桂"。地面铺卵石成席纹。

2. 其他型制

"春满庭"北侧，"双桂书屋"的格局是一个异体。住宅、别厅、书屋建成一串，但各自的朝向却不同。整体的轴线大致为东西向，住宅为"明三间"，却朝南。一侧厢房开大门，通向前院，另一侧厢房有门通入小厨房。小厨房之后是一个小院，院内有金桂、银桂各一棵。院后又是朝东的两间别厅，前面一间又分出两小间，门额上题匾"双桂书屋"。别厅之后接着是书屋。别厅和书屋都有一方小小的天井采光。书屋内用菱花格扇分隔出一间暖阁，也可以全部卸下形成一个大空间。书屋左侧是个大厨房。楼上则从前到后全部通敞，从书屋楼上可达别厅楼上。两个天井一圈都做刻花栏杆板，栏杆板上装格扇窗。"双桂书屋"独具一格，在狭窄的地段上打破常规，巧妙布局，充分利用了地段，并且造成了多变的空间。这房屋做工精致，风格典雅，很别致。建房主人汪庭辉（九十一世德沉，邑庠生）从清末到民国二十二年（1933年）在问渠书屋任经学堂塾师数十年，热爱儿童，所以"双桂书屋"中壁画及床檐画等多以儿童嬉戏为题材，十分活泼可爱。

小的学堂厅又称书斋。它型制十分自由，规格不定。有三开间上下楼的，如原汪曙画厅。也有三开间单层的，如原"八家"汪静川所建"余屋"和六家区内的"桂屏书屋"。也有单开间上下楼的，如八家令锺的"临溪书屋"和志顺公后裔汪高跃家的学堂厅。这些书屋与大型学堂厅的区别就在于，第一，规模小，都没有游廊。即使三开间的，面阔、进深也比大型学堂厅小。如"余屋"三间，明间面阔约三米，次间仅二米多一点，进深则只有三米。单间的开间和进深比较大。第二，这些小型书屋虽也有独立建造的，更多的干脆建在小花园中，如"余屋"和"容膝亦安"，但独立性不如大型学堂厅，多附属在住宅之内。

凡是三间的小书屋，明间多做八扇菱花格扇门，次间做槛墙格扇窗。因为房间较小，书屋一般三间相通不做隔断，俗称"三间菱花门"。单开间的书屋，如"临溪书屋"，上下两层，均不做门窗而全面敞开，仅在檐枋之下做精美华丽的挂落。楼上除挂落外，还有花栏杆。涵远楼也是一种小型学堂厅，只有一个暖阁。

小型学堂厅，也做与大型学堂厅类似的装饰，活泼而富有生气。

3. 园林式学堂厅

八十七世汪国仁在乾隆年间（1736—1795）与造承德堂同时，在他的住宅(今吴富仁宅)北侧先造了一幢"南华别墅"(今程为全宅)，接着又在南华别墅北侧造了"问渠书屋"，紧挨着承德堂东南角的厨房。这问渠书屋是他四个儿子读书的地方。清末，汪庭辉在其中办学塾，习称"经学堂"。

书屋是园林式的，"中有方塘小池，有泉水冒出"，显然，选址的时候就看中了这股泉水，并借它取名为"问渠书屋"。名称来自朱熹的诗《观书有感》："半亩方塘一鉴开，天光云影共徘徊，问渠那得清如许，谓有源头活水来。"据汪觉民先生遗稿说："内中有亭台水榭……上有大厅，旁有书房小座。(按：大厅在水塘西，向东)下厅(按：即水塘东岸)一排连珠书房，小间小厅。楼上(按：指大厅楼上)为大敞开舞台型制，左右各有大书房，向前俱有大窗户，可眺远山近湖，古杏垂柳，风景甚佳。"上厅楹联："溪柳留芳韵，渊鱼察妙机"；"咬定一两句书终身师保；栽成五七竿竹满目儿孙"；"功夫若撑船稍松则退，学问同进篑积久升崇"。又有一副署名为邓石如书的楹联，写的是"幸有两眼明多交益友；苦无十年暇熟读奇书"。大书房是蒙童读书的地方，小间小厅的连珠书房则是开蒙已过，试习制艺的地方了。

水塘的北岸有一道廊子，南岸则是一片粉墙，中央有个月洞门，门内三间楼房，便是原"南华别墅"，作为塾师的书斋和住房。从连珠书房到西岸的大厅，有一条紧贴水面的石板桥。半途搭上月洞门前的月台。桥的西端，大厅的右前方，有一座水榭，翼角高翘。大厅之南，隔一条不到一米宽的夹弄，又有一幢花厅，与大厅檐廊有门相通，楼上且有飞廊连接。花厅朝西，通间用菱花格扇，它之南又接着一所小院，院的南端向巷子开券门，门额为水磨青砖，刻篆体"览辉"二字，染石绿色，十分清雅。

问渠书屋与社庙、关帝庙之间本来有一片茂盛的树林，林东侧有院墙。

这所早期的学堂厅不仅反映出当时徽商的富有和对文化的渴求，还反映出他们本身文采风流和整个徽州的文化水平之高。它造在一个僻远的小山村里，在徽州的山山水水之间该有多少文化蕴藏！
sections.content_en:
3. Guanlu Village

An extremely important feature of Guanlu Village in Yi County, Anhui, is the large number, high quality, and complete regulation of its school halls (学堂厅). A school hall is an independent building, usually built together with residences. Guanlu Village currently has only about thirty-some medium residences, but as many as fourteen school halls.

(1) Function of School Halls

The construction of school halls relates to Huizhou merchants' esteem for reading. After merchants achieved economic success and retired for old age, they still delighted in calligraphy, ink, and recitation, and did not completely give up their children entering officialdom through imperial exams. Children who read, even if "repeatedly failing exams," could "abandon Confucianism for commerce," gaining advantage in business competition through their cultural foundation. Hence some wealthy merchant families, within their clan's residence complex, built elegant study halls—both for poetry and calligraphy self-entertainment, and for setting up family schools for children's study. Families without family schools could send children to study at others' homes. Usually teachers of upright character and effective teaching were invited from other towns and villages.

School halls were built for retired Huizhou merchants to enjoy their old age and for children to study—but the imperial exam path was narrow and arduous, with few achieving success, while commerce easily brought wealth—so Huizhou merchant children mostly went out as apprentices at age twelve or thirteen. Consequently in some later schools, besides reading the Four Books and Five Classics, they practiced abacus and bookkeeping. Some merchant children treated the school hall as a place for amusement. For example, the existing Hanyuan Tower (涵远楼) has tall buildings with very exquisite painted decorations and carvings. On its left side against the gable wall is a stair corridor; at half-height a platform is set; beside the platform on the gable wall opens a brick-carved lattice window over 1m wide and nearly 1m high. This corridor was the young master's pigeon-raising room—they spent much time raising and releasing pigeons; the lattice window was for pigeons to enter and exit. The millet pigeons ate was not available nearby, so special people were sent to buy it from elsewhere. Servants were also hired to clean the pigeon room. In such a wealthy environment, some children had no heart for diligent study, a few even degenerating into "rascals" (皮赖). Nevertheless, the普及 of family schools ultimately raised Guanlu Village people's cultural level. Life had a strong bookish atmosphere.

(2) Status and Position of School Halls

Guanlu Village once had seven large school halls: "Wu'ai Wulu" (吾爱吾庐), "Hanyuan Tower" (涵远楼), "Anya Study" (安雅书屋), "Wenqu Study" (问渠书屋), "Shuanggui Study" (双桂书屋), Wang Peiyun's family school hall, and Wuting Mountain Room school hall. Small school halls included "Linxi Study" (临溪书屋), "Yu House" (余屋), Wang Shu's painting hall, Wang Gaoyue's school hall, "Rongxi Yi'an" (容膝亦安), "Guiping Study" (桂屏书屋), and "Zhongdui House" (中对屋)—seven total. Large and small school halls total fourteen, showing the important status of school halls in Guanlu Village.

Large school halls' positions within residence complexes were mostly near gardens and village-edge green spaces, with elegant environments. For example, Wuting Mountain Room school hall and Wenqu Study are both within gardens. "Wu'ai Wulu" and "Linxi Study" tightly border the stream below the peak; the former also has its own not-small garden. Hanyuan Tower has garden bamboo forest on one side and village-outside mulberry fields on the other. Before Anya Study is the village center's largest green space; Wang Peiyun's family school hall is not far north of this green space, and north of it is another garden. School hall construction underwent reasonable layout consideration.

School hall style is ornate, light, slightly smaller in scale. Its furniture resembles that in other halls, mostly using redwood, also excelling in exquisite delicacy, with some unique furniture such as flower stands and desks.

(3) Types and Forms of School Halls

Within clan residence complexes, large school halls are independently built, two-story, scale usually similar to "large-corridor three-bay" residences, quality even more refined than residence main buildings. Their forms are relatively lively, often innovative, with locally outward-facing features. Upper and lower floor doors and windows are all made relatively large—one reason being that womenfolk did not enter school halls; only men and children were inside, and since they needed to read, doors and windows might as well be large.

Small school halls mostly attach to residences as side courtyards, mostly three-bay lattice-door style, a few one-bay lattice-door style.

1. Corridor Three-Bay (Large)

This type is a three-bay upper building, two stories, with a front corridor. Before the upper building is a large courtyard, open and spacious. Corridor construction has two types: "Wu'ai Wulu" garden has corridors surrounding the courtyard on three sides; Anya Study, Hanyuan Tower, Wang Peiyun's school hall, etc., only have corridors on the courtyard's left and right sides.

The upper building's ground floor central bay is the hall; before the master's wall (太师壁) enshrines Confucius or Zhu Xi's deity seat, some enshrine "Heaven-Earth-Master-Parent-Teacher" (天地君亲师) seat. "Wu'ai Wulu" school hall's Zhu Xi deity seat is placed in the upstairs main hall; when children go to school they first worship Zhu Xi, then worship the teacher. Hall furniture arrangement is same as residence halls; between the hall's front gold pillars are installed ten lattice folding doors (菱花格扇). Both side bays of the hall are children's study classrooms, needing sufficient light—hence using lattice sill windows, mostly six per bay—so school hall upper building's front eave decoration is far more ornate than residence upper buildings. The side bay's door opens on the side facing the hall, behind the front gold pillar. The school hall's hall is also the master's important reception hall, called "Official Hall" (官厅)—sedan chairs could be carried straight in from the main gate.

Upstairs central and side bays also use lattice folding doors. Large-corridor type has exterior corridors with lattice railings or beauty-rests (美人靠). Small-corridor type has no exterior corridor, installing folding doors on front gold pillars. The central bay against the rear eave wall has a wall cabinet, framed above the staircase.

Upstairs one side bay is the teacher's bedroom; indoors mostly fixed furniture, usually including single bed, bookshelf, curio shelf, wardrobe, etc. Before the window set desk and chair. Along walls install wall-attached panels. Bedroom gable walls often open very large windows. E.g., "Wu'ai Wulu" installs four smaller lattice folding windows. Opening the windows, facing the lush forest on the coming-dragon mountain, sky high clouds light, mind as clean as washed.

Local ordinary residences' upstairs mostly use column-and-tie (穿斗式) rough framing, very simple. But school hall upstairs central bay uses post-and-lintel (抬梁式) roof framing with exposed upper construction, called "Exposed-Ridge Hall" (明脊厅). Rafters and purlins all painted red lacquer, or with painted decorations; ceiling boards painted dark indigo, imitating ceiling-brick practice with painted white mortar joints. Ridge purlin center and gold purlin ends install ornate carved gilded bronze lantern hooks. Side bay indoors make ceilings, warm in winter, cool in summer.

School hall interior colors are bright and lively; upstairs and downstairs halls all use vermilion as base color. Below the hall, on the flower beams and pad blocks above the door openings on both sides of the master's wall, thin carved gold描金, same as in residences. Below the hall and ground and second-floor side bay ceilings are fully painted, themes same as in residences. Side bay sill walls use ground bricks with tight joints (磨砖对缝). Doors and windows lattice folding doors outside are red, using indigo and green two colors with shell-chip surface decoration; inside use indigo as base, with painted decorations. Bedroom interior walls use white and indigo as base, making large landscape or figure paintings. Bed eaves paint flowers, birds, fish, insects—very rich and splendid.

The corridor is built detached from the upper building; the two structures are not connected. Corridor left and right each three bays, bay width over 2m. The corridor facing the upper building is also three bays, corresponding to the upper building. Between corridor eave pillars are lattice railings; below the horizontal tie-beams use lattice hanging decorations (菱花挂落). Corridor width about 1.5m; against the upper building's end gable wall makes a small door leading to the upper building's eave corridor—the right one is "Hanging Painting" door, the left one is "Autumn Leaf" door—i.e., door opening shaped like a hanging painting or a fallen leaf. Realistic modeling, all edged with ground brick.

In the academy courtyard plant low plants such as nandina; "Wu'ai Wulu" small courtyard plants one golden osmanthus and one silver osmanthus each, meaning "plucking osmanthus" (折桂, i.e., exam success). Ground paved with cobblestones in mat pattern.

2. Other Forms

North of "Chunman Ting" (春满庭), "Shuanggui Study" (双桂书屋)'s layout is an anomaly. Residence, separate hall, and study built in a string, but each facing differently. Overall axis roughly east-west; residence is "apparent three-bay" but faces south. One side wing opens the main gate leading to the front courtyard; the other side wing has a door leading to a small kitchen. After the small kitchen is a small courtyard, with one golden osmanthus and one silver osmanthus inside. After the courtyard is again two east-facing separate halls; the front one again divides into two small rooms, lighthouse inscribed "Shuanggui Study." After the separate hall follows the study. Both separate hall and study have a small skylight courtyard for lighting. Inside the study, lattice folding doors divide out a warm room (暖阁), which can also be fully removed to form a large space. Left of the study is a large kitchen. Upstairs is fully open from front to back; from the study upstairs one can reach the separate hall upstairs. Both skylight courtyards' perimeter all make carved railing boards, with folding windows on railing boards. "Shuanggui Study" is unique—on a narrow site breaking convention, clever layout, fully utilizing the site, and creating varied spaces. This house has exquisite workmanship, elegant style, very distinctive. Builder Wang Tinghui (91st generation Dechen, county student) from late Qing to Republic 22 (1933) served as classics-school tutor at Wenqu Study for decades, loving children—so "Shuanggui Study"'s murals and bed-eave paintings mostly use children at play as themes, very lively and adorable.

Small school halls are also called studies (书斋). Their form is very free, specifications unfixed. There are three-bay two-story, e.g., former Wang Shu's painting hall. Also three-bay single-story, e.g., former "Eight Families" Wang Jingchuan's "Yu House" and "Guiping Study" in the Six-Families district. Also single-bay two-story, e.g., Eight-Families Ling Zhong's "Linxi Study" and descendant Wang Gaoyue's school hall. These studies differ from large school halls in: first, small scale, all without corridors. Even three-bay ones, width and depth are smaller than large school halls. E.g., "Yu House" three bays: central bay width ~3m, side bays only just over 2m, depth only 3m. Single-bay ones have relatively larger width and depth. Second, though some small studies are independently built, more are simply built in small gardens, such as "Yu House" and "Rongxi Yi'an"—but independence is less than large school halls, mostly attached within residences.

All three-bay small studies: central bay mostly makes eight lattice folding doors; side bays make sill-wall lattice windows. Because rooms are small, studies generally have three bays connected without partitions, commonly called "three-bay lattice door." Single-bay studies, such as "Linxi Study," two stories, both make no doors/windows but fully open—only under eave tie-beams make exquisite ornate hanging decorations. Upstairs besides hanging decorations also have lattice railings. Hanyuan Tower is also a type of small school hall, with only one warm room.

Small school halls also make decorations similar to large school halls, lively and full of vitality.

3. Garden-Style School Hall

87th-generation Wang Guoren, in Qianlong era (1736–1795), simultaneously with building Chengde Hall, north of his residence (now Wu Furen's residence) first built "Nanhua Villa" (南华别墅, now Cheng Weiquan's residence), then north of Nanhua Villa built "Wenqu Study" (问渠书屋),紧挨着 Chengde Hall's southeast corner kitchen. This Wenqu Study was where his four sons studied. In late Qing, Wang Tinghui ran a family school in it, commonly called "Classics School" (经学堂).

The study is garden-style: "inside has a square pond small pool, with spring water bubbling up"—obviously when selecting the site they valued this spring, and borrowed it to name "Wenqu Study." The name comes from Zhu Xi's poem "Thoughts on Reading": "Half-mu square pond opens like a mirror, sky light and cloud shadows wander together; ask the channel how it stays so clear—because there is source of living water flowing in." According to Mr. Wang Juemin's surviving manuscript: "Inside has pavilions and waterside pavilions... above has a great hall, beside has small study rooms. (Note: great hall west of pond, facing east) lower hall (note: i.e., pond east bank) a row of linked-bead studies, small rooms small halls. Upstairs (note: referring to great hall upstairs) is a large open stage-type form, left and right each have large studies, forward all have large windows, can view distant mountains and nearby lake, ancient apricots and weeping willows, scenery excellent." Upper hall couplets: "Stream willows retain fragrant charm, deep pool fish observe subtle mechanism"; "Biting into one or two sentences of books becomes lifelong teacher-protector; planting five or seven bamboo stalks fills eyes with descendants"; "Kung fu is like poling a boat—slightly slack then retreat; learning is like adding basketfuls—accumulated long then rises high." Also a couplet signed as Deng Shiru's calligraphy: "Fortunate to have two bright eyes to make many worthy friends; bitter to lack ten years' leisure to thoroughly read extraordinary books." The large study was where young children learned to read; the small-room small-hall linked-bead studies were where those past initial learning practiced exam essay composition.

The pond's north bank has a corridor; south bank is a white plaster wall, center has a moon-gate door; inside three-bay two-story building is the original "Nanhua Villa," serving as tutor's study and residence. From linked-bead studies to the west bank's great hall, there is a stone slab bridge紧贴水面. Halfway搭 onto the moon-gate's front platform. At the bridge's west end, right-front of the great hall, is a waterside pavilion (水榭) with high-soaring wing corners. South of the great hall, across a less-than-1m-wide alley, is another flower hall (花厅), connected to the great hall's eave corridor by a door, upstairs also has a flying corridor connection. Flower hall faces west, full bay uses lattice folding doors; south of it again adjoins a small courtyard; the courtyard's south end opens an arched door to the alley, lighthouse of ground blue brick, carved seal-script "Lan Hui" (览辉) two characters, dyed stone-green, very elegant.

Between Wenqu Study and the village temple and Guandi Temple there was originally a lush forest, with a courtyard wall on the forest's east side.

This early school hall not only reflects Huizhou merchants' wealth and cultural craving at the time, but also reflects their own literary elegance and the high cultural level of all Huizhou. It was built in a remote small mountain village—how much cultural treasure must there be among Huizhou's mountains and waters!

sections.name: 有求必应的泛神崇拜
sections.content_zh:
一、有求必应的泛神崇拜

中国的农村到处都有庙宇。但汉族地区，庙宇虽多，正常状态下农民们有的只是功利性的泛神崇拜。两千多年下来，庶民们并不理睬《礼记》之类的规定，根据"需要"，借助于引进，无限制地扩大了神谱。泛神崇拜非常方便，非常随意，也便是非常适合中国人的性格。

乡土环境的庙宇里供奉着各种各样的神灵。除了少数在较大范围里崇祀着的之外，各地还会有自己的神，地方色彩很浓。这种泛神的崇拜，大致包含着两个组成部分，就是自然崇拜和英雄崇拜。借《礼记·祭法》说："山林川谷丘陵，能出云、为风雨、见怪物，皆曰神。有天下者祭百神。"这是自然崇拜。《祭法》又说："夫圣王之制祭祀也，法施于民则祀之，以死勤事则祀之，以劳定国则祀之，能御大灾则祀之，能捍大患则祀之。"这是英雄崇拜。这两种崇拜在乡土社会中流行，自然力、自然现象、自然物以及各种传说人物和历史人物以及外来的神祇，都可以崇拜。

实用主义主宰着汉民族的泛神崇拜，使它极具功利色彩，所求于神灵的，无非是趋吉禳凶，避祸求福。"有求必应"是一切神灵的"价值"所在。因此，来历不明，职司不清的神也是所在多有。山西省泽州县冶底村东岳庙有一座明代永乐二年（1404年）的石碑，记郡太守张奉直以民事下乡，见庙貌很好，"时蝗旱之余，饿殍相望，此乡之民独有生意，因询父老以兴建之由及利泽于人物者。咸曰：庙之始建，无从稽考，维神之利泽于此土也厚，故民之奉祀也虔。旱而乞之雨则雨，蝗而乞之除则除，岁常丰熟，民无夭扎疠疫之苦，神之惠泽于吾民者多矣。"一位"无从稽考"的神，无从证实其"利泽"的神，就这样莫名其妙地"坐享"了几百年的香火。

这样的功利主义甚至改造了外来的佛教，民间把佛教也纳入了泛神崇拜，最普及的是敬爱观音菩萨和畏惧阎王，一位是大慈大悲"普度众生"，一位是不留情面清算善恶。离村落近的佛寺，就不免世俗化，例如做"道场"挣钱和收容民间杂神，等等。中国特有的道教在乡民中间也是实用主义的泛神崇拜，并把泛神崇拜和巫术结合起来了。

实用主义把世俗的社会性带入了泛神崇拜，神界不但能有等级制组织，而且神与人之间也成了一种社会关系。神可以人化，以致人也很容易被神化。

除了泛神崇拜的庙宇外，各地还有不少名人纪念庙，主祀对一方百姓有功有德的人，如浙南、闽北、赣东一带有胡公庙和越国公庙，浙北有钱王庙，四川有川主庙，等等。不过长期以后，沾染了巫术迷信，名人就神化了。

泛神崇拜当然包含自然崇拜，乡间人们普遍崇拜日月星辰（三光）、天地山川之类。因为它们显得崇高、庄严、永恒，宏大而神秘，很难认为它们在冥冥之中不会影响人们的祸福凶吉。在南方各地，住宅堂屋香案上有"天地君亲师"的牌位。楼上当心间的窗前还有个小小的香炉，每月初一、十五上香，供的是"天"。拜天拜地，却并不向他们祈求什么。倒是小小的星辰，容易被人们的想象力捕捉，成为神谱中的重要成员，如福德五星、太白金星、奎星，等等。最重要的是紫微星，即北极星，在中国大部分地区的天象中，它恒定不动，仿佛是天体布列和运动的中枢。宋代张君房著《云笈七签》里说："北辰星者，众神之本也，凡星各有主掌，皆系于北辰"，并且说它协助玉皇大帝执掌天经地纬、日月星辰，统管诸神和四季。它成了最高的吉星，所以起屋上梁的时候，挂大红对联必称"上梁恰逢紫微星"。

自然力和自然物也被神化并且人格化了，如雷公、电母、风伯、雨师；以及五岳大帝、泰山娘娘、四海神君，等等。也有些自然神是"设想"有点儿关系的人去担当的，如江神为屈原，潮神为伍子胥。

中国民间很早就有了对天官、地官、水官的崇拜。《魏书·释老志》说："一切众生，皆是天、地、水三官所统摄。"擅长于造神的道教宣称天官职司赐福，地官职司赦罪，而水官则专管解厄，职掌分明，直接关系到人的实际生活。明代徐道在《历代神仙通鉴》里说天官、地官、水官分别就是元始天尊口中吐出来的尧、舜、禹，都创造了"天地莫大之功，为万世君师之法"。以致地无分南北，"三官庙"遍及农村。浙江省永嘉县凡路亭必祀三官，往往一村有好几个这样的亭子。同时，在赐福、赦罪和解厄三者之中，人们选择了更有积极意义和包容性的"赐福"，又把过于概括的有终极性气味的"福"具体化为农耕社会里人们最高的生活理想：长寿、多子、发财。所以天官最受尊崇，有些地方三官庙便被称为天官庙。天官的形象是白面长髯，雍容华贵，端坐在一枚大元宝之上。
sections.content_en:
1. Responsive Pantheistic Worship

Temples are everywhere in rural China. But in Han areas, despite the many temples, under normal circumstances farmers practice only utilitarian pantheistic worship. Over two thousand years, common people ignored regulations such as the Book of Rites, and according to "need," through introduction, unlimitedly expanded the pantheon. Pantheistic worship is very convenient, very casual—and thus very suited to Chinese character.

Temples in the rural environment enshrine a great variety of deities. Besides a few worshipped over larger areas, each locality has its own gods, with strong local color. This pantheistic worship roughly comprises two components: nature worship and hero worship. Quoting the Book of Rites · Sacrificial Laws: "Mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, and hills that can produce clouds, make wind and rain, and manifest strange things—all are called gods. Those who hold the world sacrifice to the hundred gods." This is nature worship. The Sacrificial Laws also says: "When the sage kings instituted sacrifices, those whose laws benefited the people were sacrificed to; those who died in diligent service were sacrificed to; those who through labor stabilized the state were sacrificed to; those who could ward off great disasters were sacrificed to; those who could resist great calamities were sacrificed to." This is hero worship. Both forms of worship prevailed in rural society—natural forces, natural phenomena, natural objects, and various legendary and historical figures, as well as imported deities, could all be worshipped.

Pragmatism dominates the Han people's pantheistic worship, giving it a strongly utilitarian cast. What people seek from deities is nothing but pursuing good fortune and averting evil, avoiding disaster and seeking blessing. "Responsive to every request" is the "value" of all deities. Hence gods of unclear origin and unclear functions are everywhere. In Dongyue Temple at Yedi Village, Zezhou County, Shanxi, there is a stone stele from Ming Yongle 2nd year (1404), recording that Prefect Zhang Fengzhi went to the countryside on civil affairs and saw the temple was well maintained: "After locust plagues and drought, with corpses of the starving lining the roads, the people of this village alone had livelihood; thus he asked elders about the reason for its construction and its benefits to people. All said: the temple's original construction cannot be traced, but the god's benefit to this land is great, so the people's worship is devout. In drought, praying for rain brings rain; in locust plague, praying for removal brings removal; years are usually abundant, people suffer no premature death or pestilence—the god's grace to our people is much." A god "untraceable in origin," a god whose "benefits" cannot be verified, thus inexplicably "enjoys" hundreds of years of incense.

Such utilitarianism even transformed imported Buddhism. Folk society incorporated Buddhism into pantheistic worship—the most widespread being loving Guanyin Bodhisattva and fearing King Yama: one is the great compassionate "savior of all beings," the other mercilessly accounts for good and evil. Buddhist temples near villages inevitably became secularized—for example, holding "ritual services" for money and housing miscellaneous folk deities. China's indigenous Daoism among villagers is also pragmatist pantheistic worship, combining pantheistic worship with witchcraft.

Pragmatism brought secular sociality into pantheistic worship. The divine realm not only has hierarchical organization, but relations between gods and humans also became a kind of social relation. Gods could be humanized, so much so that humans could easily be deified.

Besides pantheistic worship temples, various localities have many celebrity memorial temples, primarily enshrining people of merit and virtue to local people—e.g., in southern Zhejiang, northern Fujian, and eastern Jiangxi there are Hugong Temple and Yueguogong Temple; in northern Zhejiang there is Qianwang Temple; in Sichuan there is Chuanzhu Temple, etc. But over time, contaminated by witchcraft and superstition, celebrities became deified.

Pantheistic worship of course includes nature worship. Rural people普遍 worship sun, moon, and stars (the Three Lights), heaven, earth, mountains, and rivers. Because they appear sublime, solemn, eternal, grand, and mysterious, it is hard to believe they do not influence people's fortune and misfortune in the unseen world. In southern localities, on the incense table in the residence's main hall there is the tablet of "Heaven-Earth-Master-Parent-Teacher." Before the window of the upstairs central bay there is also a small incense burner; on the first and fifteenth of each month incense is burned, offering to "Heaven." Worshipping heaven and earth, yet not praying to them for anything. Rather, small stars are easily captured by people's imagination, becoming important members of the pantheon—such as the Five Fortune Stars, Great White Venus, Kuixing, etc. The most important is Ziwei Star, i.e., Polaris. In the celestial phenomena of most of China, it remains fixed, as if the center of celestial arrangement and movement. Song dynasty Zhang Junfang's Seven Slips of the Cloudy Satchel says: "The North Star is the root of all gods; every star has its own charge, all tied to the North Star"—and says it assists the Jade Emperor in governing the celestial classics and wefts, sun, moon, and stars, administering all gods and four seasons. It became the highest auspicious star, so when raising a house beam, hanging red couplets must say "beam-raising coincides with Ziwei Star."

Natural forces and natural objects were also deified and personified—such as Thunder Duke, Lightning Mother, Wind Earl, Rain Master; as well as the Five Great Mountain Emperors, Mount Tai Lady, Four Sea Lords, etc. Some nature gods were "assigned" to people thought to have some relation—e.g., the river god is Qu Yuan, the tide god is Wu Zixu.

Chinese folk society很早就 had worship of Heavenly Official, Earthly Official, and Water Official. The Book of Wei · Buddhism and Daoism Records says: "All living beings are governed by the Three Officials of Heaven, Earth, and Water." Daoism, adept at creating gods, proclaimed the Heavenly Official's function is bestowing fortune, the Earthly Official's function is pardoning sins, and the Water Official exclusively manages relieving misfortune—functions clearly divided, directly related to people's actual lives. Ming dynasty Xu Dao in Comprehensive Mirror of Generations of Immortals says the Three Officials are respectively Yao, Shun, and Yu spat from the mouth of Primordial Heavenly Venerable, all having created "the greatest merit under heaven, as the law for rulers and teachers of ten thousand generations." Consequently regardless of north or south, "Three-Official Temples" spread throughout the countryside. In Yongjia County, Zhejiang, every roadside pavilion must enshrine the Three Officials—often a village has several such pavilions. Meanwhile, among bestowing fortune, pardoning sins, and relieving misfortune, people chose the more positive and inclusive "bestowing fortune," and further具体化 the overly abstract, ultimate-sounding "fortune" into the highest life ideal in agrarian society: longevity, many sons, wealth. Hence the Heavenly Official is most revered; in some places Three-Official Temples are called Heavenly-Official Temples. The Heavenly Official's image is white-faced with long beard, dignified and elegant, sitting upright on a large gold ingot.
