sections.name: 桥
sections.content_zh:
三、桥

南方雨量大，溪河密布，因此就多桥。桥有梁桥和拱桥之分，梁桥有木质和石质的，拱桥的结构主体均为石质。拱又分真假，假拱就是多少个单券平行在一起，用很多铁质元宝楔（又称银锭楔、燕尾楔）把它们连结成整体。不论木桥还是石桥，也不论梁桥还是拱桥，都有单跨的和多跨的。连续多孔的石拱桥上面大多是平缓的，甚至是平的，两侧有石板栏杆。三孔以下的石拱桥则多呈虹形，而且往往还加高石墩，形成极美的侧影，刚柔相济却又轻快，如上海郊区朱家角村的虹桥、浙江湖州南浔拱桥和江苏苏州盛泽白龙桥，都极其轻巧挺拔。更美的是在桥顶再造一座轻巧玲珑的亭子，如浙江省武义县郭洞村村口的回龙桥。

郭洞村回龙桥是一座单跨石拱桥，初建于元至正年间（1341—1368），叫石虹桥，几度坍塌重建，清康熙年间第二次重修后，改名为回龙桥，至今良好。拱跨十四米，拱高七米，正是个半圆。桥面宽三点七米。清乾隆十九年（1754年）在桥顶上加建了一座方亭子，用四棵石质柱子。亭子平面三米见方，上覆四角攒尖顶，非常轻盈，尺度和桥的整体十分和谐。乾隆二十二年（1757年）村人何孚惠撰《回龙桥石亭记》说："或以为古代桥必有屋，所以使桥坚且足为往来者所休息。"这篇文中认识到了亭子的重量对稳定圆形拱桥的重要性，它能"使桥坚"。自桥亭建成之后回龙桥就没有再坍塌，而亭子又为往来的人提供了休息交谊场所。何孚惠接着写道："吾族居民以耕凿为务，其有戴笠负锄驱黄犊而过者，于此详菽麦之辨，月夕风晨，有连袂袖书而来者，即于此续黄石一编，亦无不可也。"

离俞源村不远，武义县去宣平县的半途，有一个樊岭脚村，村子水口建筑群中有一座桥，桥上建着一座木构的大厅堂，很宽敞。这种廊桥在浙江、江西和福建很多，是村子的集会场、戏院和某种大型群众性活动的场所，也可用作集贸市场。在河段上方造这种场所，大概也会有两种考虑：一是少占农用地面；二是防火灾的蔓延，因为戏场、市场容易引发火灾。

梁式桥里最有乡土特色的是皖南、浙江、江西、福建的木质板凳桥。板凳桥是一种多跨桥，每一节像一只长板凳，不过桥板和板凳腿并不固定连接在一起，在两节桥板交接处只用一副板凳腿同时支承相邻两节。这板凳腿有的本身像一只板凳横过来放着，有四条腿；但大多数只有两条腿，在支搭的时候要扶住，两端都架上桥板之后就稳了。桥板是用七八根杉木顺向并联而成的。每节一丈或一丈三尺，一节一节地搭，边搭边用竹篾编的缆绳把相邻两节捆住，联结是柔性的。整体搭成之后，又用一根通长的竹篾缆绳（如今多改用铁链）串连各节，一端固定在岸边的石柱桩上或大树上，另一端自由。洪水暴发的时候，桥腿架就会倒塌，但是各节桥板和支架有缆绳连系着并不会被冲走，而是顺水势靠拢固定端一边的岸线漂着，摆动如蛇。待洪水退了之后，再捞回来重新搭架。山洪很快会过去，桥的架搭又很容易，农民自己就会，材料也现成，所以这种板凳桥的应用很普遍。长的板凳桥有达到一二百米的，如江西省婺源县城（紫阳镇）南、北、东三个城门口外的板凳桥和汪口村俞氏大宗祠前的板凳桥都很长。

板凳桥在宋画中就可以见到。"鸡声茅店月，人迹板桥霜"，那板桥大概就是这种板凳桥。

石质拱桥里最有乡土特色又最显工夫的是浙东一带用大块天然卵石干砌而成的，看上去似乎不大可靠，却也能历百年而依然牢固安稳。浙江省宁波市和奉化市相邻处的岩头村，村口外不远就有两座这样的桥，一座单跨，一座双跨。跨距大约有十米。单跨的完好如初，双跨的有一跨纵向裂开，半边垮坍，但剩下的半边上仍然可以过人。

浙江省永嘉县楠溪江有些村子的村墙门洞也用这种干码的卵石拱，如廊下村。

造桥比较费钱，所以大多是宗族出资或者向众人募化的，浙江省永嘉县楠溪江畔岩头村《金氏宗谱》的"家规"里写道："桥、路、渡舟倾坏，子孙倘有余资，当助修治。"修桥铺路是第一等善事，宗谱和地方志也乐于记载，如道光《安徽通志·义行》有歙人余文义，经商而富，"构石梁以济涉，同邑罗芝之孙亦石箬岭建梁以通往来"。通常，桥头会有石碑详记建桥经过和捐钱人的芳名录。较大的桥有乡人捐赠的田亩，以其收入作为常年修桥的经费。小石板桥也有一种"孝子桥"，老人寿庆时候，子孙花钱修路造桥给老人积德祈福、延年益寿。家境较好人家，孝子独力造一座小桥；有些财力不济的人家不过一次捐一块石板而已，桥面是逐渐加宽的。光绪《婺源县志·人物·义行》载，明代富春村人吴裕，"慷慨好施，凡桥梁道路如吴村、善源、洪源、梅源诸处，独力建造，而工费浩大唯本村为最，且于其上盖亭、列肆、设义浆、施药饵，行旅赖之"。桥亭和路亭一样，也是施舍助人的地方，有柴火灶，四季清水和柴禾供应不绝。盛夏则有暑药、草鞋。

桥架在溪河之上，这里视野宽阔，景色多变，于是，顺乎自然，出现了廊桥或桥亭，能遮风避雨，所以又叫风雨桥，大多会成为一个社交中心。旧徽州六邑之一，江西省婺源县的村子，水口必有"五生"，即廊桥或桥亭、水碓、长明灯、文笔和文昌阁。郭洞村的回龙桥和樊岭脚的廊桥都是水口桥。

依"五生"的做法，桥常建于水口，水口又常有文昌阁，以致有把文昌阁建在桥上的。如江西婺源，据光绪《婺源县志·津梁》载，"灵毓桥、上溪头桥，有文昌阁。""里仁桥，蕉源，上有文昌阁，吴文熙建。"类似的记载还有不少。浙江省也有些长桥在风雨廊中央设文昌帝君神龛，香火不绝。

水口"五生"各有特殊的体形，变化很大，而且并没有严格的功能限制，所以它们经常和水口山、水口林一起组成绝佳的风景。清人方西畴在《新安竹枝词》中有句：烟村数里有人家，溪转峰回一径斜，结伴携钱沽新酒，虹梁水口看云花。

坐在水口桥上，一面和同伴饮酒聊天，一面看天阔野旷、白云变幻，那种浪漫的闲适，确是烟村人家的至乐。所以，张子房为黄石公着履，许仙魂迷白娘子，尤其是牛郎年年七夕喜迎织女，故事都安排在桥头。

村民把水口桥梁的命运与全村人的命运紧密联系了起来。看山西省阳城县郭洞下村回龙桥，何孚悦写的《重造回龙桥记》说道："……及其既坏，村中事变频兴，四民失业，比年受灾，生息不繁，"而一旦修复，"顿还旧观，嗣是民物之丰美，衣冠之赫奕，当必有倍于前者"。这种比附虽然颇多迷信色彩，然而也透出村人们通过营建，改变环境，从而塑造自己命运的愿望和信心。

来往的人多，闲坐的人也不少，水口的风雨桥因此也成了村里树立乡规民约的石碑的首选之地。江西省婺源洪村小水口上的明代正德年（1506—1521）建的居安桥里，便有两块石碑，一块是嘉庆十五年（1810年）立的《奉宪永禁赌博》，还有一块是道光四年（1824年）光裕堂的《公议茶规》，严禁在出售茶叶时缺斤短两，以次充好，"如有背卖者查出罚通宵戏一台，银五两入祠"。洪村出著名的"松萝茶"，这一条规矩不但维护了本村茶叶的市场品牌，更维护了世道人心。

江西省婺源县清华镇的西头有一座彩虹桥，五跨，四个桥墩是石头砌筑的，每个桥墩上有一座三开间的方亭，每跨桥身架在四根大木梁上，它们之间用四间或五间的廊子连接，共有桥廊三十六间，桥身全长一百四十米左右，两端还按例各有门屋。彩虹桥跨在浩淼的婺水之上，河水丰沛，水色澄碧，两岸平畴如带，远处青山层叠。桥上倚栏，望渔舟上下，每逢网起鱼跃，桥上人和舟上人便大声问答，共享欢乐。

彩虹桥东端第二个石墩的迎流"燕嘴"上，曾有过一座经幢，灰白色石头制的；桥西端的小山岗上，有过一座十几米高的文笔。这两件文物都在"文化大革命"的时候被当作"四旧"而被"革命者"砸毁了。这东端第二个石墩上的长廊里，北墙上有一座神橱，供着三个神位，正中是"治水有功大夏禹王"，左侧是"募化僧人胡济祥"，右侧是"创始里首胡永班"。神橱的楹联是"两水夹明镜，双桥落彩虹"，上面的横批书"长虹卧波"。这座桥墩是1986年水毁后重建的，神橱也是新的，当初大概会有塑像。

彩虹桥东头门屋还有一副楹联：胜地著华川爱此间长桥卧波五峰立极；治时兴古镇尝当年文彭篆字彦槐对诗。

文彭是明代嘉靖年间（1522—1566）吴派篆刻家，他来访徽派篆刻家何震，同到彩虹桥游览，如今桥东端南侧的水边石矶上有摩崖石刻"小西湖"三个字，传说是他写的。彦槐姓齐，清代嘉庆进士，精书法辞赋，难得的是曾创造过多种农用机械和天文仪器，那块石矶上刻了他写的一首诗：睢阳桥外一灯孤，五老峰前飞夜乌，绝好荷花无一柄，月明空照小西湖。

诗写得有点凄凉，不知是为什么。

《清华胡氏仁德堂世谱》和《婺源县志》都说彩虹桥建于清代乾隆年间。《县志·义行》里记载："胡班，清华人，农于里之方头溪。溪当两源之冲，架木桥通行旅，山雨暴涨，则患叵测。班故贫，幼负贩供养甘旨。尝夏月桥圮，阻不得归，誓成此桥，以济众危。自是修葺绋缡，视如已急。遇霜雪夜，辄披衣起，扫除之。如是者历二十六年。既又议易木以石，众皆首肯，推为部署，中遭洪水冲决，后督其成。"《世谱》的记载稍稍简略一些："彩虹桥在方头溪，原胡仁德孙建木桥。乾隆庚寅（1770年），德公裔宏鸿，即林坑巷庵僧济祥，与里人永班募捐，建立石垛，架亭设茶其上，至今并设祀祭之。"两则记载稍有不同，但没有大悖。

彩虹桥的创建是由于一位贫穷的农民"誓成此桥，以济众危"，桥成之后又在桥上施茶，和路亭一样。乡情无处不在，远途的过客，能坐在这桥上歇一口气，不怕雨淋日晒，还能饮一杯茶，人与人之间的互助互爱便这样在他们心里滋长起来，代代传承。这就是乡谊亲情，就是为什么故土那么难离。

最华丽的廊桥（风雨桥）是贵州、湖南、广西数省苗族村寨里的。石质桥墩上垒起木垛，木料是顺躺着的，从下往上逐层放长，形成叠涩式的下小上宽的木垛，减小了跨度，然后在上架桥面，再建一层长廊。在长廊上依桥墩的位置分段矗立起木塔楼，飞檐层叠，非常华丽，非常生动。这些桥和鼓楼一起，成了苗族村落的标志。它们常常建在水口，也是人们纳凉闲坐的场所。

侗族风雨桥上的塔楼大体是方形的，也有不少是顺向比较长，横向稍窄一些。它们少则有三四层飞檐，多的有十来层。最上的顶子往往是方形锥尖的，远远高出于两侧的檐廊，仿佛当地村子里的塔楼。

长廊、桥梁和塔楼，以活泼的体形，出现在深山林壑里，因为它们所处位置和造型的特异，往往成了一个聚落的标志，所以它们的位置和形象大多是经过仔细而有创造力的设计的，它们也就成了一方的地标。
sections.content_en:
3. Bridges

The south has heavy rainfall and dense streams and rivers—therefore many bridges. Bridges are divided into beam bridges and arch bridges—beam bridges can be wooden or stone, while the structural body of arch bridges is all stone. Arches are divided into true and false—false arches are multiple single arches parallel together, connected into a whole with many iron ingot wedges (also called silver-ingot wedges, swallow-tail wedges). Whether wooden or stone bridges, whether beam or arch bridges—there are single-span and multi-span types. Above continuous multi-hole stone arch bridges the surface is mostly gentle, even flat—with stone slab railings on both sides. Stone arch bridges with three holes or fewer mostly take rainbow shape, and often have raised stone piers—forming extremely beautiful side profiles, combining strength and softness yet light—such as the Rainbow Bridge at Zhujiajiao Village in Shanghai suburbs, the Nanxun Arch Bridge in Huzhou, Zhejiang, and the White Dragon Bridge at Shengze, Suzhou, Jiangsu—all extremely light and upright. Even more beautiful is building a light and exquisite pavilion on top of the bridge—such as the Huilong Bridge at the village entrance of Guodong Village in Wuyi County, Zhejiang.

Guodong Village's Huilong Bridge is a single-span stone arch bridge—first built in Yuan Zhizheng era (1341–1368), called Stone Rainbow Bridge—collapsed and rebuilt several times—after the second repair in Qing Kangxi era, renamed Huilong Bridge—still good today. Arch span fourteen meters, arch height seven meters—exactly a semicircle. Bridge deck width 3.7 meters. In Qing Qianlong nineteenth year (1754), a square pavilion was added on top of the bridge—using four stone pillars. Pavilion plan three meters square, covered with four-corner pyramidal roof—very light, scale very harmonious with the bridge as a whole. In Qianlong twenty-second year (1757), villager He Fuhui wrote "Record of the Stone Pavilion of Huilong Bridge": "Some think ancient bridges must have buildings, so as to make the bridge firm and sufficient for travelers to rest." This article recognized the importance of the pavilion's weight for stabilizing the circular arch bridge—it can "make the bridge firm." Since the bridge pavilion was built, Huilong Bridge has not collapsed again—and the pavilion provides a resting and socializing place for travelers. He Fuhui continued: "Our clan residents make their living by farming and digging—those wearing straw hats, carrying hoes, driving yellow calves passing by—here discuss the distinction between beans and wheat; on moonlit evenings and windy mornings, those coming with sleeves full of books—can here continue the Huangshi one book, also not impossible."

Not far from Yuyuan Village, halfway from Wuyi County to Xuanping County, there is Fanlingjiao Village—in the village's water-mouth building complex there is a bridge, on which stands a wooden great hall—very spacious. Such covered bridges are many in Zhejiang, Jiangxi, and Fujian—they are village assembly halls, opera theaters, and venues for large-scale mass activities—also used as markets. Building such venues above river sections probably has two considerations: first, less occupation of farmland; second, preventing fire spread—because opera venues and markets easily cause fires.

The most rural-characteristic among beam bridges are the wooden bench bridges of southern Anhui, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, and Fujian. Bench bridge is a multi-span bridge—each section like a long bench—but the bridge deck and bench legs are not fixedly connected—at the junction of two bridge deck sections, only one pair of bench legs simultaneously supports adjacent two sections. Some bench legs themselves are like a bench placed sideways—with four legs; but most have only two legs—need support during erection, stable after both ends have bridge decks. Bridge decks are made of seven or eight Chinese fir logs parallel along the direction. Each section one zhang or one zhang three chi—built section by section—while building, bamboo-woven cables tie adjacent sections—connection is flexible. After overall completion, a long bamboo cable (now mostly iron chain) connects all sections—one end fixed to stone pillar stakes or big trees on the bank, the other end free. When floods burst, bridge leg frames collapse—but each section's deck and supports connected by cables will not be washed away—instead drift along the water toward the fixed-end bank line, swaying like a snake. After floods recede, fish them back and rebuild. Mountain floods pass quickly—bridge erection is easy, farmers can do it themselves, materials are ready—so this bench bridge is widely used. Long bench bridges can reach 100–200 meters—such as the bench bridges outside the south, north, and east city gates of Wuyuan County town (Ziyang Town), Jiangxi—and the bench bridge in front of the Yu Clan Great Ancestral Hall at Wangkou Village are both very long.

Bench bridges can be seen in Song dynasty paintings. "Rooster crows at thatched inn moon, footprints on board bridge frost"—that board bridge was probably this kind of bench bridge.

The most rural-characteristic and most skillful among stone arch bridges are those in eastern Zhejiang built with large natural cobblestones in dry masonry—looking seemingly unreliable—yet can last a hundred years still firm and stable. At Yantou Village near the border of Ningbo and Fenghua, Zhejiang—not far outside the village entrance there are two such bridges—one single-span, one double-span. Span about ten meters. The single-span is as good as new—the double-span has one span longitudinally cracked, half collapsed—but the remaining half can still be crossed.

Some village wall gateways in the Nanxi River basin of Yongjia County, Zhejiang also use this dry-stacked cobblestone arch—such as Langxia Village.

Building bridges is relatively expensive—so mostly funded by clans or solicited from the public. In the "Family Rules" of the "Jin Clan Genealogy" at Yantou Village by the Nanxi River, Yongjia, Zhejiang: "Bridges, roads, ferry boats if damaged—descendants if having surplus funds, should help repair." Building bridges and paving roads is the first-class good deed—genealogies and local gazetteers are happy to record—such as Daoguang "Anhui General Gazetteer·Righteous Deeds" has She County person Yu Wenyi, rich from commerce—"built stone beams to aid crossing, fellow county Luo Zhi's grandson also built stone beam at Ruoling to facilitate passage." Usually, bridgeheads have stone tablets detailing bridge construction process and donors' honor roll. Larger bridges have farmland donated by villagers—income used as annual bridge repair funds. Small stone slab bridges also have a kind of "filial son bridge"—when elders celebrate birthdays, descendants spend money repairing roads and building bridges to accumulate virtue and bless elders, prolong life. Better-off families—filial sons alone build a small bridge; some financially unable families only donate one stone slab at a time—bridge deck gradually widens. Guangxu "Wuyuan County Gazetteer·Figures·Righteous Deeds" records Ming dynasty Fuchun Village person Wu Yu—"generous and charitable—all bridges and roads such as Wu Village, Shanyuan, Hongyuan, Meiyuan and other places—built alone—and the most expensive was in this village—and on them built pavilions, set up shops, provided free tea, distributed medicine—travelers relied on it." Bridge pavilions, like road pavilions, are also places for giving aid—with firewood stoves, year-round clear water and firewood supply unceasing. In midsummer there are heat-relief medicine and straw sandals.

Bridges span over streams and rivers—here vision is wide, scenery varied—so naturally, covered bridges or bridge pavilions appeared—can shelter from wind and rain—therefore also called wind-and-rain bridges—mostly become a social center. One of the old six Huizhou counties—Wuyuan County villages in Jiangxi—water mouths must have "Five Lives": covered bridge or bridge pavilion, water-powered trip hammer, eternal lamp, writing brush, and Wenchang Pavilion. Guodong Village's Huilong Bridge and Fanlingjiao's covered bridge are both water-mouth bridges.

Following the "Five Lives" practice—bridges often built at water mouths—water mouths often have Wenchang Pavilions—even to the point of building Wenchang Pavilion on the bridge. Such as Wuyuan, Jiangxi—according to Guangxu "Wuyuan County Gazetteer·Fords and Bridges": "Lingyu Bridge, Shangxitou Bridge, have Wenchang Pavilion." "Liren Bridge, Jiaoyuan, has Wenchang Pavilion on it, built by Wu Wenxi." There are many similar records. Some long bridges in Zhejiang also set Wenchang Emperor shrine in the center of the wind-and-rain corridor—incense unceasing.

Water-mouth "Five Lives" each have special forms—great variation—and no strict functional restrictions—so they often form excellent scenery together with water-mouth mountains and water-mouth forests. Qing person Fang Xichou in "Xin'an Bamboo Branch Songs" has lines: Smoke village several li has homes, stream turns peak returns one path slants; companions carry money buy new wine, rainbow beam water mouth watch cloud flowers.

Sitting on the water-mouth bridge—drinking and chatting with companions while watching wide sky and open fields, changing white clouds—that romantic leisure is indeed the greatest joy of smoke-village people. Therefore, Zhang Zifang putting on shoes for Huangshi Gong, Xu Xian enchanted by White Snake—especially Cowherd welcoming Weaver Girl every year on Qixi—stories are all arranged at bridgeheads.

Villagers closely link the fate of water-mouth bridges with the fate of the whole village. Look at Huilong Bridge at Guodongxia Village, Yangcheng County, Shanxi—He Fuyue's "Record of Rebuilding Huilong Bridge" says: "…once it was damaged, village affairs frequently changed, four occupations lost work, consecutive years suffered disasters, population did not prosper"—and once repaired—"immediately returns old view, thereafter abundance of people and goods, splendor of official dress—will surely double the former." This analogy though much superstitious—yet reveals villagers' desire and confidence to change environment through construction, thereby shaping their own destiny.

Many passersby, many idlers—water-mouth wind-and-rain bridges therefore become the first-choice place for village rules and regulations stone tablets. In Ju'an Bridge built in Ming Zhengde era (1506–1521) at the small water mouth of Hong Village, Wuyuan, Jiangxi—there are two stone tablets: one is "Imperially Ordered Forever Ban Gambling" established in Jiaqing fifteenth year (1810)—another is "Publicly Agreed Tea Regulations" of Guangyu Hall in Daoguang fourth year (1824)—strictly forbidding short weight and shoddy goods in tea sales—"if violator found, punish with all-night opera one performance, five taels silver into ancestral hall." Hong Village produces famous "Songluo Tea"—this rule not only maintained the village tea's market brand, but also maintained social morality.

At the west end of Qinghua Town, Wuyuan County, Jiangxi there is a Rainbow Bridge—five spans—four stone piers—each pier has a three-bay square pavilion—each span bridge deck on four large wooden beams—between them connected by four or five bay corridors—total thirty-six bridge corridor bays—bridge total length about 140 meters—both ends according to convention each have gate houses. Rainbow Bridge spans over the vast Wu River—river water abundant, color clear blue—both sides flat fields like belts—distant green mountains layered. Leaning on railings on the bridge—watching fishing boats up and down—whenever nets rise and fish leap—people on bridge and people on boats loudly question and answer—sharing joy.

On the upstream "swallow beak" of the second stone pier at the east end of Rainbow Bridge—there was once a sutra pillar, gray-white stone; on the small hill at the west end of the bridge—there was a writing brush over ten meters high. These two cultural relics were both smashed by "revolutionaries" as "four olds" during the Cultural Revolution. In the long corridor on this second east-end stone pier—on the north wall there is a shrine cabinet—enshrining three deity positions: center "Great Yu King of Xia with Merit in Flood Control"—left "Monk Hu Jixiang who Solicited Donations"—right "Village Head Hu Yongban who Founded It." The shrine cabinet's couplet is "Two waters sandwich bright mirror, twin bridges fall rainbow"—above the horizontal scroll reads "Long rainbow lying on waves." This pier was rebuilt after 1986 flood damage—the shrine cabinet is also new—originally probably had statues.

The east gate house of Rainbow Bridge also has a couplet: Scenic spot famous Huachuan love this long bridge lying waves five peaks stand extreme; Peaceful time ancient town taste当年 Wen Peng seal characters Yan Huai opposing poetry.

Wen Peng was a Wu-school seal carver in Ming Jiajing era (1522–1566)—he visited Hui-school seal carver He Zhen, together toured Rainbow Bridge—now on the water-side rock at the south side of the bridge east end there is cliff carving "Small West Lake" three characters—legend says he wrote it. Yan Huai surname Qi—Qing Jiaqing jinshi—skilled in calligraphy and poetry—rarely also created various agricultural machinery and astronomical instruments—that rock has a poem he wrote: Suiyang Bridge outside one lamp lonely, Five Old Peaks before fly night crows; absolutely good lotus not one stem, moon bright empty shines Small West Lake.

The poem is a bit desolate—don't know why.

Both "Qinghua Hu Clan Rende Hall Genealogy" and "Wuyuan County Gazetteer" say Rainbow Bridge was built in Qing Qianlong era. "Gazetteer·Righteous Deeds" records: "Hu Ban, Qinghua person—farmed at Fangtou Stream in the village. Stream at the confluence of two sources—built wooden bridge for travelers—mountain rain sudden rise—danger unpredictable. Ban was poor—from youth peddled to support parents. Once in summer bridge collapsed—blocked cannot return—vowed to build this bridge to aid public danger. Since then repaired and maintained—treated as own urgency. Encountering frost and snow nights—always got up dressed—swept clean. Like this for twenty-six years. Then discussed replacing wood with stone—all agreed—pushed as manager—midway suffered flood washout—later supervised completion." The "Genealogy" record is slightly simpler: "Rainbow Bridge at Fangtou Stream—originally Hu Rende's grandson built wooden bridge. Qianlong Gengyin (1770)—Rende's descendant Honghong,即 monk Jixiang of Linkeng Lane—with villager Yongban solicited donations—built stone piers—erected pavilion and set tea on it—to this day also set sacrifices." The two records slightly differ—but no major contradiction.

Rainbow Bridge's creation was due to a poor farmer "vowing to build this bridge to aid public danger"—after bridge completion, also provided tea on the bridge—same as road pavilions. Village affection is everywhere—distant travelers can sit on this bridge to catch breath—not afraid of rain and sun—can also drink a cup of tea—mutual help and love between people thus grows in their hearts—passed down generations. This is village friendship and kinship—this is why homeland is so hard to leave.

The most ornate covered bridges (wind-and-rain bridges) are in Miao villages of Guizhou, Hunan, Guangxi provinces. On stone piers stack wooden cribs—timber laid horizontally—from bottom upward progressively longer—forming corbelled small-bottom wide-top wooden cribs—reducing span—then bridge deck on top—then build a long corridor. On the long corridor, according to pier positions, sectionally erect wooden tower buildings—flying eaves layered—very ornate, very vivid. These bridges together with drum towers become the symbol of Miao villages. They are often built at water mouths—also places for people to cool off and sit.

The tower buildings on Dong wind-and-rain bridges are generally square—also many longitudinally longer, transversely narrower. They have at least three or four layers of flying eaves—some over ten layers. The topmost roof is often square pyramidal—far higher than the side eaves corridors—like the tower buildings in local villages.

Long corridors, bridges, and tower buildings—with lively forms—appear in deep mountain forests—because their location and造型 are distinctive—often become a settlement's symbol—so their position and image are mostly经过 careful and creative design—they become a local landmark.

sections.name: 文峰塔
sections.content_zh:
四、文峰塔

世界各民族，在它们发展过程中，绝大多数有过对天空、天体和天象的崇拜。天空、天体和天象，最高、最远、又最广阔，却最直接地以寒暑、晴雨、昼夜影响着所有人的生活，既直接又可感，却又不可捉摸。所以，全世界各民族，都曾经最无保留地敬畏和崇拜天体和天象，认为它们直接关系着人们的吉凶祸福。世界上绝大多数民族，不论在哪个洲里生活，都有过一种上接苍穹的愿望，为这个目标建造了各种各样的高耸的建筑物，它们都可以笼统地叫做"塔"，例如古埃及的金字塔、意大利的比萨斜塔、印度的库特勃塔和日本的五重塔，等等。

就中国人来说，地无分南北东西，在一个很长的时期里，家家户户都曾经在住宅的明间中央，恭恭敬敬地供上"天地君亲师"的牌位，晨昏礼拜。毫无疑问，这"天"是至高无上、居于第一位的。所以中国人也不例外地要造塔。

在中国，早期的塔依附于佛教，据《洛阳伽蓝记》记载，南北朝时期洛阳有了各种大小的庙宇一千三百六十七所之多，按当时洛阳寺庙的规制，它们的塔的数量是很多的。当然，其中会有不少是小小的，矮矮的。

中华民族的文化习惯不接受抽象的宗教教义而倾向功利主义的信仰和崇拜。所以，塔也就蜕化成了一种功利主义的东西，携带着人们迷信的愿望。中国乡村普遍地、大量地造塔，起始于宋、辽、金、元诸朝，尤其盛于明、清两朝。这时期，佛教的势力已经在民间退潮，混进了中国传统的功利主义的泛神崇拜里去了。塔的"功能"完全世俗化了。塔的"用处"，主要是形成村镇某种有利的风水，这风水，主要是直接可以提高地方的科举成绩。所以，农村里兴建的大量高塔，几乎都是"文峰塔"。

文峰塔的风水作用是参与封闭村落的下水口，其实就是"避免"一个村落的自然范围内的水径直痛痛快快地流出这个范围去。但是事实上，地表水当然要排出去，不能也不该闭塞，所以，这个所谓闭塞便是象征性的，比如在流出一个村域的时候，适当地打个弯。如果打弯也不能，那就在下水口，便是地表水流出村域的地点，建造一座庙、一个塔，便可以"镇住"文运，不让它随水流走。文峰塔担当的就是这个责任。

这样的实例在我国东南诸省很普遍。例如，浙江省建德市的新叶村、安徽省黟县的碧山村等等。

新叶村的小水口在村的东南角巽位上，这是风水术的惯例。那里有一座文昌阁，阁的右侧便是作为文峰塔的抟云塔，建于明代初年（万历二年，即1574年）。它是六边形，共七层，可以借木楼梯上下，总高一百四十尺（见《抟云塔记》）。底层曾有围廊，已毁（或未建）。楼板及楼梯也已毁，不能登临了。

那里的环境很开阔，巽位而无遮无拦，形成了所谓"去水无情"的形势，这在风水术上看来是不吉利的，因为水在风水术里又被认作财的象征，不能让它痛痛快快地流走。但是，只要照风水术的"道理"，这样一件"重要"的事情，造一座塔便可以一劳永逸地挡住。这措施彰显了风水术数的荒诞，但这样的"文风"塔，在东南各省很多，而且很美。"人总是按照美的规律创造一切的"，也包括了迷信的东西。

玉华叶氏十一世祖一清公（1507—1583）有一首诗写道：一柱平蹲玉嶂东，亭亭直上插苍穹；题名不羡当时雁，奋迹还期此日龙。欲并鼎钟垂盛美，岂同竹帛纪遭逢；胜散未必皆天设，人力从来赛化功。

村里的一位耆老，这样热烈地赞美自己的家乡，倒是很能动人感情的。从另一方面看，他们对风水的神奇，其实并不真的放在心上。"子不语怪力乱神"，有不少读书人是对风水术抱着不屑态度的。

但这些塔都值得称赞，它们在很大程度上美化了当年的农村。中国的农村，不分南北，占绝大多数的建筑是住宅，而中国的住宅高不过两层，平地展开，轮廓比较沉闷，所以偶然某户人家在二楼之上造一间阁楼，开几扇外向的雕花窗，就会在村口成了一个"景点"，人们异口同声叫它为"小姐绣楼"，给它编一个动人的故事。有些地方，例如广东，会在屋脊上堆砌大量琉璃装饰。但它们的影响也只有小小一个范围，而塔在村落建筑群中的"装饰"效用却大得多了。它们的体形打破了住宅所形成的平淡的村落轮廓，大大活跃了这个沉闷的村落建筑群。所以，在一些经济水平比较高的地方，山上或村子里的塔就很普遍。

有了塔，就有了村子里读书人的吟咏。打开村子居民的宗谱，这样的诗连篇累牍，生活气息十分温暖浓厚。浙江省的江山县，是浙江省、福建省和江西省的交通枢纽之一，它的水上港口夹岸有两座山，山腰上各有一座塔，东塔叫百祐塔，西塔叫凝秀塔，清代学人施闰章有诗诵《将至江山县书我见》，有句："双塔夹崖口，丹霞照岭时"。塔在许多地方成了水上航行的标志。

可惜，"文化大革命"时期，这些文峰塔被判定为属于"四旧"，用炸药大量毁灭。江西省婺源县凤山村有一座文峰塔叫龙天塔，伫立在村口。塔建于明万历年间（1573—1620），三十七米高，七层，六边形，楼阁式。"文化大革命"时期，一位"工作组"组长在炸药已经堆满了塔底层，只待喊一声"万岁"便爆炸的一刹那，挺身而出，冒着很大的政治危险，勇敢地保护了这座塔。这是婺源县几十座文峰塔中唯一保存下来的一座。如今紫草花、油菜花，一茬又一茬地开在塔下，把村子装饰得好美。
sections.content_en:
4. Literary Peak Pagodas

All ethnic groups of the world, in their development process, the vast majority have worshipped the sky, celestial bodies, and celestial phenomena. The sky, celestial bodies, and celestial phenomena—the highest, farthest, and most vast—yet most directly affect everyone's life through cold and heat, clear and rain, day and night—both direct and perceptible, yet intangible. Therefore, all ethnic groups of the world have once most unreservedly revered and worshipped celestial bodies and phenomena, believing they directly relate to people's fortune and misfortune. The vast majority of ethnic groups in the world, regardless of which continent they live on, have had a desire to reach up to the sky—for this goal built various towering buildings—they can all be generally called "pagodas"—such as the ancient Egyptian pyramids, the Leaning Tower of Pisa in Italy, the Qutb Minar in India, and the Five-Story Pagoda in Japan, etc.

For Chinese people—regardless of north, south, east, west—for a very long period, every household once respectfully enshrined the "Heaven, Earth, Sovereign, Parent, Teacher" tablet in the center of the main room of their residence, worshipping morning and evening. Undoubtedly, this "Heaven" is supreme and ranks first. Therefore Chinese people also, without exception, build pagodas.

In China, early pagodas were attached to Buddhism—according to "Record of Buddhist Temples in Luoyang"—during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period Luoyang had various large and small temples as many as 1,367—according to the temple regulations of Luoyang at that time—the number of their pagodas was very large. Of course, many of them would be small and short.

The Chinese nation's cultural habit does not accept abstract religious doctrines but tends toward utilitarian belief and worship. Therefore, pagodas also degenerated into a utilitarian thing—carrying people's superstitious wishes. Chinese villages universally and massively built pagodas—starting from Song, Liao, Jin, Yuan dynasties—especially flourishing in Ming and Qing dynasties. During this period, Buddhist power had already ebbed among the people—mixed into traditional Chinese utilitarian pantheistic worship. The pagoda's "function" was completely secularized. The pagoda's "use" was mainly to form some favorable feng-shui for villages and towns—this feng-shui mainly could directly improve local imperial examination results. Therefore, the large number of high pagodas built in rural areas were almost all "Literary Peak Pagodas" (Wenfeng Pagodas).

The feng-shui function of Literary Peak Pagodas is to participate in sealing the lower water mouth of a village—actually it is to "avoid" the water within a village's natural range from flowing straight and happily out of this range. But in fact, surface water of course must be drained out—cannot and should not be blocked—so this so-called sealing is symbolic—for example, when flowing out of a village domain, appropriately make a bend. If bending also cannot—then at the lower water mouth—the point where surface water flows out of the village domain—build a temple, a pagoda—can "suppress" literary fortune—not letting it flow away with water. The Literary Peak Pagoda takes on this responsibility.

Such examples are very common in the southeastern provinces of China. For example, Xinye Village in Jiande City, Zhejiang, and Bishan Village in Yi County, Anhui, etc.

Xinye Village's small water mouth is at the southeast corner of the village in the Xun position—this is the convention of feng-shui. There is a Wenchang Pavilion—to the right of the pavilion is the Tuanyun Pagoda as a Literary Peak Pagoda—built in early Ming dynasty (Wanli second year, i.e., 1574). It is hexagonal—seven stories total—can go up and down by wooden stairs—total height 140 chi (see "Record of Tuanyun Pagoda"). The bottom floor once had a surrounding corridor—already destroyed (or not built). Floor boards and stairs also destroyed—cannot climb.

The environment there is very open—the Xun position with no obstruction—formed the so-called "water leaving without affection" situation—this is considered inauspicious in feng-shui—because water in feng-shui is also recognized as a symbol of wealth—cannot let it flow away happily. But—according to feng-shui "reason"—such an "important" matter—building a pagoda can block it once and for all. This measure demonstrates the absurdity of feng-shui numerology—but such "literary style" pagodas are many in southeastern provinces—and very beautiful. "People always create everything according to the laws of beauty"—including superstitious things.

The 11th-generation ancestor of Yuhua Ye clan, Mr. Yiqing (1507–1583), wrote a poem: One pillar squats east of Jade Barrier, gracefully straight up piercing the blue sky; inscribing names not envying contemporary geese, striving for achievement expecting this day's dragon. Wanting to join tripod bells to pass down prosperity, how same as bamboo and silk recording encounters; victory scattered not necessarily all heaven-set, human power always surpasses transformation.

A village elder—so warmly praising his hometown—is quite moving. From another perspective—they actually didn't really take the magic of feng-shui to heart. "The Master does not speak of strange forces, disordered spirits, and gods"—many scholars held a disdainful attitude toward feng-shui.

But these pagodas are all praiseworthy—they greatly beautified the rural areas of that time. Chinese rural areas—north and south—the vast majority of buildings are residences—and Chinese residences are no higher than two stories—spread flat—outline relatively dull—so occasionally a household builds an attic above the second floor—opens a few outward carved windows—will become a "scenic spot" at the village entrance—people unanimously call it "Young Lady's Embroidery Tower"—make up a moving story for it. Some places—such as Guangdong—will pile a lot of glazed decorations on roof ridges. But their influence is only a small range—while the pagoda's "decorative" effect in the village building group is much greater. Their body shape breaks the dull village outline formed by residences—greatly enlivens this dull village building group. Therefore—in places with relatively high economic levels—pagodas on mountains or in villages are very common.

With pagodas—there are the chants of village scholars. Opening the village residents' genealogy—such poems are numerous—life atmosphere very warm and rich. Jiangshan County in Zhejiang—is one of the transportation hubs between Zhejiang, Fujian, and Jiangxi—its water port has two mountains on both banks—each mountainside has a pagoda—east pagoda called Baiyou Pagoda—west pagoda called Ningxiu Pagoda—Qing dynasty scholar Shi Runzhang has a poem "Approaching Jiangshan County, Book What I See"—with lines: "Twin pagodas sandwich cliff mouth, red glow shines on ridge time." Pagodas in many places became markers for water navigation.

Unfortunately—during the "Cultural Revolution"—these Literary Peak Pagodas were judged as belonging to the "Four Olds"—destroyed in large numbers with explosives. In Fengshan Village, Wuyuan County, Jiangxi—there is a Literary Peak Pagoda called Longtian Pagoda—standing at the village entrance. The pagoda was built in Ming Wanli era (1573–1620)—37 meters high—seven stories—hexagonal—pavilion style. During the "Cultural Revolution"—a "work team" leader—at the moment when explosives had already filled the bottom floor of the pagoda—only waiting to shout "Long Live" to explode—stepped forward—braving great political danger—bravely protected this pagoda. This is the only one of dozens of Literary Peak Pagodas in Wuyuan County that survived. Today—purple grass flowers, rapeseed flowers—crop after crop bloom under the pagoda—decorating the village so beautifully.
key_terms: 世界各民族发展过程中绝大多数有过对天空天体天象崇拜
天空天体天象最高最远最广阔最直接以寒暑晴雨昼夜影响所有人生活既直接可感又不可捉摸
全世界各民族都曾经最无保留地敬畏和崇拜天体天象认为直接关系吉凶祸福
世界上绝大多数民族不论在哪个洲生活都有过上接苍穹愿望为这个目标建造各种各样高耸建筑物都可以笼统叫做塔
古埃及金字塔意大利比萨斜塔印度库特勃塔日本五重塔
中国人地无分南北东西在很长时期里家家户户都曾经在住宅明间中央恭恭敬敬供上天地君亲师牌位晨昏礼拜
天是至高无上居于第一位所以中国人也不例外地要造塔
中国早期的塔依附于佛教据洛阳伽蓝记载南北朝时期洛阳有各种大小庙宇一千三百六十七所之多按当时洛阳寺庙规制塔数量很多当然其中会有不少小小的矮矮的
中华民族文化习惯不接受抽象宗教教义而倾向功利主义信仰和崇拜所以塔蜕化成功利主义东西携带着人们迷信愿望
中国乡村普遍大量地造塔起始于宋辽金元诸朝尤其盛于明清两朝
这时期佛教势力已经在民间退潮混进中国传统功利主义泛神崇拜里去了塔的功能完全世俗化了
塔的用处主要是形成村镇某种有利的风水这风水主要是直接可以提高地方的科举成绩所以农村里兴建的大量高塔几乎都是文峰塔
文峰塔的风水作用是参与封闭村落的下水口其实就是避免一个村落的自然范围内的水径直痛痛快快地流出这个范围去
地表水当然要排出去不能也不该闭塞所以所谓闭塞便是象征性的比如在流出一个村域的时候适当地打个弯
如果打弯也不能那就在下水口便是地表水流出村域的地点建造一座庙一个塔便可以镇住文运不让它随水流走文峰塔担当的就是这个责任
这样的实例在我国东南诸省很普遍浙江建德新叶村安徽黟县碧山村等等
新叶村的小水口在村的东南角巽位上这是风水术的惯例
新叶村有一座文昌阁阁的右侧便是作为文峰塔的抟云塔建于明代初年万历二年即1574年
抟云塔六边形共七层可以借木楼梯上下总高一百四十尺见抟云塔记底层曾有围廊已毁或未建楼板及楼梯也已毁不能登临了
新叶村环境很开阔巽位而无遮无拦形成了所谓去水无情的形势这在风水术上看来是不吉利的因为水在风水术里又被认作财的象征不能让它痛痛快快地流走
只要照风水术的道理这样一件重要的事情造一座塔便可以一劳永逸地挡住这措施彰显了风水术数的荒诞但这样的文风塔在东南各省很多而且很美
人总是按照美的规律创造一切的也包括了迷信的东西
玉华叶氏十一世祖一清公1507-1583有一首诗一柱平蹲玉嶂东亭亭直上插苍穹题名不羡当时雁奋迹还期此日龙欲并鼎钟垂盛美岂同竹帛纪遭逢胜散未必皆天设人力从来赛化功
村里的一位耆老这样热烈地赞美自己的家乡倒是很能动人感情的
他们对风水的神奇其实并不真的放在心上子不语怪力乱神有不少读书人是对风水术抱着不屑态度的
这些塔都值得称赞它们在很大程度上美化了当年的农村
中国的农村不分南北占绝大多数的建筑是住宅而中国的住宅高不过两层平地展开轮廓比较沉闷
偶然某户人家在二楼之上造一间阁楼开几扇外向的雕花窗就会在村口成了一个景点人们异口同声叫它为小姐绣楼给它编一个动人的故事
有些地方例如广东会在屋脊上堆砌大量琉璃装饰但它们的影响也只有小小一个范围
塔在村落建筑群中的装饰效用却大得多了它们的体形打破了住宅所形成的平淡的村落轮廓大大活跃了这个沉闷的村落建筑群
在一些经济水平比较高的地方山上或村子里的塔就很普遍
有了塔就有了村子里读书人的吟咏打开村子居民的宗谱这样的诗连篇累牍生活气息十分温暖浓厚
浙江江山县是浙江福建江西交通枢纽之一水上港口夹岸有两座山山腰上各有一座塔东塔叫百祐塔西塔叫凝秀塔
清代学人施闰章有诗诵将至江山县书我见有句双塔夹崖口丹霞照岭时
塔在许多地方成了水上航行的标志
文化大革命时期这些文峰塔被判定为属于四旧用炸药大量毁灭
江西婺源凤山村有一座文峰塔叫龙天塔伫立在村口塔建于明万历年间1573-1620三十七米高七层六边形楼阁式
文化大革命时期一位工作组组长在炸药已经堆满了塔底层只待喊一声万岁便爆炸的一刹那挺身而出冒着很大的政治危险勇敢地保护了这座塔
这是婺源县几十座文峰塔中唯一保存下来的一座
如今紫草花油菜花一茬又一茬地开在塔下把村子装饰得好美

sections.name: 水碓和碾子
sections.content_zh:
五、水碓和碾子

我国江南各省多丘陵，又多雨。雨水在丘陵里奔流，形成小溪。正常天气，溪水不大不小，流速不快不慢，可以控制起来利用。利用方法之一，便是造水碓，引水做工。浙江南部、福建北部，大致每个山村都有一座水碓房。大村可能有两座，一般根据水轮和溪水的相对位置叫做上水碓和下水碓。

乡人用不大的沟渠把山溪水引到水碓，控制起来。需要的时候，打开闸板，水便流动冲击一个水轮的木板翼片，推动水轮旋转。经过几个环节，除去稻谷的砻糠、细糠，便有了可以煮饭的米。

这种水碓，是村落公益性的装备，村民都可以使用。它的建造和维修大多由富户负担。村民都很爱惜它，有不少村子把它列入水口"五生"之中，因此，它往往有浓荫常绿的老树覆盖，并且成了村子"十景"之一。浙江省永嘉县的上坳村、武义市的郭洞村，江西省婺源县的清华镇和黄村，以及福建省的不少村落，它们的水碓至今还在使用。

在华北农村，有功能与南方的水碓相仿而形态大不相同的公共场所，这就是碾场。

一户人家稍稍富裕了一点，便会在屋子门外空地上安置一个大石碾盘，配上碾子，供乡邻们各家随意使用。因为所费不多，所以一个村子里会有好几个。家产更富裕些的，就再把它用屋子盖上，成了碾子房，那就是"全天候"的了。

碾盘是一整块大石板，圆形的，直径两米上下。碾子是圆柱形的石块，中心有直通两端的圆洞。用一根木棒穿过碾子，一头套在碾盘中心的木轴上，另一头长出碾盘，人工推着碾子走圈子，就可以把碾盘上的玉米碾成细粒，叫棒子碴，这是当地的主食，相当于南方的大米。

也可以套上小毛驴或骡子，捂上他们的眼睛，代替人力。

和南方的水碓一样，这些碾子旁也常常是邻居亲友们聚会的地方，主要是妇女们，抱着娃儿聊天。因为碾子绝大多数是露天的，没有盖房，所以靠边不能种树，以防虫鸟污染。

但也有大户人家出钱造个碾子房，不过，拉碾子的牲口不懂守规矩，所以房内气味很差，人们宁愿在露天操作。北方雨水不多，露天操作很好，就是要避开大风天。
sections.content_en:
5. Water Trip Hammers and Mills

The Jiangnan provinces of China are mostly hilly and rainy. Rainwater rushes through the hills, forming small streams. In normal weather, stream water is neither too large nor too small, flow speed neither too fast nor too slow—can be controlled and utilized. One method of utilization is building water trip hammers, diverting water to do work. In southern Zhejiang and northern Fujian—roughly every mountain village has a water hammer house. Large villages may have two—generally called upper water hammer and lower water hammer according to the relative position of the water wheel and stream.

Villagers use not-too-large ditches to divert mountain stream water to the water hammer, controlling it. When needed, open the gate board—water flows and strikes the wooden board blades of a water wheel, pushing the water wheel to rotate. After several stages—removing the husk and fine bran of rice—there is rice that can be cooked.

This kind of water hammer is village public welfare equipment—all villagers can use it. Its construction and repair are mostly borne by wealthy households. Villagers cherish it—many villages include it in the water-mouth "Five Lives"—therefore, it often has shade from evergreen old trees—and becomes one of the village's "Ten Scenes." The water hammers of Shang'ao Village in Yongjia County, Zhejiang, Guodong Village in Wuyi City, Qinghua Town and Huang Village in Wuyuan County, Jiangxi, and many villages in Fujian—are still in use today.

In North China rural areas—there are public places with functions similar to southern water hammers but very different forms—these are mill yards.

A household that becomes slightly wealthier will place a large stone mill disc on the open ground outside their house—equipped with a millstone—for neighbors to use freely. Because the cost is not much—a village will have several. Wealthier households will cover it with a house—becoming a mill house—that is "all-weather."

The mill disc is a whole large stone slab—circular—diameter about two meters. The millstone is a cylindrical stone block—with a round hole through the center from both ends. Use a wooden stick through the millstone—one end套 on the wooden axle at the center of the mill disc—the other end extends beyond the disc—manually push the millstone in circles—can grind corn on the disc into fine grains—called corn grits—this is the local staple food—equivalent to southern rice.

Can also hitch a small donkey or mule—cover their eyes—replacing human power.

Like southern water hammers—beside these mills are also often gathering places for neighbors and relatives—mainly women—holding babies and chatting. Because mills are overwhelmingly open-air—no house built—so cannot plant trees by the side—to prevent insect and bird contamination.

But there are also wealthy households paying to build a mill house—however—the animals pulling the mill don't understand rules—so the smell inside is bad—people prefer to operate in the open. North China has little rain—open-air operation is fine—just need to avoid windy days.

sections.name: 枯童塔
sections.content_zh:
六、枯童塔

在一个很长的历史时期里，尤其在农村，儿童的死亡率很高，因此，未成年的儿童，只有乳名，没有按宗族辈分而起的"正式"名字。未成年儿童不幸夭折，被认为"不吉利"，既进不了宗谱，也进不了祖茔。

一些管理比较好的宗族，这些夭折了的孩子有一个公有的集体坟墓，叫做"枯童塔"或者"宝童塔"之类，以免被野狗或者兽类吞食。它们有简单的包裹，却没有丧衣。

浙江省兰溪市的诸葛村，于清朝中叶在村南经堂山上造了一座枯童塔，于1936年重修，塔身为六边形，边宽一点五米，高三点五米，全身由青石板建成。北面塔身刻"枯童塔"三个大字，南面塔身有一个直径大约四十五厘米的洞口，作为弃尸之用。西面塔身上刻着"启骸门"三个字，用砖块封砌，下面刻小字："此处下掘去泥即见砖门，启开便可取尸骸别埋"。这是送童尸和整理枯童塔时用的。

诸葛村的枯童塔用一块大青石板做顶，六边都出挑檐口于塔身之外，翼角微微上翘，中央矗立大石葫芦一个，高一米有余。塔身六面薄薄地浮雕着植物花纹。这座荒地里的小小公墓，造型水平很高，显示出父母对骨血儿女的怜爱。

浙江省缙云县的厚吴村，也有一座为夭折孩子建造的公墓，叫"宝童塔"。塔建于清道光己酉年（1849年），塔身六角形，由青砖砌筑，上部采用攒尖顶，出挑瓦檐下是层层叠涩，建造得十分讲究。塔大致方向为坐北朝南，略略偏东。南侧为塔的正面，塔身高三点二六米，塔顶高四点六八米，每边宽一点四二米。六面体的塔身每一面墙的檐下嵌有一块匾额。正面刻着："宝童塔"三个大字，匾下面是弃尸洞口，距地面一点六九米。从塔身正面顺时针旋转，匾额内分别刻有："道光"、"己酉"，为塔的建造的年代。塔朝东一面的匾上写有"东门"字样，据说下面有取尸骸别埋时用的垒砖封闭的小门。

村里的老人说，宝童塔一直使用到20世纪50、60年代，为了给夭折的孩子们一个安宁、洁净的处所，让父母们放心，每年清明前后族人还要修缮和整理这个小小的公墓。孩子们虽然进不了祖茔，但从没有离开过祖先的庇佑，没离开过家族的关心和爱护。
sections.content_en:
6. Child Pagodas

For a very long historical period—especially in rural areas—child mortality was very high. Therefore, underage children only had milk names—no "formal" names according to clan seniority. When an underage child不幸 died young—it was considered "inauspicious"—could neither enter the genealogy nor the ancestral cemetery.

Some better-managed clans—these deceased children had a public collective grave—called "Child Pagoda" or "Precious Child Pagoda" etc.—to avoid being eaten by wild dogs or beasts. They had simple wrapping—but no funeral clothes.

At Zhuge Village in Lanxi City, Zhejiang—in mid-Qing dynasty—a Child Pagoda was built on Jingtang Mountain south of the village—rebuilt in 1936. The pagoda body is hexagonal—side width 1.5 meters—height 3.5 meters—entirely built of bluestone slabs. The north face of the pagoda body is engraved with "Child Pagoda" three large characters—the south face has a hole about 45 centimeters in diameter—for depositing bodies. The west face is engraved with "Bone-Opening Gate" three characters—sealed with bricks—below engraved small characters: "Dig down here removing mud to see brick gate—open to take bones for separate burial." This is used when sending child bodies and organizing the Child Pagoda.

Zhuge Village's Child Pagoda uses a large bluestone slab as roof—all six sides have overhanging eaves beyond the pagoda body—wing corners slightly upturned—center stands a large stone gourd—over one meter high. The six faces of the pagoda body have shallow relief plant patterns. This small cemetery in the wasteland—has very high modeling level—showing parents' love for their blood children.

At Houwu Village in Jinyun County, Zhejiang—there is also a cemetery built for deceased children—called "Precious Child Pagoda." Built in Qing Daoguang Jiyou year (1849)—pagoda body hexagonal—built of blue bricks—upper part uses pyramidal roof—under overhanging tile eaves are layered corbels—built very exquisitely. The pagoda's general direction is facing south slightly east. The south side is the front—pagoda body height 3.26 meters—pagoda top height 4.68 meters—each side width 1.42 meters. Under the eaves of each wall face of the hexagonal body—a plaque is embedded. The front face is engraved: "Precious Child Pagoda" three large characters—below the plaque is the body-depositing hole—1.69 meters from ground. Rotating clockwise from the front—the plaques are respectively engraved: "Daoguang", "Jiyou"—the construction era. The east-facing plaque has "East Gate" characters—reportedly below there is a brick-sealed small door for taking bones for separate burial.

Village elders say—the Precious Child Pagoda was used until the 1950s–60s—to give deceased children a peaceful, clean place—to reassure parents—every year around Qingming Festival clan members also repair and organize this small cemetery. Although the children could not enter the ancestral cemetery—they never left ancestral protection—never left clan care and love.

浙江缙云县厚吴村也有一座为夭折孩子建造的公墓叫宝童塔
厚吴村宝童塔建于清道光己酉年1849年塔身六角形由青砖砌筑上部采用攒尖顶出挑瓦檐下是层层叠涩建造得十分讲究
塔大致方向为坐北朝南略略偏东南侧为塔的正面
塔身高三点二六米塔顶高四点六八米每边宽一点四二米
六面体的塔身每一面墙的檐下嵌有一块匾额
正面刻着宝童塔三个大字匾下面是弃尸洞口距地面一点六九米
从塔身正面顺时针旋转匾额内分别刻有道光己酉为塔的建造的年代
塔朝东一面的匾上写有东门字样据说下面有取尸骸别埋时用的垒砖封闭的小门
村里的老人说宝童塔一直使用到20世纪5060年代
为了给夭折的孩子们一个安宁洁净的处所让父母们放心每年清明前后族人还要修缮和整理这个小小的公墓
孩子们虽然进不了祖茔但从没有离开过祖先的庇佑没离开过家族的关心和爱护

sections.name: 浙江省建德市新叶村住宅的施工
sections.content_zh:
七、浙江省建德市新叶村住宅的施工

建造房屋，都要组织一个专门的班子。小型的建筑，工程可以全部由大木工匠完成，而建造做工精、规模大的建筑，如大祠堂、文昌阁和比较讲究的住宅等等，各项工程就要有专业工匠。大木工匠只管大木架，小木工匠管门窗，雕饰则由花工和油漆匠担任。石匠包揽石柱、石础、天井阶沿、夹杆石、抱鼓石等石作部分。

建房的事主对拟建房屋有了比较明确的要求之后，便委托一位堪舆师来相地观风水，选定基址，确定建筑的朝向以及与周围环境的关系。再由事主及各行匠师根据材料和财力协商建筑的规模、布局、朝向和形式，再由老工匠画出简单的平面图和屋架图，叫做"起屋样"。老匠人把"屋样"所需的全部大木尺寸画在一支木杆上，木杆的断面为矩形，长度与全屋最长的构件即堂屋明间的檩子相等。这木杆叫"杖杆"，由大木师傅掌握。老师傅还根据设计将全部木构件，包括它们的一切榫卯位置和尺寸用竹条做出一套制尺，工匠称"造篾"，一类构件一支篾。做好造篾，工匠们便可以按造篾所示尺寸下料加工。营建工程即将开始。

从架马（木工用三段圆木构成一个架子叫"木马"，把木料搁在木马上才好加工）、清场、定磉、拼架、立架到踏栋（上脊檩），都要请阴阳先生择日子和时辰。

下料先从正厅的一榀梁架的前小步柱、栋柱和后小步柱开始。将这三棵木料的下端，即伐木时斧子砍成的略呈锥形的一端先行锯下。锯的时候，由事主先捧住这部分，锯断不得落地而把它们放到漆盘中。建祠堂便将盘供在旧祠堂内，建住宅则将它供在原住宅的"上横头"，即太师壁前条案正中。这三块木头称为"班头"，"班"指鲁班。也有说是代表鲁班、班妻、班母的，或者说是代表鲁班及木工和泥水工二位徒弟的。"踏栋"之日，再将三块木头迎往工地，放在供桌上拜祭。

经过选料、齐柱脚、弹墨线、下料、刮木取直，开榫卯等工作，备齐所有木构件。备料要考虑到木材生长时的情况，垂直构件，梢端居上，根端居下；水平构件，梢端向西，根端居东；或者梢端向北，根端居南。大至栋梁立柱，小至门窗格扇，用材都须如此。

在备料的同时或略后，在建房现场平整地基，请"马甲将军"。"马甲将军"是一张红纸，上书"天无忌，地无忌；年无忌，月无忌，日无忌，时无忌，阴阳无忌。"有的还写上"姜太公在此、大吉大利"的条幅，将它贴在工地上，以求保佑施工顺利。基地平整后，由泥水匠或石匠定好柱网中心线，挖磉坑，安放平磉（柱顶石），再把柱础位置以一个十字形落墨于平磉上。打地基时，打夯工人要一起叫号："一步土，两步土，步步登高卿相府；打好夯，盖好房，房房俱出状元郎。"要多说些吉利话。

然后，将备好的木料运到现场，由木工指挥，将柱、梁、枋等构件合榫拼装，穿上木簪，便成为"扇架"（这套工序称"拼架"）。每榀梁架栋柱顶上装"尖头"（也有称"肩头"）的榫卯缝里夹进一叠五色布头，有黄、青、蓝、红、黑五色，代表金、木、水、火、土五行。

每拼装完一榀屋架，就把它竖立起来，三开间的屋，左侧两榀，右侧两榀，暂时成对靠在一起。竖立齐四榀后，安放柱础，便把每榀屋架就位，立在柱础上，临时固定。然后上檩、枋，把木构架横向连成整体。当全部构架竖立完毕后，只留明间的脊檩不入榫卯，在卯口搁一支叫"造篾"的竹片垫着，等待风水师择黄道吉日，举行隆重的"踏栋"仪典。

踏栋前，先在脊檩中段盖好红布，上面挂一个筛子、一束万年青，再交叉放几根青竹。红布兆大喜；筛子有千只眼，能看穿一切鬼魅和不吉，以便予以排除；万年青象征永久的兴旺，青竹则意味着节节高。

仪典这天，正房明间中央设供桌，供上先前留下的三只"班头"。祭品有果盒、香烛、肉、饭、豆腐等。人们热烈地聚集在一起，坐在前面的是事主、堪舆师、工匠师傅和宗族中的长者。吉时一到，随着一声高唱，由事主恭请木匠头和泥水匠头，腰扎红布带，手握大木槌登场。他们临场先洗脸、喝茶、上香。然后，木匠头手握木槌向左边中榀屋架的前大金柱打去，一声响，踏栋这时真正开始了。再打右边中榀屋架的前大金柱，然后是左后大金柱和右后大金柱。他边打边唱，泥水匠们齐声逐句叫"好"。

"一打金鸡叫，"泥水匠和："好！"
"二打凤凰住，"泥水匠和："好！"
"三打百无禁忌，"泥水匠和："好！"
"四打四柱落地，"泥水匠和："好！"

和"好"之后，木匠在右，泥水匠在左，各自登梯向明间左右屋架中央脊檩两端上攀。木匠边攀登边唱而泥水匠以"好"相和：

"脚踏金梯银梯步步高，"泥水匠和："好！"
"八仙过海捧仙桃，"泥水匠和："好！"
"仙桃头上生贵子，"泥水匠和："好！"
"柱子头上状元郎，"泥水匠和："好！"

攀到位置后，木匠接唱一切"开光"都要唱的《开光大吉》："日出时良，天地开昌；太公到此，万事吉祥。天无忌、地无忌、年无忌、月无忌、日无忌、时无忌、阴阳无忌。良工到此，大吉大利。"

和前面一样，木匠每唱一句，泥水匠跟着和一声"好"！

木匠再唱《护身咒》：我身依泰山，泰山依我身，泰山问慈悲，常护各人身。上元将军，走护我身；中元将军，隔护我身；下元将军，挡护我身。奉请东方九夷兵，南方八蛮兵，西方六戎兵，北方五狄兵，中央三真兵，救急切切如律令。

泥水匠依旧对口喊："好"！

唱毕，木工左右依次一一抽掉垫在正栋梁卯口的"造篾"，打入榫卯，整个木架最后完成。随后，把施工用的"杖杆"恭恭敬敬放置到后下金檩下方专设的一根枋子上，永久供奉，表示对工匠师傅的感谢。

随着最后一槌的响声，放起火炮。同时，早已在屋架上等待的其他工匠们将印上红喜字的馒头向四方抛去，丢给围观者。馒头在当地又称"兴隆"，上梁抛馒头有祝祷兴发、隆盛的意思。（有些村子还抛甜甜的糖果和避邪的金刚锤。金刚锤是木制的立方体，切角，棱长大约二厘米，染上紫苏汁，有竹签做的柄。）前来贺喜的和看热闹的人，双手向上接馒头和金刚锤的姿态被看作作揖，弯身捡地上的馒头则看做打躬，图的是热闹吉利有喜气。

建造祠堂，则以抛银锞、银元代替抛馒头。但下面有四位宗族的头首，各抓被单一角，张开，接住它们，仍旧归宗祠公有。抛银锞、银元不过是象征性的仪式，取个吉利，以图宗族发达罢了。

抛过银锞或馒头，举行"回红"仪式，即取下栋梁上的红布和万年青。并将红布截为三段：东家一份，木匠头和泥水匠头各得一份。

事主和匠人师傅等捧起三块"班头"，护送它们走出村东南水口百步之外，丢在外溪溪水中，慢慢冲走。然后在丢弃处再设祭：供上鲜肉、豆腐、米饭，并燃烧纸元宝。元宝烧尽，踏栋的全部礼仪才宣告结束。以后的垒墙铺瓦，抹地面等工作均不再有任何仪式。

这一套"踏栋"仪式，既隆重庄严，又喜气洋洋。兴造房屋，不论祠堂或者住宅，是宗族或家庭的头等大事。为了它们，需要节衣缩食，多年攒积。在农业社会里，宗族也好，家庭也好，都要在土地上生根，才能生存。而除了农田之外，房屋才是宗族或家庭立足于一方土地的根。房屋庇护着乡人们，世世代代在一方土地上劳作、生育。房屋也刻印在偶然离乡背井、远涉天涯去谋生的人心上，使他们永远记得乡土和乡土的亲人们。暮年晚景，他们还要回来，一回来，就有一个家。所以乡人们在房屋上倾注着那么深的感情。乡土建筑，这是千千万万勤劳人民心灵的寄托。
sections.content_en:
7. Construction of Residences at Xinye Village, Jiande City, Zhejiang Province

Building a house requires organizing a specialized team. For small buildings, the project can be entirely completed by major carpenters. But for exquisitely crafted, large-scale buildings—such as great ancestral halls, Wenchang Pavilions, and more elaborate residences—various projects require specialized craftsmen. Major carpenters only manage the large wooden frame; minor carpenters manage doors and windows; carvings are handled by ornament workers and painters. Stone masons handle stone parts such as stone pillars, stone plinths, courtyard steps, clamping stones, and drum-shaped bearing stones.

After the owner has relatively clear requirements for the proposed house, they commission a feng-shui master to survey the land and observe feng-shui, select the site, determine the building's orientation and relationship with the surrounding environment. Then the owner and various craftsmen negotiate the building's scale, layout, orientation, and form based on materials and financial resources. Then the old craftsman draws simple floor plans and roof frame diagrams—called "making the house sample." The old craftsman draws all major timber dimensions needed for the "house sample" on a wooden pole—the pole's cross-section is rectangular, its length equal to the longest component of the whole house, i.e., the purlin of the main room's central bay. This wooden pole is called the "measuring pole," held by the master carpenter. The master also makes a set of measuring rulers from bamboo strips according to the design—including all tenon-and-mortise positions and dimensions—craftsmen call them "making strips," one strip per type of component. After making the strips, craftsmen can cut and process materials according to the dimensions shown on the strips. The construction project is about to begin.

From setting up the horse (carpenters use three round logs to form a stand called a "wooden horse," placing timber on it for processing), clearing the site, setting plinths, assembling frames, erecting frames, to "stepping the ridge" (placing the ridge purlin)—all require a yin-yang master to choose the day and hour.

Cutting materials starts from the front small-step pillar, ridge pillar, and rear small-step pillar of one truss of the main hall. The lower ends of these three timbers—the slightly conical ends cut by axes during felling—are sawed off first. During sawing, the owner first holds this part—after sawing it must not touch the ground but be placed in a lacquer tray. For building an ancestral hall, the tray is enshrined in the old ancestral hall; for building a residence, it is enshrined in the original residence's "upper horizontal head"—i.e., the center of the long table in front of the master wall. These three pieces of wood are called "class heads"—"class" refers to Lu Ban. Some say they represent Lu Ban, Lu Ban's wife, and Lu Ban's mother—or represent Lu Ban and his two apprentices, the carpenter and the mason. On the "ridge-stepping" day, the three pieces of wood are escorted to the construction site and placed on the offering table for worship.

After material selection, pillar foot trimming, ink line snapping, material cutting, wood planing straight, and tenon-and-mortise cutting—all wooden components are prepared. Material preparation must consider the timber's growth direction: for vertical components, the tip end is up, the root end is down; for horizontal components, the tip end faces west, the root end faces east—or tip end north, root end south. From major beams and pillars down to door and window lattice—all materials must follow this.

Simultaneously with or slightly after material preparation—the construction site foundation is leveled, and the "Horse Armor General" is invited. "Horse Armor General" is a red paper with writing: "Heaven has no taboos, earth has no taboos; year has no taboos, month has no taboos, day has no taboos, hour has no taboos, yin-yang has no taboos." Some also write a banner "Jiang Taigong is here, great fortune and great luck"—pasted on the construction site to pray for smooth construction. After the site is leveled, the mason or stone mason sets the pillar grid center lines, digs plinth pits, places flat plinths (pillar top stones), and marks the pillar base positions with a cross in ink on the flat plinths. During foundation ramming, ramming workers chant together: "One step earth, two steps earth, step by step rising to minister's mansion; ram well, build good house, every house produces top scholars." Must say many auspicious words.

Then the prepared timber is transported to the site—under the carpenter's command—pillars, beams, lintels and other components are assembled with tenons and mortises, secured with wooden pins—becoming a "fan frame" (this process is called "frame assembly"). In the tenon-and-mortise joints at the top of each truss's ridge pillar—"pointed head" (also called "shoulder head")—a stack of five-colored cloth heads is inserted—yellow, green, blue, red, black—representing the five elements metal, wood, water, fire, earth.

After assembling each roof truss—it is erected—for a three-bay house, two trusses on the left, two on the right—temporarily leaned in pairs. After all four trusses are erected, pillar bases are placed—each truss is positioned on its pillar base—temporarily fixed. Then purlins and lintels are placed—connecting the wooden frame horizontally into a whole. When all frames are erected—only the central bay's ridge purlin is left not joined into tenon-and-mortise—with a bamboo strip called "making strip" placed in the mortise opening as a spacer—waiting for the feng-shui master to choose an auspicious day for the grand "ridge-stepping" ceremony.

Before ridge-stepping—the middle section of the ridge purlin is covered with red cloth—above it hang a sieve, a bundle of evergreen, and several green bamboos crossed. Red cloth foretells great joy; the sieve has a thousand eyes—can see through all ghosts and misfortune to eliminate them; evergreen symbolizes eternal prosperity; green bamboo means rising step by step.

On the ceremony day—an offering table is set in the center of the main room's central bay—with the three previously left "class heads" placed on it. Offerings include fruit boxes, incense and candles, meat, rice, tofu, etc. People gather enthusiastically—sitting in front are the owner, feng-shui master, craftsman masters, and clan elders. When the auspicious moment arrives—with a loud chant—the owner respectfully invites the head carpenter and head mason—wearing red cloth sashes, holding large wooden mallets—to enter. They first wash faces, drink tea, and burn incense. Then the head carpenter holds the mallet and strikes the front large golden pillar of the left middle truss—with a sound—the ridge-stepping truly begins. Then strikes the front large golden pillar of the right middle truss—then the left rear large golden pillar and right rear large golden pillar. He strikes while singing—the masons chorus "good" sentence by sentence.

"First strike golden rooster crows," masons respond: "Good!"
"Second strike phoenix dwells," masons respond: "Good!"
"Third strike hundred taboos gone," masons respond: "Good!"
"Fourth strike four pillars landed," masons respond: "Good!"

After the "good" responses—the carpenter on the right, mason on the left—each climbs a ladder toward both ends of the central ridge purlin between the left and right frames. The carpenter sings while climbing—the mason responds with "good":

"Feet step golden ladder silver ladder rising high," mason: "Good!"
"Eight immortals cross the sea holding peaches of immortality," mason: "Good!"
"On the immortal peach head a noble son is born," mason: "Good!"
"On the pillar head a top scholar," mason: "Good!"

After reaching position—the carpenter sings the "Great Opening Light" sung at all "opening light" ceremonies: "Sun rises at auspicious time, heaven and earth open prosperously; Grand Duke arrives, all things auspicious. Heaven no taboos, earth no taboos, year no taboos, month no taboos, day no taboos, hour no taboos, yin-yang no taboos. Skilled craftsmen arrive, great fortune and great luck."

As before—the carpenter sings each line—the mason follows with a "good"!

The carpenter then sings the "Body-Protecting Spell": My body relies on Mount Tai, Mount Tai relies on my body, Mount Tai asks compassion, always protects all persons. Upper Yuan General, walks protecting my body; Middle Yuan General, separates protecting my body; Lower Yuan General, blocks protecting my body. Invoke Eastern nine Yi soldiers, Southern eight Man soldiers, Western six Rong soldiers, Northern five Di soldiers, Central three True soldiers—urgent urgent as the law commands.

The mason still shouts "good" in response!

After singing—the carpenters left and right sequentially remove the "making strips" placed in the main beam mortise openings—drive in the tenons—the entire wooden frame is finally completed. Then the construction "measuring pole" is respectfully placed on a specially set lintel below the rear lower golden purlin—permanently enshrined—expressing gratitude to the craftsman masters.

With the sound of the final mallet strike—firecrackers are set off. At the same time—other craftsmen already waiting on the roof frame throw steamed buns printed with red happiness characters in all directions—to the onlookers. Steamed buns are locally also called "prosperity"—throwing buns at beam raising has the meaning of praying for development and prosperity. (Some villages also throw sweet candies and evil-avoiding diamond hammers. Diamond hammers are wooden cubes with cut corners—edge length about two centimeters—dyed with perilla juice—with bamboo stick handles.) People coming to congratulate and watch—holding hands up to catch buns and diamond hammers is seen as making a respectful gesture—bending to pick up buns from the ground is seen as bowing—seeking liveliness, auspiciousness, and joy.

For building an ancestral hall—silver ingots and silver coins are thrown instead of buns. But below there are four clan leaders—each holding a corner of a quilt spread open—to catch them—still belonging to the clan common treasury. Throwing silver ingots and coins is just a symbolic ceremony—seeking auspiciousness—hoping for clan prosperity.

After throwing silver ingots or buns—the "return red" ceremony is held—i.e., removing the red cloth and evergreen from the ridge beam. The red cloth is cut into three sections: owner gets one, head carpenter and head mason each get one.

The owner and craftsman masters etc. pick up the three "class heads"—escort them out beyond a hundred steps from the village's southeast water mouth—throw them into the outer stream—slowly washed away. Then another sacrifice is held at the disposal site: offering fresh meat, tofu, rice—and burning paper ingots. When the ingots are burned out—the entire ridge-stepping ceremony is declared concluded. Subsequent wall building, tile laying, floor plastering etc. no longer have any ceremonies.

This set of "ridge-stepping" ceremonies—is both solemn and grand, and full of joy. Building a house—whether ancestral hall or residence—is the most important event for a clan or family. For them—requires living frugally and saving for years. In agricultural society—clan or family—must take root on the land to survive. And besides farmland—the house is the root of a clan or family taking root on a piece of land. Houses shelter villagers—generation after generation working and giving birth on the land. Houses are also imprinted on the hearts of those who occasionally leave home and travel far to make a living—making them always remember their homeland and homeland relatives. In old age—they will return—once back, there is a home. Therefore villagers pour such deep feelings into their houses. Vernacular architecture—this is the spiritual sustenance of millions of hardworking people.

建房事主对拟建房屋有明确要求后委托堪舆师相地观风水选定基址确定建筑朝向及与周围环境关系
事主及各行匠师根据材料和财力协商建筑规模布局朝向形式
老工匠画出简单平面图和屋架图叫做起屋样
老匠人把屋样所需全部大木尺寸画在一支木杆上木杆断面矩形长度与全屋最长构件即堂屋明间檩子相等
这木杆叫杖杆由大木师傅掌握
老师傅根据设计将全部木构件包括一切榫卯位置和尺寸用竹条做出一套制尺工匠称造篾一类构件一支篾
做好造篾工匠们按造篾所示尺寸下料加工营建工程即将开始
从架马木工用三段圆木构成架子叫木马把木料搁在木马上才好加工清场定磉拼架立架到踏栋上脊檩都要请阴阳先生择日子和时辰
下料先从正厅一榀梁架的前小步柱栋柱和后小步柱开始
将这三棵木料下端即伐木时斧子砍成略呈锥形一端先行锯下
锯时由事主先捧住这部分锯断不得落地而放到漆盘中
建祠堂将盘供在旧祠堂内建住宅供在原住宅上横头即太师壁前条案正中
这三块木头称为班头班指鲁班也有说代表鲁班班妻班母或者代表鲁班及木工和泥水工二位徒弟
踏栋之日再将三块木头迎往工地放在供桌上拜祭
经过选料齐柱脚弹墨线下料刮木取直开榫卯等工作备齐所有木构件
备料考虑木材生长时情况垂直构件梢端居上根端居下水平构件梢端向西根端居东或者梢端向北根端居南大至栋梁立柱小至门窗格扇用材都须如此
备料同时或略后在建房现场平整地基请马甲将军
马甲将军是一张红纸上书天无忌地无忌年无忌月无忌日无忌时无忌阴阳无忌有的还写姜太公在此大吉大利条幅贴在工地上求保佑施工顺利
基地平整后由泥水匠或石匠定好柱网中心线挖磉坑安放平磉柱顶石再把柱础位置以十字形落墨于平磉上
打地基时打夯工人一起叫号一步土两步土步步登高卿相府打好夯盖好洋房房俱出状元郎要多说吉利话
备好木料运到现场由木工指挥将柱梁枋等构件合榫拼装穿上木簪便成为扇架这套工序称拼架
每榀梁架栋柱顶上装尖头也有称肩头的榫卯缝里夹进一叠五色布头黄青蓝红黑五色代表金木水火土五行
每拼装完一榀屋架就竖立起来三开间的屋左侧两榀右侧两榀暂时成对靠在一起
竖立齐四榀后安放柱础把每榀屋架就位列在柱础上临时固定然后上檩枋把木构架横向连成整体
全部构架竖立完毕后只留明间脊檩不入榫卯在卯口搁一支叫造篾的竹片垫着等待风水师择黄道吉日举行隆重踏栋仪典
踏栋前先在脊檩中段盖好红布上面挂一个筛子一束万年青再交叉放几根青竹
红布兆大喜筛子有千只眼能看穿一切鬼魅和不吉以便排除万年青象征永久兴旺青竹意味着节节高
仪典天正房明间中央设供桌供上先前留下三只班头祭品有果盒香烛肉饭豆腐等
人们热烈聚集坐在前面的是事主堪舆师工匠师傅和宗族中长者
吉时一到随着一声高唱由事主恭请木匠头和泥水匠头腰扎红布带手握大木槌登场
他们临场先洗脸喝茶上香然后木匠头手握木槌向左边中榀屋架前大金柱打去一声响踏栋真正开始
再打右边中榀屋架前大金柱然后是左后大金柱和右后大金柱他边打边唱泥水匠们齐声逐句叫好
一打金鸡叫泥水匠和好二打凤凰住泥水匠和好三打百无禁忌泥水匠和好四打四柱落地泥水匠和好
和好之后木匠在右泥水匠在左各自登梯向明间左右屋架中央脊檩两端上攀木匠边攀登边唱泥水匠以好相和
脚踏金梯银梯步步高泥水匠和好八仙过海捧仙桃泥水匠和好仙桃头上生贵子泥水匠和好柱子头上状元郎泥水匠和好
攀到位置后木匠接唱一切开光都要唱的开光大吉日出时良天地开昌太公到此万事吉祥天无忌地无忌年无忌月无忌日无忌时无忌阴阳无忌良工到此大吉大利
木匠每唱一句泥水匠跟着和一声好
木匠再唱护身咒我身依泰山泰山依我身泰山问慈悲常护各人身上元将军走护我身中元将军隔护我身下元将军挡护我身奉请东方九夷兵南方八蛮兵西方六戎兵北方五狄兵中央三真兵救急切切如律令
泥水匠依旧对口喊好
唱毕木工左右依次一一抽掉垫在正栋梁卯口的造篾打入榫卯整个木架最后完成
随后把施工用的杖杆恭恭敬敬放置到后下金檩下方专设的一根枋子上永久供奉表示对工匠师傅感谢
随着最后一槌响声放起火炮同时早已在屋架上等待的其他工匠们将印上红喜字的馒头向四方抛去丢给围观者
馒头在当地又称兴隆上梁抛馒头有祝祷兴发隆盛意思
有些村子还抛甜甜的糖果和避邪的金刚锤金刚锤是木制立方体切角棱长大约二厘米染上紫苏汁有竹签做的柄
前来贺喜和看热闹的人双手向上接馒头和金刚锤姿态被看作作揖弯身捡地上馒头则看做打躬图热闹吉利有喜气
建造祠堂则以抛银锞银元代替抛馒头下面有四位宗族头首各抓被单一角张开接住它们仍旧归宗祠公有
抛银锞银元不过象征性仪式取个吉利以图宗族发达罢了
抛过银锞或馒头举行回红仪式即取下栋梁上的红布和万年青并将红布截为三段东家一份木匠头和泥水匠头各得一份
事主和匠人师傅等捧起三块班头护送它们走出村东南水口百步之外丢在外溪溪水中慢慢冲走
然后在丢弃处再设祭供上鲜肉豆腐米饭并燃烧纸元宝
元宝烧尽踏栋全部礼仪才宣告结束以后垒墙铺瓦抹地面等工作均不再有任何仪式
这一套踏栋仪式既隆重庄严又喜气洋洋兴造房屋不论祠堂或者住宅是宗族或家庭头等大事
为了它们需要节衣缩食多年攒积在农业社会里宗族也好家庭也好都要在土地上生根才能生存
除了农田之外房屋才是宗族或家庭立足于一方土地的根
房屋庇护着乡人们世世代代在一方土地上劳作生育
房屋也刻印在偶然离乡背井远涉天涯去谋生的人心上使他们永远记得乡土和乡土的亲人们
暮年晚景他们还要回来一回来就有一个家所以乡人们在房屋上倾注着那么深的感情
乡土建筑这是千千万万勤劳人民心灵的寄托
